sample_outputs.explanation: Two injected regions found in svchost.exe (PID 1204). Region 0x1f3a0000 starts with MZ (4d 5a) — a PE header — meaning a full DLL or EXE has been reflectively loaded into svchost memory without touching disk. Region 0x2c4d0000 shows the byte sequence fc 48 83 e4 f0 e8 c8 — this is the canonical x64 Cobalt Strike stager/shellcode prologue (stack alignment + call to delta). PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE on both regions is the critical flag: legitimate DLLs loaded by the Windows loader are PAGE_EXECUTE_READ; RWX is the hallmark of shellcode injection or reflective loading. Next steps: (1) dump both regions with windows.dumpfiles or the malfind --dump flag, then run the extracted blobs through 1768.py (Cobalt Strike config extractor) to recover the C2 IP, beacon interval, and jitter — this gives you the attacker's infrastructure; (2) run windows.netstat to correlate svchost.exe PID 1204 against any ESTABLISHED connections to external IPs, identifying the live C2 channel; (3) run windows.dlllist --pid 1204 to enumerate all loaded modules and identify any with no path on disk (memory-only DLLs), then cross-reference against windows.handles to find any named pipe handles (Cobalt Strike SMB beacons use named pipes for lateral movement, e.g., \\.\pipe\msagent_*).

legal_notes: US CFAA boundary: Acquiring a memory dump from any system you do not own or have explicit written authorization to image is a federal crime under 18 U.S.C. § 1030(a)(2) regardless of whether you 'only read' the data. RAM contains credentials, encryption keys, and personal communications — unauthorized acquisition carries the same exposure as unauthorized file access, and prosecutors have successfully argued higher severity due to the breadth of data captured in a single dump.

Engagement scope — acquisition method must be explicitly authorized: Your rules of engagement must specify not just 'access to host X' but the specific acquisition method (live acquisition via agent, crash dump, hypervisor snapshot, physical access). A client authorizing 'penetration testing of server 10.10.5.20' does NOT implicitly authorize crashing that server to force a dump, running a kernel driver on it, or exfiltrating a 32 GB file over their network. Get each method in writing before the engagement.

Cloud and AD consideration: On cloud-hosted VMs (AWS EC2, Azure VM, GCP Compute), memory acquisition via hypervisor snapshot (e.g., aws ec2 create-snapshot, Azure disk snapshot of OS disk) is logged immutably in CloudTrail / Azure Monitor Activity Log with your IAM caller identity. For Active Directory domain controllers, acquiring DC memory dumps exposes the entire domain's Kerberos keying material (krbtgt hash) and all user NTLM hashes — this data must be handled under the same controls as the most sensitive data classification in the engagement, and destruction/return procedures must be agreed upon in writing before the engagement begins.
false_positives: windows.malfind flags ALL RWX memory regions, including legitimate JIT-compiled code from .NET CLR, Java HotSpot, V8 (Chrome/Electron), and Mono runtimes. On a developer workstation or any host running a modern browser, malfind will produce dozens of false positives. Always check whether the flagged region's base address falls within a known JIT heap by cross-referencing windows.dlllist for clr.dll, jvm.dll, or v8.dll loaded in the same process before declaring injection.

windows.pslist and windows.pstree can miss DKOM (Direct Kernel Object Manipulation) rootkits that unlink EPROCESS structures from the ActiveProcessLinks doubly-linked list. A process hidden this way will not appear in pslist output at all — absence of a process is not proof it doesn't exist. Cross-reference with windows.psscan (which scans raw memory for EPROCESS pool tags rather than walking the linked list) to detect unlinked processes.

windows.netstat reflects the network state AT THE MOMENT OF DUMP ACQUISITION. Short-lived connections (C2 beacons with fast jitter, DNS-over-HTTPS exfiltration, one-shot lateral movement) will not appear if they completed before the dump was taken. A clean netstat output does not mean no network activity occurred — correlate with pcap or EDR telemetry for temporal coverage.

windows.hashdump only extracts hashes from the SAM hive for local accounts. It will return empty or partial results on domain-joined machines where interactive logon uses cached domain credentials stored in the SECURITY hive (LSA secrets), not SAM. For domain credential extraction from memory, use windows.lsadump or target the lsass.exe process directly with windows.dlllist and manual LSASS parsing — hashdump silence on a DC is expected, not a tool failure.

Symbol resolution failures produce misleading output: if Volatility cannot locate the correct PDB symbol file for the exact kernel build (e.g., a custom OEM kernel, a patched enterprise build, or a non-English Windows locale with a different ntoskrnl.exe hash), plugin output may show incorrect offsets, misidentified structures, or silently skip objects. Always verify the ISF (Intermediate Symbol File) matches your dump's exact ntoskrnl.exe version via the banners plugin before trusting structural analysis results.

autopsy.description: Open-source digital forensics platform. Analyzes disk images, file systems, and mobile devices. Recovers deleted files, extracts artifacts (web history, emails, documents), timestamps, and builds timelines. Used by law enforcement and incident responders worldwide.
autopsy.teach_intro: Autopsy is the GUI layer over The Sleuth Kit. When you have a disk image from a compromised system, Autopsy carves through it to find deleted files, recover artifacts, and build a timeline of activity. It's used for both offensive intelligence gathering and defensive incident response.

File Recovery.label: Deleted File Recovery
File Recovery.desc: Recover deleted files from disk images.
File Recovery.example: Open case → Add data source → Enable file recovery module
File Recovery.teach: Files are 'deleted' but the data stays on disk until overwritten. Autopsy recovers them. Deleted malware, wiped logs, erased documents — all potentially recoverable.

Web Artifacts.label: Browser History
Web Artifacts.desc: Extract browser history, downloads, cookies, cached images.
Web Artifacts.example: Open case → Run Recent Activity module
Web Artifacts.teach: Browser artifacts reveal attacker research: what sites they visited before the attack, C2 infrastructure they accessed, tools they downloaded.

Timeline.label: Timeline Analysis
Timeline.desc: Build a chronological timeline of file system activity.
Timeline.teach: Timeline shows exactly when files were created, modified, and accessed. Correlate with attack timestamps to build the kill chain narrative.

Keyword Search.label: Keyword Search
Keyword Search.desc: Search disk image for specific strings: passwords, IPs, domains.
Keyword Search.example: Open case → Keyword Search → enter terms
Keyword Search.teach: Search for C2 domains, malware hashes, victim data, or keywords from the investigation. Even encrypted files often have metadata or strings that match.

opsec_notes: Beginner-grade noise: Autopsy itself is a forensic analysis tool run OFFLINE against a disk image — it generates no network traffic and makes no live system calls against the target. The opsec risk is not in running Autopsy, but in HOW you acquired the image (dd, FTK Imager, live acquisition tools) and where you store/process it. Acquisition tools touching a live system write to memory, modify access timestamps, and may trigger EDR process-creation alerts.

Concrete artifact a defender sees during acquisition: If you use a live acquisition agent (e.g., Velociraptor, CrowdStrike RTR, or a custom dd-over-SSH session) to pull the image, the acquiring process appears in the target's Sysmon EID 1 (process creation) and EID 3 (network connection) logs. The parent-child tree (e.g., sshd.exe -> cmd.exe -> dd.exe reading \\.\PhysicalDrive0) is a high-fidelity detection signal in CrowdStrike Falcon's process tree view and will score high on behavioral anomaly models.

2025-2026 cutting edge — EDR telemetry on raw disk reads: Windows 11 22H2+ and Server 2025 expose kernel callbacks via PsSetCreateProcessNotifyRoutineEx and volume filter drivers. CrowdStrike Falcon and SentinelOne both instrument IRP_MJ_READ against \Device\HarddiskVolume* at the minifilter layer. A process opening a raw volume handle (GENERIC_READ on PhysicalDrive0) without being a known backup or AV binary will trigger a high-severity alert in both platforms as of their 2025 sensor versions. Use a hardware write-blocker and image from outside the OS to avoid this entirely.

2025-2026 cutting edge — cloud forensics acquisition: When the 'disk' is an AWS EBS volume or Azure managed disk, acquisition means snapshotting and mounting — actions logged in CloudTrail (ec2:CreateSnapshot, ec2:AttachVolume) and Azure Monitor (Microsoft.Compute/snapshots/write). These API calls are visible to the cloud tenant's SIEM. On an authorized IR engagement, coordinate with the cloud team so these events don't trigger their own incident. On a red-team engagement, snapshotting a volume you're not authorized to touch is a CFAA violation regardless of whether you already have EC2 access.

Autopsy's case database (SQLite, stored in the case directory) and extracted artifacts are written in plaintext to the analyst's workstation. If that workstation is on a corporate network, DLP tools monitoring file writes or network shares may flag large SQLite files or bulk document extraction. Process your cases on an air-gapped forensic workstation or an encrypted offline VM, not on your daily-driver laptop connected to the SOC network.

Timeline correlation gotcha: Autopsy's timeline module ingests MAC times (Modified, Accessed, Changed) from the file system. On NTFS, the $STANDARD_INFORMATION attribute is trivially manipulable by timestomping tools (e.g., Metasploit's timestomp, PowerShell Set-ItemProperty). Always cross-reference $STANDARD_INFORMATION times against $FILE_NAME attribute times — Autopsy surfaces both, and discrepancies between them are a strong indicator of anti-forensic activity. Defenders hunting for timestomping should look for $SI < $FN (standard info timestamp earlier than filename attribute timestamp), which Autopsy's timeline will visually expose.

Running targeted ingest with custom keyword list and hash filtering.

legal_notes: US CFAA boundary: Autopsy analysis of a disk image is legally permissible only when you have explicit authorization to examine the data on that image. Acquiring and analyzing a disk image from a system you do not own, administer, or have written authorization to examine constitutes unauthorized access under 18 U.S.C. § 1030 regardless of whether the system is 'already compromised.' On IR engagements, obtain a signed Statement of Work and explicit data handling authorization before imaging — the image itself contains PII, credentials, and privileged communications that carry their own legal exposure (HIPAA, GDPR, attorney-client privilege).

Rules of engagement — scope of analysis: Your engagement authorization defines what you may IMAGE, not just what you may ACCESS. A penetration test authorizing you to 'test 10.0.0.0/24' does not authorize you to image and forensically analyze the workstations in that range. Forensic acquisition and analysis requires a separate, explicit authorization clause. Confirm with your client whether the engagement scope includes forensic artifact collection, and document the chain of custody for every image you acquire — courts have thrown out forensic evidence for broken chain of custody even in authorized investigations.

Cloud and modern AD consideration: When the 'disk' is a cloud-hosted VM (AWS EC2, Azure VM, GCP Compute), forensic acquisition via snapshot crosses cloud provider terms of service boundaries and may implicate the provider's own legal obligations. AWS, Azure, and GCP all have law enforcement request processes — if this is a criminal matter, coordinate with legal counsel before snapshotting. On Azure, analyzing a managed disk snapshot may expose data governed by Microsoft's data residency commitments; processing that data outside the designated region may violate your organization's data sovereignty agreements. For hybrid AD environments, the NTDS.dit file recovered from a DC image contains all domain credential hashes — treat it as the most sensitive artifact in your case and restrict access accordingly.
false_positives: Timestamp anomalies from legitimate software: Many enterprise applications (antivirus, backup agents, DLP tools) routinely modify file metadata as part of normal operation. Autopsy's timeline will flag these as activity spikes. A Symantec or CrowdStrike sensor touching thousands of files during a scheduled scan looks identical in the timeline to an attacker staging data. Always correlate timeline spikes against known scheduled task times (pulled from the SOFTWARE hive's Task Scheduler entries) before attributing them to malicious activity.

Deleted file carving produces false file type identifications: Autopsy's file carver (backed by PhotoRec-style signature matching) identifies files by header magic bytes, not by file system metadata. A carved file with a PDF header (25 50 44 46) may be a fragment of a larger file, a file that was partially overwritten, or a false positive from data that happens to start with those bytes. Always validate carved files by opening them in the appropriate application or running file(1) against them — do not treat a carved file's type identification as authoritative without secondary confirmation.

VSS shadow copy timestamps do not equal file creation times: When you mount a VSS snapshot and ingest it into Autopsy, the file system timestamps reflect when files were last modified BEFORE the snapshot was taken, not when the snapshot was created. Analysts frequently misread a snapshot taken at 03:00 as meaning all files with 02:59 timestamps were 'created just before the attack.' Those timestamps may be months old. Always document the snapshot creation time separately and treat it as an upper bound, not a creation time.

Browser history artifacts reflect cached data, not confirmed visits: Autopsy's Recent Activity module extracts Chrome and Edge history from SQLite databases (History, Cookies, Web Data). These databases cache data aggressively — a URL appearing in history may reflect a redirect, a prefetch, an embedded resource load, or a background sync, not a deliberate user visit. A user's history showing a visit to a file-sharing site does not prove they intentionally downloaded something; the visit may have been triggered by an ad, a redirect chain, or a browser extension.

Prefetch files are absent on servers by default: Autopsy's ingest modules look for Windows Prefetch files (C:\Windows\Prefetch\*.pf) to reconstruct execution history. On Windows Server editions, prefetching is disabled by default (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Memory Management\PrefetchParameters\EnablePrefetcher = 0). The absence of prefetch data on a server image does NOT mean no executables were run — it means prefetch was disabled. Check for alternative execution artifacts: Shimcache (AppCompatCache in SYSTEM hive), Amcache.hve, and Windows Event Log EID 4688 (process creation, if audit policy was enabled).

theharvester.description: OSINT gathering tool for email addresses, subdomains, IPs, URLs, and employee names. Queries search engines (Google, Bing, DuckDuckGo), social media, Shodan, VirusTotal, and dozens more. Pre-engagement recon gold.
theharvester.teach_intro: theHarvester searches public sources for information about a target organization. Before you touch a single system, you can find email addresses (for phishing), subdomains (attack surface), employee names (social engineering), and IP ranges. All completely passive and legal.

-d.label: Target Domain
-d.teach: Your target domain is the seed. theHarvester finds everything publicly associated with it — emails, subdomains, employee names.

-b.label: Data Sources
-b.desc: Which sources to query: google, bing, shodan, virustotal, all
-b.teach: 'all' queries every available source. Individual sources: shodan finds exposed services, virustotal finds subdomains, linkedin finds employees (for social engineering).

-l.label: Result Limit
-l.teach: More results = more complete picture. 500 is a good starting point. Increase for large organizations.

-f.label: Output File
-f.desc: Save results to HTML and XML: -f output_file
-f.teach: HTML output is readable, XML is machine-parseable. Always save — you'll reference these findings throughout the engagement.

-v.label: Verify Hosts
-v.desc: Verify found hosts via DNS resolution.
-v.teach: Resolves found subdomains to confirm they're live. Dead subdomains are less interesting than live ones.

opsec_notes: BEGINNER — theHarvester makes outbound HTTPS requests to Google, Bing, DuckDuckGo, and other search engines FROM YOUR MACHINE. Your public IP appears in those search engines' access logs. If you're running this from a corporate network or home ISP, that IP is attributable to you. Always route through a VPS or dedicated recon infrastructure you control.

CONCRETE ARTIFACT — When theHarvester uses the 'shodan' or 'virustotal' source, it issues authenticated API calls. Both Shodan and VirusTotal log every API query with your API key, timestamp, and queried domain. Defenders who own the target domain can purchase Shodan Monitor or VirusTotal Enterprise and receive alerts when their domain is queried. Your API key is a direct attribution artifact stored in Shodan's and VT's logs indefinitely.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025 — Enterprise SOCs running Palo Alto Cortex XDR or CrowdStrike Falcon with DNS telemetry enabled will see the DNS resolution burst that theHarvester's host-verification flag (-v) generates. A single workstation resolving 50-200 subdomains of the same apex domain within 60 seconds is a high-confidence recon indicator. Cortex XDR's Analytics Engine flags this as 'DNS Enumeration' with MITRE T1596 tagging. Avoid -v on engagements where the client's DNS resolver logs to a SIEM.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025 — Microsoft Defender for Endpoint (MDE) on Windows hosts running theHarvester via Python will generate process-tree telemetry: python.exe spawning network connections to google.com, bing.com, and api.shodan.io in rapid succession. MDE's command-line entropy scoring and parent-child anomaly detection can flag this as suspicious reconnaissance behavior, especially if python.exe is not a common process on the endpoint. Run theHarvester from a dedicated Linux recon box, not from a Windows host inside the client environment.

When using the '-b all' flag, theHarvester queries every configured source sequentially. This generates a recognizable traffic fingerprint: a single source IP making structured HTTPS GET requests to 30+ distinct external domains within minutes, all with similar User-Agent strings. Network-layer DLP solutions (Zscaler, Netskope) and CASB platforms log and can alert on this pattern. Rotate sources manually (-b google,bing,duckduckgo) across separate sessions with time delays to reduce fingerprint density.

theHarvester's default User-Agent is a Python requests string (e.g., 'python-requests/2.x.x'). Many search engines and data providers rate-limit or block non-browser User-Agents. More critically, WAFs protecting target-adjacent infrastructure (Cloudflare, Akamai) log User-Agent strings. A defender reviewing Cloudflare logs for their domain will see 'python-requests' hitting their DNS or web infrastructure and can correlate timing with other recon activity. Patch your recon tooling to use a realistic browser UA or proxy through a headless browser.

legal_notes: US CFAA BOUNDARY — theHarvester queries only public third-party sources (search engines, Shodan, VirusTotal, certificate logs). It does NOT directly touch the target's systems, so it does not constitute 'unauthorized access' under 18 U.S.C. § 1030 in the traditional sense. However, if your engagement scope explicitly prohibits passive OSINT against the target domain, or if you use harvested data to access systems outside your authorized IP scope, you have crossed into CFAA territory. The tool itself is legal; what you do with its output determines your exposure.

AUTHORIZATION SCOPE — theHarvester's -d flag accepts any domain. Before running it, confirm the target domain is explicitly listed in your Rules of Engagement (RoE) or Statement of Work (SoW). A common mistake: the client authorizes testing of 'targetcorp.com' but theHarvester discovers 'targetcorp-subsidiary.io' — querying Shodan or VirusTotal for that subsidiary domain may be outside scope even though it's the same corporate family. Get explicit written authorization for every apex domain you intend to harvest.

MODERN CLOUD CONSIDERATION — When theHarvester discovers S3 bucket CNAMEs, Azure Blob Storage endpoints (*.blob.core.windows.net), or GCP Storage URLs (*.storage.googleapis.com) associated with the target domain, accessing those cloud resources — even if publicly exposed — may implicate the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act AND the cloud provider's Terms of Service. AWS, Azure, and GCP all prohibit unauthorized security testing of their infrastructure without explicit permission from both the resource owner AND the cloud provider. Accessing a misconfigured public S3 bucket without authorization is legally ambiguous and has resulted in prosecutions. Confirm your RoE covers cloud asset testing and that the client has notified their cloud provider if required.
false_positives: EMAIL COLLISIONS — theHarvester frequently returns email addresses from cached or archived pages that no longer reflect current employees. An address like 'j.smith@targetcorp.com' may belong to an employee who left three years ago, making it useless for phishing but potentially triggering account lockout policies if used in a password spray. Always cross-reference harvested emails against LinkedIn to confirm current employment before using them in an active attack phase.

SUBDOMAIN GHOST RECORDS — DNS records for subdomains like 'dev.targetcorp.com' or 'staging.targetcorp.com' frequently persist in search engine caches and certificate transparency logs long after the actual host has been decommissioned. theHarvester will report these as valid hosts. Without -v (host verification), you have no idea if the IP is live. Even with -v, a host that responds to DNS but returns a 404 or connection refused on all ports is a dead lead. Always validate with httpx or naabu before investing recon time.

SHODAN IP ATTRIBUTION ERRORS — Shodan's banner data is crawled on a schedule and can be weeks or months stale. An IP that Shodan associates with 'jenkins.targetcorp.com' may have been reassigned, the service may have been moved behind a CDN, or the port may have been closed since the last crawl. Shodan timestamps its data — check the 'last_update' field in the raw Shodan JSON before treating a banner as ground truth.

LINKEDIN DATA STALENESS AND MISATTRIBUTION — theHarvester's LinkedIn source relies on Google-cached LinkedIn pages, not live LinkedIn API data. Job titles and employer associations can be 6-18 months out of date. More critically, common names produce false matches: 'David Chen' at 'financialgroup.io' in the harvester output may actually be a David Chen who listed the company as a past employer, not a current employee. Treat LinkedIn results as leads requiring manual verification, not confirmed targets.

CERTSPOTTER AND CT LOG OVER-INCLUSION — Certificate transparency logs record every TLS certificate ever issued for a domain, including wildcard certs, test certs, and certs for infrastructure that was spun up and immediately torn down. theHarvester using certspotter as a source will return subdomains that existed for hours during a cloud deployment test and were never intended to be persistent. A subdomain appearing in CT logs does not mean it is currently live, in scope, or meaningful. Filter CT results aggressively against live DNS resolution before treating them as attack surface.

maltego.description: Visual intelligence gathering and link analysis platform. Transforms data about organizations, people, domains, and infrastructure into interactive graph visualizations. Shows hidden relationships between data points. Industry standard for OSINT graph analysis.
maltego.teach_intro: Maltego builds a visual graph of connections. Start with a domain → transforms find associated IPs, email addresses, people → those people have social media → their connections reveal other targets. It's like Palantir but for pentesters. The graph view makes complex relationships obvious at a glance.

Transforms.label: Run Transforms
Transforms.desc: Automated OSINT lookups called transforms. Right-click any node to run transforms against it.
Transforms.example: Right-click domain → Run Transform → DNS from Domain
Transforms.teach: Each transform queries a different data source and adds new nodes to the graph. Chain transforms: domain → subdomains → IPs → ASN → other domains on same ASN.

Machine.label: Machine Mode
Machine.desc: Automated transform chains that run multiple queries sequentially.
Machine.example: Machines tab → Company Stalker → enter target domain
Machine.teach: Machines are automated investigation workflows. 'Company Stalker' finds email addresses, people, and social profiles automatically. 'Footprint L1' does basic infrastructure mapping.

opsec_notes: Beginner noise: Every Maltego transform fires real DNS lookups, WHOIS queries, and API calls against live infrastructure. If you run transforms against a target domain, that domain's DNS servers log your resolver IP (or your API provider's IP). The target may notice unusual WHOIS query spikes or see your Maltego API provider's netblock in their access logs.

Maltego's built-in transforms route through Paterva's cloud transform servers (transform.maltego.com). Your query data — target domains, IPs, email addresses — transits Paterva's infrastructure. On a sensitive engagement, this means a third party sees your OSINT targets. Use local transforms or self-hosted MISP/Shodan API keys routed through your own VPS to avoid this.

Concrete defender artifact: Shodan, Censys, and VirusTotal API calls originating from Maltego's transform hub appear in those platforms' access logs attributed to Paterva's ASN (AS197695 or similar). A security-aware target monitoring their own Shodan exposure alerts may see a spike in lookups against their IP ranges correlated with your engagement timeline.

2025-2026 cutting edge: Modern threat intelligence platforms (Recorded Future, Mandiant Advantage) now fingerprint OSINT tool behavior patterns. Maltego's transform call sequences — rapid-fire WHOIS → PassiveDNS → certificate transparency → LinkedIn scrape in under 60 seconds — produce a behavioral signature that TI platforms flag as automated reconnaissance. Slow your transform execution and interleave manual browsing to break the pattern.

2025-2026 cutting edge: If you are running Maltego on a corporate SOC-monitored endpoint (common in internal red-team engagements), CrowdStrike Falcon's process tree telemetry will log maltego.exe spawning Java child processes (Maltego runs on JVM) with outbound connections to transform APIs. Falcon's network containment rules may alert on the volume of unique external DNS resolutions per process. Run Maltego on a dedicated, isolated VM outside the monitored estate.

OAuth and API key hygiene: Maltego integrations with LinkedIn, Hunter.io, Have I Been Pwned, and FullContact require personal API keys stored in the Maltego client config (~/.maltego/ on Linux, %APPDATA%\Maltego\ on Windows). These keys are stored in plaintext XML. On a shared assessment VM or if your machine is compromised, these keys leak and can be used to attribute your OSINT activity back to your personal accounts.

sample_outputs.scenario: Beginner: Starting from a single domain, running built-in DNS and WHOIS transforms to discover associated infrastructure. Student is learning what Maltego's graph output looks like after basic transforms.
sample_outputs.command: Maltego GUI: Create new graph → drag 'Domain' entity → set value 'targetcorp.com' → right-click → Run Transforms → 'To DNS Name [DNS]' and 'To IP Address [DNS]'

(2) Run 'To DNS Name [Reverse DNS]' on the /24 containing 198.51.100.45 to find other domains hosted on the same server. (3) Note that dev.targetcorp.com and staging.targetcorp.com are high-value targets — development environments often have weaker authentication and expose internal tooling.

Operator chains transforms across domain → email addresses → people → LinkedIn → leaked credentials → infrastructure, then pivots to certificate transparency for shadow IT discovery.

The HIBP hit on James Morrison (Senior Network Engineer) with a RockYou2024 plaintext entry is critical — this is a credential stuffing candidate for VPN, OWA, and the Azure tenant. Next steps: (1) Feed j.morrison@targetcorp.com + leaked password candidates into a password spray against sso.targetcorp.com using a tool like MSOLSpray or TeamFiltration with lockout-safe delay. (2) Enumerate targetcorp-dev.azurewebsites.net with ffuf for exposed endpoints and check for Azure managed identity metadata abuse. (3) Export the Maltego graph as a CSV and import into BloodHound's custom query interface or a Neo4j instance to correlate with any AD data collected later.

legal_notes: CFAA boundary: Running Maltego transforms against a target organization's domain, email addresses, or IP infrastructure constitutes active data collection even though it feels passive. Under 18 U.S.C. § 1030, accessing computer systems without authorization includes automated querying that causes measurable load or triggers access controls. Transforms that hit the target's own servers (e.g., DNS zone transfer attempts, direct WHOIS to the target's registrar) may cross the authorization line if not explicitly permitted in your rules of engagement.

Scope authorization: Maltego's graph expansion is non-linear — one domain becomes 200 nodes spanning dozens of third-party organizations (hosting providers, email vendors, CDN partners, subsidiary domains). Ensure your rules of engagement explicitly authorize OSINT against discovered infrastructure, not just the seed target. Many engagements authorize testing against 'targetcorp.com and all owned IP space' but the Maltego graph will surface Azure tenants, AWS accounts, and SaaS platforms that are technically owned by the client but may have separate authorization requirements or third-party data.

Cloud and SaaS consideration: Transforms that enumerate Azure AD tenants (via login.microsoftonline.com tenant discovery), AWS S3 bucket names, or GCP project IDs may trigger automated abuse detection in Microsoft, Amazon, and Google's security systems. Microsoft in particular logs unauthenticated tenant enumeration and may flag your source IP for enhanced scrutiny or block it, which can interfere with later phishing infrastructure or OAuth consent abuse phases of the engagement. Coordinate timing of OSINT phases with your client's IT team if stealth is not a requirement.
false_positives: Certificate transparency transforms will surface SANs for wildcard certs (*.targetcorp.com) and report dozens of 'discovered' subdomains that do not actually resolve or host services. Operators frequently mistake SAN entries for live hosts — always validate every CT-discovered hostname with active DNS resolution before treating it as a live target.

Hunter.io and similar email harvesting transforms return email addresses with confidence scores, but those scores reflect format pattern matching against observed email conventions, not confirmed deliverability. Addresses like 'it-admin@targetcorp.com' are often role accounts that bounce, are monitored by a team rather than an individual, or are honeypot addresses that trigger alerts when contacted.

LinkedIn transforms via FullContact or similar enrichment APIs frequently return stale employment data. A person shown as 'Senior Network Engineer at TargetCorp' may have left the organization 18 months ago. Their email address may still exist as a forwarding alias or may be completely dead. Targeting former employees for credential stuffing is both legally risky (they may have no connection to the current target) and operationally wasteful.

IP geolocation data surfaced by Maltego's IP transforms is notoriously inaccurate for cloud-hosted infrastructure. An IP in AWS us-east-1 may geolocate to Ashburn, Virginia in one database and Seattle in another. More critically, Cloudflare, Akamai, and Fastly anycast IPs will geolocate to wherever the nearest PoP is to your resolver — not where the origin server is. Do not use Maltego geolocation data to make infrastructure attribution decisions.

Maltego's 'To Person' transforms frequently conflate individuals with the same name. A transform on 'j.morrison@targetcorp.com' may return LinkedIn profiles, social media accounts, and breach data for multiple James Morrisons globally. The graph will visually link these as if they are the same person. Always cross-validate person-entity enrichment with at least two independent data points (employer, location, profile photo) before treating the enriched data as accurate.

shodan.description: Command-line interface for Shodan — the search engine for internet-connected devices. Finds exposed services, default credentials, vulnerable software versions, industrial control systems, cameras, databases, and more. Essential for external attack surface mapping.
shodan.teach_intro: Shodan continuously scans the entire internet and indexes what it finds. You search it like Google but for devices. 'org:TargetCorp port:3389' finds all of their RDP servers. 'hostname:target.com vuln:CVE-2021-44228' finds their Log4j-vulnerable hosts. It's the fastest way to understand an organization's external exposure.

search.label: Search Shodan
search.desc: Query the Shodan database with filters.
search.teach: Powerful filters: org: (company name), hostname:, port:, os:, product:, version:, country:, vuln: (by CVE). Combine them: 'org:Target Corp port:3389 os:Windows'

host.label: Host Lookup
host.desc: Get all Shodan data for a specific IP.
host.teach: Shows every open port, service banner, vulnerabilities, and historical data Shodan has for an IP. Like a passive nmap from Shodan's perspective.

stats.label: Statistics
stats.teach: See which countries target's servers are in, which ports are most common, what OS versions they run. Great for understanding the overall infrastructure.

download.label: Download Results
download.desc: Download search results to a file.
download.example: shodan download results 'org:Target Corp' && shodan parse results.json.gz
download.teach: Download all matching hosts for offline analysis. Parse with shodan parse to extract IPs, ports, and banners.

myip.label: My IP Address
myip.desc: Show your current external IP address.
myip.teach: Quick check of what IP you're appearing as externally. Important for engagement tracking and for verifying VPN/proxy is working.

opsec_notes: Shodan itself makes NO network requests to your target — all queries hit Shodan's own API servers over HTTPS (port 443). Your IP appears in Shodan's API logs, not in the target's firewall or web logs. A defender watching their own perimeter will see nothing from a passive Shodan query.

Your Shodan API key is transmitted in every CLI request as a query parameter or header. If you run 'shodan' commands in a shared shell environment, the key appears in shell history (~/.bash_history, ~/.zsh_history) and in process listings visible via 'ps aux' to other users on the same host. Rotate keys after engagements and store them in a secrets manager, not in dotfiles.

CrowdStrike Falcon and SentinelOne both instrument process creation events. If you invoke the Shodan CLI from within a post-exploitation shell (e.g., a Sliver or Mythic implant), the parent-child process tree — cmd.exe or powershell.exe spawning 'shodan' or 'python.exe shodan' — is a high-fidelity behavioral anomaly. EDR command-line telemetry will capture the full argv including your API key and search terms. Prefer running recon tooling from a clean operator workstation, never from an implant.

Defender for Endpoint (MDE) on Windows 11 24H2 with Attack Surface Reduction rules enabled will flag Python-based CLI tools (the Shodan CLI is pip-installed Python) if they attempt outbound connections to non-categorized endpoints. The Shodan API domain (api.shodan.io) may not be in the corporate proxy allowlist, causing a DNS query for api.shodan.io to appear in DNS security logs (e.g., Cisco Umbrella, Palo Alto DNS Security) — a concrete artifact: DNS query log entry for api.shodan.io from an internal workstation is anomalous and alertable.

The concrete defender artifact for Shodan CLI use on a corporate host: Windows Event ID 4688 (process creation with command line auditing enabled) or Sysmon EID 1 will record the full command line including search terms and API key. On Linux, auditd rule '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S execve' captures the same. Log path on Linux: /var/log/audit/audit.log. On Windows: Security event log or Sysmon operational log.

When using 'shodan download' to pull large result sets, the CLI writes compressed JSON (.json.gz) files to disk. On a monitored endpoint, file creation events (Sysmon EID 11) for .json.gz files in unusual directories (Downloads, Temp, or a red-team staging directory) combined with a prior network connection to api.shodan.io creates a correlated detection chain that modern XDR platforms (Palo Alto Cortex, Microsoft Sentinel with Fusion) will surface as a multi-stage alert.

sample_outputs.scenario: Beginner: operator has a target company name and wants to find all their internet-exposed hosts with open RDP (port 3389). Single search query, no download, just reading results.
sample_outputs.output:
ip_str          port    org                  hostnames

203.0.113.45    3389    Acme Logistics       vpn-gw.acme-logistics.com

sample_outputs.explanation: Each row is a host Shodan's scanners found with port 3389 open and responding. The 'org' field comes from WHOIS/BGP ASN data — it's how Shodan groups IPs by owner. 'hostnames' is populated from reverse DNS. What this tells you: Acme has at least 5 RDP-exposed hosts, one named 'legacy-ts01' which suggests an older terminal server — a high-value target for credential spraying or BlueKeep-class vulns. Next steps: (1) Run 'shodan host 203.0.113.201' to pull the full banner for that legacy host including OS fingerprint and any CVE tags Shodan has flagged. (2) Cross-reference hostnames against certificate transparency logs (crt.sh) to find additional subdomains. (3) Note that direct RDP exposure without a VPN gateway in front is a significant misconfiguration — document it for the report.

sample_outputs.scenario: Advanced: operator is mapping a target's full external attack surface before a red-team engagement. Hunting for exposed management interfaces, cloud metadata endpoints, and Shodan-flagged vulnerable services across the target's ASN. Downloading results for offline analysis.

203.0.113.199   6379    -                        Redis            7.2.x
sample_outputs.explanation: This query targets the entire ASN (AS64512) rather than org name — ASN is more reliable because org strings in Shodan are inconsistent. The compound query hunts for three high-value categories simultaneously: (1) VPN/gateway appliances (Fortinet, Ivanti/Pulse, Citrix) — these are the current crown jewels for initial access given the cadence of critical vulns in 2024-2025; (2) exposed data stores (Elasticsearch port 9200, MongoDB 27017, Redis 6379) which are frequently unauthenticated. The Ivanti PCS result with a CVE tag is the immediate priority — verify the exact CVE against the NVD before acting, Shodan's vuln tags can lag or misattribute. Next steps: (1) Run 'shodan host 203.0.113.18' for full banner and confirm the version string matches a known-exploitable release. (2) Feed all IPs into 'httpx -l ips.txt -title -tech-detect -status-code' for live validation — Shodan data can be days to weeks stale. (3) For the unauthenticated data stores, use 'nuclei -l datastores.txt -t exposures/' to confirm open access before touching them directly. (4) Cross-reference the Fortinet version against the FortiGuard advisory portal — 7.0.9 may or may not be patched for current SSL-VPN vulns depending on the exact build.

legal_notes: Under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (18 U.S.C. § 1030), querying Shodan's database is passive and does not constitute unauthorized access to the target's systems — Shodan's scanners collected the data, not you. However, using Shodan results to then access a system you are not authorized to test IS a CFAA violation. The recon is legal; acting on it without authorization is not. This distinction matters in court and in your engagement contract.

Your rules of engagement must explicitly define the IP ranges and ASNs in scope. Shodan queries against an org name or ASN will return ALL their internet-facing infrastructure, including hosts outside your authorized scope (subsidiary companies, cloud tenants, CDN edges, third-party-hosted services). Document every IP you intend to interact with and confirm it falls within the signed scope before proceeding. Scope creep discovered via Shodan is a common source of engagement disputes.

In cloud environments (AWS, Azure, GCP), an organization's internet-facing IPs may be owned by the cloud provider's ASN (e.g., AS16509 for AWS), not the target's own ASN. Searching by org name may miss cloud-hosted assets entirely, while searching by cloud ASN will return thousands of unrelated tenants. Use 'ssl.cert.subject.cn:target.com' or 'hostname:target.com' queries to find cloud-hosted assets attributable to the target — but confirm authorization covers cloud-hosted infrastructure explicitly, as some clients exclude their cloud environments from scope.
false_positives: Shodan's scan data has a freshness problem: results can be anywhere from hours to several weeks old depending on the port and protocol. A service that was exposed last month and has since been firewalled off will still appear in Shodan results. Always validate with a live probe (httpx, nmap against confirmed in-scope hosts) before treating a Shodan result as current ground truth.

The 'org' field is populated from BGP/WHOIS data and is notoriously inconsistent. A company that recently acquired another, rebranded, or uses a holding company for IP registration will have assets scattered across multiple org strings. Searching 'org:"Acme Corp"' will miss assets registered under 'org:"Acme Holdings LLC"' or 'org:"Acme-Legacy"'. Always supplement org searches with ASN lookups and SSL certificate CN/SAN searches.

Shodan's vulnerability tags (the 'vulns' field) are generated by matching banner version strings against CVE databases using heuristic rules — they are NOT the result of active exploitation or authenticated version checks. A host running Apache/2.4.51 may be tagged for a vuln that was backport-patched by the OS vendor (common in RHEL/CentOS/Debian). Treat Shodan vuln tags as leads requiring manual verification, not confirmed findings.

Load balancers, CDNs (Cloudflare, Akamai, Fastly), and reverse proxies cause Shodan to index the edge node's banner, not the origin server's. A target behind Cloudflare will show Cloudflare's nginx version and Cloudflare's IP in Shodan, not the real origin. The 'org' field will show 'Cloudflare, Inc.' — you may completely miss the target's actual infrastructure unless you find the origin IP through other means (historical DNS, certificate transparency, direct IP references in JS).

Port 443 results with generic 'http.title' values like 'Access Denied', '403 Forbidden', or empty titles often indicate WAF or load balancer interception — Shodan's crawler hit the edge, not the application. The product and version fields in these cases reflect the WAF or proxy, not the backend. Operators who act on these results (e.g., attempting to exploit an 'Apache 2.4.x' version shown by Shodan) may be targeting a Cloudflare or AWS ALB edge node, wasting time and generating noise.

responder.description: LLMNR/NBT-NS/mDNS poisoning tool for credential capture on local networks. When Windows systems fail DNS, they broadcast LLMNR requests — Responder answers them, captures NTLMv2 hashes, and cracks them offline. Also runs rogue SMB, HTTP, FTP, and other servers to capture auth attempts.
responder.teach_intro: Windows fails a DNS lookup → broadcasts LLMNR on the local network asking 'who has this name?' → Responder answers 'that's me!' → Windows sends NTLMv2 credentials to authenticate. You capture the NTLMv2 hash and crack it offline. In corporate environments this produces credentials within minutes of running.

-I.label: Network Interface
-I.desc: Interface to listen on: -I eth0 or -I wlan0
-I.teach:
Responder listens on your interface and responds to broadcast queries. Must be on the same network segment as victims.

Interface: -I eth0

-r.label: Enable NBNS
-r.teach:
NBNS is another Windows name resolution fallback. Combined with LLMNR poisoning you capture more hashes.

Enable rogue DNS

-d.label: Enable DHCP
-d.desc: Enable DHCP poisoning to inject Responder's IP as WPAD proxy.
-d.teach:
DHCP poisoning injects WPAD configuration pointing to Responder's HTTP server. All browsers that auto-configure proxy send credentials.

Enable DHCP replies

-w.label: WPAD Server
-w.desc: Start a rogue WPAD proxy server.
-w.teach:
WPAD (Web Proxy Auto-Discovery) tricks browsers into authenticating to your proxy. Transparent credential capture from browser traffic.

Enable WPAD rogue proxy server

-P.label: Force NTLMv1
-P.desc: Force downgrade from NTLMv2 to NTLMv1 for easier cracking.
-P.teach: NTLMv1 is weaker and cracks much faster than NTLMv2. Some systems accept downgrade, others don't.

--lm.label: LM Downgrade
--lm.desc: Enable LM hash downgrade (very old systems).
--lm.teach:
LM hashes are trivially crackable. Only older Windows systems (XP era) still use them, but some configs still negotiate LM.

Downgrade to LM hashes (older Windows)

-F.label: -F
-F.teach: Force NTLM authentication in WPAD responses

output_read.meaning: informational event
machine asked for something, you replied — they'll send hashes
the NTLMv2 hash — crack it with hashcat -m 5600
NTLMv2 is strong but crackable with rockyou if password is weak
Username and client IP tell you who the hash belongs to

opsec_notes: BEGINNER NOISE: Responder floods the local broadcast domain with LLMNR (UDP/5355), NBT-NS (UDP/137), and mDNS (UDP/5353) responses. Any packet capture running on the segment — even a junior SOC analyst's Wireshark session — will see your machine answering queries it has no business answering. This is not subtle. Every poisoned response has your attacker IP as the source.

CONCRETE ARTIFACT — Network IDS: Suricata and Snort ship default rules (ET POLICY LLMNR Response and similar) that fire on LLMNR poisoning responses. The defender sees: src_ip=<your box>, dst_ip=<victim>, udp/5355, payload matching the poisoned name. Zeek logs this as dns.log entries with rcode=0 (NOERROR) for names that should not resolve. Correlation of your IP answering dozens of different hostnames in seconds is a near-certain IOC.

CONCRETE ARTIFACT — Windows Event Log: On the victim host, a successful NTLM authentication attempt to a rogue SMB server generates Security EID 4625 (failed logon) or EID 4624 (successful logon) with Logon Type 3 (network) and an unfamiliar target workstation name. Microsoft Defender for Identity (MDI) specifically has a detection rule 'LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning and relay attack' that fires on exactly this pattern — it correlates the broadcast query with the subsequent NTLM auth to an unexpected host.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025-2026 — CrowdStrike Falcon / SentinelOne: Modern EDR with network telemetry (Falcon's Network Containment, SentinelOne's Deep Visibility) ingests raw socket events. Responder binding to UDP/5355, UDP/137, and TCP/445 simultaneously from a non-domain-controller process is a high-confidence behavioral indicator. Falcon's Threat Graph correlates the process tree (python.exe or Responder binary) → socket bind → inbound SMB auth → NTLM hash capture as a single attack chain. In 2025 deployments with Falcon Complete, this chain auto-quarantines within seconds.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025-2026 — Microsoft Defender for Endpoint (MDE) + Sentinel: MDE's advanced hunting table DeviceNetworkEvents captures Responder's listener sockets. A KQL query joining DeviceNetworkEvents (LocalPort in (137,5355,5353,80,443,21)) with DeviceLogonEvents (LogonType==3, RemoteIP==attacker) surfaces the full chain. Azure Sentinel analytic rules shipped in 2024-2025 include 'LLMNR Poisoning Detected' as a scheduled query. Assume any mature SOC with MDE E5 licensing sees this within one beacon interval.

EVASION CONSIDERATION — Analyze-Only Mode: Running Responder with -A (analyze mode) suppresses poisoning responses entirely — you observe broadcast queries without answering them. This is near-silent from a network perspective and lets you map which hostnames are being queried (revealing internal naming conventions, misconfigured clients, and high-value targets) before committing to active poisoning. Use -A first on any engagement where stealth matters; switch to active only in a defined window.

sample_outputs.explanation: Several things are happening simultaneously: (1) -w enables the WPAD rogue proxy server — Windows clients configured for 'auto-detect proxy settings' query 'wpad' via LLMNR/DNS, Responder answers, and the browser authenticates to the fake WPAD server, yielding HTTP NTLMv1 hashes; (2) -F forces NTLM authentication on the WPAD/HTTP server even when the client would prefer anonymous; (3) -P forces NTLMv1 on the HTTP server — NTLMv1 hashes (mode 5500 in hashcat) crack dramatically faster than NTLMv2 and are also crackable via rainbow tables (crack.sh); (4) '--lm' attempts LM hash downgrade for legacy clients. The capture shows svc_backup (likely a service account — high value for persistence) via HTTP/NTLMv1, and da_admin via SMB/NTLMv2. Next actions: (a) crack svc_backup NTLMv1 with 'hashcat -m 5500' or submit to crack.sh; (b) for da_admin NTLMv2, pivot to relay — kill Responder's SMB server, launch 'ntlmrelayx.py -tf targets.txt --no-http-server -smb2support' to relay the DA hash to a target without SMB signing; (c) run BloodHound to map what da_admin can reach; (d) if relay succeeds to a DC, attempt secretsdump via impacket.

legal_notes: CFAA (18 U.S.C. § 1030): Responder actively intercepts network authentication traffic and captures credential material. Running it on any network you do not own or have explicit written authorization to test constitutes unauthorized interception of computer communications and unauthorized access to computer systems — both felony-grade CFAA violations. The 'I was just on the network' defense does not apply; credential capture is an affirmative act beyond mere presence.

RULES OF ENGAGEMENT — SCOPE: Confirm your RoE explicitly permits credential capture and LLMNR poisoning before running Responder. Many client engagements authorize scanning but explicitly prohibit credential interception (especially in environments with PCI-DSS or HIPAA obligations where captured hashes may constitute regulated data). Verify the authorized IP subnet — Responder poisons the entire broadcast domain, which may extend beyond your scoped /24 into VLANs you are not authorized to touch if the network is misconfigured.

MODERN CLOUD / HYBRID AD CONSIDERATION: In hybrid Azure AD / Entra ID environments, captured NTLMv2 hashes may belong to accounts synchronized to the cloud via Azure AD Connect. Cracking or relaying these hashes could yield access to cloud resources (M365, Azure portal, Intune) far beyond the on-prem scope defined in your RoE. Explicitly confirm with the client whether cloud-synchronized accounts are in scope before using captured credentials against any cloud endpoint.
false_positives: WPAD FALSE CAPTURE — LEGITIMATE PROXY CLIENTS: In environments where a real WPAD server exists, some clients may query 'wpad' via LLMNR as a fallback after DNS succeeds. Responder may capture authentication attempts from clients that are legitimately trying to reach the real proxy and are confused by the race condition between the real DNS response and Responder's poisoned LLMNR response. The hash is real, but the client may immediately fail over to the real proxy — you get the credential but the client session continues normally, making detection harder to attribute.

MACHINE ACCOUNT HASHES — NOT USER CREDENTIALS: A significant portion of Responder captures in Active Directory environments are NTLM authentications from computer accounts (e.g., CORP\WORKSTATION01$) rather than user accounts. Machine account hashes are computationally infeasible to crack with standard wordlists (they are 120-character random passwords rotated every 30 days by default). Operators who don't filter these out waste cracking cycles. Filter with: grep -v '\$::' hashes.txt before submitting to hashcat.

MULTICAST SUPPRESSION — SWITCHES WITH IGMP SNOOPING: On networks where managed switches enforce IGMP snooping and multicast filtering, LLMNR (224.0.0.252) and mDNS (224.0.0.251) multicast packets may be suppressed at the switch level. Responder will appear to run normally but will capture zero hashes because its poisoned responses never reach the querying hosts. NBT-NS (broadcast, not multicast) is unaffected. If you see zero LLMNR/mDNS captures but the network is clearly active, suspect multicast filtering and rely on NBT-NS or pivot to SMB relay instead.

ANALYZE MODE GHOST QUERIES — RESPONDER'S OWN PROBES: When running in -A (analyze) mode, Responder itself generates some network traffic to enumerate the environment. On networks with other security tools (e.g., a blue team running their own Responder in analyze mode, or a honeypot), you may see your own probes reflected back, creating the appearance of additional LLMNR query sources that don't correspond to real victim hosts.

NTLMv2 RELAY FAILURE — SMB SIGNING ENFORCED: Responder captures NTLMv2 hashes for relay via ntlmrelayx, but if the target has SMB signing required (enforced by default on all Windows Server 2022 domain controllers and increasingly on workstations via GPO in hardened 2024-2025 deployments), relay attacks fail silently. The hash capture succeeds, the relay attempt returns STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED or a signing negotiation failure, and operators may incorrectly conclude the credentials are invalid. Verify SMB signing status with 'nmap --script smb2-security-mode' or CrackMapExec before investing time in relay chains.

bettercap.description: The Swiss Army knife of network attacks. Performs ARP spoofing, man-in-the-middle attacks, WiFi hacking, BLE (Bluetooth) sniffing, network discovery, and credential capture. Replaces ettercap with a modern modular architecture.
bettercap.teach_intro: Bettercap positions itself between you and network traffic (MITM). ARP poisoning tricks devices into sending traffic through you. Once in the middle, you see all unencrypted traffic, can inject content into HTTP pages, strip HTTPS (with SSLstrip), or capture credentials from protocols that use plaintext auth.

-iface.label: Network Interface
-iface.teach: Specifies your network interface. wlan0 for WiFi MITM, eth0 for wired. Bettercap starts an interactive console.

net.probe.label: Network Probe
net.probe.desc: Discover hosts on the network segment.
net.probe.teach: Sends ARP/mDNS/UPnP probes to discover all hosts. Shows IP, MAC, hostname, and vendor. Your target list.

arp.spoof.label: ARP Spoofing
arp.spoof.desc: Perform ARP poisoning to MITM traffic.
arp.spoof.teach: Tells victim 'the gateway is at MY MAC address'. All their traffic flows through you. Combine with net.sniff to capture it.

net.sniff.label: Network Sniffing
net.sniff.desc: Sniff and display/log captured network traffic.
net.sniff.teach: Captures and parses all traffic. Credentials from HTTP forms, FTP, POP3, IMAP, Telnet — all visible in cleartext.

https.proxy.label: HTTPS Proxy / SSLstrip
https.proxy.desc: Act as HTTPS proxy for SSL inspection and stripping.
https.proxy.teach: SSLstrip intercepts HTTPS redirects and serves HTTP instead. User thinks they're on HTTPS but you see plaintext. Modern HSTS protects most sites.

wifi.recon.label: WiFi Recon
wifi.recon.desc: Scan and monitor nearby WiFi networks.
wifi.recon.teach: Shows all APs and clients in range with signal strength, BSSID, encryption type. Foundation for WiFi attacks.

wpscan.description: Black box WordPress vulnerability scanner. Enumerates WordPress version, installed plugins, themes, users, and checks them all against a database of known vulnerabilities. The definitive tool for WordPress security assessment.
wpscan.teach_intro: WordPress powers 43% of the web. WPScan specifically targets the WordPress ecosystem — outdated plugins are the most common attack vector. A single vulnerable plugin can give you remote code execution regardless of how well the core WordPress installation is secured.

--url.label: Target URL
--url.teach: Give wpscan the WordPress URL. It auto-detects WordPress, version, and begins enumeration.

--enumerate.label: Enumerate
--enumerate.desc: What to enumerate: p=plugins, t=themes, u=users, vp=vulnerable plugins only.
--enumerate.teach: p finds all plugins (each is a potential vuln). u finds usernames for brute forcing. vp only shows vulnerable plugins — cleaner output.

--api-token.label: API Token
--api-token.desc: WPScan vulnerability database API token. Free at wpscan.com.
--api-token.teach: The API token unlocks vulnerability data. Without it you see plugins/themes but not which ones are vulnerable. Free 25 API calls/day with registration.

--passwords.label: Password File
--passwords.teach: If you found admin username via enumeration, brute force the wp-login.php endpoint. WordPress doesn't rate-limit by default.

--usernames.label: Username(s)
--usernames.teach: Use usernames found during --enumerate u. Author archives reveal usernames. xmlrpc.php also exposes them.

-t.label: Threads
-t.teach: More threads = faster but more detectable. Default 5 is safe. Plugin enumeration with many threads completes much faster.

opsec_notes: BEGINNER NOISE: WPScan sends dozens of HTTP GET requests to paths like /wp-login.php, /wp-json/wp/v2/users, /readme.html, and /?author=1 in rapid succession. Any web server access log (Apache /var/log/apache2/access.log, Nginx /var/log/nginx/access.log) will show these requests clustered within seconds from your source IP, making automated scanning trivially obvious to even a basic log review.

CONCRETE ARTIFACT — WAF/IDS SIGNATURE: WPScan sets a default User-Agent string of 'WPScan v3.x.x (https://wpscan.com/wordpress-security-scanner)'. This string is in the default ruleset of ModSecurity, Cloudflare WAF, Wordfence, and Sucuri. A defender watching their WAF dashboard will see a block or alert with this UA verbatim. Override with --user-agent 'Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36' to blend into browser traffic.

RATE LIMITING DETECTION: WordPress sites running Wordfence or iThemes Security will auto-block source IPs after a configurable threshold of 404s or login attempts (default is often 20 requests/minute). The --throttle flag (milliseconds between requests) and -t 1 (single thread) dramatically reduce this signature. On a hardened target, aggressive scanning will lock you out before enumeration completes.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025-2026 — CLOUD WAF TELEMETRY: WordPress deployments behind AWS CloudFront + WAF or Azure Front Door generate structured JSON logs (CloudFront access logs in S3, Azure Monitor WAF logs) that include client IP, URI, User-Agent, and rule match IDs. These logs feed directly into SIEM pipelines (Sentinel, Splunk). A defender with a Sentinel analytic rule on 'WPScan' UA or high-frequency wp-json enumeration will get an incident within minutes. If the target is behind a CDN, your scan hits the CDN's origin shield IP pool — but your source IP is still logged at the CDN edge.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025-2026 — API TOKEN FINGERPRINTING: The --api-token flag causes WPScan to make authenticated requests to the WPScan Vulnerability Database API (wpscan.com). This is an outbound connection FROM YOUR HOST to an external SaaS. On a corporate red-team engagement, endpoint DLP or network proxy inspection (Zscaler, Palo Alto NGFW with SSL inspection) will log this outbound connection. The domain wpscan.com may be categorized as 'Security/Hacking Tools' and blocked or alerted on. Pre-stage the vulnerability database locally using --update and operate offline where possible.

PLUGIN ENUMERATION DEPTH: The --enumerate p flag with --plugins-detection aggressive sends a request for every plugin path in WPScan's database (thousands of requests). This is statistically anomalous in any web server log — a legitimate user never requests /wp-content/plugins/[obscure-plugin]/readme.txt. Passive mode (--plugins-detection passive) only reads plugin references from the homepage HTML and is orders of magnitude quieter, though less complete.

sample_outputs.explanation: This output reveals a multi-vector attack surface on a production e-commerce site. Key findings: (1) WooCommerce 8.4.0 has an unauthenticated stored XSS — this is immediately exploitable without credentials and could be used to steal session cookies from admin users or inject a keylogger into the checkout page affecting customers. (2) The Elementor XSS requires Contributor-level authentication — pair this with the enumerated usernames for a targeted credential attack. (3) Two real usernames (sarah.mitchell, j.torres) were extracted from the WP-JSON API — this endpoint (/wp-json/wp/v2/users) is enabled by default and leaks display names. These are likely Active Directory or SSO usernames on a corporate target. Next steps: (a) Use the enumerated usernames against the organization's OWA, VPN portal, or Azure AD login with a password spray tool like spray or o365spray — corporate WordPress often uses the same username format as AD; (b) Exploit the unauthenticated WooCommerce XSS by injecting a payload into the order tracking form and sending a crafted link to an admin (stored XSS persists in the DB); (c) Check if the Flatsome theme version has its own CVEs via searchsploit flatsome or the WPScan DB; (d) Attempt authenticated enumeration of additional plugins by registering a Contributor account if open registration is enabled.

legal_notes: CFAA BOUNDARY: WPScan actively requests URLs on the target server, reads files (readme.html, license.txt, wp-cron.php), and optionally attempts authentication brute force. Each of these constitutes 'access' under 18 U.S.C. § 1030. Running WPScan against any WordPress installation you do not own or have explicit written authorization to test is a federal crime regardless of whether the site is 'public-facing.' The fact that readme.html is publicly accessible does not constitute authorization to enumerate the site's vulnerability surface.

RULES OF ENGAGEMENT — SCOPE SPECIFICITY: Your engagement SOW must explicitly authorize WordPress-specific enumeration. A generic 'web application penetration test' authorization may not cover automated scanning tools, brute-force of wp-login.php (which generates authentication log entries and may trigger account lockouts on real user accounts), or enumeration of the /wp-json/ API. Confirm with your client whether WordPress user enumeration is in scope — leaking employee usernames (sarah.mitchell, j.torres) may violate data handling clauses in the contract.

CLOUD/SAAS CONSIDERATION: If the target WordPress site is hosted on WordPress.com (managed), WP Engine, Kinsta, or Flywheel, your scan may hit shared infrastructure. WordPress.com explicitly prohibits automated scanning in its ToS, and WP Engine's WAF will block and report scanning activity to their security team, who may contact your client. Confirm the hosting provider and whether their platform ToS permits third-party security testing — some managed hosts require a separate authorization letter from the hosting provider in addition to the site owner's permission.
false_positives: VERSION DETECTION FROM CACHED PAGES: WPScan detects WordPress version from multiple sources including the readme.html, RSS feed generator tag, and meta generator tag. If the site uses a caching plugin (WP Super Cache, W3 Total Cache) or a CDN serving stale HTML, the version string in the page source may reflect a cached copy from before a recent update. The site may actually be running a patched version while WPScan reports the old one. Always cross-reference version detection with the 'Found By' field — 'Script In Homepage (Passive Detection)' is more reliable than a cached readme.

PLUGIN FALSE NEGATIVES FROM PASSIVE DETECTION: In passive mode (--plugins-detection passive), WPScan only identifies plugins referenced in the homepage HTML source. A plugin that is installed and active but not referenced in any frontend asset (a backend-only plugin like a security scanner, backup plugin, or admin tool) will be completely invisible to passive enumeration. This creates a false sense of completeness — the operator may believe they have a full plugin inventory when significant attack surface is hidden. Aggressive mode is required for complete enumeration but carries the noise tradeoff.

USER ENUMERATION BLOCKED BY SECURITY PLUGINS: Wordfence, iThemes Security, and All In One WP Security can disable the /?author=N redirect and block the /wp-json/wp/v2/users endpoint. When these controls are active, WPScan will report 'No Users Found' even if valid accounts exist. This is a false negative, not evidence of a single-user or headless installation. The absence of enumerated users should prompt the operator to attempt login error message analysis manually or use OSINT (LinkedIn, email harvesting) to identify likely usernames.

VULNERABILITY DATABASE LAG: WPScan's vulnerability data is only as current as the last --update or API query. A plugin version flagged as 'Latest, no known vulnerabilities' may have had a CVE published in the last 24-48 hours that hasn't propagated to the WPScan DB yet. For high-value targets, cross-reference plugin versions against the NVD (nvd.nist.gov), Patchstack, and the plugin's own changelog on wordpress.org — the WPScan DB is comprehensive but not real-time.

MULTISITE AND SUBDIRECTORY INSTALLS: WPScan assumes a standard single-site WordPress installation at the provided URL. WordPress Multisite networks (where /wp-admin/ is at the network root but individual sites are at /site1/, /site2/) will produce incomplete results if you scan a subsite URL. The tool may fail to detect the correct WordPress version, miss network-activated plugins, or report the wrong theme. Always identify whether the target is a Multisite installation before interpreting results — look for 'wp-signup.php' or 'wp-activate.php' at the root as indicators.

searchsploit.description: Offline command-line search tool for the Exploit-DB database. Contains 45,000+ exploits for every platform and software version. Find public exploits for any software version without internet access. Links directly to downloadable exploit code.
searchsploit.teach_intro: After nmap discovers 'Apache 2.4.29' or 'OpenSSH 7.4', searchsploit tells you what public exploits exist for that exact version. It searches the offline copy of Exploit-DB — the internet's largest database of known exploits — and gives you the exact file to use.

-t.label: Title Search Only
-t.desc: Search only in exploit title, not description.
-t.teach: Title-only search reduces false positives. 'searchsploit apache' returns thousands. 'searchsploit -t apache 2.4' narrows to the version.

-e.label: Exact Match
-e.teach: Exact matching for precise version strings from nmap output. Copy the service/version string from nmap -sV and paste it.

-x.label: View Exploit Code
-x.desc: Read exploit source code directly in terminal.
-x.teach: Always read exploit code before running it. Understand what it does, what requirements it has, and whether it's stable or a PoC that might crash the service.

-m.label: Copy Exploit
-m.desc: Mirror exploit file to current directory.
-m.teach: Copies the exploit to your working directory so you can modify it. Always copy before editing — don't modify the database original.

--cve.label: Search by CVE
--cve.desc: Find exploits for a specific CVE number.
--cve.teach: Found a CVE in a Nuclei or Nessus scan? searchsploit --cve gives you the public PoC exploit code immediately.

-u.label: Update Database
-u.teach: Run monthly to keep your local DB current. New exploits are added daily to Exploit-DB. Fresh = more hits.

opsec_notes: SearchSploit itself is a fully offline tool — it reads from a local copy of Exploit-DB stored on disk (typically /usr/share/exploitdb/). Running 'searchsploit apache 2.4.29' generates ZERO network traffic, DNS queries, or HTTP requests. This is its primary operational advantage: you can enumerate public exploit coverage for a target's software stack without touching the wire at all.

The danger is not in running searchsploit — it is in what you do NEXT. When you copy an exploit with '-m' and then compile or execute it, that action IS visible. Process creation events (Sysmon EID 1) will log gcc, python3, or msfconsole spawning from your shell, with the exploit filename in the command-line field. CrowdStrike Falcon's process tree analysis will flag a terminal session that reads a .c file and immediately invokes gcc followed by a network connection as a high-confidence suspicious chain.

If you run 'searchsploit -u' to update the database, it calls 'git pull' against the Exploit-DB GitHub repository. This generates outbound HTTPS traffic to github.com and api.github.com. On a monitored network, this is a concrete artifact: a DNS query for github.com followed by a TLS session to 140.82.x.x. Zeek/Bro will log this as conn.log and dns.log entries. Do not update on a client network — update at home before the engagement.

SentinelOne and Defender for Endpoint (MDE) both score command-line entropy and flag high-entropy arguments. Exploit filenames from Exploit-DB often contain version strings and CVE numbers (e.g. 'apache_2.4.49_rce.py'). If you copy an exploit with '-m' and then execute it, MDE's AMSI integration will scan the script content at runtime. Python and PowerShell exploits are especially exposed — AMSI hooks the script engine before execution. Obfuscate or stage payloads off-disk where possible.

When you view exploit source with '-x', searchsploit pipes the file through 'less' or 'cat'. On a shared or monitored jump box, shell history (HISTFILE) and audit logs (auditd, EID 4688 on Windows equivalents) will record the exact filename you examined. If the filename contains a CVE number, a defender reviewing logs post-incident can reconstruct exactly which vulnerability you were researching and when. Clear history or use 'HISTFILE=/dev/null searchsploit -x ...' on sensitive assessments.

A concrete defender artifact: when searchsploit is installed via apt or the Kali metapackage, the database lives at /usr/share/exploitdb/. Any EDR or HIDS with file-access monitoring (Falco on Linux, Sysmon for Linux with EID 11) will log reads from this path. On a compromised Linux host where you've dropped a copy of searchsploit or the exploitdb directory, Falco rules matching 'read from /usr/share/exploitdb' or 'open of known offensive tool path' will fire. Rename or relocate the database directory if operating on a sensitive host.

sample_outputs.scenario: Beginner: nmap found Apache 2.4.29 on a CTF box. Student wants to know what public exploits exist for that exact version before touching Metasploit.
sample_outputs.output:
