sample_outputs.explanation: Each row is one public exploit. The left column is the title — read it carefully because searchsploit matches on keywords, not exact version logic, so some results (like the PHP CGI entry) are for a different product that happens to share the word 'Apache'. The right column is the path RELATIVE to the exploitdb root (/usr/share/exploitdb/exploits/). The prefix before the slash tells you the target platform: 'linux/webapps' means a Linux web app exploit, 'multiple/dos' means it works cross-platform but causes a denial of service. For a beginner: your next three actions are (1) read the exploit with 'searchsploit -x multiple/dos/42745.py' to understand what it does before running anything, (2) check whether the target actually has the vulnerable module loaded (OPTIONS request to the server), (3) search for a Metasploit module with 'search type:exploit name:optionsbleed' inside msfconsole. The DoS entries are rarely useful on a CTF — focus on the 'webapps' and 'remote' category entries.

sample_outputs.scenario: Advanced: operator has nmap XML output from a full internal scan. Piping version strings into searchsploit to triage the entire attack surface for exploitable services before starting manual testing.
sample_outputs.command: searchsploit --nmap internal_scan.xml 2>/dev/null | grep -v 'No Results' | grep -E '(remote|webapps|local)' | sort -t'|' -k2
sample_outputs.explanation: The '--nmap' flag parses nmap XML directly, extracting service/version strings per host and running a searchsploit query for each — this compresses what would be 20 manual queries into one command. The output is triaged by host and port, giving you an immediate priority list. Reading this output as an operator: (1) vsftpd 2.3.4 with 17491.rb is the classic backdoor — port 6200 shell, trivially exploitable, almost certainly a honeypot or intentional CTF flag; verify with 'nc 10.10.20.11 6200' before touching Metasploit. (2) Ghostcat (CVE-2020-1938) on Tomcat 9.0.31 is a real AJP connector file read — use 48143.py to read WEB-INF/web.xml and extract credentials, then pivot to manager console RCE with 'msfconsole -x "use exploit/multi/handler"' or the Tomcat WAR upload path. (3) Samba on 10.10.20.19 — 42084.rb is EternalBlue-adjacent module load; confirm Samba version with 'crackmapexec smb 10.10.20.19' before firing. Next-step tools: crackmapexec for SMB validation, impacket-smbclient for share enumeration, and curl -v 'ajp://10.10.20.14:8009/' to confirm AJP is exposed before running Ghostcat.

legal_notes: Under 18 U.S.C. § 1030 (CFAA), possessing and searching searchsploit is legal — it is a research tool querying a public database. The legal line is crossed when you USE an exploit against a system you are not authorized to access. Copying an exploit with '-m' and executing it against a target outside your written scope of work is unauthorized access regardless of whether the exploit is publicly available. 'It was on Exploit-DB' is not a legal defense.

Your rules of engagement (RoE) must explicitly authorize exploitation attempts, not just scanning. Many client contracts authorize vulnerability identification (running searchsploit, running nuclei) but NOT exploitation. Before you move from 'searchsploit found a match' to 'I am running the exploit', confirm your RoE language covers active exploitation of that service on that host. If the RoE says 'no production systems', a Tomcat server serving live traffic is out of scope even if it is in the IP range.

In cloud environments (AWS, Azure, GCP), exploiting a vulnerable service on an EC2 instance or Azure VM that you are authorized to test may still violate the cloud provider's Acceptable Use Policy if the exploit generates traffic patterns that affect shared infrastructure (e.g., a DoS exploit on a shared host). AWS's penetration testing policy requires pre-authorization for certain attack types. Always check provider AUP alongside client RoE — they are separate authorization layers.
false_positives: SearchSploit matches on keywords in the title string, not on version logic. Searching 'apache 2.4.29' will return results for Apache OpenMeetings, Apache Struts, and Apache Tomcat because all contain the word 'apache'. Always read the full exploit title and verify the target product matches before spending time on an exploit. The path prefix (linux/webapps vs windows/remote) is a secondary filter, not a guarantee of relevance.

Version strings from nmap are often wrong or imprecise. nmap fingerprints banners and HTTP headers, which administrators frequently modify (ServerTokens Prod in Apache, for example). If nmap reports 'Apache 2.4.x' because the server suppressed the minor version, searchsploit will return results for every 2.4.x release. You may spend time on a CVE that was patched two minor versions ago. Always cross-reference with the application's own version disclosure (error pages, /server-status, readme files) before committing to an exploit path.

The '--nmap' XML parsing mode silently drops services where nmap did not capture a version string (STATE open but VERSION unknown). If nmap ran without '-sV' or the service fingerprint timed out, those ports produce no searchsploit output. An operator who relies solely on '--nmap' output will miss exploitable services on ports where version detection failed. Always audit the raw nmap XML for 'open' ports with empty version fields and follow up manually.

Exploit-DB contains many proof-of-concept (PoC) entries that demonstrate a vulnerability exists but are NOT weaponized — they crash the service, print a message, or require significant modification to produce a shell. The title will say 'Remote Code Execution' but the actual exploit code may be a 10-line Python script that sends a malformed packet and exits. Always read the exploit source with '-x' before assuming a 'Remote Code Execution' entry gives you a shell. Check the comments at the top of the file for 'PoC only' or 'requires modification' notes.

SearchSploit's local database is only as current as its last update ('searchsploit -u'). On a Kali installation that has not been updated in six months, the database may be missing exploits for CVEs disclosed in the last quarter. For recently disclosed vulnerabilities (within 90 days), always supplement with a direct Exploit-DB web search, GitHub search for the CVE number, and nuclei template checks — the offline database is a starting point, not a complete picture of the current exploit landscape.

binwalk.description: Firmware analysis and extraction tool. Identifies embedded file systems, compressed data, bootloaders, encryption, and executable code within binary firmware images. Essential for IoT security research and CTF firmware analysis challenges.
binwalk.teach_intro: Firmware from IoT devices, routers, and embedded systems often contains Linux file systems, configuration files, and hardcoded credentials compressed inside a single binary blob. Binwalk finds and extracts all of it — revealing the actual operating system, user accounts, and running services.

-e.label: Extract
-e.teach: The most useful flag — extracts everything binwalk finds. Creates a _firmware.bin.extracted/ directory with all recovered files. Look for /etc/passwd, config files, and binaries.

-E.label: Entropy Analysis
-E.desc: Calculate entropy to identify compressed/encrypted regions.
-E.teach: High entropy = compressed or encrypted data. Low entropy = plaintext/code. Entropy graph reveals the structure of the firmware at a glance.

-A.label: Opcode Scan
-A.desc: Scan for common executable opcodes to identify CPU architecture.
-A.teach: Unknown firmware? -A identifies the CPU architecture (MIPS, ARM, x86). Guides your disassembly setup.

-D.label: Extract by Type
-D.teach: Extract specific file types when you know what you're looking for. Pulls all JPEG images, all certificate files, or all ELF binaries.

opsec_notes: Beginner noise: Binwalk itself runs entirely offline against a local file — it generates NO network traffic, DNS queries, or ICMP packets. The operational noise is entirely on the analyst's own machine: disk I/O, CPU spikes during entropy analysis, and file writes to the extraction directory. If you're on a monitored analyst workstation, those file-system artifacts are visible.

Concrete defender artifact: When binwalk extracts firmware with the -e flag, it writes a directory named '<firmware_file>.extracted' containing decompressed file systems, kernel images, and raw binary blobs. On a monitored Linux host, auditd with 'watch' rules on /tmp or ~/Desktop will log these writes via AUDIT_SYSCALL records (type=SYSCALL, syscall=openat/mkdirat). The directory tree and inode creation timestamps are forensic artifacts if the analyst machine is later examined.

2025-2026 cutting edge — EDR process tree: CrowdStrike Falcon and SentinelOne both score process trees for anomalous child-process chains. If binwalk is invoked from a suspicious parent (e.g., a browser download handler, a Python script spawned by a phishing macro, or a reverse shell), the parent-child relationship will flag even though binwalk itself is a legitimate tool. Running binwalk from a clean, documented analyst terminal session avoids this scoring penalty.

2025-2026 cutting edge — command-line entropy and argument scoring: Modern EDR telemetry (Defender for Endpoint via MDE's Advanced Hunting, SentinelOne's STAR rules) scores command-line strings for entropy and rare argument combinations. Binwalk invocations with -D 'squashfs:squashfs' or custom regex extraction types can appear high-entropy to automated classifiers. On a managed corporate endpoint, document your tooling in the engagement record before running; unexpected high-entropy process invocations generate analyst queue items.

Extracted firmware file systems frequently contain hardcoded private keys, certificates, and password hashes. If you copy these off the analysis machine to a cloud storage service or personal device without authorization, you may be creating a secondary data-handling violation under the engagement's rules of engagement — even if the firmware analysis itself was authorized. Treat extracted credential material as in-scope sensitive data.

Entropy analysis (-E flag) writes a PNG plot to disk using matplotlib. On air-gapped or restricted analyst environments, this may fail silently or trigger DLP alerts if the PNG is auto-synced by a cloud backup agent (OneDrive, Dropbox, iCloud). Disable sync agents or redirect output to an isolated analysis directory before running entropy scans on sensitive firmware.

sample_outputs.explanation: The entropy graph (-E) is the critical artifact here: the spike to 0.997-0.998 at offset 0xE00000 indicates either strong encryption or a compressed+encrypted partition — distinguishable by block alignment. AES-CBC at 16-byte alignment with near-perfect entropy (0.998) strongly suggests an encrypted update partition or secure boot payload, not just compression. The extracted ELF at 0x1000040 is a 32-bit ARM binary — likely the main application daemon. Next actions: (a) Run 'file' and 'strings' against the extracted ELF, then load it into Ghidra or Binary Ninja for static analysis — look for hardcoded keys, API endpoints, and authentication logic. (b) Mount the SquashFS: 'sudo mount -t squashfs -o loop squashfs-root.squashfs /mnt/fw' and enumerate /etc/shadow, /etc/ssl/private/, and any .conf files. (c) For the encrypted partition, check the extracted ELF and SquashFS for key material — firmware update keys are frequently stored in /etc/ or compiled into the update daemon. Use 'binwalk -R \x00\x01\x02\x03' style raw searches or run 'entropy-analysis' tooling from the FACT framework for deeper automated analysis. (d) If the device is physically accessible, consider UART/JTAG extraction to dump the decrypted partition at runtime using a tool like OpenOCD.

legal_notes: US CFAA boundary: Binwalk analysis of firmware you did not obtain with authorization may constitute unauthorized access to a protected computer system under 18 U.S.C. § 1030 if the firmware was obtained by circumventing access controls (e.g., extracted from a device you do not own, downloaded from a vendor's restricted portal, or obtained via an unauthorized dump). Analyzing firmware you legally purchased and own, or firmware provided by a client under a signed statement of work, is the correct authorization baseline. 'I found it on the internet' is not authorization.

Engagement scope: Firmware analysis engagements must explicitly authorize the specific firmware images and device models in the rules of engagement. Extracting and analyzing firmware from a device model outside the agreed scope — even if physically present in the client's environment — is out-of-scope work. Credential material, private keys, and configuration data extracted from firmware must be handled per the engagement's data classification requirements and returned or destroyed per the agreed data-handling clause.

Modern IoT/OT consideration: Smart building controllers, ICS/SCADA devices, and medical IoT firmware frequently contain proprietary protocols and safety-critical logic. Extracting and reverse-engineering this firmware may implicate additional legal frameworks beyond CFAA: the DMCA § 1201 anti-circumvention provisions (if encryption is bypassed), export control regulations (EAR/ITAR if the device has defense applications), and FDA cybersecurity guidance for medical devices. Confirm with legal counsel before analyzing firmware from regulated device categories, even under an authorized engagement.
false_positives: Binwalk's signature database matches on magic bytes, which means it will report false positives when random binary data happens to match a known file signature. A common example: LZMA properties bytes (0x5D 0x00 0x00) appear frequently in compressed data streams, causing binwalk to report multiple 'LZMA compressed data' hits at offsets that are actually inside an already-identified SquashFS — these are not separate LZMA streams, they are internal SquashFS block headers.

Entropy analysis (-E) will report 'high entropy' for both encrypted data AND well-compressed data (e.g., lz4, xz, zstd). An entropy score of 0.95+ does NOT definitively mean encryption — it means high information density. Operators frequently misidentify compressed SquashFS partitions as 'encrypted' based on entropy alone. Confirm by checking block alignment (AES-CBC is always 16-byte aligned) and looking for IV prepended to the block.

Binwalk's -A opcode scan will report ARM/MIPS/x86 opcodes in data sections, string tables, and compressed regions that happen to contain byte sequences matching valid instructions. This produces long lists of 'ARM executable code' hits inside what is actually a JPEG or a compressed kernel — the opcode scanner has no context about whether the bytes are actually executed. Always validate ELF hits with 'file' and 'readelf' before investing reverse-engineering time.

The automatic extraction (-e) of nested archives can recurse into binwalk extracting binwalk's own extraction output, creating infinite loops or extremely deep directory trees when firmware contains self-referential or multiply-nested compression. Binwalk has a recursion depth limit but it can still fill a disk partition on large firmware images. Always run extraction on a partition with monitored free space, or use '--depth 2' to cap recursion.

Vendor firmware images sometimes contain intentional padding regions filled with 0xFF (flash erase state) or 0x00. Binwalk will report these as 'data' or attempt signature matches against them, generating noise entries. A long run of 0xFF bytes between partitions is not a file — it is flash padding. Filter these by checking that the reported offset contains a valid magic byte sequence before treating it as a real finding.

mitre_attack.name: Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Supply Chain

gdb.description: GNU Debugger enhanced with PEDA or GEF (GDB Enhanced Features) for exploit development. Analyzes program execution, finds memory corruption vulnerabilities, develops buffer overflow exploits, and reverse engineers binaries. Core tool for binary exploitation and CTF challenges.
gdb.teach_intro: GDB lets you run a program in slow motion — pause execution, inspect memory and registers, step through instructions, and understand exactly what happens during a crash. Buffer overflows, format string vulnerabilities, and heap exploits are all found and exploited using GDB. GEF adds color, pattern generation, and exploit-development commands.

pattern create.label: Cyclic Pattern (GEF)
pattern create.desc: Generate De Bruijn sequence to find buffer overflow offset.
pattern create.teach: Creates a unique 200-char pattern. Put in the input, crash the program, read the value in RIP/EIP, then 'pattern offset VALUE' tells you exactly how many bytes until the return address.

checksec.label: Security Checks
checksec.desc: Show enabled exploit mitigations: ASLR, NX, Stack Canary, PIE, RELRO.
checksec.teach: Before exploiting: know your defenses. NX means no shellcode in stack. PIE means addresses are randomized. No canary = easier stack overflow. No PIE = fixed addresses.

run.label: Run Program
run.desc: Execute the target binary inside GDB.
run.teach: Start the program. With a crash it shows the instruction pointer value — the foundation of understanding the overflow.

info registers.label: View Registers
info registers.desc: Show current register values (RIP, RSP, RBP, etc.)
info registers.teach: After a crash: what's in RIP? That's your target. RSP points to the stack. Understanding registers is the foundation of exploit development.

x/20wx $rsp.label: Examine Stack
x/20wx $rsp.desc: Examine 20 words from the stack pointer.
x/20wx $rsp.teach: Shows what's on the stack right now. Find your pattern, shellcode, or gadgets here. x/s $rsp for strings, x/i $rip for instructions.

b *address.label: Set Breakpoint
b *address.desc: Set breakpoint at specific memory address or function.
b *address.teach: Pause execution at interesting points. Before the vulnerable function to see input. After strcpy to see overflow. At the return to verify control.

opsec_notes: BEGINNER — GDB itself makes no network noise, but the binary you're debugging might. If you're running a network service under GDB to catch a crash, that service still opens sockets, sends packets, and writes logs. The debugger is invisible; the target process is not.

GDB attaches to a process via ptrace(). On Linux, ptrace attachment is logged by auditd when audit rules include '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S ptrace -k debug'. Defenders with auditd enabled will see your UID, the target PID, and the timestamp in /var/log/audit/audit.log as SYSCALL type=PTRACE records.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025-2026 — CrowdStrike Falcon and SentinelOne both instrument ptrace-family syscalls via eBPF probes on modern kernels (5.15+). Attaching GDB to a running production process — especially one owned by root or a service account — generates a high-confidence 'Debugger Attached to Sensitive Process' behavioral indicator. On hardened hosts, this may trigger an automatic kill or quarantine of the debugger process.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025-2026 — Microsoft Defender for Endpoint on Linux (MDE Linux agent, GA since 2022) uses fanotify and eBPF to monitor process injection patterns. Running GDB against a SUID binary or a process running as a different UID is flagged under the 'Suspicious Debugger Activity' detection family. The parent-child process tree (bash -> gdb -> target_suid_binary) is a high-entropy anomaly scored by MDE's command-line behavioral engine.

CONCRETE ARTIFACT — When GEF's 'pattern create' or 'pattern search' commands are used, they write a De Bruijn sequence to the process's stdin or memory. If the target binary logs its input (e.g., a web server logging POST bodies), the cyclic pattern string (e.g., 'aaaaaaaabaaaaaaacaaaa...') is a distinctive artifact in application logs and any network capture. Defenders with DLP or SIEM rules on high-entropy input strings will alert.

Running GDB with 'set follow-fork-mode child' against a forking daemon (Apache, nginx, sshd) causes the debugger to follow child processes. On systems with Sysmon for Linux (available since 2022), EID 9 (RawAccessRead) and EID 10 (ProcessAccess) equivalents are generated for each fork-follow. A sequence of rapid process-access events from a single GDB parent is a detectable pattern in any SIEM ingesting Sysmon Linux telemetry.

sample_outputs.scenario: Beginner CTF — 32-bit ELF binary 'vuln' crashes on long input. Operator uses GEF's cyclic pattern to find the exact offset to EIP for a classic stack buffer overflow.

sample_outputs.explanation: checksec confirms: NX blocks shellcode injection, but no PIE means binary gadgets are at fixed addresses — a stable ROP chain is viable. No stack canary means no cookie to bypass. The 'x/6gx $rsp' output shows 72 bytes of 'A' padding before RIP is overwritten with 'B's (0x4242...), confirming the offset. The 'pop rdi; ret' gadget at 0x4012a3 is the first link in a ret2plt chain: load the GOT address of puts into RDI, call puts@plt to leak the libc address of puts, compute libc base, then ret2system('/bin/sh'). Next steps: (1) use 'ropper' or 'ROPgadget' to find 'ret' for stack alignment before system(); (2) use 'x/gx 0x<puts_got>' to confirm the GOT entry address; (3) script the full chain in pwntools — pwnlib.elf.ELF + pwnlib.rop.ROP automates gadget chaining and libc offset resolution against a known libc version fingerprinted via the leak.

legal_notes: US CFAA (18 U.S.C. § 1030) — Attaching GDB to a process on a system you do not own or have explicit written authorization to test constitutes unauthorized access to a protected computer. This applies even if the binary is world-readable or the service is publicly exposed. 'I was just debugging it' is not a defense. Authorization must be documented before you attach a debugger to any production or third-party system.

Engagement scope — In a penetration test, your rules of engagement (RoE) must explicitly authorize binary exploitation and local privilege escalation, not just network scanning. Many RoE documents permit external recon but prohibit post-exploitation steps like SUID binary abuse or kernel exploit development. Confirm in writing that local exploit development against in-scope hosts is authorized before running GDB against SUID binaries or kernel modules.

Cloud and container consideration — In AWS, Azure, and GCP environments, attaching a debugger to a containerized process or a managed service binary (e.g., the AWS SSM agent, Azure Monitor agent) may violate the cloud provider's acceptable use policy independently of your customer authorization. On EKS/AKS/GKE nodes, ptrace across container boundaries (via --pid=host or privileged container escape) is a container breakout technique that almost certainly exceeds standard pentest scope unless explicitly listed in the RoE.
false_positives: ASLR makes addresses non-reproducible across runs. If you find a gadget address or stack offset in one GDB session and hardcode it into your exploit, it will fail outside GDB unless ASLR is disabled (echo 0 > /proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space) or the binary has no PIE. GDB disables ASLR by default via 'set disable-randomization on' — your exploit offsets inside GDB will NOT match offsets in a live non-GDB run unless you account for this.

GDB adds environment variables to the process environment (LINES, COLUMNS, and sometimes GDB-specific vars), which shifts the stack layout relative to a non-GDB execution. A buffer overflow offset that works perfectly inside GDB may be off by 16-64 bytes when run outside it. Use 'env -i' wrappers or pwntools' 'process()' with explicit env to control this.

GEF's 'pattern search' can return false offset matches when the cyclic pattern appears multiple times in memory — for example, if the binary copies the input into multiple buffers (stack and heap). The first match is not always the one controlling RIP/EIP. Always verify by running with a controlled 4/8-byte value at the suspected offset and confirming the register value.

Heap layout inside GDB differs from outside GDB because the debugger itself allocates memory in the same address space on some configurations, and because glibc's malloc uses different arenas depending on thread count and environment. Heap exploit offsets (tcache poisoning, fastbin dup) developed inside GDB frequently fail outside it — always test heap exploits with and without GDB attached.

On binaries compiled with '-fstack-protector-strong' (the default in most modern distros), GDB will show a SIGSEGV or __stack_chk_fail before you reach your RIP overwrite if your padding crosses the canary. The canary value changes each run (when ASLR is on). Operators sometimes mistake the canary-triggered crash for a wrong offset — use 'checksec' first and look for the canary value in registers/stack before assuming your offset calculation is wrong.

mitre_attack.name: Hijack Execution Flow: Dynamic Linker Hijacking

radare2.description: Open-source reverse engineering framework. Disassembles, debugs, analyzes, and patches binaries for any architecture. Supports x86/x64, ARM, MIPS, PowerPC, and more. The free alternative to IDA Pro and Ghidra for binary analysis.
radare2.teach_intro: Radare2 lets you take apart compiled programs and understand what they do without source code. Malware analysis, CTF binary challenges, vulnerability research — all done in r2. The command syntax is cryptic but incredibly powerful once learned. aa = analyze all, pdf = print disassembly of function.

-A.label: Analyze on Open
-A.desc: Run full analysis when opening binary.
-A.teach: Full auto-analysis finds functions, strings, cross-references. Equivalent to typing 'aaa' after opening. Always use -A for a clean start.

-d.label: Debug Mode
-d.teach: Debug mode lets you run the binary, set breakpoints, and inspect memory. Use for dynamic analysis.

aaa.label: Deep Analysis
aaa.desc: Run all analysis passes: functions, symbols, xrefs.
aaa.teach: aaa finds all functions, resolves imports, and builds the call graph. Takes longer than aa but gives complete picture.

pdf.label: Print Disassembly
pdf.desc: Print disassembly of current function: pdf @ main
pdf.teach: Shows assembly of a function. pdf @ sym.vulnerable_function shows the function you're targeting. Start with main, follow calls.

iz.label: List Strings
iz.desc: List all strings found in the binary.
iz.teach: Strings reveal hardcoded credentials, URLs, C2 domains, flag hints in CTFs. One of the first things to run on any binary.

afl.label: List Functions
afl.teach: After analysis, afl shows every function. grep for: main, vuln, login, check, admin, flag. Start your analysis from interesting function names.

opsec_notes: BEGINNER NOISE: Radare2 itself makes no network connections during static analysis — it is a local process. However, launching r2 against a binary creates a new process with the binary path as an argument. On any monitored endpoint, this is immediately visible in process telemetry: parent process (your shell), child process (radare2), and the full command line including the target binary path are logged by Sysmon EID 1 and EDR process-creation hooks.

ARTIFACT — FILE SYSTEM: r2 writes a project file and a history file to disk by default. The history file lands at ~/.config/radare2/history and logs every command you typed in the session. On a shared analyst box or a compromised host you are analyzing from, this file is a forensic artifact that reveals your entire analysis workflow. Wipe it or redirect with R2_HISTORY env var.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025-2026 — EDR PROCESS TREE: CrowdStrike Falcon and SentinelOne both score process trees for anomaly. If you launch r2 from a suspicious parent (e.g., a web shell, a macro-spawned cmd.exe, or a LOLBin), the child process inheriting that suspicious lineage will receive an elevated threat score even if r2 itself is benign. On a red-team engagement where you are analyzing a dropped payload on a live target, prefer analyzing the binary off-box (exfiltrate it first) rather than running r2 on the target host.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025-2026 — DEFENDER FOR ENDPOINT: Microsoft Defender for Endpoint (MDE) on Win11 24H2 with Tamper Protection enabled instruments kernel callbacks (PsSetCreateProcessNotifyRoutineEx) that fire on every process creation. r2 in debug mode (-d flag) calls ptrace (Linux) or DebugActiveProcess (Windows). On Windows, DebugActiveProcess is a high-fidelity MDE signal — it is the same API used by debuggers and injectors alike. MDE's behavioral engine correlates this with the parent process and command-line entropy. Running r2 -d against a suspicious binary on a monitored Windows host will almost certainly generate a MDE alert in the 'Suspicious debugger activity' category.

CONCRETE ARTIFACT — LINUX AUDIT: On hardened Linux hosts with auditd running, r2 debug mode triggers syscall audit rules for ptrace (syscall 101 on x86_64). The audit log at /var/log/audit/audit.log will contain SYSCALL records with syscall=101, the PID of r2, and the PID of the target process. If the host ships logs to a SIEM (Splunk, Elastic), this is a high-fidelity detection for unauthorized debugging activity.

EVASION CONSIDERATION: If you must run r2 on a monitored host for legitimate authorized analysis, prefer static analysis mode (no -d flag) and rename the r2 binary to something less conspicuous only if your rules of engagement explicitly permit binary renaming. Be aware that CrowdStrike Falcon uses file hash and import table analysis, not just process name, so renaming alone does not evade hash-based detections. The better operational choice is always to exfiltrate the sample and analyze it in an isolated VM.

sample_outputs.scenario: Beginner CTF — analyzing a simple Linux ELF binary challenge to find a hardcoded password or flag string. Operator opens the binary in r2 and lists all strings.
sample_outputs.output:
[x] Analyze all flags starting with sym. and entry0 (aa)
[x] Analyze function calls (aac)
[x] Analyze len bytes of instructions for references (aar)
[x] Finding and parsing C++ vtables (avrr)
[x] Type matching analysis for all functions (aaft)
[x] Propagate noreturn information (aanr)
[x] Use -AA or aaaa to perform additional experimental analysis
 -- r2 is brought to you by pancake and the community
[0x00401060]> iz
[Strings]
Nth Paddr      Vaddr      Len Size Section  Type  String
000 0x00002008 0x00402008  24  25 (.rodata) ascii Enter the secret password:
001 0x00002021 0x00402021   9  10 (.rodata) ascii CTF{r2_1s_
002 0x00002030 0x00402030  14  15 (.rodata) ascii Wrong password!
003 0x0000203f 0x0040203f  13  14 (.rodata) ascii Access granted!
sample_outputs.explanation: The iz command lists all printable strings embedded in the binary's data sections. Here we can see four strings: a prompt asking for a password, a partial flag string starting with 'CTF{r2_1s_', a failure message, and a success message. The partial flag at address 0x00402021 tells us the flag is stored in .rodata (read-only data), which means it is compiled in as a constant — the program is doing a direct string comparison. Next steps: (1) run 'afl' to list all functions and find the comparison function, (2) run 'pdf @sym.main' to disassemble main and see the strcmp or memcmp call, (3) look at the bytes immediately following 0x0040202b to recover the rest of the flag that iz may have split across entries. The beginner takeaway: strings in .rodata are never encrypted by default — always run iz first on a CTF binary before spending time on disassembly.

sample_outputs.scenario: Advanced malware analysis — operator has recovered a suspected implant (x86_64 ELF) from a compromised Linux server. Goal: identify C2 callback logic, persistence mechanism, and any anti-analysis tricks before detonating in a sandbox.
sample_outputs.output:
[x] Analyze all flags starting with sym. and entry0 (aa)
[x] Analyze function calls (aac)
[x] Analyze len bytes of instructions for references (aar)
[0x00401080]> afl
0x00401080    1     42 entry0
0x004010b0    4    112 sym.imp.pthread_create
0x004011a0    8    347 sym.beacon_loop
0x00401300    3     89 sym.resolve_c2
0x00401360    5    203 sym.xor_decrypt
0x00401420    2     61 sym.anti_debug_check
0x00401480   12    891 sym.main
[0x00401080]> pdf @sym.anti_debug_check
/ (fcn) sym.anti_debug_check 61
|   sym.anti_debug_check ();
|           0x00401420      55             push rbp
|           0x00401421      4889e5         mov rbp, rsp
|           0x00401424      bf01000000     mov edi, 1
|           0x00401429      e8b2feffff     call sym.imp.ptrace
|           0x0040142e      4885c0         test rax, rax
|           0x00401431      7c12           jl 0x401445
|           0x00401433      bf00000000     mov edi, 0
|           0x00401438      e873feffff     call sym.imp.exit
\           0x0040143d      5d             pop rbp
sample_outputs.explanation: The function list (afl) immediately reveals the implant's architecture: beacon_loop (likely the C2 callback thread), resolve_c2 (DNS or IP resolution for the C2 server), xor_decrypt (payload or config decryption), and critically anti_debug_check. Disassembling anti_debug_check shows a classic ptrace(PTRACE_TRACEME, ...) anti-debug trick — if the process is already being traced (i.e., you attached r2 with -d), ptrace returns -1 and the binary calls exit(). This is why we analyzed statically first. Next steps: (1) run 'pdf @sym.resolve_c2' to extract the C2 hostname or IP — look for string references or hardcoded byte arrays, (2) run 'pdf @sym.xor_decrypt' and identify the XOR key — often a single byte or short repeating sequence visible as an immediate value in the disassembly, (3) use r2's patching capability ('wa nop' at 0x00401429) to NOP out the ptrace call if you need to debug dynamically, then reopen with -d. Cross-reference findings with YARA rules for the identified XOR key and C2 pattern before submitting to a sandbox like Any.run or Cape. If the resolve_c2 function uses a DGA (domain generation algorithm), extract the seed and algorithm for threat intel reporting.

legal_notes: US CFAA BOUNDARY: Radare2 is a static and dynamic analysis tool. Running it against a binary you do not own or have explicit written authorization to analyze may violate 18 U.S.C. § 1030 if that binary contains proprietary code protected by license or if analyzing it requires circumventing access controls. Reverse engineering for interoperability has limited safe harbor under the DMCA (17 U.S.C. § 1201(f)), but this is narrow and jurisdiction-dependent. Always obtain written authorization before analyzing binaries belonging to a client, employer, or third party.

ENGAGEMENT SCOPE: On a penetration test, your rules of engagement (RoE) define what you are authorized to do with artifacts you recover. Recovering a binary from a compromised host and analyzing it with r2 is generally within scope for malware triage, but exfiltrating that binary to an off-site analysis machine may constitute data exfiltration that requires explicit RoE language permitting it. Confirm with your client before moving binaries off the target network — especially in regulated environments (HIPAA, PCI-DSS, FedRAMP) where the binary may contain sensitive data in its strings or embedded config.

MODERN CONSIDERATION — SOFTWARE SUPPLY CHAIN: If you are analyzing a binary as part of a software supply chain security assessment (e.g., auditing a vendor's compiled artifact for backdoors), be aware that some vendors embed license-enforcement telemetry that phones home when the binary is loaded or debugged. r2 in debug mode will trigger this telemetry. Conduct supply chain binary analysis in a fully air-gapped environment with outbound network blocked to prevent inadvertently alerting the vendor or triggering license invalidation.
false_positives: STRIPPED BINARIES — FUNCTION NAMES: When a binary is stripped (no symbol table), r2's 'afl' output replaces named functions with addresses like 'fcn.00401080'. The auto-analysis heuristics (aa/aaa) attempt to recover function boundaries by looking for function prologues (push rbp; mov rbp, rsp on x86_64), but they frequently split one logical function into multiple fcn.* entries or merge two adjacent functions into one. Always cross-check function boundaries manually with 'pdf' before drawing conclusions about code structure.

THUMB/ARM INTERWORKING: On ARM binaries that mix Thumb and ARM instruction sets, r2 can misidentify the instruction set mode for a given code region, producing completely wrong disassembly — instructions that look like garbage or nonsensical opcodes. If ARM disassembly looks wrong, check the current analysis mode with 'e asm.bits' and manually set it with 'e asm.bits=16' for Thumb or 'e asm.bits=32' for ARM. This is a common false positive when analyzing Android native libraries (.so files).

PACKED OR OBFUSCATED BINARIES: r2's static analysis (aa/aaa) operates on the binary as it exists on disk. If the binary is packed (UPX, custom packer) or uses self-modifying code, the disassembly of the packed stub will look like the entire program — the actual payload code is not visible until runtime unpacking occurs. Operators frequently mistake the unpacking stub's entropy-heavy data section for 'the malware' and report incorrect IOCs. Always check for packer signatures with 'rabin2 -I' before trusting static analysis results.

RELOCATION AND PIE BINARIES: Position-Independent Executables (PIE) have a load address of 0x0 in the binary on disk. r2 will display virtual addresses starting from 0x0 or a small base. When correlating r2 addresses with runtime addresses from a debugger, GDB, or a crash dump, you must add the actual runtime base address (visible in /proc/PID/maps on Linux or the module list in a debugger). Operators frequently report wrong offsets in vulnerability research because they forget to account for ASLR-shifted base addresses.

CROSS-ARCHITECTURE ANALYSIS: r2 supports many architectures, but auto-detection can fail on firmware blobs or raw binary dumps without ELF/PE/Mach-O headers. If you open a raw ARM firmware image without specifying '-a arm -b 32', r2 will default to x86 analysis and produce entirely wrong disassembly. Always explicitly set architecture and bit-width when analyzing raw or exotic binaries: 'r2 -a arm -b 32 firmware.bin'.

ghidra.description: NSA-developed open-source reverse engineering suite with decompiler. Converts compiled binaries back into readable C-like pseudocode. Supports x86, ARM, MIPS, PowerPC, and more. Free alternative to IDA Pro that rivals its decompilation quality.
ghidra.teach_intro: Ghidra's decompiler is the magic — it takes raw assembly and produces readable C code. Instead of reading assembly for hours, you get something close to the original source code. Malware analysis, vulnerability research, and CTF binary challenges become dramatically easier with a decompiler.

CodeBrowser.label: Code Browser
CodeBrowser.desc: Main GUI for code analysis, disassembly, and decompiler.
CodeBrowser.example: Open Ghidra → New Project → Import file → Open CodeBrowser → Analyze
CodeBrowser.teach: Always run auto-analysis (A key) after importing. Decompiler window (right side) shows C pseudocode. Navigate by clicking function names.

Decompiler.label: Decompiler View
Decompiler.desc: See C-like pseudocode for any function.
Decompiler.example: Click any function → Decompiler pane auto-updates
Decompiler.teach: The decompiler is Ghidra's killer feature. For CTF challenges: find the password check function, read the decompiled C, understand the logic without touching assembly.

Scripting.label: Ghidra Scripts
Scripting.desc: Automate analysis with Java or Python scripts.
Scripting.teach: Automate repetitive analysis: extract all strings, find crypto constants, batch rename variables, export function signatures. Python scripts run via Jython.

opsec_notes: Beginner baseline: Ghidra is a local analysis tool — it generates NO network traffic during normal use. The noise it makes is entirely on the analyst's machine: disk I/O from project creation, JVM heap activity, and file writes to ~/.ghidra/ and the project directory. No DNS queries, no outbound connections, no PCAP artifacts from the tool itself.

Artifact footprint on analyst host: Ghidra writes a project directory (*.rep folder + *.gpr file) containing the imported binary, analysis results, and any applied labels. If you're analyzing a sample on a shared or monitored workstation, these project files contain a copy of the malware binary and will be flagged by any AV/EDR scanning the filesystem. Analyze on an isolated VM with real-time protection disabled or exclusions set.

2025-2026 cutting-edge — EDR process tree anomaly: Launching ghidraRun (a JVM process) from a terminal spawned by a C2 beacon or unusual parent (e.g., winword.exe -> cmd.exe -> java.exe) will score high on CrowdStrike Falcon's process tree behavioral analytics and SentinelOne's STAR rules. If you're doing live malware triage on a compromised host, do NOT run Ghidra there — exfiltrate the binary and analyze offline. Parent-child chain java.exe under any Office or browser process is an immediate high-fidelity alert.

2025-2026 cutting-edge — Defender for Endpoint file-open telemetry: On Windows, MDE (Microsoft Defender for Endpoint) logs file-open events via ETW-TI (Threat Intelligence ETW channel) when a process reads a PE file that matches known malware hashes or exhibits suspicious entropy. If you open a packed sample in Ghidra on a MDE-enrolled host, the file-read event may trigger an automatic investigation even if real-time protection is off. Use an air-gapped or non-enrolled VM for malware RE work.

Concrete defender artifact — Sysmon EID 11 (FileCreate): When Ghidra imports a binary and writes its project database, Sysmon EID 11 fires for every file written under the project directory. A defender with a Sysmon rule watching for PE files written to non-standard paths (e.g., ~/Desktop/ghidra_projects/) will see the original binary copied into the .rep folder. This is a forensic artifact that proves the analyst touched that specific binary at a specific time.

Script execution risk: Ghidra's scripting engine (Java and Python via Jython) can execute arbitrary code on the analyst machine. Malicious Ghidra scripts (.java or .py files) distributed alongside 'cracked' tool bundles or poisoned CTF challenge packages have been observed in the wild. Never run Ghidra scripts from untrusted sources without reviewing them first — they run with full JVM permissions on your host.

sample_outputs.scenario: Beginner — CTF binary challenge. Participant has a stripped ELF binary 'crackme' and wants to find the hardcoded password check. Using Ghidra's CodeBrowser and Decompiler to locate the comparison logic.
sample_outputs.command:
ghidraRun &
# Then via GUI: File > Import File > crackme (ELF x86-64)
# Auto-analyze: Yes (default options)
# CodeBrowser: Functions panel > main > Decompiler pane
sample_outputs.explanation: The decompiler has reconstructed the original C logic from raw x86-64 assembly. Key observations: (1) local_48 is a 64-byte stack buffer — Ghidra named it by its stack offset. (2) The strcmp call compares user input against the literal string 's3cr3t_k3y_2025' — this is the hardcoded password. (3) The return value iVar1 == 0 means strings matched. Beginners should understand that Ghidra didn't magically find the password — it translated the assembly MOV/CMP/CALL instructions into readable C. Next steps: (1) Search for other string references via Window > Defined Strings to find all hardcoded values at once. (2) If the binary is packed or obfuscated, the decompiler output will look like garbage — that's a signal to run it through 'detect-it-easy' or 'die' first to identify the packer.

sample_outputs.scenario: Advanced — Malware analyst reverse-engineering a suspected implant (Windows x86-64 PE) recovered from an incident. Goal: identify C2 beacon logic, decode obfuscated strings, and extract IOCs. Using Ghidra headless analyzer plus custom script for XOR string decoding.
sample_outputs.command:
# Headless import and auto-analysis (no GUI, scriptable in CI pipelines)
ghidraRun ~/ghidra_10.4/support/analyzeHeadless \
  ~/projects implant_analysis \
  -import /evidence/implant_b64dec.exe \
  -postScript ExtractXorStrings.java 0x41 \
  -scriptPath ~/ghidra_scripts/ \
  -log /tmp/ghidra_analysis.log

# Script output appended to log:
sample_outputs.output:
[INFO]  ANALYZING: implant_b64dec.exe (PE 64-bit)
[INFO]  Auto-analysis complete. 1,847 functions identified.
[INFO]  Running post-script: ExtractXorStrings.java (key=0x41)
[SCRIPT] XOR-decoded string @ 0x140003a20 -> "api.telemetry-cdn[.]net"
[SCRIPT] XOR-decoded string @ 0x140003b44 -> "/v2/checkin"
[SCRIPT] XOR-decoded string @ 0x140003c10 -> "Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64)"
[SCRIPT] XOR-decoded string @ 0x140003d88 -> "POST"
[SCRIPT] XOR-decoded string @ 0x140003e02 -> "X-Session-Token"
[SCRIPT] Decoded 5 strings. Results written to: /tmp/xor_strings_0x41.txt
[INFO]  Function @ 0x140001230 flagged: calls VirtualAlloc + WriteProcessMemory + CreateRemoteThread
[INFO]  Function @ 0x14000a910 flagged: calls CryptEncrypt (advapi32)
[INFO]  Analysis complete. Project saved: ~/projects/implant_analysis.rep
sample_outputs.explanation: This headless run demonstrates production-grade malware triage without touching the GUI. Key findings: (1) The XOR-decoded strings reveal the C2 domain 'api.telemetry-cdn[.]net', URI '/v2/checkin', and a spoofed User-Agent — these are immediate network IOCs to push to your SIEM and DNS sinkholes. (2) The flagged function at 0x140001230 using VirtualAlloc + WriteProcessMemory + CreateRemoteThread is the classic process injection triad — this implant injects into a remote process. (3) CryptEncrypt usage suggests the beacon traffic is encrypted, meaning PCAP alone won't give you plaintext C2 comms. Next steps: (1) Open the project in CodeBrowser GUI and navigate to 0x140001230 — use 'Find References' to trace what process name is passed to OpenProcess. (2) Run the binary in a sandbox (ANY.RUN, Cape) with network capture to correlate the decoded domain against live beacon traffic. (3) Feed 'api.telemetry-cdn[.]net' into Shodan/Censys to pivot on the C2 infrastructure — look for shared TLS certificates or ASN clustering. (4) Use Ghidra's 'Version Tracking' feature if you suspect this is a variant of a known family — diff against a reference sample from MalwareBazaar.

legal_notes: US CFAA boundary: Ghidra itself is a passive analysis tool — running it generates no unauthorized access. However, the binary you import may be legally protected. Reverse engineering software to bypass copy protection, license checks, or DRM may violate the DMCA Section 1201 (anti-circumvention) even if you own a copy of the software. Security research exemptions exist (17 U.S.C. § 1201(j)) but are narrow — document your research purpose before analyzing commercial software. Analyzing malware samples recovered from your own authorized incident response engagement is clearly within scope.

Authorization scope — evidence handling: In a paid engagement or incident response context, the binary you're analyzing may contain sensitive client data (credentials, PII, proprietary code). Your rules of engagement should explicitly authorize reverse engineering of recovered artifacts. Storing a client's malware sample in a personal Ghidra project on a non-client-controlled system may violate data handling clauses in your SOW. Use client-provisioned or contractually authorized analysis infrastructure.

Modern cloud/supply chain consideration: If you are reverse engineering a container image layer, a Lambda deployment package, or a compiled cloud function binary recovered from a compromised environment, the artifact may contain embedded cloud credentials (AWS access keys, Azure SAS tokens, GCP service account JSON). Ghidra's string search and decompiler will surface these. Treat any recovered credentials as live until rotated — report them to the client immediately per your incident response retainer terms, and do not use them to access cloud resources without explicit written authorization.
false_positives: Decompiler type inference errors on optimized binaries: When a compiler applies aggressive optimizations (O2/O3, LTO), Ghidra's decompiler frequently misidentifies variable types and sizes. A uint32_t loop counter may be decompiled as a char*, making pointer arithmetic look like string manipulation. Always cross-reference decompiler output against the raw disassembly listing — if the C code looks semantically wrong, the assembly is ground truth.

Stripped binaries produce generic function names: Without debug symbols, Ghidra names functions FUN_140001230, DAT_140003a20, etc. The decompiler may correctly reconstruct the logic but assign it to the wrong semantic category. Analysts frequently misidentify a crypto routine as 'custom obfuscation' because the function name gives no hint — always check if the byte patterns match known algorithms using Ghidra's 'Find > For Scalars' or the CAPA plugin before concluding something is novel.

Indirect calls and vtables break decompiler call graphs: C++ binaries with virtual dispatch, or malware using function pointer tables for API resolution (a common evasion technique), will show calls like (**(code **)(param_1 + 0x28))() in the decompiler. Ghidra cannot statically resolve these without manual annotation. The call graph will appear to have dead ends, and automated script-based IOC extraction will miss dynamically resolved API calls entirely — this is a significant false negative risk in malware analysis.

Packed or encrypted sections decompile as garbage: If a binary is packed (UPX, custom packer) or has encrypted code sections, Ghidra will attempt to disassemble the unpacking stub correctly but will produce nonsensical decompiler output for the encrypted payload region. Analysts sometimes mistake the XOR/ROR unpacking loop for the actual malware logic. Always check section entropy (high entropy > 7.0 in .text or .data sections signals packing) before trusting decompiler output for those regions.

ARM Thumb/Thumb-2 interworking misidentification: On ARM binaries (common in mobile malware and IoT firmware), Ghidra occasionally misidentifies Thumb-mode code as ARM-mode at interworking boundaries, producing completely wrong disassembly and decompiler output for affected functions. Symptom: decompiler shows implausible operations like reading from address 0x1 or 0x3. Fix by manually setting the instruction set mode at the affected address via right-click > Set Instruction Set.

setoolkit.description: Automated framework for social engineering attacks. Creates phishing sites (credential harvesting), spear-phishing emails, infectious media payloads, and more. Integrates with Metasploit. The standard tool for demonstrating human-factor attacks to clients.
setoolkit.teach_intro: The most secure network can be bypassed by targeting the humans who use it. SET automates phishing campaigns: clone any website, send convincing emails, harvest entered credentials, and deliver Meterpreter payloads via malicious links. Used to demonstrate to clients why security awareness training matters.

1.label: Social Engineering Attacks
1.desc: Main menu option 1 — all SE attack vectors.
1.teach: The social engineering menu. Credential harvesting, tabnabbing, web jacking, multi-attack web. Most engagements start here.

2.label: Website Cloning
2.desc: Clone any website for credential harvesting.
2.teach: SET downloads the target site and hosts a perfect copy on your machine. Victims enter credentials, you capture them. Used with convincing phishing emails.

Spear.label: Spear Phishing
Spear.desc: Create targeted phishing emails with malicious attachments.
Spear.teach: Spear phishing is targeted — crafted for a specific person using OSINT. Much higher success rate than mass phishing. Can attach Meterpreter payload documents.

gophish.description: Open-source phishing simulation platform with a professional web dashboard. Create and manage phishing campaigns, track email opens, link clicks, credential submissions, and attachments. The standard for authorized phishing assessments.
gophish.teach_intro: GoPhish makes phishing campaigns measurable. You set up an email template, a landing page (can be a cloned site), a target list, and a sending profile — then track who opened, who clicked, who entered credentials. Perfect for demonstrating risk to clients with concrete data.

Dashboard.label: Web Dashboard
Dashboard.desc: Access at https://localhost:3333 with default admin:gophish
Dashboard.teach: The dashboard shows campaign results in real time. Who opened the email, who clicked the link, who submitted credentials. Data-driven social engineering assessment.

Campaign.label: Campaign Setup
Campaign.desc: Create sending profile → email template → landing page → target list → campaign.
Campaign.teach: Each component is separate. Sending profile = SMTP server. Email template = the phishing email. Landing page = the fake site. Target groups = who gets phished.

opsec_notes: BEGINNER NOISE: Every GoPhish campaign generates SMTP traffic with a distinct sending profile. Your 'From' header, X-Mailer, and DKIM/SPF alignment are logged by every major email gateway (Proofpoint, Mimecast, Microsoft Defender for Office 365). If SPF/DKIM/DMARC are not properly configured on your sending domain, your emails will be quarantined or flagged before they ever reach the target inbox — and the attempt is still logged.

CONCRETE ARTIFACT: GoPhish's default landing page injects a tracking pixel and appends a unique RId parameter to every link (e.g., ?rid=aB3xKq). This query parameter pattern is fingerprinted by Proofpoint TAP and Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Safe Links sandboxes. Defenders inspecting URL logs will see repeated hits to your phishing domain with the same RId prefix structure. Rotate your parameter names and obfuscate the GoPhish source before deployment.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025-2026: Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Plan 2 now performs detonation-based analysis of landing pages in a sandboxed browser. If your cloned credential-harvesting page contains the default GoPhish JavaScript event listeners or the unmodified form POST handler pointing to /post, the detonation engine will classify it as a phishing kit and retroactively pull delivered emails from user inboxes via ZAP (Zero-hour Auto Purge). Strip all GoPhish-default JS artifacts and proxy credential submissions through a legitimate-looking relay.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025-2026: CrowdStrike Falcon's email telemetry integration (via Microsoft Graph API or O365 connector) correlates GoPhish campaign timing with endpoint process trees. When a user clicks a link and a browser spawns a child process (e.g., a macro-enabled Office doc download triggers winword.exe -> cmd.exe), Falcon scores the parent-child anomaly and can attribute it back to the originating email thread. If your campaign delivers payloads, assume the click event and the process spawn are correlated in the SIEM within seconds.

INFRASTRUCTURE OPSEC: GoPhish's default TLS certificate is self-signed and its HTTPS listener fingerprint (port 3333, specific TLS handshake parameters) is indexed by Shodan and Censys. Exposed GoPhish admin panels have been publicly catalogued. Always bind the admin dashboard to 127.0.0.1 or a VPN-only interface, change the default port, and place a reverse proxy (Caddy or nginx) in front of the phishing listener with a valid Let's Encrypt certificate on a domain aged at least 30 days.

SENDING DOMAIN ARTIFACT: Email headers written by GoPhish include a default X-Mailer value and a Message-ID format that is documented in public threat intelligence feeds. Proofpoint and Mimecast rule sets specifically match the GoPhish Message-ID entropy pattern. Before any authorized engagement, patch the GoPhish source (models/email.go) to randomize Message-ID generation and remove or spoof the X-Mailer header to match the client's legitimate mail platform (e.g., Microsoft Exchange Online).
