tshark.description: Command-line version of Wireshark. Same dissectors, same display filter syntax, but scriptable. Essential for headless captures, scripted analysis, and live IDS
tshark.teach_intro: Wireshark is for staring at packets; tshark is for grepping them. Capture for an hour, then 'tshark -r capture.pcap -Y http.request.method==POST -T fields -e http.host -e http.request.uri' to find every POST request in the capture. Useful in engagements where the on-disk pcap is too large to open in Wireshark, or when you're scripting credential extraction from cleartext protocols (HTTP-AUTH, FTP, telnet, SMTP). Pairs with capinfos for capture metadata and editcap for splitting/filtering captures.
opsec_notes: Beginner noise: tshark in capture mode (-i eth0) puts the NIC into promiscuous mode. On managed switches with port security or 802.1X, promiscuous mode changes are visible to NAC solutions and can trigger quarantine events. On a shared segment, the NIC driver logs a mode change that Sysmon EID 11 (file create) may catch if tshark writes a temp ring buffer to disk.

The tshark process itself is a concrete artifact: on Linux, 'ps aux | grep tshark' or 'ss -p' will show the process holding a raw socket (SOCK_RAW). Any EDR with process enumeration telemetry (CrowdStrike Falcon's process tree, SentinelOne's storyline) will flag a non-root user spawning a process with CAP_NET_RAW or running as root with a command line containing '-i' and a live interface name.

On Windows, tshark relies on Npcap (or legacy WinPcap). Npcap driver load events appear in the Windows System event log (EID 7045 — 'A new service was installed') if Npcap is not already present. Defender for Endpoint's kernel sensor tracks driver loads via ETW-TI; a first-time Npcap install on an endpoint during an engagement is a high-fidelity IOC. Pre-stage Npcap silently or use an already-instrumented jump box.

When using tshark for post-capture analysis (-r file.pcap) rather than live capture, no raw socket is opened and no NIC mode change occurs. This is the stealthy path: exfiltrate the pcap from a compromised host and analyze offline. The exfiltration itself is the risk — a 2 GB pcap transferred over SMB or HTTP will trip DLP rules and NetFlow anomaly detectors watching for large outbound transfers.

Command-line entropy scoring: modern EDR products (Defender for Endpoint's MDAV behavioral engine, CrowdStrike's Falcon Prevent ML) score process command lines for entropy. A tshark invocation like 'tshark -r cap.pcap -Y "http.request.method==POST" -T fields -e http.host -e http.request.uri -e http.file_data' is low-entropy and readable, but piping output through base64 or xargs in the same shell session raises the parent-child command entropy score. Keep post-processing in a separate shell invocation.

Concrete defender artifact — pcap files on disk: tshark ring-buffer captures (-b filesize:102400 -w /tmp/.cap) write files that any EDR with file-write telemetry will log. On Linux, Sysmon for Linux (EID 11) captures file creation events. Choose write paths that blend with existing application log directories, and clean up ring buffer files before leaving the host. Forensic tools like Volatility and bulk_extractor can recover partial pcap data from memory even after file deletion.

sample_outputs.scenario: Beginner: operator has a pcap from a lab network and wants to see all HTTP POST requests — hunting for cleartext credentials submitted via a login form
sample_outputs.command: tshark -r lab_capture.pcap -Y "http.request.method == POST" -T fields -e frame.number -e ip.src -e ip.dst -e http.host -e http.request.uri -e http.file_data
sample_outputs.output:
frame.number  ip.src          ip.dst          http.host              http.request.uri        http.file_data
47            192.168.1.105   192.168.1.10    intranet.corp.local    /login.php              username=jsmith&password=Summer2024!
112           192.168.1.107   192.168.1.10    intranet.corp.local    /login.php              username=admin&password=P@ssw0rd123
198           192.168.1.105   192.168.1.10    intranet.corp.local    /upload.php             filename=report.docx
231           192.168.1.112   192.168.1.10    intranet.corp.local    /login.php              username=bwilson&password=Welcome1
309           192.168.1.105   192.168.1.10    intranet.corp.local    /api/v1/auth            user=svc_backup&pass=Backup$2024
sample_outputs.explanation: Each row is one HTTP POST. The http.file_data field contains the raw POST body — here it's URL-encoded form data, which is how most legacy web login forms transmit credentials. Frame 47 gives you jsmith:Summer2024!, frame 112 gives admin:P@ssw0rd123, and frame 309 gives a service account credential. Why does this work? HTTP (port 80) is unencrypted; the entire request body travels in plaintext on the wire. HTTPS (port 443) would encrypt this and you'd see only TLS handshake records. Next steps: (1) take these credentials to crackmapexec or evil-winrm to test against the domain, (2) check if any of these users appear in BloodHound as high-value targets, (3) run 'tshark -r lab_capture.pcap -Y ftp -T fields -e ftp.request.command -e ftp.request.arg' to check for FTP credentials in the same capture.

sample_outputs.scenario: Advanced: operator has a 4-hour ring-buffer capture from a compromised Linux pivot box sitting on a flat internal segment. Hunting for Kerberos AS-REQ traffic to identify domain users authenticating, and correlating with NTLM SSP negotiate packets to fingerprint legacy auth — building a target list for AS-REP roasting and NTLM relay
sample_outputs.command: tshark -r internal_pivot_4h.pcap -Y "kerberos.msg_type == 10 or ntlmssp.identifier" -T fields -e frame.time_relative -e ip.src -e ip.dst -e kerberos.CNameString -e kerberos.realm -e ntlmssp.auth.username -e ntlmssp.auth.domain 2>/dev/null | sort -u | tee /tmp/auth_targets.txt
sample_outputs.explanation: Kerberos AS-REQ (msg_type 10) reveals the CNameString — the plaintext username requesting a TGT — and the realm. NTLMSSP negotiate/authenticate frames expose username and domain for legacy NTLM auth. From this output: (1) svc_mssql and svc_backup are service accounts — high-value Kerberoasting targets; run 'GetUserSPNs.py CORP.LOCAL/jsmith:Summer2024! -dc-ip 192.168.10.5 -request' to pull their TGS hashes. (2) bwilson appears only in Kerberos, not NTLM — likely a modern workstation; jsmith and svc_backup appear in both, suggesting they're hitting legacy SMB shares or old applications that fall back to NTLM. (3) The krbtgt entry at frame ~2187s is anomalous — a workstation requesting a TGT for krbtgt is a red flag for a golden ticket validation attempt or a misconfigured service; investigate 192.168.10.200. Follow-up chain: feed auth_targets.txt into crackmapexec for password spray validation, run Responder on the segment to capture NTLM hashes from the NTLM-authenticating hosts, and use ntlmrelayx.py targeting hosts that don't appear in the Kerberos list (likely SMB signing disabled).

legal_notes: US CFAA (18 U.S.C. § 2511 / Wiretap Act intersection): capturing live network traffic with tshark on a segment you do not own or administer — even if you have shell access to a host on that segment — may constitute unlawful interception under the Wiretap Act, which is separate from CFAA authorization. A signed rules-of-engagement document authorizing 'network traffic capture' on the specific subnet is required. 'I had admin on a box in that VLAN' is not sufficient authorization.

Scope boundary — pcap retention and data handling: tshark captures everything on the wire, including traffic from out-of-scope hosts that happen to share the segment. Your engagement SOW must explicitly address how captured data containing third-party credentials, PII, or out-of-scope host communications is handled, stored, and destroyed. Many enterprise clients require pcap files to be encrypted at rest (e.g., written to a LUKS volume) and destroyed within 24 hours of engagement close.

Cloud and container consideration: in AWS VPC environments, you cannot passively sniff traffic between EC2 instances — the hypervisor enforces isolation. Capturing traffic in cloud environments requires either a VPC Traffic Mirroring session (which requires explicit AWS account authorization and leaves CloudTrail logs under event 'CreateTrafficMirrorSession') or capturing only traffic on the local instance's own interfaces. Attempting to enable promiscuous mode on an ENI without Traffic Mirroring will silently fail — you will only see your own instance's traffic, which can create a false sense of completeness in your capture.
false_positives: TLS 1.3 with ESNI/ECH (Encrypted Client Hello) will make http.host fields empty or show the CDN's shared hostname rather than the actual destination. A capture showing all HTTPS traffic to 'cloudflare-ech.com' or a blank host field does not mean the traffic is unidentifiable — it means the SNI is encrypted. Do not conclude 'no interesting HTTPS destinations' from a modern capture without also correlating IP destinations against passive DNS or Shodan.

TCP segment reassembly: tshark's default behavior reassembles TCP streams before applying display filters. If you disable reassembly ('tshark -o tcp.desegment_tcp_streams:FALSE') to speed up processing on large pcaps, http.file_data fields will be empty or truncated for POST bodies that span multiple TCP segments. You'll see the request but miss the credential. Always verify reassembly is enabled when hunting for application-layer data.

VLAN tagging and 802.1Q: if the capture interface is a trunk port, packets will have 802.1Q headers. tshark will decode these correctly, but display filters like 'ip.src == 192.168.10.0/24' may miss packets if the VLAN tag shifts the IP header offset in a way that confuses a filter written without 'vlan' context. Use 'tshark -Y "vlan and ip.src == 192.168.10.0/24"' or strip VLAN tags with editcap before analysis.

Loopback and localhost traffic: tshark on '-i lo' (Linux loopback) captures inter-process traffic on the local host, including Redis, PostgreSQL, and internal API calls. This is extremely useful for finding cleartext internal service credentials, but the output volume is enormous and most of it is noise. Filtering on '-Y tcp.port == 6379' (Redis) or '-Y tcp.port == 5432' (Postgres) is necessary — but be aware that Redis AUTH commands and Postgres md5 password hashes appear in the stream and are easy to miss without explicit field extraction.

Capture filter vs. display filter confusion: tshark supports both BPF capture filters (-f 'tcp port 80') applied at capture time and Wireshark display filters (-Y 'http.request') applied at read time. A BPF capture filter of 'tcp port 80' will drop UDP DNS traffic entirely from the capture — you won't be able to go back and add DNS analysis later. Operators frequently set overly narrow capture filters during live captures and then discover they needed the traffic they filtered out. When in doubt, capture everything and filter at analysis time, accepting the larger pcap size.

mitre_attack.name: Gather Victim Network Information: IP Addresses

ettercap.description: Network sniffer/interceptor for MITM attacks on LANs. ARP poisoning, ICMP redirects, DHCP spoofing, DNS spoofing, plus SSL/TLS interception with installed CA. O
ettercap.teach_intro: Ettercap teaches MITM fundamentals because it makes the attack surface visible: you see the ARP tables update, the victims' traffic flow through your machine, and the filter modules let you watch credentials, cookies, and session tokens stream past in real-time. Modern engagements increasingly prefer bettercap (Go, scriptable, better UI) for the same job. Ettercap's plugin/filter language is still uniquely powerful for old-school protocol manipulation: write an etterfilter rule that swaps a binary in transit during an HTTP download.
opsec_notes: Beginner noise: ARP poisoning floods the local broadcast domain with gratuitous ARP replies. Every host on the segment updates its ARP cache, and any network monitoring tool (Wireshark, ntopng, even a managed switch's MAC table) will see your MAC address claiming to own two IPs simultaneously — the gateway and the victim. This is the loudest possible MITM signal on a LAN.

Concrete artifact — Sysmon EID 3 (Network Connection) will log ettercap's outbound connections when it spawns plugin subprocesses or contacts DNS. More critically, on the victim host, Windows Event ID 4 (ARP cache change) is visible via 'arp -a' delta monitoring; enterprise tools like Darktrace and Vectra AI baseline ARP behavior per VLAN and alert on cache churn within seconds of poisoning starting.

Modern EDR detection: CrowdStrike Falcon's network containment and SentinelOne's Ranger module both perform passive ARP monitoring on enrolled endpoints. When Falcon's sensor sees a host's default gateway MAC change mid-session without a DHCP renewal, it scores the event as a lateral movement indicator and can auto-contain the affected endpoint. Ettercap's ARP storm is a near-certain trigger on any segment with >30% EDR coverage.

SSL/TLS interception with ettercap's bundled CA only works if the victim trusts your CA — which requires a prior foothold (GPO push, MDM profile, or social engineering). In 2025, HSTS preloading, certificate transparency logs, and browser-enforced pinning (Chrome, Firefox) mean ettercap's sslstrip plugin fails silently against modern HTTPS targets. The operator sees decrypted traffic; the victim sees a certificate warning or a broken connection. Do not assume SSL stripping works without pre-validating the target's TLS posture.

Advanced evasion: To reduce ARP storm volume, use ettercap's '-q' (quiet) flag combined with a targeted '/M arp:remote/' specification naming only the two hosts you want to intercept rather than poisoning the entire subnet. This reduces ARP reply rate from broadcast-storm levels to two targeted streams, cutting Vectra/Darktrace anomaly scores significantly — but does NOT eliminate detection by switch-level port security or dynamic ARP inspection (DAI), which is enabled by default on Cisco Catalyst 9000 series and Aruba CX switches in 2025 enterprise deployments.

Packet capture artifact: ettercap writes a unified sniff log to '/tmp/etter.log' by default (or the path specified with '-w'). On a shared pentest box or a compromised host used as a pivot, this file contains plaintext credentials and session tokens. Defenders performing incident response will find this file during triage. Operators must explicitly redirect output and wipe the file post-engagement; failure to do so constitutes a data handling violation under most rules of engagement.

Note: SMBv1 downgrade via etterfilter is increasingly blocked by Windows Defender's SMB hardening (enabled by default on Server 2022 and Win11 22H2+) — verify SMBv1 status with 'Get-SmbServerConfiguration | Select EnableSMB1Protocol' before relying on this path.

legal_notes: US CFAA (18 U.S.C. § 1030): ARP poisoning and traffic interception constitute 'unauthorized access' and 'intentional interception of electronic communications' under both CFAA and the Wiretap Act (18 U.S.C. § 2511) when performed without explicit written authorization. The fact that ettercap is a 'passive' sniffer once poisoning is established does not reduce liability — the ARP manipulation itself is an active unauthorized modification of network state on systems you do not own. Penalties include felony charges with up to 10 years imprisonment for first offenses involving financial data or credentials.

Rules of engagement scope: ARP poisoning is a broadcast-domain attack — it affects ALL hosts on the VLAN segment, not just your named targets. Even with '/M arp:remote /victim// /gateway//', gratuitous ARP replies are visible to every host on the segment and can disrupt non-target hosts (VoIP phones, printers, IoT devices) that update their caches. Your engagement authorization must explicitly cover the entire VLAN, not just the named target IPs. Confirm with the client whether 'collateral disruption' to non-scoped hosts is acceptable before running any MITM attack.

Cloud and hybrid AD consideration: In environments using Azure AD-joined or Hybrid-joined Windows 11 endpoints (common in 2025 enterprise), primary authentication flows use cloud-brokered tokens (PRT — Primary Refresh Token) over HTTPS to login.microsoftonline.com, not NTLM over SMB. Ettercap will not capture these flows. Additionally, Microsoft Entra ID Conditional Access policies can detect impossible travel or token replay from an unexpected IP, invalidating captured tokens within minutes. Ettercap-based MITM on modern hybrid environments requires a separate strategy for cloud token theft (e.g., Evilginx2 for OAuth flows) and is not a substitute for understanding the target's identity architecture before the engagement.
false_positives: Dynamic ARP Inspection (DAI) on managed switches silently drops ettercap's poisoned ARP replies without notifying the attacker. The tool reports 'ARP poisoning victims: GROUP 1 / GROUP 2' and appears to be running successfully, but zero traffic is redirected. Operators frequently spend 20+ minutes troubleshooting 'why am I not seeing credentials' before realizing DAI is enabled. Verify by checking whether your own ARP cache on the attacker machine shows the victim's IP mapped to your MAC — if not, DAI is blocking you.

Ettercap's SSL dissector reports 'SSL dissection needs a valid redir_command_on script' and silently skips HTTPS sessions if iptables/nftables redirect rules are not configured. The operator sees HTTP credentials but assumes HTTPS traffic is also being decrypted — it is not. The tool gives no per-session warning that an HTTPS flow was passed through unmodified. Always verify SSL interception is working by testing against a known HTTP vs HTTPS endpoint before trusting that you have full visibility.

The dns_spoof plugin matches on the DNS query name string using a simple substring or exact match from 'etter.dns'. If the victim's application uses DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) — enabled by default in Firefox since 2020 and configurable in Chrome/Edge — ettercap's dns_spoof plugin receives no DNS queries to intercept and silently fails. The operator sees no spoofed DNS entries in output and may incorrectly conclude the victim is not browsing to the target domain.

On switched networks with port security (MAC address limiting), ettercap's ARP poisoning causes the victim's switch port to see two MACs claiming the same IP. Some switch configurations will trigger a port-security violation and shut down the attacker's port rather than the victim's — effectively kicking the attacker off the network. This looks identical to a successful poisoning from ettercap's perspective until traffic stops flowing.

Ettercap's protocol dissectors for modern application protocols (Kerberos over non-standard ports, LDAPS, RDP NLA) are outdated and will silently pass traffic without extracting credentials, even when the dissector appears to be loaded. The '42 protocol dissectors' count in startup output includes dissectors for protocols like telnet and FTP that are rarely seen in 2025 enterprise environments. Operators who see the dissector list and assume comprehensive coverage will miss credential material in protocols ettercap cannot parse.

sslscan.description: TLS/SSL configuration scanner. Identifies supported ciphers, protocol versions (SSLv2/3, TLS 1.0/1.1/1.2/1.3), heartbleed, BEAST, POODLE, certificate weakness,
sslscan.teach_intro: Run sslscan against every TLS-bearing target on day 1 of an engagement. The output tells you which crypto attacks might still work (TLS 1.0 means BEAST might be on the table, SSLv3 means POODLE) and which certs are expired, self-signed, or use weak signatures (MD5, SHA1). Modern engagements rarely find pre-2014 protocols outside of forgotten IoT appliances, but compliance teams pay for the audit anyway. testssl.sh is the spiritual successor — more thorough but slower.
opsec_notes: BEGINNER — sslscan initiates a full TLS handshake with the target on every cipher it tests. This generates a burst of TCP connections to the target port (typically 443) in rapid succession, each with a different ClientHello cipher suite. Any web server access log will record these as repeated TLS negotiation attempts from your source IP within seconds. Check /var/log/nginx/access.log or /var/log/apache2/access.log on the target — your IP will appear dozens of times in a tight timestamp window.

sslscan's cipher enumeration pattern is a well-known signature: it sends ClientHello packets with single cipher suites in sequence rather than the browser-standard list of 20-30 suites in one handshake. Network-layer IDS rules (Snort SID 2024897, Suricata TLS anomaly rulesets) and WAFs like Cloudflare and Akamai flag this pattern. If the target is behind a WAF, expect your source IP to be blocked or rate-limited within the first 10-15 probes.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025 — CrowdStrike Falcon's network telemetry (via its kernel sensor) tracks process-to-socket associations. If sslscan is launched from a compromised host during post-exploitation, Falcon will correlate the unusual process (a non-browser binary) making rapid sequential TLS connections to external or internal hosts and score it as anomalous network behavior. The parent-child process tree (e.g., cmd.exe → sslscan.exe or bash → sslscan) is a high-fidelity indicator. Prefer running TLS enumeration from a dedicated recon host outside the target environment, not from a foothold.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025 — Microsoft Defender for Endpoint's advanced hunting (DeviceNetworkEvents table) will surface sslscan activity if run on or from a Windows host: the tool's command-line arguments are captured via ETW process-creation events (EID 4688 with command-line auditing enabled, or Sysmon EID 1). The string 'sslscan' in InitiatingProcessCommandLine is a trivial hunt query. Rename the binary and strip or modify the User-Agent string in the TLS ClientHello if operating from a monitored host — though binary renaming alone does not change the cipher-enumeration packet pattern.

CONCRETE ARTIFACT — On the target's TLS terminator (nginx, HAProxy, F5 BIG-IP), each sslscan cipher probe appears as a separate SSL_do_handshake() call in debug-level TLS logs. On F5 BIG-IP, the /var/log/ltm log will show repeated 'SSL Handshake failed' or 'no shared cipher' entries from your source IP as sslscan tests unsupported suites. This is a reliable defender artifact even when the target returns no HTTP response.

If the engagement scope includes cloud-fronted targets (AWS CloudFront, Azure Front Door, GCP Cloud Armor), sslscan will enumerate the CDN's TLS configuration, NOT the origin server's. The CDN terminates TLS and presents its own certificate and cipher policy. Results will reflect the CDN's hardened posture (TLS 1.2/1.3 only, strong ciphers) and will not reveal origin misconfigurations. Always resolve the origin IP through certificate transparency logs or DNS history and scan it directly if authorized.

sample_outputs.explanation: This output is a critical finding on a modern engagement — this device is running firmware from approximately 2011 and has never been updated. Prioritize these findings: (1) Heartbleed (CVE-2014-0160) is confirmed across all TLS versions — use metasploit auxiliary/scanner/ssl/openssl_heartbleed or the standalone heartbleed PoC to extract up to 64KB of server memory per request, potentially recovering session tokens, private key material, or credentials in plaintext. (2) SSLv3 enabled without SCSV support means POODLE (CVE-2014-3566) is viable — a MITM attacker can force SSLv3 fallback and decrypt session cookies. (3) EXPORT-grade ciphers (EXP-RC4-MD5, 40-bit DES) mean FREAK (CVE-2015-0204) and DROWN attacks may apply. (4) MD5 certificate signature with a 512-bit RSA key is trivially forgeable — the private key can be factored with commodity compute. (5) CRIME is possible since TLS compression is enabled. Next tools: run testssl.sh --full 10.10.40.12:8443 for a comprehensive structured report suitable for the finding writeup; use arp-spoof + sslstrip2 or bettercap's tls.proxy module to position for POODLE/BEAST exploitation on the OT segment; check whether this gateway has a web management interface on port 80 or 443 and run nuclei -t ssl/ against it for templated vuln confirmation. Document the firmware version string from the certificate CN and cross-reference against the vendor's advisory database for known RCE chains.

legal_notes: US CFAA (18 U.S.C. § 1030) boundary: initiating TLS handshakes against a host you are not authorized to test constitutes 'unauthorized access to a protected computer' even though sslscan does not exploit vulnerabilities — it actively connects to and negotiates with the target service. The fact that TLS is a public-facing protocol does not grant implicit authorization to enumerate it. Ensure written authorization explicitly covers the target IP and port before running sslscan.

Rules of engagement scope: sslscan will follow the IP you give it, not the hostname. If your authorized scope is 'app.corp.com' and that hostname resolves to a shared CDN IP (e.g., a Cloudflare or Akamai anycast address), sslscan will enumerate the CDN's TLS stack, which is NOT your client's infrastructure and is explicitly out of scope. Always verify the resolved IP is within the authorized CIDR range before executing. Conversely, if scope is defined by IP range, confirm that the TLS certificate's CN/SAN matches the expected target — you may be scanning the wrong virtual host on a shared IP.

Cloud and modern infrastructure consideration: in AWS environments, scanning an Elastic Load Balancer (ALB/NLB) endpoint enumerates AWS's TLS policy, not the application's. AWS ALB TLS policies are controlled at the AWS account level and findings against them may not be remediable by the application team. If the engagement includes cloud infrastructure review, confirm whether the client has authorized AWS-level configuration review separately from application-level testing, and note that AWS's Acceptable Use Policy prohibits scanning AWS infrastructure without prior approval even with customer authorization.
false_positives: TLS termination offloading: if the target sits behind a reverse proxy (nginx, HAProxy, AWS ALB, F5 BIG-IP) that terminates TLS, sslscan reports the proxy's cipher and protocol configuration, not the backend application server's. A backend running an ancient OpenSSL version may be completely hidden behind a hardened proxy. Operators frequently report 'TLS 1.3 only, strong ciphers' on a target whose backend is running OpenSSL 1.0.1 — the finding is accurate for the proxy but misleading about actual risk. Always check whether you can reach the backend directly on an internal port.

Firewall-enforced TLS version filtering: some stateful firewalls and DPI appliances (Palo Alto NGFW, Fortinet FortiGate) will silently drop SSLv2/SSLv3 ClientHello packets at the network layer before they reach the server. sslscan will report these protocols as 'disabled' on the server when in fact the server may support them — the firewall is blocking the probe. This produces a false negative for legacy protocol support. Verify by scanning from a network segment that bypasses the firewall (e.g., from inside the DMZ if authorized).

Self-signed certificate expiry false urgency: sslscan flags expired certificates as a finding, but on internal OT/IoT networks, self-signed certificates are frequently used with manually managed validity periods that are intentionally long or have been allowed to expire without operational impact because the devices don't perform certificate validation anyway. An expired self-signed cert on an internal SCADA HMI is a real finding, but the actual risk is the lack of mutual TLS validation, not the expiry date itself. Don't let the expiry finding overshadow the more critical 'no certificate validation enforced' issue.

SNI-dependent cipher presentation: some servers present different cipher suites depending on whether a Server Name Indication (SNI) value is sent in the ClientHello. sslscan by default uses the target hostname as the SNI value, but if you specify an IP address directly, it may send no SNI or an IP-format SNI, causing the server to respond with a default vhost configuration that differs from the named vhost's TLS policy. A target may appear to support weak ciphers when scanned by IP but present only strong ciphers when the correct SNI hostname is used. Always use --sni-name or specify the FQDN when the target is a named virtual host.

OpenSSL version dependency for legacy protocol testing: sslscan's ability to test SSLv2 and SSLv3 depends on whether the version of OpenSSL it was compiled against has those protocols enabled. Most modern Linux distributions ship OpenSSL 3.x with SSLv2/SSLv3 compiled out entirely. If sslscan reports 'SSLv2 disabled' and 'SSLv3 disabled' on a target you have reason to believe is ancient, verify whether your sslscan binary was built with legacy protocol support (sslscan --version will show the OpenSSL version). A false 'disabled' result here is a tooling limitation, not a server configuration finding.

snmpwalk.description: Walks an SNMP MIB tree from a starting OID. Foundational tool for enumerating network devices that expose SNMP with default community strings (public, private).
snmpwalk.teach_intro: snmpwalk -v2c -c public 10.10.10.5 dumps the entire MIB tree of a target. On unhardened devices that's interface names, ARP tables, routing tables, even SSH/Telnet credentials (Cisco IOS sometimes stores them in MIBs reachable with the 'private' community). Try public/private/cisco/community first; for SNMPv3, use snmpwalk -v3 with auth. Often paired with onesixtyone for fast community-string discovery across a subnet.
opsec_notes: BEGINNER NOISE: Every snmpwalk session sends a stream of UDP packets to port 161 on the target. A single full MIB walk against one host can generate hundreds to thousands of UDP datagrams in seconds — this is visible in any NetFlow/IPFIX collector, firewall log, or IDS with SNMP anomaly rules. Defenders watching for 'UDP 161 burst from a single source' will see you immediately.

CONCRETE ARTIFACT: On Cisco IOS and many managed switches, SNMP GET/GETNEXT requests are logged to syslog (facility local7 by default) when 'snmp-server enable traps' or 'logging buffered' is configured. The log line includes the source IP of the querying host, the community string attempted, and the OID requested — e.g., '%SNMP-3-AUTHFAIL: Authentication failure for SNMP request from host 10.10.14.22'. This is written to the device's local buffer AND forwarded to any configured syslog server.

COMMUNITY STRING ATTEMPTS: Failed community string guesses (wrong community = SNMP AUTHFAIL) are logged separately from successful walks. If you try 'public', 'private', 'cisco', and 'community' sequentially against a Cisco device, you generate four distinct AUTHFAIL syslog entries per host before you even get data. On a subnet sweep with onesixtyone, this becomes thousands of AUTHFAIL events — a trivial SIEM correlation rule fires immediately.

2025-2026 CUTTING EDGE — NDR/NTA DETECTION: Modern Network Detection and Response platforms (Darktrace, ExtraHop Reveal(x), Cisco Secure NDR) fingerprint SNMP walk behavior by analyzing the sequential OID traversal pattern in UDP payloads. A legitimate NMS polls specific OIDs on a schedule; snmpwalk traverses the entire tree in lexicographic order at wire speed. This behavioral signature — full sequential OID traversal from a non-NMS source IP — is a high-confidence detection in any mature NDR deployment as of 2025. Evasion requires throttling requests (--sleep equivalent via scripted loops) and spoofing source IP to match the known NMS.

2025-2026 CUTTING EDGE — CLOUD/HYBRID ENVIRONMENTS: In AWS environments, EC2 instances running network management software may have SNMP exposed on internal VPC subnets. AWS VPC Flow Logs capture UDP 161 traffic and feed into GuardDuty. As of 2024-2025, GuardDuty's 'UnauthorizedAccess:EC2/MaliciousIPCaller' and network anomaly findings can trigger on SNMP sweep patterns originating from non-baseline IPs. If the target org uses AWS Network Firewall with managed threat intelligence rules, SNMP enumeration from a pentest box may be blocked and alerted before a single packet reaches the target.

SNMPv3 TRAP SOURCE EXPOSURE: When you authenticate with SNMPv3 (-v3 -u username -l authPriv -a SHA -A passphrase -x AES -X privpass), the authentication handshake itself reveals your source IP and the username you're probing. SNMPv3 engines log failed authentication attempts with the username tried — this is more attributable than v2c community string failures because usernames are often tied to real accounts in the org's NMS configuration.

(5) The IP address table reveals a SECOND subnet (192.168.100.1) not visible from your current position — this is network discovery gold. sample_outputs.explanation: OID 1.3.6.1.2.1.4.22 is the ipNetToMediaTable — the ARP table. This output gives you a live map of every IP-to-MAC binding the switch has seen on VLAN 4 (interface index 4). Key observations: (1) MAC prefixes starting with 00:50:56 are VMware vNICs — you're looking at a virtualized environment, likely vSphere. The prefix 00:0c:29 is also VMware (workstation/fusion). This tells you the hypervisor layer is present and these are VMs, not physical hosts. (2) The static entry at .105 (00:00:5e:00:01:01) is a VRRP virtual MAC — there's a first-hop redundancy protocol running, meaning this network has HA gateway pairs worth mapping. (3) You now have a live host list (10.10.20.10, .15, .22, .30, .50, .100) that bypasses the need for active scanning — these hosts are confirmed live because the switch has active ARP entries for them. Next steps: (a) Feed this IP list directly into crackmapexec or nmap -sV --open for service fingerprinting without a noisy ping sweep. (b) Run 'snmpwalk -v3 [same auth] 10.10.20.1 1.3.6.1.4.1.9.9.23.1.2.1' to pull Cisco CDP neighbor table — this reveals adjacent switches, routers, and their platform strings, building your full network topology without touching those devices directly. (c) Cross-reference MAC OUIs against your target's known hardware vendors using macvendors.com or a local OUI database to identify device types (printers, cameras, servers) before scanning. (d) If the SNMPv3 credentials work on adjacent devices discovered via CDP, you can chain this walk across the entire infrastructure.

legal_notes: CFAA BOUNDARY: Sending SNMP queries to a device you are not authorized to administer constitutes unauthorized access to a computer under 18 U.S.C. § 1030(a)(2) regardless of whether the community string is 'public' and the device is misconfigured. 'Public' does not mean publicly authorized — the string is a credential, and using it without authorization is legally equivalent to using a found password. Ensure your rules of engagement explicitly authorize SNMP enumeration against the target IP range before running any snmpwalk command.

SCOPE AND ROE: SNMP walks against network infrastructure (routers, switches, firewalls) are often treated as a separate authorization category from host scanning in enterprise engagements. A client may authorize you to scan servers in 10.10.0.0/16 but explicitly exclude network infrastructure. Confirm with your client whether 'network devices' are in scope — the ARP table and routing table data you extract can reveal subnets and hosts far outside your authorized IP range, and acting on that data may constitute scope creep even if the initial query was authorized.

CLOUD/MODERN CONSIDERATION: In cloud environments (AWS, Azure, GCP), SNMP is rarely exposed on the public internet but may be accessible on internal VPC/VNet subnets from a compromised instance. Querying SNMP on cloud-managed network appliances (AWS Transit Gateway, Azure Virtual WAN hubs) may violate the cloud provider's acceptable use policy in addition to your client's ROE, and may trigger provider-side incident response independent of the client's security team. Clarify whether cloud-managed networking infrastructure is explicitly in scope.
false_positives: FIREWALL RATE-LIMITING TRUNCATES WALKS: Many enterprise firewalls and ACLs rate-limit SNMP responses or silently drop packets after a threshold. snmpwalk will appear to complete successfully but return only a partial MIB tree — you may see interfaces 1-4 but miss interfaces 5-12. There is no error message; the walk simply stops at the last successfully received OID. Always compare the interface count from SNMP against what nmap sees on the same host to detect truncation.

SNMP PROXY AND AGGREGATOR RESPONSES: In environments using SNMP proxy agents or network management aggregators (SolarWinds, PRTG acting as SNMP proxy), snmpwalk may return data from the NMS database rather than the live device. The sysUpTime, interface counters, and ARP tables you receive may be cached and hours or days stale. A device that appears 'up' with active ARP entries may have been decommissioned — verify with active scanning before acting on SNMP-derived host lists.

COMMUNITY STRING 'PUBLIC' ON HONEYPOTS: Security teams increasingly deploy SNMP honeypots that respond to 'public' community string queries with plausible-looking but fabricated MIB data — fake hostnames, fake IP ranges, fake routing tables designed to waste attacker time or trigger alerts when acted upon. If the MIB data looks unusually clean or the device has no corresponding entry in your passive recon (Shodan, certificate transparency, DNS), treat it as potentially deceptive.

SNMPv3 ENGINE ID MISMATCH: When targeting SNMPv3 devices, if the engineID of the target doesn't match what snmpwalk expects during the discovery handshake, the tool may silently fail or return 'No Such Object' for all OIDs even with correct credentials. This is commonly misread as 'SNMP not running' or 'wrong community string' when the actual issue is an engineID negotiation failure. Use 'snmpget -v3 -u user -l noAuthNoPriv -e <engineID> ...' to manually specify the engine ID if auto-discovery fails.

VIRTUAL IP AND CLUSTER RESPONSES: On clustered devices (HSRP/VRRP active-standby pairs, F5 BIG-IP clusters), snmpwalk against the virtual IP may return the active node's MIB data, but the same query repeated seconds later may return the standby node's data if a failover occurred. Interface indexes, ARP tables, and routing entries may differ between nodes — what appears to be a 'changed network topology' between two walks may simply be a failover event, not actual network changes.

volatility.description: Original Python 2 memory forensics framework. Many older incident-response runbooks still call vol.py directly. Volatility 3 (volatility3 in the registry) is th
volatility.teach_intro: Memory forensics is the answer to 'attacker used in-memory payloads, no disk artifacts'. Volatility parses a RAM image (acquired via WinPMem, LiME, AVML, or VMware snapshot) and reconstructs process lists, network connections, registry hives, loaded DLLs, and injected code. Key plugins: pslist, psscan (for hidden processes), netscan, malfind (heuristics for unpacked code), mimikatz (extract credentials from lsass). Volatility 2 vs 3: v2 has wider profile coverage for old Windows versions; v3 is faster and Python 3.
opsec_notes: Volatility is a READ-ONLY offline analysis tool — it parses a memory image file on the analyst's workstation and generates zero network traffic, zero disk writes to the target, and zero process activity on the compromised host. The only 'noise' is the acquisition step (WinPMem, LiME, AVML) that preceded it. If you're running vol.py, the opsec risk window is already closed.

The acquisition artifact IS the opsec exposure: WinPMem (winpmem_mini_x64.exe) dropped to disk and executed as SYSTEM generates Sysmon EID 1 (process create) with a high-entropy executable name, EID 11 (file create) for the .raw output, and a kernel driver load event (EID 6) — CrowdStrike Falcon and Defender for Endpoint both alert on unsigned kernel driver loads in 2025 hardened environments. Acquire via a pre-signed, allowlisted binary or use a hardware DMA device (PCILeech/FPGA) to avoid this entirely.

On live-response engagements, running vol.py against a mounted image on a Windows analyst box can trigger Defender for Endpoint's behavioral engine if Python spawns child processes that touch LSASS-pattern strings in memory (e.g., malfind output piped through grep for 'lsass'). Run analysis in an isolated Linux VM or air-gapped workstation to avoid telemetry leaking back to the client's tenant.

Volatility 2's profile system requires matching the exact OS build. If you load the wrong profile (e.g., Win7SP1x64 against a Win7SP0x64 image), plugin output silently produces garbage — KDBG offsets misalign and pslist walks corrupted pointers. Defenders reviewing your IR report will catch fabricated process lists. Always verify the profile with imageinfo or kdbgscan before running any plugin.

When exporting malfind regions to disk for further analysis (--dump-dir), the extracted PE files will be written to the analyst's filesystem. Modern EDR on the analyst box (SentinelOne, Falcon) may detonate these extracted payloads in its local sandbox and generate alerts — quarantine the dump directory or disable real-time protection on the isolated analysis VM before dumping.

ETW-TI (Event Tracing for Windows Threat Intelligence) telemetry is captured at acquisition time in the memory image itself — a skilled analyst can recover ETW buffers from the image using the 'raw' plugin chain and reconstruct what the EDR saw in the moments before acquisition. This means a memory image is also a record of the attacker's evasion attempts, not just their artifacts.

sample_outputs.scenario: Beginner IR scenario: analyst has a Windows 10 memory image suspected of running a RAT. Running pslist to enumerate all processes and spot obvious anomalies.
sample_outputs.explanation: The critical anomaly is on the second-to-last line: 'svch0st.exe' (PID 5544) — note the zero replacing the letter 'o', a classic masquerading technique. Its parent is explorer.exe (PID 2344, a user desktop process), whereas legitimate svchost.exe processes are always children of services.exe (PID 612). It also spawned cmd.exe (PID 6012) one second later, indicating interactive command execution. Next actions: (1) run 'malfind -p 5544' to check for injected shellcode in its memory regions, (2) run 'dlllist -p 5544' to enumerate loaded DLLs for suspicious or unsigned modules, (3) run 'netscan' to check if PID 5544 has active network connections to a C2 address.

sample_outputs.explanation: Two injected regions found inside MsMpEng.exe (Windows Defender's own engine process — a high-value hollowing target because it's typically excluded from EDR scanning). Address 0x1d0000 shows an MZ header (4d 5a) in a PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE private VAD region — this is a reflectively loaded PE, consistent with Cobalt Strike's reflective DLL injection. Address 0x2f0000 shows the classic x64 Cobalt Strike shellcode stub (fc 48 83 e4 f0 e8 c8 — the 'and rsp, 0xfffffff0' alignment prologue). Extracted PE files land in ./extracted/ for static analysis. Next actions: (1) run 'python2 vol.py ... netscan' and grep for PID 1488 to find the C2 beacon IP and port, (2) carve the extracted PE through '1768.py' (Didier Stevens's Cobalt Strike config extractor) to recover the malleable C2 profile, sleep jitter, and watermark, (3) run 'handles -p 1488 -t mutant' to find mutex artifacts that fingerprint the specific CS team server, (4) pivot to Volatility 3 (vol3) for the same image if you need ISF-based symbol resolution on the 2019 kernel structures — v2 profiles for Server 2019 can misparse some pool tags.

legal_notes: Under 18 U.S.C. § 1030 (CFAA), acquiring a memory image from a system you do not own or have explicit written authorization to image is a federal offense regardless of whether you later analyze it with a read-only tool like Volatility. The acquisition step — not the analysis step — is the legal exposure point. Ensure your rules of engagement explicitly authorize memory acquisition, not just 'forensic analysis'.

Scope boundary: if your engagement authorizes forensic analysis of 'the compromised workstation,' that authorization does not extend to imaging domain controllers, file servers, or other hosts that appear in the memory image's network connections. Each host requires its own authorization. Memory images of DCs contain domain-wide credential material (Kerberos tickets, cached hashes) — treat them under the same data-handling controls as a full AD dump.

Cloud and virtualization consideration: in AWS, Azure, and GCP environments, taking a memory snapshot of a VM (via hypervisor snapshot, VM suspend, or cloud-provider forensic APIs) may be governed by the cloud provider's terms of service AND your client's data residency and privacy obligations (GDPR, HIPAA, SOC2 scope). Confirm with legal counsel before snapshotting VMs that process regulated data — the memory image will contain plaintext PII, credentials, and encryption keys in RAM.
false_positives: malfind flags every PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE private VAD region as suspicious, but .NET CLR, JIT compilers (V8 in Chrome, SpiderMonkey in Firefox), and legitimate packed installers all create RWX regions at runtime. On a typical Windows 10 workstation, malfind may return 50-200 'hits' of which fewer than 5 are malicious. Always correlate with the process name, parent, and whether the region contains an MZ header or recognizable shellcode stub before concluding injection.

pslist walks the EPROCESS doubly-linked list — a rootkit that unlinks its process from the list (DKOM, Direct Kernel Object Manipulation) will be invisible to pslist but visible to psscan (which scans pool tags). Conversely, psscan will show terminated processes whose pool memory hasn't been overwritten yet, producing 'ghost' entries with no Exit time that look like hidden malware but are just stale allocations. Cross-reference both plugins before concluding a process is hidden.

netscan on Windows 8+ images frequently shows connections in CLOSE_WAIT or TIME_WAIT state that were already terminated before acquisition — these are not active C2 channels. The timestamp on the connection state is the last-seen time, not the acquisition time. A connection showing a foreign address does not mean that address is currently reachable or that the process is still running.

Wrong profile selection silently corrupts all output. If imageinfo suggests multiple candidate profiles (e.g., Win10x64_14393 and Win10x64_17134), running pslist with the wrong one will produce a list that looks plausible — correct process names, reasonable PIDs — but with subtly wrong PPID relationships and timestamps because the EPROCESS offsets differ between builds. Always validate with kdbgscan and cross-check at least one known-good process (System, PID 4) before trusting any plugin output.

On memory images acquired from VMs under heavy I/O load (database servers, busy DCs), the image may contain torn writes — a process structure partially updated mid-acquisition. This causes malfind or dlllist to throw Python exceptions mid-run or silently skip entries. The absence of output for a PID is not proof the process had no injected code; it may be an artifact of acquisition timing. Re-acquire with a quiesced snapshot when possible.

rizin.description: Fork of radare2 focused on stability and clearer UX. Same core capabilities (disassembly, decompilation via Ghidra plugin, ROP gadget search, binary patching) w
rizin.teach_intro: Rizin's commands mostly match radare2 (aaa for analyze, pdf for disassembly, V for visual mode) but the project has aggressively de-cruftified the CLI. Cutter is the GUI for Rizin (sister project). The pf (print format) and Ghidra decompiler plugin make Rizin viable as a primary RE workstation for malware analysis or CTF binary challenges.
opsec_notes: Rizin is a static analysis tool that runs entirely on the analyst's local machine — it makes NO network connections, generates NO packets, and leaves NO network-layer artifacts. A defender watching the wire will see nothing from rizin itself. The risk surface is entirely on the analyst's host.

When rizin loads a binary for analysis (e.g., a malware sample), the binary is NOT executed — it is mapped into memory as data. However, some plugins (notably the Ghidra decompiler plugin, rz-ghidra) spawn a child process (rizin -> rz-ghidra JVM subprocess). On an analyst workstation monitored by CrowdStrike Falcon or SentinelOne, this parent-child process tree (rizin spawning a JVM) can look anomalous if the analyst machine is in a monitored corporate environment. Ensure your malware analysis VM is isolated and its process telemetry is understood by your SOC before running.

Concrete artifact a defender sees on the analyst host: rizin writes analysis cache files to ~/.cache/rizin/ (Linux/macOS) or %APPDATA%\rizin\ (Windows). If you are analyzing a malware sample on a shared or monitored workstation, these cache files contain disassembled function names, strings, and metadata extracted from the malware binary. Incident responders triaging the analyst machine will find these artifacts. Use an isolated, air-gapped VM for sensitive sample analysis.

In 2025-2026 EDR environments (Defender for Endpoint, SentinelOne Singularity), opening a known-malicious binary with ANY tool — including rizin — can trigger a file-open telemetry event via ETW (Event Tracing for Windows) kernel callbacks registered since Win11 22H2. The binary hash is logged even if it is never executed. If your analysis VM is domain-joined or has MDE onboarded, the SOC will see the hash of the sample you opened. Analyze in a purpose-built, non-domain, non-EDR-enrolled VM.

If you use rizin's binary patching capabilities (w, wx, wv commands) to modify a live malware sample on disk, the resulting write operation will be flagged by any EDR with file-integrity monitoring. Sysmon EID 11 (FileCreate) and EID 23 (FileDelete) will fire on the modified binary. Patch in a copy, never the original, and do so only in your isolated analysis environment.

The rz-ghidra plugin (Ghidra decompiler integrated into rizin) requires a working Java runtime. On Windows analysis hosts, java.exe or javaw.exe spawned as a child of rizin.exe is a high-entropy parent-child relationship that CrowdStrike Falcon's process tree anomaly detection may score as suspicious. Pre-approve this relationship in your Falcon policy exclusions if you run a persistent malware analysis lab.

sample_outputs.explanation: The `aaa` command runs rizin's full auto-analysis pass — it identifies functions, cross-references, and symbols. The `iz` command (print strings in data sections) dumps all ASCII/UTF-8 strings found in the binary's data and rodata sections. Here, the flag `CTF{h4rdc0d3d_s3cr3t_f0und}` is sitting in plaintext in `.rodata` — the binary never encrypted or obfuscated it. The `Paddr` column is the physical file offset; `Vaddr` is the virtual address where the string lives when the binary is loaded into memory. Next steps: (1) use `pdf @ main` to disassemble the main function and see how the string is used in a comparison, (2) use `axt 0x00402021` to find all cross-references TO the flag string to understand the control flow that guards it.

sample_outputs.scenario: Advanced — malware analyst reverse-engineering a suspected Windows implant (PE32+). Hunting for C2 beacon logic: identifying suspicious function calls, decoding an obfuscated string, and locating a ROP gadget chain for shellcode staging.

sample_outputs.explanation: This output tells a story: `fcn.00401a30` is the beacon initialization function. Key observations: (1) `lea rcx, [0x00402020]` loads a pointer to an obfuscated blob, then immediately calls `fcn.00401800` — that is almost certainly an XOR or ROL decode stub. The decoded result at `0x00402026` is the C2 hostname. (2) `ws2_32_ptr` is an indirect call through a stored pointer to `WSAStartup` — this is API hashing / dynamic import resolution, a classic anti-static-analysis technique to avoid having `ws2_32.dll` in the IAT. (3) Port `0x1bb` = decimal 443 — HTTPS C2 over standard port. (4) Two `pop rdi; ret` gadgets at `0x00401234` and `0x00404ab2` are usable for ROP chain construction if the implant stages shellcode. Next steps: (1) Use `pz @ 0x00402020` to dump the raw obfuscated blob, then script the XOR decode in Python or CyberChef to recover the plaintext C2 domain. (2) Use `axt fcn.00401800` to find every call site of the decode stub — each one is another obfuscated string. (3) Feed the recovered C2 domain into passive DNS (SecurityTrails, RiskIQ) to pivot on infrastructure. (4) Cross-reference the ROP gadgets against known shellcode stagers (donut, sRDI) to fingerprint the staging mechanism.

legal_notes: Under 18 U.S.C. § 1030 (CFAA), rizin itself is a passive analysis tool and its use is not restricted — however, the binary you analyze may be subject to legal constraints. Analyzing a binary you do not own or have no license to reverse-engineer may violate the DMCA (17 U.S.C. § 1201) anti-circumvention provisions, particularly for commercial software with technical protection measures. Malware samples obtained from threat intel feeds are generally analyzed under implicit research exemptions, but confirm with your organization's legal counsel before distributing analysis artifacts.

If you are using rizin as part of a penetration test engagement — for example, reverse-engineering a client's custom application to find vulnerabilities — your rules of engagement must explicitly authorize binary analysis of that application. 'Network penetration testing' authorization does not automatically cover reverse-engineering proprietary client software. Get written authorization that specifically names binary analysis and decompilation as in-scope activities.

In cloud and containerized environments, binaries you pull from a running container (via `docker cp` or K8s `kubectl cp`) for offline rizin analysis may contain secrets, credentials, or proprietary code belonging to the client. Your data-handling obligations under the engagement contract govern how you store, transmit, and destroy these artifacts. Do not upload client binaries to online sandboxes (VirusTotal, Any.run) without explicit written authorization — this constitutes unauthorized disclosure of potentially proprietary or sensitive data.
false_positives: rizin's auto-analysis (`aaa`) uses heuristics to identify function boundaries. In heavily optimized binaries (compiled with Clang -O3 or MSVC /O2 with LTCG), tail-call optimization and function inlining cause rizin to misidentify function boundaries, splitting one logical function into several `fcn.XXXXXXXX` stubs or merging two functions into one. Always cross-reference with the call graph (`agC`) and do not trust function size counts from `afl` as authoritative.

The `iz` / `izz` string extraction commands will surface every sequence of printable bytes above a minimum length threshold (default 4 bytes). In binaries with large binary data blobs, lookup tables, or embedded resources (icons, certificates, compressed payloads), rizin will report hundreds of false-positive 'strings' that are actually structured binary data that happens to contain printable byte sequences. Filter aggressively and cross-reference string addresses against actual data section boundaries.

rizin's Ghidra decompiler plugin (rz-ghidra) produces C pseudocode that is a best-effort reconstruction — it is NOT the original source. For functions with complex stack manipulation, indirect jumps, or hand-written assembly (common in shellcode stagers and packers), the decompiler output will be wrong or incomplete. Treat decompiler output as a hint, not ground truth. Always verify against the raw disassembly (`pdf`) before drawing conclusions about control flow.

When analyzing packed or self-modifying binaries (UPX, custom packers, .NET with ConfuserEx), rizin's static analysis operates on the packed stub, not the unpacked payload. `aaa` will analyze the decompression routine and report it as the entire program. The actual malicious code is invisible until runtime unpacking occurs. rizin alone cannot unpack these — you need dynamic analysis (x64dbg, WinDbg with a dump-on-OEP script) to extract the unpacked image, then reload it in rizin.

rizin's ROP gadget search (`rop` command or `/R` search) operates on the binary as statically laid out on disk. If ASLR is enabled on the target system, all gadget virtual addresses will be offset by a random slide at runtime. The gadget offsets from rizin are relative to the binary's preferred load address — you must add the runtime base address (leaked via an info disclosure or calculated from a known symbol) before using them in an actual exploit. Treating rizin's gadget VAs as absolute addresses in a live exploit will cause immediate crashes.

cutter.description: Qt-based GUI for Rizin. Free, open-source alternative to IDA Pro for reverse engineering. Native Ghidra decompiler integration, graph view, hex view, debugger i
cutter.teach_intro: Cutter is what students reach for when Ghidra feels too heavy and r2's curses UI feels too austere. Open a binary, hit Ctrl+R to refresh analysis, navigate to main, F5 for Ghidra decompiler output. Native plugin system supports YARA scanning, signature matching, and custom analysis scripts in Python. Pairs cleanly with rizin command-line for automation.
opsec_notes: Beginner baseline: Cutter is a local GUI application — it makes NO network connections during normal analysis. Opening a binary in Cutter does not generate DNS queries, ICMP, or HTTP traffic. The only network noise risk is if you enable remote debugging against a live target or use a plugin that phones home. Your analysis artifact is entirely local.

File system artifact: Cutter writes analysis databases and config to disk. On Linux, look for ~/.local/share/rizin/cutter/ and ~/.config/rizin/. On Windows, %APPDATA%\rizin\cutter\. If you are analyzing malware on a shared or monitored workstation, these directories will contain the binary path, function names, and your annotations — treat them as sensitive artifacts and wipe them post-engagement.

Process tree detection (2025-2026): CrowdStrike Falcon and SentinelOne both instrument process creation. If you launch Cutter from a shell that was spawned by a suspicious parent (e.g., a C2 beacon, a macro-spawned cmd.exe), the process tree anomaly — cutter.exe or rizin.exe as a child of an unusual parent — will score high on behavioral ML models. Analyze on a clean, isolated VM with a benign process lineage.

Defender for Endpoint (MDE) script scanning (2025-2026): If you use Cutter's Python scripting console to automate analysis and your script touches AMSI-monitored APIs (e.g., invoking subprocess, writing decoded shellcode to disk for comparison), MDE's AMSI integration will scan the script content. Keep analysis scripts that handle live shellcode buffers off Windows hosts with MDE enabled, or run them inside a hardened analysis VM with ETW-TI sinks disabled.

Concrete defender artifact — Sysmon EID 11 (FileCreate): When Cutter auto-saves an analysis project or exports a decompiled C file, Sysmon EID 11 will log the file creation path. On a monitored host, a FileCreate event for a .rzdb file or a .c export in a temp directory alongside a suspicious binary name is a high-fidelity indicator that reverse engineering activity is occurring. Defenders hunting for insider threat or malware analyst evasion watch this pattern.

Remote debugging exposure: Cutter supports remote debugging via rizin's rzr:// and gdb:// protocols. If you attach Cutter to a remote process for dynamic analysis, the debug session opens a listening socket on the analysis host. On a pentest, ensure this port is firewalled to localhost — an open rizin debug port is an unauthenticated RCE vector if discovered by another actor on the same network segment.

sample_outputs.scenario: Beginner: CTF participant opens a simple ELF crackme binary in Cutter to find the password-check function. No flags — just GUI navigation to main and Ghidra decompiler view.
sample_outputs.explanation: The Ghidra decompiler has reconstructed the C-like source of the password check function. The strcmp call at 0x080484b6 compares user input against the hardcoded string 's3cr3t_k3y_2025' — that is the flag. Beginners should note: (1) Cutter's Strings panel (shortcut: Shift+S) would have surfaced this string directly without needing to reach the decompiler — always check strings first. (2) The function was found because Cutter's auto-analysis traced cross-references from main() down the call graph. Next steps: verify by running the binary with the found string, then explore the Imports panel to understand what libc functions the binary uses — this teaches you the attack surface of any binary you analyze.

sample_outputs.scenario: Advanced: Red-team operator reverse-engineering a custom C2 implant beacon captured from a compromised host. Goal is to extract the C2 URL, XOR key, and beacon interval from the binary without executing it. Using Cutter with Ghidra decompiler and a custom Python analysis script via the Cutter scripting console.
sample_outputs.output:
[Cutter 2.4.0 | Rizin 0.7.2]
Opening: implant_beacon.exe (PE32+ executable, x86-64, Windows)
Analysis completed in 1.87s
  Functions found : 203
  Strings found   : 412 (47 obfuscated/encoded)
  Imports found   : 61
  Sections        : .text .rdata .data .rsrc .reloc

[Scripting Console — Python]
>>> import cutter
>>> fcn = cutter.core().cmdj('pdfj @ sym.beacon_init')
>>> # Hunting XOR decode loop — found at 0x140003c2a
>>> cutter.core().cmd('px 16 @ 0x14001a080')
0x14001a080  2f 78 4b 39 71 4d 21 5a  3c 00 00 00 00 00 00 00  /xK9qM!Z<.......
>>> # Decoded C2 string after XOR 0x41:
>>> bytes([b ^ 0x41 for b in [0x2f,0x78,0x4b,0x39,0x71,0x4d,0x21,0x5a]]).decode()
'nYjxP|ah'
>>> # Beacon interval extracted from .data offset 0x14001b010: DWORD 0x0000EA60 = 60000ms
sample_outputs.explanation: The operator has identified three critical IOCs without executing the implant: (1) an XOR-encoded C2 hostname fragment at 0x14001a080 with key 0x41 — the full decode loop in sym.beacon_init would yield the complete URL; (2) a beacon interval of 60 seconds (0xEA60 ms) stored as a DWORD in .data — this is a behavioral signature for network defenders; (3) 47 obfuscated strings flagged by Cutter's entropy analysis, indicating the implant uses single-byte XOR obfuscation throughout. Next steps: (a) use Cutter's YARA plugin to generate a signature from the XOR decode loop bytes for hunting across other collected samples with 'yara-scan'; (b) pivot to rizin CLI with 'rizin -c "aaa; iz~http" implant_beacon.exe' to batch-extract all decoded strings; (c) feed the beacon interval and C2 pattern to your SIEM as a network detection rule — 60-second beaconing with this byte pattern is a high-fidelity hunt query in Splunk or Elastic.

legal_notes: CFAA boundary: Cutter is a static analysis tool — opening a binary you lawfully possess (a CTF challenge, a binary you compiled, a sample provided by a client) carries no CFAA exposure. However, if you obtained the binary by extracting it from a system you are not authorized to access, the analysis activity does not launder the unauthorized access. Authorization to analyze a binary must trace back to authorization to possess it.

Engagement scope — malware samples: If a client provides you a malware sample for analysis during an IR engagement, your rules of engagement should explicitly authorize reverse engineering of that sample. Some organizations have legal holds or chain-of-custody requirements on malware artifacts — confirm with the client's legal team before exporting decompiled code, annotated databases, or YARA rules derived from the sample, as these may constitute derivative works of proprietary or criminal-origin code.

Software licensing consideration: Cutter is GPL-licensed and free to use. However, if you are reverse-engineering a commercial binary (e.g., a vendor's closed-source product) to find vulnerabilities, check whether the software's EULA prohibits reverse engineering. In the US, DMCA Section 1201 has a security research exemption (as clarified by the 2021 triennial rulemaking), but the exemption has conditions — the research must be conducted on lawfully acquired copies and the findings used for good-faith security research. Document your authorization before beginning.
false_positives: Ghidra decompiler output is a reconstruction, not ground truth: The Ghidra decompiler integrated into Cutter will sometimes misidentify calling conventions on x86-32 binaries, producing phantom parameters or incorrect return types. A function that takes two arguments may decompile as taking three if the stack frame analysis is confused by compiler optimizations. Always cross-reference decompiler output against the disassembly view — if the decompiler shows a parameter that has no corresponding push/mov in the asm, it is a decompiler artifact.

String entropy false positives: Cutter's entropy-based obfuscation detection will flag legitimate compressed resources, icon data, and certificate blobs as 'obfuscated strings.' A PE binary with a large .rsrc section containing PNG icons will show dozens of high-entropy 'strings' that are actually pixel data. Filter by minimum length and printable-ASCII ratio before concluding a binary is heavily obfuscated.

Function boundary misdetection in stripped binaries: When analyzing a stripped binary with no symbols, Cutter's auto-analysis (inherited from rizin's 'aaa') uses heuristics to find function prologues. On binaries compiled with link-time optimization (LTO) or with non-standard prologues (e.g., MSVC /GL builds), functions will be split, merged, or missed entirely. A 'function' in the graph view may actually be the tail of a different function that fell through — always verify by checking if the identified prologue (push rbp / mov rbp,rsp or equivalent) is actually present.

Import table lies: Delay-loaded DLLs and manually resolved imports (LoadLibrary/GetProcAddress chains) will not appear in Cutter's Imports panel. A malware sample that resolves all its WinAPI calls at runtime via hashed API lookup will show an almost-empty import table — do not conclude a binary is benign because its imports look clean. The absence of suspicious imports is itself a suspicious indicator in a PE binary of non-trivial size.

Debugger attach on self-modifying code: If you use Cutter's integrated debugger on a binary that unpacks itself at runtime (a common packer pattern), the static analysis view and the live debugger view will diverge — the disassembly shown in the graph view reflects the on-disk bytes, not the unpacked in-memory code. Breakpoints set on static addresses may land in the wrong location post-unpack. Use memory dump + re-analysis workflow: let the packer run to OEP, dump the process with a tool like pe-sieve or hollows-hunter, then open the dump in a fresh Cutter session for accurate static analysis.

frida.description: Dynamic instrumentation toolkit for native apps on Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, Android, QNX. Inject JavaScript snippets into a running process to hook functions
frida.teach_intro: Frida is the universal hook-everything tool for runtime analysis. On Android: connect to a jailbroken/rooted device, frida-ps -U to list processes, frida-trace to log every API call, or write a JS script that overrides Java.use('javax.net.ssl.X509TrustManager') to bypass SSL pinning. On iOS: same workflow, requires jailbreak or repackaged IPA. Foundational for mobile pentesting and DRM/anti-cheat bypass research. Objection is a turnkey CLI built on top of frida for common mobile-pentest tasks.
opsec_notes: Beginner noise: Frida's default gadget injection on Android/iOS causes the target process to pause briefly during attach — this is visible as an ANR (Application Not Responding) event in Android logcat and in iOS crash logs under /var/mobile/Library/Logs/CrashReporter/. Any MDM solution monitoring device health will see these pauses.

Frida-server on Android runs as a persistent daemon (typically on TCP port 27042 by default). Any network scan of the device or host-based firewall log will show this open port. Change the port with frida-server -l 0.0.0.0:CUSTOM_PORT and tunnel over ADB (adb forward tcp:CUSTOM_PORT tcp:CUSTOM_PORT) to avoid exposing it on the network interface.

CrowdStrike Falcon for Mobile and SentinelOne Singularity Mobile (2024-2025 builds) both instrument Android's /proc/[pid]/maps and detect the frida-agent shared library (frida-agent-64.so or frida-agent-32.so) mapped into a process's address space. Renaming the .so alone is insufficient — modern detections hash the gadget's internal strings and exported symbol table, not just the filename.

On iOS, Frida requires either a jailbreak or a repackaged IPA with the FridaGadget.dylib embedded. Repackaged IPAs break Apple's code-signing chain — any MDM solution enforcing managed app integrity (Jamf, Microsoft Intune with Conditional Access) will flag or block the app on enrollment check. The artifact is a mismatched TeamID in the embedded provisioning profile versus the signing certificate.

Concrete defender artifact: On Android, Frida's ptrace-based attach writes to /proc/[pid]/mem and calls PTRACE_ATTACH. This is logged by SELinux audit daemon (check /var/log/audit/audit.log or dmesg for 'avc: denied { ptrace }' if SELinux is enforcing). On rooted devices with Magisk + Zygisk, the Zygisk module DenyList can block Frida injection into specific processes — operators must check whether the target app is on the DenyList before assuming injection will succeed.

2025-2026 cutting edge: Anti-Frida detection in hardened apps (banking, DRM, anti-cheat) now commonly uses inline integrity checks that scan their own process memory for Frida's JavaScript runtime (QuickJS/V8 heap signatures) and check for the presence of frida-helper threads in /proc/self/task/. Bypassing these requires custom Frida builds with stripped/renamed internals (e.g., the 'Frida-stripped' community forks) or gadget injection via a custom linker namespace to hide the mapped region from /proc/self/maps reads.

sample_outputs.scenario: Beginner: Rooted Android device connected via USB. Operator wants to list running processes and attach to a banking app to observe SSL traffic by bypassing certificate pinning using Objection.
sample_outputs.output:
PID  Name
----  -----------------------------------------------
  312  adbd
  891  com.android.systemui
 1042  com.android.phone
 1387  com.google.android.gms
 2201  com.targetbank.android
 2389  com.android.chrome

sample_outputs.explanation: The output lists every running process on the USB-connected Android device by PID and package name. The operator can see com.targetbank.android at PID 2201 — this is the target. The PID is needed for direct Frida attachment. Next steps: (1) Use 'objection -g com.targetbank.android explore' to attach via package name and get an interactive shell with pre-built SSL pinning bypass, certificate inspection, and memory search commands. (2) Alternatively, write a custom Frida JS script: 'frida -U -n com.targetbank.android -l sslpinning_bypass.js' to hook javax.net.ssl.X509TrustManager and return empty arrays from checkClientTrusted/checkServerTrusted, forcing the app to accept your Burp Suite proxy cert. (3) Verify the bypass worked by checking Burp's HTTP history for decrypted HTTPS traffic from the app.

sample_outputs.scenario: Advanced: iOS app (repackaged IPA with FridaGadget.dylib embedded, sideloaded via AltStore) implements multi-layer anti-tampering: jailbreak detection, Frida detection via /proc/self/maps scan, and ObjC method swizzling guards. Operator uses a custom Frida script to hook the anti-tamper check function before it runs, then pivots to dumping the app's decrypted class-dump for further static analysis.
sample_outputs.output:
[iPhone::com.targetapp.ios ]-> 
[*] Frida attached to PID 4821
[*] Hooking -[AppIntegrityChecker performChecks]
[*] Original return value: 1 (TAMPERED)
[*] Patched return value: 0 (CLEAN)
[*] Hooking -[JailbreakDetector isJailbroken]
[*] Patched return value: NO
[*] SSL pinning hook installed on Security.framework SecTrustEvaluateWithError
[*] Intercepted SecTrustEvaluateWithError -> forcing errSecSuccess
[*] App resumed. Monitoring ObjC method calls...
[*] [AppSession initWithToken:] called with token: eyJhbGciOiJSUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9...
[*] [NetworkManager sendRequest:toEndpoint:] -> https://api.targetapp.com/v3/user/profile
sample_outputs.explanation: The script successfully patched three layers of defense before the app's main logic ran: (1) AppIntegrityChecker.performChecks was hooked to return 0 (clean) instead of 1 (tampered), preventing the app from self-terminating. (2) JailbreakDetector.isJailbroken was patched to return NO. (3) SecTrustEvaluateWithError in Apple's Security.framework was intercepted to force errSecSuccess, bypassing native SSL pinning that sits below the ObjC layer and would have survived a pure ObjC swizzle. The output then shows live method call interception revealing a JWT token and an API endpoint. Next steps: (1) Feed the JWT to jwt_tool or CyberChef to decode claims and check for algorithm confusion (alg:none, RS256->HS256 downgrade). (2) Use the discovered endpoint 'https://api.targetapp.com/v3/user/profile' as a starting point for Burp Suite API enumeration — look for IDOR by substituting user IDs in the path. (3) Run 'frida-ios-dump' or 'bagbak' against the attached process to dump the decrypted binary from memory for offline analysis in Ghidra or IDA Pro, bypassing the App Store FairPlay DRM encryption.

legal_notes: US CFAA boundary: Attaching Frida to any process on a device you do not own, or on a device owned by an organization without explicit written authorization, constitutes unauthorized access to a computer under 18 U.S.C. § 1030. This applies even if the device is physically in your possession (e.g., a corporate-issued phone). 'Rooting the device yourself' does not constitute authorization to instrument third-party apps whose terms of service prohibit reverse engineering — civil liability under the DMCA (17 U.S.C. § 1201) may apply separately from CFAA.

Rules of engagement scope: Mobile app pentests must explicitly enumerate which apps are in scope, which device OS versions are authorized, and whether the engagement covers the app binary only or also the backend API. Frida's runtime hooks will inevitably touch backend endpoints — ensure your RoE covers server-side testing, not just the client binary, before any network traffic is generated by your hooked app.

Modern MDM/cloud consideration: In enterprise environments, iOS devices enrolled in Apple Business Manager (ABM) and Android devices enrolled in Android Enterprise (fully managed) report app inventory and integrity status to the MDM server (Jamf Pro, Microsoft Intune, VMware Workspace ONE). Sideloading a repackaged IPA or installing Frida-server on a managed device will trigger compliance policy violations visible to the enterprise security team in near-real-time — this is an out-of-band detection channel completely separate from the app's own anti-tamper logic.
false_positives: SSL pinning bypass confirmation is unreliable when the app uses multiple pinning layers at different stack levels. A Java-layer X509TrustManager hook via Frida may succeed while a native OkHttp CertificatePinner or a Conscrypt-level check still blocks traffic — the operator sees no errors in Frida but Burp still shows no decrypted traffic. Always verify bypass success by checking Burp's HTTP history AND the device's logcat simultaneously.

frida-ps -U will list processes by the name the OS reports, which on Android is the package name for foreground apps but may be a generic process name (e.g., 'app_process64') for services or apps in the background that haven't fully initialized. Attaching to the wrong PID because two processes share a similar name is a real risk — always cross-reference with 'adb shell ps -A | grep <package>' to confirm the correct PID before attaching.

On Android 12+ with the new app hibernation feature, apps that haven't been used recently are placed in a cached/stopped state. Frida will appear to attach successfully (no error returned) but hooks will not fire because the target process is not actively executing — the operator may incorrectly conclude the hook logic is wrong when the real issue is the process state. Force the app to the foreground before attaching.

Frida's --no-pause flag (used to avoid the startup pause that triggers ANR detection) means your script runs after the process has already started. If the target function you want to hook is called during early initialization (e.g., in Application.onCreate() on Android), you will miss those calls entirely. The output will show your hook installed successfully but you'll never see the early-lifecycle events — use spawn mode ('frida -U -f com.package.name -l script.js') instead of attach mode for initialization-time hooks.

On jailbroken iOS devices running Dopamine or palera1n (2024-2025 jailbreaks for iOS 16-17), Frida-server compatibility is version-sensitive. A Frida client version mismatch of even a minor version (e.g., client 16.2.x vs server 16.1.x) will produce a successful-looking connection but cause silent hook failures or crashes with no useful error message. Always verify 'frida --version' on the host matches the frida-server binary on the device exactly.
